Earl Warren

R E

Grand Ma•ler 1955

Earl Warren is the sixty-ninth Grand Master of Masons in California.
On November 1st, 1919, he was raised to the sublime degree of Master
Mason in Sequoia Lodge No. 349, at Oakland. He was appointed a Steward
of that Lodge in 1922 and 1923; Junior Deacon in 1924; Senior Deacon in
1925; and was thereafter elected as Junior Warden in 1926; Senior Warden
in 1927; and Master in 1928. He served the Lodge as Marshal in 1929. From
1928 to 1933 he served as a member of various committees of Grand Lodge.
He was elected Senior Grand Warden in 1933; Deputy Grand Master in
1934; and Grand Master in 1935. He is a member (32°) of Oakland Bodies
No. 2, Scottish Rite, A. and A. S. R., and of Aahmes Temple, A.A.O.N.M.S.,
having served as Potentate of the Temple in 1933-4.
The foregoing Masonic record closely indicates that, from the beginning of his Masonic career, Brother Warren has shown a keen interest in
our ancient and honorable fraternity.
He was born at Los Angeles March 19, 1891, and received his elementary and high school education in the public schools of Bakersfield. In 1912
he was graduated from the University of California. He received the degree
of Juris Doctor from the University of California School of Jurisprudence
in 1914, and was thereupon admitted to the practice of the law. He has
achieved outstanding success at the bar, but his greatest success was in his
marriage on October 14, 1925, to Nina E. Meyers, a beautiful woman of
rare grace and mental attainments who is loved by a multitude of friends.
The Warrens have six children: three boys and three girls, and their home
life is ideally happy.
Our retiring Grand Master entered the service of the United States
army on September 7, 1917, being originally assigned to the 363rd Infantry
of the Ninety-first Division at Camp Lewis, Washington. He was honorably discharged as a Lieutenant on December 9, 1918. On his return to
civil life, he at once became active in the public service. From January to
May, 1919, he was Clerk of the Judiciary Committee of the Assembly in the
State Legislature. From October, 1919, to May, 1920, he served as Deputy
City Attorney of the City of Oakland. In May, 1920, he was appointed
Deputy District Attorney of Alameda county and served in that capacity
until January, 1925, when he was appointed District Attorney of that
county, which office he has held since that time, having been three times
elected. In 1931-2 he was President of the District Attorneys' Association
of California, and, since his retirement from the presidency of that organization, has served as its secretary. He is known throughout the United States
as an outstanding, fearless public officer, who performs the duties of his
office without fear or favor.
In addition to his duties as District Attorney of Alameda county, he
has been Chairman of the Board of Managers of the State Bureau of
Criminal Investigation and Identification since 1927. He is also Research
Associate of the Bureau of Public Administration of the U niversity of
California.
From the above sketch we can see that, from the time he entered the
service of his country during the World War up to the present time, he
has devoted himself to the public service and particularly to the cause of
law enforcement. In this field he has carried into practical effect the principles of Free Masonry, which have been his guiding star.

Devotional Service
THE MASONIC UNIVERSE

By Harold Camp, D. D.
Masonry conceives the Sovereign Mind of the universe as the Great
Architect and Supreme Builder with whom we, as Masons, work together
for the building of the Temple of Brotherhood. I want to speak of the
four fundamental classes of things with which the Great Architect works
and with which, under Him, we have to do.
First, the things which never get out of repair.
Second, the things which get out of repair and repair themselves.
Third, the things which get out of repair and can n'ever be repaired.
Fourth, the things which get out of repair and which we, as Masons,
must help to repair.
1. There are things which never get out of repair. They belong to the
perfect mechanism of the universe; the coming and going of the great
constellations, the sequences of the seasons, the ebb and flow of the tides,
the ascent of the sap in the trees in the springtime and the descent of the
sap into the roots in the fall, the perfect adjustment of rainfall to sunshine,
of heat to cold, of storm to calm. We live in a universe that never gets
out of repair, the source of boundless cosmic comfort to us all.
2. There are things which get out of repair and repair themselves.
Perhaps you have had the misfortune to break an arm or a leg. You sent
for your physician. He did not pretend that it was his skill to mend those
broken parts, but rather to put them into a position favorable for their own
mending, relying upon the beneficent ministry of nature to repair the
broken parts. Perhaps there has come the time when through strain of
overwork, long continued uninterrupted application to your task, your
nerves have threatened to give way, and to you has come the wise counsel,
"Go off into the woods, or down by the seashore, or back amid the scenes
of your childhoo!l and youth and let the ministry of nature repair your
shattered spirit." And so you have come back with a steady hand and. a
clear mind and a fresh perspective of your task. We all need that ministry
which, when things get out of repair, is the power by which they repair
themselves. There are just three classes of people in the world: people
who have had a nervous breakdown, people who are having a nervous
breakdown, and people who are about to have a nervous breakdown.
3. The things which get out of repair and can never be repaired. It
is one of the supreme purposes of Masonry to keep some things from
getting out of repair, and one is a wasted life. Masonry seeks to hold
before us the vision of the right life, and all the beauty of its symbolism
and the significance of its ritual and the power of its fellowship is to lure
the members of the craft towards the prize of its attainment. One thing
which is the source of continual marvel to every thoughtful life is the
pricelessness of individual personality. Each self is profoundly unique and
infinitely different. No one has ever lived just like you. Each of us has
something to express of the gracious goodness and fullness of the Lord
which none other can express. Each is different, not only physically, but
mentally and spiritually. Once we have wasted the opportunity of life to
fulfill our truest self and to express that unique image of God within our
lives, the opportunity never returns.

10

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

4. There are things which get out of repair and we must help to repair
them. We live in a world in which things are always getting out of repair.
I shall remind you only of two. One is our friendship as man with man.
It was a great Mason who said, "Above all else let us keep our friendship
in repair." The greatness of Masonry is not in its ritual, impressive as that
ritual is; it is not in its temples, beautiful as those temples are; it is not
in its wealth, vast as that wealth may seem to be. The greatness of
Masonry is in its fellowship. A man must have Masonry in his heart to
understand the true meaning of that friendship which our craft expresses
in its symbols and ceremonies. Most of us know the sorrow of a neglected
friendship of which the poet speaks:
Around the corner I have a friend,
In this great .city that has no end;
Yet days go by and weeks rush on,
And before I know it a year is gone,
And I never see my old friend's face;
For life is a swift and terrible race.
Still he. knows I love him just as well
As in the days I rang his bell
And he rang mine. We were younger then;
And now we are busy, tired menTired with playing a foolish game;
Tired with trying to make a name.
Tomorrow I say I will call on Jim,
Just to show that I'm thinking of him.
But tomorrow comes-and tomorrow goes;
And the distance between us grows and grows.
Around the corner-yet miles away" Here's a telegram, sir!" "Jim-died-today I"
And that's what we get, and deserve, in the end,
Around the corner, a vanished friend.
Fitially, it is the friendship of God which you must keep in repair.
Without God· Masonry could not be. Its origin, its history, its passion, its
future, are all wrap.p ed up in that great word "God." God, out of the
vision of Whom love comes, out of the vision and love ·of Whom service
comes, out of the vision and love and service of Whom character comes.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

The · Grand Lodge of California having been opened in Ample Form
for its eighty-seventh annual communication, I -will in obedience to our
Constitution, set forth in this written message, my official acts during the
year, the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and some
recommendations for legislation which to me seem expedient for the welfare of the Craft :
General Condition of Masonry
The year has been an uneventful one if peace and harmony among
the 582 Lodges of the jurisdiction and an almost total lack of unpleasantness can be called uneventful. During the entire year there has not been,
to my knowledge, a serious disagreement between any of the Lodges of
the jurisdiction. No individual Lodge has conducted itself in a manner
to warrant the discipline or censure of the Grand Master. No serious
derelictions of duty or personal misconduct on the part of any officer of
the constituent Lodges has been called to my attention, and but 32 trials
of individual members for Masonic offenses out of a membership of approximately 128,000. I have had many contacts with the inspectors and
officers of our Lodges and have counselled with them on matters of
importance to their Lodges and to Masonry in general, but the nature of
the matters discussed have pertained to Masonic business and policy and
have contained an almost irreducible minimum of unpleasantness. When
I assumed this exalted office one year ago, I did not believe that it was
possible, particularly in troubled times such as the world is now passing
through, for an institution as large as ours to live an entire year with so
little discord as it has been my happy lot to experience, even though that
organization should be guided in all things by the great moral and fraternal principles of Freemasonry. My. experience has · been such as to
teach me that, even among well-intentioned men, the possibility of error,
occasioned by the frailty of human nature and the misunderstandings that
naturally arise from lack of appreciation of the other fellow's point of view
would lead to a larger number of conflicts than· have confronted me. In
passing, may I say that I have not attempted to avoid knowledge of any
such matters if they existed, but, on the contrary, have invited a free
discussion of the problems of the Craft on the part of all concerned. I am
conscious of the fact that this happy condition never could have existed
but for the unselfish devotion to duty on the part of all the officers and
inspectors of Grand Lodge and the officers of the constituent Lodges. To
them I publicly acknowledge my gratitude for the whole-hearted assistance which they have given to me and for the uniform courtesy and
respect which they have shown to the office of Grand Master during my
incumbency.
It is impossible to summarize their numerous activities on this occasion or even to mention •them by name, but I know I will not offend if I
particularly acknowledge with thanks the patient and devoted service of
the grand old man of Masonry, the man who has put more of his life and
imparted more of his character into Masonry in this jurisdiction, than

Hawaiian Lodges
It would be difficult for me to describe my feelings as the official representative of· this Grand Lodge while visiting our Loclges in that most
distant part of the jurisdiction, the Hawaiian Islands. It was not only the
great hospitality of those warm-hearted · people that impressed me, nor the
beauties of the shore-line nor the verdure of the Islands; but also the fact
that these little dots in the great Pacific Ocean, which were until almost
within the memory of living men unproductive and untouched by modern
life, are now teeming with the activity of Western civilization and their
people are improving the lot of the man working in the fields and in the
canneries in a m·a nner that would merit emulation on the mainland. And
my greatest satisfaction came from the fact that our Masonic Lodges there
-eight in number--are making a great contribution to this social development and to the spread of our civilization. These Lodges are happy in
their · association with this Grand Lodge. The visit of the Grand Master
with them and the attendance of their inspectors and representatives upon
our communications stimulate their interest and I am profoundly convinced that these eight Lodges, situated as they are and practicing Masonry
as they practice it in these outposts of Western civilization, are of importance to the Masonry of this jurisdiction and of the world far beyond the
weight of their numbers.

Visitations
For me the year has been one filled with a succession of delightful
experiences, the greatest of which were the contacts made with the· brethren
during my official visitations in all parts of the jurisdiction. From the
semi-tropical Imperial Valley to th.e glaciers on Mount Shasta, and from
the rugged mountains of -the Mother Lode to the paradise of flowers in
the Hawaiian Islands, I found the same fraternal spirit, the same warm
hospitalit,Y, and the same love for our ancient Craft. While I appreciate
the fact that the uncommon courtesy and hospitality shown to me was of
an official rather than a personal nature, still I must admit to you that
it filled me with great pride and satis.fa,ction to be so honored, and I shall
never forget it. .
I .regret that it was not possible ·f or me to visit every Lodge in the
jurisdiftion, but that is a physical impossibility. I have, however, done
my best to sit in some Lodge room in every part of the state. I h·a d
hoped to make an officfal visitation to every· Masonic District outside o.f
the larger cities and, up to a very recent date, believed that this objective
would, be accomplished. As the year ends, however, I must acknowledg·e
that I have fallen short of the mark and that the pleasure of meeting with
some of you has been denied me. It is unfortunate that time and circumstances did not permit these visitations, but I want you to know that I
had them constantly in mind, and that I shall never be satisfied until I
have visited the brethren in these districts, even though it may be long
after I have left the oriental chair.
My visitations in the .larger cities have been comparatf~ely few, but
I kno":' that .l?Y brethre1J. will understand when I ·explain that my entire
Masonic career has been spent in and around metropolitan Lodges and
that I have had heretofore very little opportunity to visit in the· more
distant parts of the jurisdiction. My decision ·to visit mainly in the nonmetropoJitan districts was therefore partly from a selfish desire to ~an·t ·
to know these Lodges better, and pa1 tly . from a conviction that the real
s.trens:th o~ Masonry lies in its univer~ality. Masonry would mean very

Inter-jurisdictional Contacts
Our contacts with our sister iurisdictions throughout the country have
been most pleasant, and I am happy to report that not a single incident
has occurred during the year to disturb the cordial relations with these
jurisdictions which we prize ·so highly. I was surprised at the' small number
of instances in which we contact the other jurisdictions, both domestic and
foreign, and as a result I have given c9nsiderable thought to the question
as to whethe.r or riot we have made a serious mistake in fail.i ng to keep
up our Masonic .c orrespondence and to publish our conclusions 't herefrortj
in the Annual Pr6ce~dings. In this day and age, when world affairs change
so rapidly, it is difficult at best for the average person to keep abreast of
the times and, ·unless we know what is .h appening MasoniCally in othet
parts of-the world, our Masonic horizon is being limited day by day. TM
officers of the Lpdges to whom we look for the education of our novitiates
wouid· have difficulty today in obtaining ari accurate and composite' picture
of Masonry throughout · the world because there are no documents or auth'e nticated publications in this jurisdiction available to them. If we do
not know what is happening to Masonry and what it is · doin11 throughout
the· world, we cannot know in whiCh direction we «ire traveling. If we do
not know whither we are traveling, we are but groping in darkness. We
concern ourselves with -Masonic education, 'and particularly with the education of those who have been recently admitted to the Craft, but · in
neglecting our· relations with other jurisdictions are we not at the same
time depriving them· and those who could teach them of- the most valuable
:
information that could be made available?
I am informed that the cost of incorporating the report of the Maso.nic
. Correspondence Committee; including the preparation·, of ·the material and
the printing thereof; on the :basis heretofore followed would not exceed
one thousand dollars. i therefore recoommend· that provision be made for
rehabilitating the Correspondence Committee and that an adequate appropriation be made for gathering the material and publishing the same in
the· Annual Proceedings.

in a manner that is not burdensome or expensive to the Lodges of th·e
jurisdiction or misleading to the brethren engaged therein. On the other
hand, irr the event that Grand Lodge does not desire to take such action,
I recomme11d that it repeal the present regulation agah1st gambling in
order that it shall not continue to remain uninforced to the embarrassment
of Grand Lodge and of future Grand Masters.

Gambling
The question most seriously discussed and the one in which there was
absolute unanimity of opinion was the growing evil of lotteries and· other
illegal gambling enterprises sponsored by Master Masons to secure funds
for the use of organizations collateral to Masonry. I trust it is not necessary for me to say in this gathering that every Grand Master who
expressed himself on the subject did so in opposition to all illegal gambling
conducted by or in the name of Masonry, ostensibly or otherwise. In
answer to a direct question as to what the situation was in this jurisdiction, I was embarrassed to admit that, although the conduct of such enterprises has been declared to be unmasonic conduct (Ross Digest, Sec. 387),
in recent years the rule of Grand Lodge has been honored more in the
breach than in the observance-that within the last four years two Grand
Masters have made strong recommendations for the proper handling of
such matters, but that no definite action has been taken by Grand Lodge
or Grand Masters, including myself to enforce our anti-gambling regulations. This was not a pleasant admission to make, but it is the truth.
Perhaps the.re will be those who disapprove of these gambling enterprises,
but who believe that the remedy of expulsion for unmasonic conduct which
now exists in the Lodge of the offender is sufficient. With these I am
constrained to disagree, because in all of the instances that have come to
my attention, our constituent Lodges as such are not concerned. I have
not had called to my attention a single instance where any one of those
Lodges has offended in this regard. Whenever an illegal gambling enterprise of this character is engaged in, hundreds of Master Masons. are
induced to lay themselves open to Masonic trial. To discipline all of them
would be impossible from the standpoint of time and expense as well as
from other considerations. To discipline less than all the participants
would be considered discrimination against those who are tried and favoritism toward those who are not tried.
It is not the duty of the individual Lodges acting independently of
each other, to assume the responsibility of solving a problem of such jurisdictionally wide concern. It is the responsibility of Grand Lodge. In the
past, correspondence between Grand Masters and participants in these
enterprises has ended in humiliation of the Grand Master and in a loss of
prestige to Grand Lodge. For this result Grand Lodge is largely responsible because it has not been decisive in its action. In making this observation, I assume a fair share of that responsibility. During the past year,
to my knowledge several of these illegal enterprises have been promoted
in the jurisdiction, and for which hundreds of our brethren could have
been disciplined had I seen fit to direct that they be tried in the constituent
Lodges which claim them as members but which had nothing to do with
the illeg~I enterprise. It may be that I have been negligent in failing to
take action to that end as some few Grand Masters have done in their
jurisdictions with varying results. However I desire to say in defense of
what might be considered unjustifiable inaction that in my opinion it is
the illegal gambling enterprises which are offe~sive 'to the good na:ne of
Masonry rather than the brothers who have, through the complacency of
Grand Lodge, been lulled into a false sense of security in the promotion

XII.
The following letter, which I sent to the Master of a lodge, states a
question which was asked regarding the proper use of lodge funds and my
reply thereto:
"I have before me your letter of March 18th, 1936, asking whether
it is a proper expenditure of lodge funds to contribute fifteen dollars
thereof to 'the Johnson Chimes Fund' established in memory of a late
departed brother who served for many years as Chaplain.
"The use of lodge funds is regulated by Sections 87, 88, 89, and 90
of our Constitution. The proposed expenditure is, of course, not within
the express terms of any of those sections. Furthermore, the use of lodge
funds has, through the years, been very jealously guarded and restricted
by various decisions in order that such funds may he sufficient at all t1mes
to meet the demands of charity upon the lodge. In 1877 and in 1896 it
was decided that a lodge could not contribute to any charity outside of
the fraternity, even to such an established organization as the Salvation
Army.
"Under the circumstances, while I appreciate the laudable purpose
for which the Johnson Chimes Fund has been established, I hold that
the lodge may not lawfully contribute any of its money to it."

XIII.
I was asked whether the officers of ll lodge, without authority having been
previously obtained from the lodge itself, could expend lodge funds for refreshments, when the proposed expenditures would not exceed the limited per-·
centage allowed, I replied that to answer the question in the affirmative would
be equivalent to handing the officers a blank check upon the lodge funds up
to the amount of the limitation. I referred to the report of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Charters, appearing in Ross' Digest, at p. 405 : "No moneys
(except such as may be disbursed by the charity committee) can legally be
drawn from the treasury· of a lodge without its express consent and under its
instructions." Consequently, I ruled that the officers of the lodge must put
the bills for refreshments and entertainment before the lodge before the same
could be paid.

XVI.
I was asked to approve an amendment · to a standing resolution, which
resolution was adopted according to Section 129 of the Constitution ; the
amendment was to increase the fee for a life membership for $150 to $200.
Before · giving my approval to the amendment I wrote the secretary of the
lodge as follows :
"Life memberships are authorized by Section 129 of the Constitution,
· which sets forth · the steps which must be taken before the requested standing resolution can become effective. One of those steps is that written
notice must be forwarded by maii to every member prior to the stated
meeting at which the resolution is to be considered. While the section does
.. not expressly provide that the standing resolution shall not be amended
until af~r similar notice has been sent, nev,ertheless, in my opinion, the
reasons for requiring the mailing of notices to every member before the
passage of the original standing resolution apply with equal force to the
consideration and passage of any amendment thereto, particularly an
amendment which raises the amount of the fee. Inasmuch as the taking
out of life memberships directly affects the amount of current dues paid
in· yearly by the members, it is a matter that vitally concerns every member of the lodge and the entire membership should be notified before any
change is made in the system of life memberships."

XVII.
I was asked whether or not it would be proper for a lodge to purchase
a building in which to meet, in view of the fact that the lower floor of the
building. was rented to a tenant who was · operating a pool hall and selling
spirituous, vinous, and malt liquors, it being represented that the sale of liquor
had been legally licensed- and was being lawfully conducted. My answer was
in . accord with .the decision of Grand Master Gist ( 1934 Proceedings, pp. 2627).. .. I .replied as follows :

22

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"While the Constitution does not expressly prohibit a Masonic lodge
from holding regular meetings in a building also occupied by a liquor
selling establishment, nevertheless such a situation would be contrary to
the principles and ideals of the fraternity. The consistent attitude of Masonry toward the saloon is expressed in those sections of our Constitution-89 and 129A-which prohibit the expenditure of lodge funds for
liquor and make ineligible for membership those who are engaged in that
business. I entertain the opinion, therefore, that it would not be proper
for your lodge to consider purchasing the property in question unless and
at the same time the business of selling liquor could be eliminated from the
premises."
XVIII.
The secretary of a lodge wrote me asking for rulings upon the eligibility
for the degrees of two candidates. He stated that the first of these candidates
"works in a local lunch room. While this place serves meals of all kinds this
young man also serves drinks as well as food"; and that the other candidate
"is now employed as a bartender on one of the cross channel steamers."
After quoting Section 129A of the Constitution, I replied as follows:
"This section was adopted in 1912 when saloons and public bars were
legal under the laws of this state. In 1920, with the advent of prohibition, saloons and public bars became outlawed under the 18th Amendment
to the Constitution of the United States, and since its repeal that outlawry
has continued under Section 22 of Article XX of the Constitution of
California. The latter section reads in part as follows:
'Intoxicating liquors, other than beers, shall not be consumed, bought,
sold, or otherwise disposed of for consumption on the premises in any
public saloon, public bar y or public barroom within the State; provided,
however, that subject to the aforesaid restriction, all intoxicating liquors
may be kept and may be bought, sold, served and consumed, and otherwise disposed of in any bona-fide hotel, restaurant . . . or other public
eating place, . . . '
"In the determination of the questions which you ask, it must, there. fore, be kept in mind that under the Constitution of this state it is contemplated that there shalt be no public saloons, bars or barrooms in California. It must also be recognized as a fact, however, that this fundamental law has been nullified and that rhe saloon in its worst form and
with all its attendant evils is again with us under the name of 'cocktail
lounge,' 'tavern,' 'buffet,' etc. This has been caused by the total indifference of the Board of Equalization, the liquor authority of the State,
to the clear mandates of the Constitution and the enabling acts of the
Legislature, and we now find many thousands of saloons licensed by the
State Board on the theory that they are bona-fide restaurants. As long
as the State authorities continue thus to ignore the law, it is impossible
for us to decide questions such as those submitted by you, according to
the regulations, pronouncements or licenses emanating from the Board of
Equalization. The character of a liquor dispensary-for the purpose of
deciding the eligibility of its employes for the degrees of Masonry-must
be determined according to the particular facts in any given case. If the
place in question is actually a bona-fide restaurant, the persons serving
the liquor merely as an incident to the service of meals, are not, by reason of their occupation, ineligible for the degrees of Masonry. If, on the
other hand, the person who makes application for the degrees serves liquor
by the drink, other than as an incident to the serving of meals, he is, in
my opiniOI}, ineligible, regardless of the manner of service. In arriving
at this conclusion I make no distinction ·between the serv'ice of either

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

23

food or drinks at or over a counter and the service thereof at tables. The
only distinction I make in this connection is between bona-fide restaurants
and public drinking houses, under whatever name the latter may be mas.querading.
"Under Section 129A of our Masonic Constitution the determination
of whether a particular place of business is a bona-fide r~staurant or a
saloon must of necess+ty be left primarily to the Master and his lodge.
Their conclusions, however, must be in accordance with common experience in such matters, and be sub}ect to review by Grand Lodge. I realize
that it is not always an easy task to distinguish between the two, but it
should be borne in mind that it is the letter and spirit of our law that
bar keepers be not admitted to Masonry. Where there is any doubt as to
the eligibility of an applicant on this score, that doubt should be resolved
in favor of the craft and against the eligibility of the applicant, 'to avert
the shadow of any scandal or reproach against the fraternity.'
"Upon the facts stated in your letters, my answers are that the first
candidate mentioned is not ineligible and that the second candidate is
ineligible."

A brother inquired whether or not his occupation as owner of a retail

under Section 129A of the Constitution. I answered in the following language:
"It is my opinion that that section was directed against the saloon
business and bar keepers ·and not against the retail sale of liquor, where
the liquor is sold ·for consumption other than on the premises and that,
therefore, a brother does not become liable to suspension or expulsion
from the fraternity by reason of his occupation as owner of an establishmen~ i_n the latter class.''.

Masonic Homes Endowment Board
I shall not attempt to report upon the activities of the various committees since our last Communication other than to say that they have
responded to every request made of them. Each committee will make a
report of its own activities for your consideration. In passing, however, it
would only be fair for me to make some comment upon the work of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board, which has worked so faithfully during
the entire year to build up the fund which all thoughtful Masons consider
to be so important to the welfare of our two greatest charities-the
Masonic Homes at Decoto and Covina. This Board, in spite of its splendid
service, will report contributions somewhat smaller in the aggregate than
have been reported by it in recent years, and it may feel some embarrassment in stating the reason for this fact. But at all events Grand Lodge
should know that it was my action and not that of the board which is
responsible for the result.
For some time I have felt that, during the economic depression through
whic'h we have been passing and from which we have not entirely emerged
at the present time, it is not entirely consistent for Grand Lodge to institute
a drive for funds for any purpose whatsoever, except in the event it should
become necessary for the immediate relief of our distressed brethren. There
has been so much distress on the part of our brethren as a result of
their own unemployment and the dependency of relatives that thousands
are in no position to give to any cause, even to one as worthy as the
endowment of our Masonic Homes. We want our brethren so situated
to attend Masonic Lodges and other gatherings, because it is at such times
when the souls of men are being tried, that tkey need the association of
their brethren and the comfort which they can receive by participating in
our Masonic rites. Men under such circumstances are extremely sensitive,
and are undoubtedly embarrassed when solicited in the Lodge Room or
otherwise for a contribution which they cannot give. If embarrassed in
this regard once, they might remain away from the Lodge during the
period of their lives when they need it most.
I therefore requested the Endowment Board t:iot to authorize any
solicitation of funds, but merely to offer .g enerally the opportunity of
conitributing to those who might feel capable of doing so. With this request
it cheerfully complied. Under the circumstances, the $37,181.00 which will
be reported by the Board, is a splendid accomplishment. Every dollar of
it comes from the hearts of our brethren and without embarrassment to
any one of them. It represents appreciable progre.ss in the accumulation
of our Endowment Fund and the Board may be proud of the manner and
the results of its accomplishment. It is reassuring to know that employment conditions are improving throughout .the jurisdiction, and that tthe
time should soon come when there will be a job for every Master Mason
who needs one. Until that time arrives, I would suggest that Grand Lodge
sponsor no drives for funds other than when necessary for the immediate
relief of distressed brethren and their families.

Relief
While on the subject of relief, I should like to report briefly my
observations concerning that important activity of our Crafit. I am convinced tthat the Lodges, acting through Boards of Relief, unemployment
services, and through their own officers, committees and members, have
fully measured up to their Masonic obligations in relieving the distress
of our own brethren and of those sojourning with us.
During the year, there have been three major catastrophes in sister
jurisdictions that seem to call for .a: tender of assistance on our part.

26

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Accordingly, I offered financial assistance on behalf of this Grand Lodge
to the Grand Jurisdiction of Montana, d~ring its d_estructive earthqua~es,
to the Grand Jurisdiction of Pennsylvama at the time of the devastatmg
winter- floods in that state and to the Grand Jurisdiction of Oregon on
the occasion of the recent widespread fires. All of these Grand Jurisdictions replied with gratitude, but stated that, while assistance was n~t
necessary at the moment in tpe event it became so they would gladly avail
themselves of our fraternal offer. However, the distress in the flooded
districts of Pennsylvania 'was so great that, in my opinion, we were
justified in making a contribution for general relief. Accordingly Grand
Lodge donated $500 to the Red Cross for that purpose.

Grand Lecturer
· Since the death of our late lamented Brother Tom Baker, Grand Lodge
has set up a · new system for teaching the ritual. In doing so it .departed
from its established practice of having a full-time paid Grand Lecturer,· and,
by resolution, delegated this important work to a part-time Gra~d Lecturer
and four unpaid assistants. These brethren have worked faithfully f~r
three years without even the recognition of having the system or their
offices made a part of the Constitution or established by legislation. Their
position is an unsatisfactory one, it not being known by them whether
Grand Lodge intends eventually to make the system permanent or not.
Knowing that this is a subject that is discussed throughout the jurisdiction
and realizing that in any discussion of it on the floor of Grand Lodge, all
the brethren could not ex;>ress themselves, I submitted a questionnaire
to the 1746 Masters and Wardens and to the 121 Inspectors and requested
their opinion on the following questions among others: (1) In your
opinion, is the present system working satisfactoril:i;? and (2) D.o you
believe that the present system should now be mcorporated m the
Constitution? In order that I might have a .frank reply from everyone, I
stated that it would not be necessary to sign the questionnaire, but merely
to return it to me filled out and with any remarks that might be considered pertinent. In order that we might know whether or not there
was any difference of opinion as between metropolitan and non-metropolitan Lodges, I used different colored stationery to distinguish between
them. For the purposes of this questionnaire, I considered only the three
largest cities as metropqlitan areas.
I received 857 replies, or 45 per cent of the total number sent out.
The answers were as follows: (1) In your opinion is the present system
working satisfactorily? Inspectors metropolitan areas: Yes, 21, No, 4;
Inspectors non-metropolitan areas: Yes, 43, No, 12; Masters and Wardens,
metropolitan areas : Yes, 157, No, 110; Masters and Wardens non-metropolitan areas: Yes, 241, No, 239; Total: Yes, 4?2, No, 365. ~2) Do you
believe t·hat the present system should now be mcorporated m the Constitution? Inspectors, metropolitan areas: Yes, 15, No, 9; Inspectors, nonmetropolitan areas: Yes, 28, No, 23; Masters and Wardens, metropolitan
areas: Yes, 111, No, 154; Masters and Wardens, non-metropolitan areas:
Yes, 136, No, 319; Total: Yes, 290. Total No, 505.
Many of these questionnaires offered suggestions and criticisms which
should be of value in the future. I submit these figures to you for your
information and leave it to your individual judgment what value, j.f any,
they may have in any discussion of the Grand Lecturer system, which
question I also leave with the members of Grand Lodge in the belief that
those who are most intimately connected with the ritualistic work are best
able to work out a satisfactory solution of the problem.

In connection with this subject, however, my attention has been called
to the fact that the four assistant Grand Lecturers have not been provided
with any sort of regalia. If Grand Lodge decides at this Communication
to continue the present mode of teaching the ritual, manifestly some
provision should be made for proper regalia and proper jewels for those
officers. I therefore recommend that if Grand Lodge maintains the present
system, the Committee on Ritual be instructed to devise a suitable form
of regalia, including jewel, for the Assistant Grand Lecturers, and when
so devised and approved by the Grand Ma·s ter, that the Grand Secretary
be authorized to purchase such aprons and jewels.
Incidentally I also call your attention to another fact respecting the
jewels worn by the officers of Grand Lodge, and that is we have never
officially prescribed the jewels of any other than Grand Master, Past Grand
Master and Past Master. I suggest that this matter also be referred to
the Committee on Ritual for appropriate action.
Public Schools
I note with interest that there was a widespread observance .of our
17th Annual Public Schools Week, and that another Grand Jurisdiction,
Georgia, initiated a similar observance this year. It is also gratifying to
note that as time passes, Public Schools Week is becoming more of a civic
affair than formerly and that greater emphasis is now being placed upon
presenting to the general public a real picture of the activities and school
life of the children rather than upon mere entertainment.
The more I see of life, the more firmly I am convinced that the hope
of the future lies in the education of our youth-not of some children but
of all children-not according to so-called classes of society, but according
to a wisely conceived and efficiently executed plan that will make available
to every child, regardless of his station in life, an equal opportunity to
study, learn, and progress upon his own merits in this complicated and
ever changing world. This can best be done, indeed it can only be done by
a system of free public education. It is for this reason that the Grand
Lodge of California, ever striving as it does, to replace darkness with
light, is so vitally interested in the public schools of our state. One of
the greatest leavening influences in society today is the public school.
It does more to break down distinctions between social and economic
groups and to eliminate class consciousness than any other man-made institution. It offers the strongest proof to the world that "he who is on the
lowest spoke of fortune's wheel may be entitled to our regard." By destroying prejudice and planting reason in its place it prepares the foundation of a liberty loving people for free government, the greatest blessing
that this or any other nation ever had.

Our Country
Brethren, at this critical time in the world's history, we would do well
to offer thanks for the greatest of all free governments-the government
of the United States of America. It is the government which has brought
more opportunity and happiness to the underprivileged of the world than
all others combined. It 'h as been the admiration and the envy of the world
and, for upwards of one hundred and fifty years, not only attracted to our
shores millions of troubled and oppressed people from other parts of the
globe, but also served as an example for other nations to emulate. Country
after country copied our institutions as closely as their foreign background
and conditions would permit, until only a few years ago it appeared to be
inevitable that free government would spread its mantle over the entire
face of the earth. Now conditions are changed and instead of striving

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

for liberty, people in other parts of the world are exchanging their freedom
for some form of autocracy. They rarely call these autocracies by the same
name but, regardless of form or name, they are the same thing, in that
they are the opposite of free government and human liberty becomes dead.
Where free government dies, Masonry dies with it, and in all of these
countries today our Lodge rooms are dark, their property has been confiscated, our brethren are persecuted for their beliefs and all men are
denied the freedom of speech, of assemblage, of the press and of religionthose rights, which to Americans and all liberty loving people are the very
essence of life itself. In all of those countries we now find war or .frantic .
preparations for war, civil strife or threatened civil strife, and a mad rush '
of different classes to plant the heel of ruthless government upon the
chests of their weaker neighbors. It is only in those countries where
people have a passion for free government that we find any degree of peace
and contentment, and nowhere on earth is there to be found any greater
measure of those blessings than in this country of ours. Let us love it
and cherish it as we do few other things, and let us pledge the future of
our Masonry to its principles as strongly as did our brethren who did so
much to bring it into being.

The Deputy Grand Master referred the message to the following committee on Segregation:
Fred B. Zimmerman, Roland R. Israel, and William W. Skelton.

GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
In presenting my report as Grand Treasurer of the Masonic Homes of
California, I wish to advise this Grand Lodge that never in my recollection
has such difficulty been encountered in the selection of bonds for investment for the Endowment Fund and stocks and bonds in investing for the
Grand Lodge.
Before the appointment of a committee to as~ist the Grand Master and
Grand Treasurer in the selection of investments, many investments were
made of my own selection. The Committee, consisting of such eminent
brethren as P.G.M.'s W. Rhodes Hervey, Arthur S. . Crites and Robert B.
Gaylord, has been most helpful. But, as the financial condition of our country grew more complicated with apparent uncertainties confronting the
market, even the efforts of t'his Committee and the Grand Treasurer were
of such uncertainty that it was finally decided to secure the services of an
adviser whose function is to furnish advice upon the subject of investments.
The services of the Standard Statistics Co., Inc., of New York, were subscribed to at a fee of $750.00 per year. It was then found that the recommendations of this adviser, in order to take advantage of market conditions, were such, that immediate action was necessary, that time was the
essence, that the changing conditions of the market rendered it impossible
to contact the members o"f the Committee in time to make purchases at the
t·hen market price. All members of the Committee waived their individual
opinions in favor of the Standard Statistics .Co., and the recent investments
in the Endowment Fund have been made in accordance with the plan proposed' and purchases made by me on recommendations of the Standard
Statistics Co., at the earliest possible time. Most if not all of these purchases have appreciated in value.

Just how long the present market condition will prevail there is no
conjecture. The fact that heretofore, during a Presidential campaign, bonds
reflected marked uncertainties, is no criterion now as the market price of
many U. S. Government, State and Municipal bonds is slowly increasing.
All bonds recently purchased have required a premium.
Another matter concerning the policy of purchasing securities for our
Endowment Fund. Our present Grand Lodge constitutional regulation prescribes that our investments be made in U . S. Government, State or Municipal bonds. Some of our brethren believe that this regulation should be
changed to include high grade industri~l, public utilities and railroad bonds,
from which we would derive greater revenue. This is referreCl to you without recommendation. ·

Sec. 22. Each Lodge represented by a Master, Warden, Past Master,

Report of Auditors
To the Finance Committee, Grand Lodge:
In accordance with your instructions, we have completed an audit of
the books of account of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California for
the fiscal year ended July 31, 1936. The following statements are submitted
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's report of cash receipts and disbursements-General Fund.
Exhibit B: Grand Secretary's analysis of cash received for the account
of Masonic Homes of California.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's report of cash receipts and disbursements-General Fund.
Exhibit D: Grand Treasurer's report of assets on hand July 31, 1936.
The scope of our examination included a verification of total cash
funds received during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1936, from the annual
returns covering the fiscal year 1934-35. Funds received and on hand held
in suspense based upon the annual returns for 1935-36 in amount $6,220.00
were not included in our examination. Total receipts due ·from subordinate
Lodges as per individual annual returns were found to be in proof by
total number of membership, classification of source of revenue, and total
amount of gross revenue received, as evidenced by the recapitulation record
of all subordinate Lodges. Total of all receipts were found accounted for
and the cash received therefrom deposited in bank accounts. Bank accounts
were reconciled and verified, and sufficient examination of detailed vouchers
was made as to satisfy ourselves as to the correctness of the accounting.
The following amounts due Grand Lodge are entered in the books
and covered by notes:

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
In submitting my second annual report to this Grand Lodge, I do so
wit.h the full realization of the responsibilities which rest upon the shoulders
of one holding this important office. I regret that I have been unable to
answer all the calls made upon me, as time would not permit; but I take
consolation in the fact that I have faithfully and conscientiously fulfilled the
duties imposed upon me to the best of my ability.
Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller, chairman of the Ritual Committee with the Assistant Grand Lecturers and myself have met four times
during the past year for the purpose of studying the ritual. These meetings
were two day sessions, making eight full days devoted to this work.
Due to the prolonged illness of Oscar L. Harris, Assistant Grand
Lecturer for the northern district, I found it necessary to take over his
work during t'he past year.
Lodges of Instruction have been held for the Inspectors in every district in the jurisdiction (with the exception of the Hawaiian Island group)
at least twice during the year and in many cases four and five visits have
been made. This does not include the Lodge of Instruction held immediately
preceding this .communication of Grand Lodge.
It has been a pleasure to this comdtittee to work with the Inspectors,
who have so generously given of their time and cooperation.

43

the hands of the officers, a .greater uniformity has resulted in the performance of these ceremonies.
. Early in the year, Inspectors' register sheets were furnished all In:,.
spectors. This record is used at the Inspectors' Lodges of Instruction, and
shows where the meetings were held, the degrees worked in and carries the
signature, office and Lodge of each officer attending.
I asked the Inspectors to have these records signed by the officers at
their Lodges of Instruction and immediately forward them to the Assistant
Grand Lecturer in charge of the district.
It is pleasing to note that the majority of Inspectors have· held Lodges
of Instruction for their officers at frequent intervals and that the attendance has been satisfactory.
Death of Oscar L. Harris

In computing the mileage covered in this work, I find that 14,830 miles
have been traveled .d uring the past year. Many visits made to districts in
the metropolitan areas have not been taken into consideration.
In my report last year I mentioned that the expense of this work to
Grand Lodge had totaled less than eighteen hundred dollars. It is again
my pleasure to report that this year our expenses have run slightly over
seventeen hundred dollars.

On July first this committee suffered a severe loss through the death
of brother Osc;ir L. Harris, Assistant Grand Lecturer for the northern
secti?n. Having been sick with tuberculosis for more than a year, the news
of his deat·h was not received with surprise, but with sincere regret and
sorrow. His sunny disposition and pleasing personality won him a host of
friends.
It is not my intention to eulogize Brother Harris in this report but I
cannot refrain from making the statement that his work for this' Grand
Lodge was well done. His was a service of love for the organization in
which he believed so sincerely and completely. His life proved him to be a ·
good man and true Mason. More than this cannot be said of any man. His
passing will be missed more by those who knew him best.
In August the vacancy created by t·he death of Brother Harris was
filled by appointment of Brother Gilbert C. DeForest, who for the past
twelve years has served as Inspector of the sixth district at Redding. As a
splendid ritualist and enjoying a wide acquaintance in the northern section
of the jurisdiction, I am sure his appointment has met with the approval
of the Lodges in his district and that he will merit the same cooperation and
success as did his predecessor.

Condition of Lodges

Visitations

The condition of Lodges generally, seems to be much improved. From
the number of petitions received by some of the Lodges, it would seem
that, so far as Masonry is concerned, the depression is over. A happier and
more optimistic feeling prevails among the officers and members. I trust
that in the anxiety to obtain new members, the Lodges will not relax their
vigilance and that none but good men and true will be conducted through
the doors of our institution. Membership in this fraternity is a privilege ani
honor, not to be accorded all men. We pride ourselves on the quality of our
membership-Let us keep it so.

During the past year I have been privileged to install the officers of
twenty-one of our Lodges and to assist the M. W. Grand Master at the
installation of several others.
Through the courtesy of the Grand Master I had the pleasure of officiating at the corner-stone laying ceremonies of the new post office bui.Jding at
Lod·i and the Lake County Museum at Lakeport.
.
I have been requested to attend many meetings of Lodges and Officers'
Associations and where possible, have accepted. When called upon, I have
endeavored to address the brethren upon subjects, both interesting and instructive. At several of these meetings, questions have been asked, relative
to various Lodge activities, chiefly among them the question, bow to create
a better attendance. To attempt to lay down a fixed set of rules to remedy
this situation would be impossible; but it might be well for Lodge Officers
to bear in mind certain cardinal rules, which if conscientiously followed
will without doubt, cause the members to become more Lodge minded. '
It should be remembered, there are just two directions · in which a
Lodge can go--forward or backward. There is no middle ground on which
it . ca? stand still. I_f it is not progressing and prospering, then it is surely
shppmg back, and 1t would be well to thoroughly investigate, to determine
the cause and make an effort to effect a remedy. In many cases it will be
found that other interests have outbid the Lodge for the attention of its

Mileage and Expense

Supplies
Many of our written ceremonies have, for years been printed on cards
and sheets of paper, to be distributed to the Lodges as needed. As a result
of this, bu.t few Lodges were in possession of all these parts.' To overcome
this condition, and to save the cost of printing so many forms, we compiled
all the :various ceremonies in one booklet, called the Officers' Manual. Three
thousand copies of this booklet were printed and four copies were mailed
to each Lodge. Requests for additional copies came in so fast that; within
two months the supply was exhausted. By placing all this information in

44

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

members. It is inconceivable that Masonry should be regarded by many
as being in competition with the theatre, the radio and other forms of entertainment, but . the statement is frequently made and seems to be the
favorite alibi when the question of Lodge attendance is mentioned. No
Lodge will run itself; and if the meetings are not properly programmed in
advance, a lack of attendance will be the inevitable result.
Too often a Master gauges the success of his year by the numbe rof his
candidates and feels all that is necessary to ·hold the interest of the members
is to confer one degree after another. There is no denying the fact that
our ritual is one of the most beautiful and important parts of Masonry, and
when properly rendered, inspiring and enlightening to all who witness it. By
it we are enabled to teach the candidate many valuable truths concerning
the fraternity and inform him about those underlying principles, upon which
Masonry is founded. To the candidate, the ritual is the most important of
our functions; for him it is a vehicle, by means of which he becomes a
member of the fraternity. Rightly does he consider it as the means to an
end-the means to enter our fraternity that he might be taught further
about those divine principles, the practice of which has made Masonry lead
the way through the ages, and become a powerful force for good in every
community of the civilized world. But too often, to his disappointment, does
he find that the ritual is the end itself, so far as instruction is concerned.
He is initiated, passed and raised and then apparently forgotten while the
Lodge turns it attention to the next candidate. He comes back a few times
to enjoy the beauties of our degrees, and tiring of the same performance,
soon becomes one of the absentees.
If a theatre should give the same act or show the same picture month
after month, the patrons would soon go elsewhere and the theatre would
go out of business. Yet, some of our Lodges expect the members to come
to the meetings and witness the same degree time after time without complaint. I do not, in any way speak disparagingly of our ritual, for I realize
that without it, Masonry would not long endure ; but we should not overlook the fact t:hat there are other equally important phases, not to be
ignored.
The average man affiliates with the fraternity, not to be joining another Lodge, but to enjoy the fellowship of his brethren and to receive instruction, which he has every right to believe we can give him. I have tecommended to some Lodges that the Master appoint a committee to assist him to
properly program the meetings of his Lodge. This suggestion, where acted
upon has resulted in a more evenly balanced calendar, consisting of entertainment, where fellowship can be enjoyed to the fullest and meetings
where the desire for instruction and enlightenment can be satisfied. I have
received reports from some of these Lodges that the attendance has picked
up remarkably. It does not take an analytical mind to discover, that where
the members are given something worth while to come for, there is no lack
of attendance.
I quote from a letter received from the Master of one of our Lodges :
" ..... Shortly after your visit to our Lodge in April, I adopted the suggestion you gave us, relative to the appointment of a committee from among
the members, to assist me in arranging the meetings of our Lodge."
"This committee has functioned well and the ideas they have advanced
have resulted in more interesting meetings. Our program is varied to suit
the tastes of all ciur members ... although we have not had many candidates so far this year, still I feel we are usefully employing our time in
bringing back to the Lodge many members who have not been in the habit
of attending."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

45

"Our Senior Warden tells me he intends to continue this practice next
year and from the results so far shown, . I am of the opinion that the question of attendance or rather non-attendance in our Lodge has been solved."
I have made the statement many times at Lodge gatherings and I repeat it here; Masonry is not m·ade up of numbers and is not dependent so
much on its large membership as it is upon the quality of the membership.
Masonry needs good men and true if it is to carry on its vast program;
but in receiving the new candidates into our midst, let us not make the mistake of neglecting those who are already carried on our rolls.
I <lo not say that we are paying too much attention to the ritual, but
rather that we are paying too little attention to matters of equal importance.
Conclusion
To the M. W. Grand Master, Brother Earl Warren, I express my deep
appreciation for his many ·c ourtesies throughout the past year and for the
kind of support he has .g iven me in the administration of this office.
I am indebted to the V. W. Grand Secretary, Brother John Whicher
and the members of his office for many favors and offers of assistance.
Working with Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller and the Assistant
Grand Lecturers has been a pleasure not to be forgotten.
I wish to thank the Inspectors and Lodge Officers for their loyal cooperation and to assure them this association has been most pleasant.
In closing, may I say that I truly appreciate the honor conferred upon
me by this Grand Lodge and hope my efforts have shown the confidence
has not been entirely misplaced.
Respectfully submitted,
LESLIE E. Woon, Grand Lecturer.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ANNUAL ORATION
By ALBERT F. ROSS ..

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
With pride I undertake the task allotted to me by our Most Worshipful
Grand Master, but with humility I realize that the task is a burden and ii
responsibility, as well as a pleasure and a privilege,
At my installation one year ago I was reminded of my duty in the one
short sentence, "It shall be the duty of the Grand Orator, at each annual
communication; to deliver an address to the Grand Lodge upon matters
appertaining to the craft."
Today the Grand Lodge of California convenes for the eighty-seventh
time in annual communication, and during a11 these past years Grand
Orators have performed the duty just stated and have delivered addresses
upon matters pertaining to the craft. If I may be pardoned for just one
personal reference, I thrill with pride to be reminded that my own grandfather sat in this Grand Lodge in 1859, and my father in 1888, both as
Masters of the same little pioneer Lodge, Northern Light No. 190, and each
listened to an exposition of Masonic history, Masonic symbolism and
Masonic ideals. Masonic history is now a few years longer, but the symbolism and the ideals are the same now as then.
During the eighty-six years of this Grand Lodge's life, many distinguished and able speakers have filled the post where I now stand. Many
of them have confessed their humility and their diffidence in attempting
to address such an assemblage. When I recall the names of just a few of
the grand orators of the past-Past Grand Masters Hervey, Adams, Burke,
Boynton, Fischer, and Gaylord, our present Senior Grand Warden, the
distinguished brother who is Chief Justice of the California Supreme Court,
Judge Waste, and his Associate Justice, Brother Ira Thompson, those eloquent brethren, John L. McNabb, Fletcher A. Cutler, Rufus B. Von KleinSmid, Ezra Decoto, Tully C. Knoles, Leslie Learned, 0. K. Morton,
Reynold E. Blight, the late William C. Hassler, and others of an earlier
day-I pray .that I may accomplish my task in any measure as well as
they; Back in 1897, thirty-nine years ago, we find the Grand Orator,
Brother Francis Ellsworth Baker, complaining that the subjects and
thoughts proper for the occasion had been so often treated by abler minds
than his that there was nothing left for a grand orator to say. And, to use
the words of Brother Waste in his oration to the Grand Lodge in 1914,
"I bring to you today only a simple message from the heart."
I speak to you not of the past as a historian. In our Grand Lodge
library there are many volumes, and in most of the subordinate Lodges,
some, and to these the attention of the craft is directed and their study
is recommended. It is urged that all you masters and wardens familiarize
yourselves with the background of present-day Masonry, and carry the
information to the craft in your various Lodges. The history of Masonic
symbolism, the works of our ancient brethren who were both operative
and speculative, the story of the Roman Collegia and of the Cathedralbuilders of the Middle Ages, the evolution of Ancient Craft Masonry as it
exists today, all this should be unfolded to the brethren that they may
know our institution and glory in its history.
The lessons of the past, in Masonry as in all else, teach us how to act
in the present. From the experiences of our ancestors we may govern our
conduct to the best advantage of both our fellow creatures and ourselves.
The present is the big time. We must give thought to the past, we
should reverence those who have preceded us, we should give memory its

what is to come.
But the time to act is now. The greatest man of a hundred years ago
can do nothing now, but each of you are here in the living present. As

How can Masonry help us to make the most of the present? How
can it do otherwise if we but make our hearts and minds recepdve to its
teaching?
Early in our Masonic careers we learn that this is an institution having
for its foundation the practice of the social and moral virtues. An ardent
application and promulgation of the great fundamental principles, and a
generous devotion of our time and attention to their realization will add
joy to our lives and the !iv.es of those around us, as well as promote success
for our endeavors in whatever work we are pursuing.
A survey of those Masonic principles is thus something we should
attempt at times, not only when, as here, we are in convention assembled,
but when we are alone with our thoughts. The ritual of our order is filled
with beautiful gems and wise and serious truths, but they must be made
more than words. We must think them; then we must act them.
Masonry as we know it is symbolic. The great Mason and scholar,
Albert Pike, said: "The symbolism of Masonry is the soul of Masonry.
E very symbol of a L odge is a religious teacher, the mute teacher also of
morals and philosophy."
.To get the value of Masonry we must understand this symbolism. One
may be a·b le to repeat every line of the .Ritual without .an error, but if he
does not understand the meaning, not just the language but the underlying
thought, he does not know his Masonry.
·I might add, however, that I am a firm believer in letter-perfection in
rendering the ritual. The words of the ritual accurately express the symbolism of our emblems, ceremonies and traditions, and to preserve this
accuracy no word should be omitted nor changed except by Grand Lodge
authority, and then the change will be uniform throughout the jurisdiction.
This is no time to discuss what may be a controversial matter before
this communication as to the so-called "new system" a nd t he so-called

50

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"old system" of lectureship in California, but regardless of what system
w~ use, I take this opportunity to say that we should adopt that which
will lead to a letter-perfect and uniform rendition of the ritual, and no
fals_e e~ono~y should be considered. We can do without banquets and
social times 1f need be, but we owe a duty, not only to our Masonic predece~sors,_ but to our Masonic posterity, that to the latter may be "transmitted
ummpa1red the most excellent tenets of our insti-tuion."
But, to repeat, to get the values from the various symbols we must
understand them. Each symbol, each emblem, each allegory has a lesson
for us which will help us in meeting the needs and grasping the opportunities of the "living present."
From the blindfold before initiation by which we are made more sightless than the new-born babe to the acacia which symbolizes immortality
after _the body has matured, and aged, and died, every single emblem and
teaching has an important place.
In the New Testament is told how Jesus of Nazareth was asked
"Master, what is the great commandment in the law " and his answer'
"Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart a~d with all thy soui
and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the
second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. On these
two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
There was the Sermon on the Mount of the New Testament there
were the Ten Commandments given to Moses, the Psalms of Dav.id, the
Proverbs of Solomon, and the preachments of the many prophets; yet of
these four short sentences was truly said, "On these two commandments
hang all the law and the prophets."
So in Masonry, can we with reverence paraphrase the words of Jesus
and say of certain emblems, "On these hang all the Masonic tenets and
principles?"
I think. we can. The Three Great Lights of Masonry cover the whole
field.
The purity of the lambskin apron, the innocence of the lamb the
friendship and brotherly love of the two right hands joined, the r~ugh
ashlar made perfect by a proper use of the common gavel, the five orders
of architecture, the globes which give us knowledge of the world we live
in and of the universe through which that world and even its mother sun
fly as but specks of dust, the trowel by which friendship is cemented and
made enduring, the geometrical problem of Euclid which exemplifies
science, and the beehive which exemplifies industry, all these deserve careful
consideration and appreciation, but all are comprehended within the lessons
taught by the Great Lights.
"The Holy Bible is given to us as the rule and guide of our faith the
square to square our actions and the compass to circumscribe our de~ires
and keep our passions within due bounds toward all mankind."
The meanings of the square and compass are many. To walk and act
upon the square is a familiar phrase of · popular significance. Among the
sacred symbols of the ancient Egyptians the square was found. The same
is true of China long before the Christian era.
Shakespeare uses the phrase, "I have not kept my square" in a play
where one is confessing his shortcomings. M<1ny of you no doubt have
heard of the old square found in the foundations of a bridge in Ireland
dated 1517, and inscribed with 'these words:
'
"I will strive to live with love and care
Upon the level by the square."

51

The square is at once the jewel of the Master and the working tool
of the Fellowcraft.
The square and compass together are often given this significance: the
square represents the worldly side of man, as . the earth in ancient times
was supposed to be flat and oblong, while the compass represents the
heavenly side, the curves which the compass makes possible being found
in the star-decked dome of heaven. This explanation should make plain
to the brethren the reason for the change in position of the square and
compass in the three degrees, from the point where the wor!dly nature
overlies the heavenly to that where the heavenly achieves supremacy over
the worldly.
"T)le most important tenets of Free Masonry," we are told, "are contained within ·the points of the extended compass. They are Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth." These tenets are early brought to the attention
of the Entered Apprentice and should never be forgotten. It is Brotherly
Love that should actuate us when we go on foot and out of our way to
assist a brother, when we stretch forth a helping hand, and when we
whisper good counsel in his ear. We are linked together by an indissoluble
chain and, although it may be a duty to relieve the distressed, it should be
a sp~ntaneous result of sincere affection for our troubled brethren, their
widows and orphans.
Truth, as explained to the Entered Apprentice, is sincerity, honesty of
expression and plain-dealing among men. The higher idea is that of
Divine Truth, a knowledge of God. Allegorically we search for that which
is lost, but this allegory points out that mankind must forever keep up
the search for Divine Truth, for only when that Truth permeates all
humanity will perfection among men and women be approached.
The compass also teaches us to circumscribe our desires, and as the
square governs our conduct with our ·fe llow-men, the compass points out
the duty of self-control, that our divine minds and spirits should have the
ascendancy over our animal natures and instincts.
The Holy Bible is not only one of the Great Lights ; it is the Great
Light. The square and compasses are only emblems and t ools when used
by themselves; it is only when upon the open Bible that they become great
lights also. No Lodge can be opened without the presence of the Bible. In
fact, we define a Lodge as "a certain number of brethren assembled with
a Holy Bible, square and compass, and a charter or dispensation." We use
the English Bible, but it is only a symbol of the book of Truth. Mohammedan Masons may use the Koran, Jews, the Old Testament only, and that
book should be used which to the Masons using it most fully represents
Divine Truth.
Masonry is said to unite men of every sect and opinion, and in doing
this it leaves each one to interpret the Bible in his own way. A Mason of
one sect or religious denomination may believe in certain practices and base
them on biblical reading, while to another the interpretation has a different
effect. So long as both believe in one true and living God, a ll-powerful and
ever-present, they can meet harmoniously as Masons and brothers before the
Holy Bible as a symbol of God's truth.
We who use the English Bible can do so with the knowledge that,
aside from its symbolical use, it is one of the greatest books ever given to
mankind. Whether as literature, philosophy or theology, it should be read
more by Masons than I think it is. When we install the Chaplain of our
Lodges he is told, "That Holy Book ... forever sheds its benignant rays
upon every lawful assemblage of Free and Accepted Mas·ons," and then he
is enjoined, "Teach us from its life-giving precepts."

Our Method of Training Children
It goes without argument that the proper training of a child taxes the
mind and thought of every parent. The same problems, multiplied many
times confront the management of an institution having the care and
responsibility of properly training a family of nearly two hundred children. Your Trustees, with the cordial and intelligent co-operation of the
Superintendent and his household staff at our Home for children at
Covina, have made the problems of child training a major study.
T.here are two schools of thought in the rearing of children in institutions: one (now largely discarded) is that boys and girls should be
cared for separately, without contact between them. The other, to which
we adhere, is that co-educational training is better in an institution as it is
in a normal home. We believe positively in the encouragement of free
association between boys and girls, of course with intelligent supervision.
For instance, we make the dining room more than merely a place to eat.
We make it a social center, with boys and girls at each table. We find
that this makes for far better manners and more really intelligent conversation than would result if boys only were at one table and girls only
at· another table. When this arrangement was inaugurated, something more
than a year ago, there was some demur among boys of the type who pride
themselves on their ultra masculinity, who delight in dirty cords and to be
rough. You all know this type. They' are in nearly all families. Our boys
soon became reconciled to the idea of sitting with g irls and the association has had a marked effect on the manners and courtesy of not only the
boys, but has tended to enlarge and liberalize the point of view of the
girls. This commingling · extends to all the activities of the Home, and has
not added to any of the problems of child-rearing. On the contrary we
have found it has fine possibilities, particularly for the practice of the art
of living outside t he Home, after. dismissal. We have no hesitation in

57

PROCEEDINGS OF THE-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

declaring our faith that mixed association, carefully managed, has splendid
cultural and moral possibilities for both boys and girls.
In this connection, and with a view to check some phases of the
mode of operation of the Home for children, Mrs. Jessie C. Fenton, of the
California Bureau of Juvenile Research, a well-known authority in child
welfare work, made a special survey of our .practices in the training of
children, and particularly in the matter of the relationships of the boys and
girls. She indorsed our methods. We refer you to her comments as contained in the report of the Superintendent in the pages following.

thoughtful and .g enerous donor was Warren G. Bailey, a m~mber of

will thereby be enab'ted to see and hear, at frequent i~tervals, the plays

A Large Donation
Brother Charles N. Flint (Pentalpha Lodge No. 202) and his wife
donated stocks and bonds of the par value of $90,000, and real estate of the
value of $25,000, the income from all of which is to be used for the benefit
of the residents of the Decoto Home.
Endowment Fund
At the close of the year 1935 the amount due on our note for money
borrowed from the Endowment Fund, to complete the buildings at Decoto
and Covina, amounted to $175,000. During the last preceding fiscal year
$25,000 was paid and since August 1, 1936, we have paid an additional sum
of $50,000, leaving now an indebtedness of only $100,000.00.
The Endowment Fund, as of July 31, 1936, had grown to the respectable sum of $889,621.51. The report of the Endowment Board will show
in detail the condition of the Fund.
