secure original data for a working basis. The list consisted of eighty-five
reports, which in most cases were followed by a thorough investigation by
field worker. The results led to the discontinuance and reduction, with the
approval of the northern Trustees, of twenty-six outside relief cases, a
total monthly sum of $466.50. This was accomplished through several substantial reasons: Adult State Aid, legally responsible children furnishing
support, Spanish-American War pension, sufficient income in the home,
admittance to Decoto and Covina where it was deemed adviS"able, children
having reached the age limit, and requests for discontinuance after field
worker secured a r eport from the Lodge and a visit had been made.
A statistical report is submitted to give a more detailed analysis of the
work accomplished.

To the Trustees of the Masonic Honie of California:
On November l, 1935, I was appointed northern California field worker
by the Board of Trustees for the Masonic Homes of California. My previous training in social service work was acquired through experience in
family case work with the San Francisco Emergency Relief Administration, and State Relief Administration. The month of November was utilized in traveling with Miss Noel, field worker in Southern California, to
discuss various phases of the work involved, as well as for the purpose of
orienting myself with Masonic Homes policies and procedures. My active
work began December 1, 1935. The territory which I have covered includes
Fresno and the jurisdiction north of it, although no specific boundaries
were designated. My travels have entailed approximately nine thousand
miles. All clerical work including reports, correspondence, etc., is done
entirely by me.
Being the first to undertake the position of social worker in the northern territory, considerable organization was essential, which I have proceeded to do slowly so as not to err at the mercy of those dependent upon
the fraternity. My main purposes are coalesced under the fallowing: (1)
Investigate all new applications (where applicant resides in the north) for
admission to the Decoto and Covina Home. (2) Interview relatives of children in the Home with the view of obtaining monthly payments for the
maintenance of their children. (3) Secure suitable homes with relatives for
children who cannot adjust themselves in the Home. (4) Secure an up-todate report on the circumstances of all recipients of outside relief, heretofore under no direct' supervision, including those residing out of the State
of California. (5) Assist in reducing the amount of outside relief now being
extended in northern California. (6) Assist Lodges in securing State Aid
for adults in lieu of making formal application for reHef from the Masonic
Homes. (In most cases, $35.00 is the usual amount allotted for State aid;
this is generally in excess of the amount granted by the Masonic Homes
for one individual. (7) Investigate original applications and renewals for
State Aid for children in the Home where the mother or relative resides
in northern California.
. Not only do I wish to lessen the increasing financial burden imposed on
the Masonic fraternity, but also consider the needs and comforts for the
future welfare of the recipients of relief, and app'iicants to the Masonic
Homes. Legally responsible relatives are contacted in all instances, either
through correspondence or personal interviews. Attitudes of applicants, interested persons, relatives, and Lodges, represent an important part in each
application. .Facts are gathered to give a complete picture of the family
circumstances in order that the Trustees may be better equipped to approve or disapprove an application. In every instance, I have made no
promises to the people involved, as all decisions are determined by the
Trustees. Liberal recommendations have been made, giving the applicant
the benefit ·of their requests, rather than to save a few dollars and cause
a greater hardship for those less fortunate.
Much detail work was required in checking over the list of families in
receipt of outside relief. It was necessary to communicate with each Lodge
concerned to discover the present whereabouts of the applicants, also to

To the Board of Trustees:
In subm:tting my twenty-seventh annual report as Superintendent of
the Decoto Home, I have to state that with few exceptions the general
conditions have been satisfactory during the past year.
We have endeavored to create a homelike atmosphere, where the members of our family can enjoy the peace and comfort so necssary to those
who are· entering the evening of life, and as far as possible to encourage
them to take an active interest in the daily life of the Home.
At the beginning of the fiscal year, there were enrolled at the Home,
363. There were admitted from September 1, 1935 to August 31, 1936, 61,
making a total of 424. During the year, there passed away 68. Voluntary departures 2, leaving now a total of 354 residents. 191 men and 161 women. Of the
men and women, 28 are married couples.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The health of the residents has been good with the exception of those who
are growing feeble, due to advancing years. The average age of the men
is 74 years, and the women 73 years.
Many of our men and women who are physically able, render assistance in the routine work of the several departments, and on the grounds;
a:nd by their labors they have been a great help in the well-being of the
Home.
As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been leased, or on
cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of eggs, fruits, nuts, vegetables
for table use. The return from the hay crop has been good this year.
All the fruit, shrubs and ornamental trees planted last year are doing
well. More trees and shrubs will be planted this year.
All the road beds are in good condition. All the necessary repairs have
been made on the boundary fences.
During the year, all necessary repairs have been made. Many rooms
!n the building have been painted. The walls and ceilings of the halls and
corridors have been repaired. Many articles of furniture have been repaired and varnished.
During the year, our water supply has been ample for our needs. Our
reservoirs, with a capacity of 500,000 gallons, have been full at all times.
The steady growth of our library continues. Many books have been
donated during the year. A large number of newspapers and magazines are
regularly received, and contribute very materially to the enjoyment of the
patrons of the reading and club rooms.
The Alameda County Free Library maintained at the Home is greatly
enjoyed by the members of the family.
We have enjoyed many splendid programs for the entertainment of
the Home family.
The social life of the Home has been greatly enriched during the year
by literary and musical entertainments, stage plays, dances, games, card
parties, etc., made possible by generous volunteers from Lodges, Eastern
Star Chapters, and friends, assisted by residents of the Home.
The special exercises which stand out prominently, were held on New
Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's and Washington's Birthdays,
Memorial Day, Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Many members of the Home have, from time to time, enjoyed moving
picture shows at towns in the vicinity of the Home-also the opportunity to ·
visit, occasionally, a Lodge or Eastern Star Chapter located at either one
0f the nearby towns, or at the Home.
Masonic degrees are at times conferred in our Temple by visiting
Lodges for the benefit of the brethren of the Home.
A visit was recently made by a large number of the residents to Stanford University at Palo Alto, Golden Gate and Sutro Parks, and the Cliff
House, San Francisco.
Sound Moving picture equipment has been completely installed in the
Assembly Hall, through the generosity of Brother Warren G. Bailey, a
member of Balder Lodge No. 393, San Francisco. Work is now being done
to correct the acoustics of the Hall. When this is attended to, weekly
pictures will be given, which will contribute greatly to the entertainment
of the members of the Home.
Every Sunday afternoon finds the residents of the Home, and visiting
friends, congregated in the Assembly Hall for Divine service. Many of the
services are conducted by visiting clergymen, assisted by church choirs,

soloists and orchestras to render the service more interesting and impressive; bringing a message of good cheer and hope to all those who attentl.
Also, Sunday morning and evening sermons over the Radio broadcast from
various Stations are enjoyed by members of the family.
The Listeners' club," for those who cannot see to read, is held daily.
Residents of the Home, and others, read. Discussions are held and sociability promoted.
Various other forms of recreation are provided ; croquet grou.nds, and
i::idoor games, weekly dances, etc. The men have their club rooms, equipped
with radios, billiard, pool and card tables; and the ladies have their social
halls.
Christmas day is a happy time. Presents, some of which are made h y
Eastern Star Chapters, are given; others are bought with money contributed by various Lodges and friends.
•
We have been honored, during the year, by visits of officers of the
Grand Lodge, members of the Board of Trustees, and members of various
Lodges and friends of the Home.
The Matron and I wish to thank a ll the officers and employees of the
Home for the conscientious service rendered in their respective departments; also to thank the Grand Lodge officers, the Board of Trustees and
all members of the fraternity for the loyal support they have at all times
given during the year.

Report of the Superintendent-CQvina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California :
Herewith I present my tenth annual report as superintendent of the
Covina Home. During these ten years 275 children have entered the Home
and 277 have departed. Of those who have been discharged, 97 were graduated from the Covina Union High School. Most of the others were returned to parents or relatives whose improved domestic or fi nancial condition enabled them to resume care. A few were removed from the Home
by reason of conduct which was judged to be detrimental to the interests
of the other children in the Home. Of those who have been removed for
the benefit of the general group, a considerable proportion have received

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

subsequent outside care at our hands. In many instances they have profited
by the opportunities thus placed before them and have turned out successfully.
Providing for Graduates-What becomes of boys and girls upon their
discharge from the Home must be a matter of vital concern especially in
these times, when the economic world seems to have so little place for
young people offering themselves for work. The Lodge which places a
chil<l in the Home is primarily responsible to receive him and help get
him started in life when he is discharged. In practice it has been found that
efforts of Lodges toward this end are oftentimes not effective; hence widespread appeal has been made for help from other Masonic sources. The
Southern California Past Masters' Association has an active committee
for this purpose. The Employment Services of the Los Angeles, San Francisco and Oakland Boards of Relief have cooperated most heartily. Appeals made by members of the Board of Trustees of the Home have been
productive. One boy of the present year's class, a full orphan, has been
received into the home of a Mason, who proposes to give him a college
education and to legally adopt him.
A fine piece of practical service for our graduates has been rendered by
the Masonic Digest of Los Angeles, which has made available to Masonic
Home graduates each year for the past three years ten free scholarships
in a leading business college in Los Angeles.

ant supply of good milk, from our own dairy is the basis of our feeding
program. A study which we recently made of other comparable institutions
in Los Angeles county showed that we were spending 30 per cent more
for food, and 27 per cent less on salaries, per child per day, than the average of these other institutions. Our expense for food during the past year
has constituted 30 per cent of our total expense.
Aims and Objects--During the past y ear there has been little change
in our methods of operation. The chief aim continues to be to give to the
children a h.o me approximating in its effect a good natural family home. We
try to get along with the minimum amount of organization and rules which
are compatible with the welfare of the children. The atmosphere is more
relaxe<l and informal than in most children's institutions. W hile we require
and generally secure obedience, we are more concerned with the development of human personality than with discipline. "Discipline in the military
sense has no more place in a children's institution than in a private family.
Authority ~hould not be maintained on a fear basis." We conceive it to
be our duty to send our boys and girls into the world with the largest
possible resources of good health, enthusiasm and self-confidence.
The continuing practice by which each boy or girl after the age of
fifteen must seek and obtain annual reappointment to continued membership
in the Home has abundantly justified itself. The same is true of the practice of requiring older children to buy their clothes and luxuries with
money earned in the Home. Both of these methods have the same end in
view: to develop responsibility in the youngster who is crossing the bridge
from childhood to adulthood.
The Home as Seen by a Child-A fifteen-year-old girl who has grown
up in the Home since she was seven was asked to write her ideas of what

Health-The health program in a children's institution must include not
only caring for the sick, but much preventive work. During the past year
our Knights Templar Hospital has had a daily average of 11 patients. This
comparatively large amount of hospitalization was occasioned primarily
by epidemic conditions prevalent in the community, influenza and mumps
being the chief ailments. While there were a few cases of severe illness, all
made a good recovery, and at present, health conditions in the Home are
extremely good. We employ a full time resident trained nurse, and supplementary nursing help as needed. Medical and surgical work is done, as it
has been for many years past, by the staff of Dr. W. P. Magan of Covina.
In the public schools attended by our children, periodical tests are made
for defects in vision, hearing, and for tuberculosis. Dental work is done
regularly for all children. We regret that on ac<:ount of the expense, it has
been impossible to provide orthodontia for certain children who are in sore
need of it.

An Authority Views Us-Seeking to check some phases of our mo<le of
operation, we recently asked Mrs. Jessie C. Fenton, of the California Bureau of Juvenile Research, to make a special study of our practices in
training children in the use of money and also in the matter of relationships of boys and girls in the Home. Mrs. Fenton spent time enough in
observation t'o enable her to form well considered conclusions, after which
she submitted a report from which the following is quoted:
"I have very few suggestions to offer, and these only with great diffidence. The plan under which you are handling the problems of money and
of social relationships seems to be operating smoothly and effectively, and
to be fully accepted by the children. And these points, of course, are the
real criteria of the value of any program.
"I was delighted to notice the very obvious happiness of the children
at the Home, and their frank affection for their supervisors. The wholesomeness and freedom from any hint of repression in the atmosphere at
the Masonic Home were clearly apparent and gave me very great pleasure.
The morale of your institution seems to be exceptionally fine, and I congratulate you on it most warmly.
"In general I feel that the plan in use at the Covina Masonic Home
for training the children in the handling of money, is an exceptionally
valuable one. It is open to certain theoretical objections, to be sure, but
it would be impossible to evolve a system which would be beyond criticism. On the whole, I am heartily in sympathy with your money arrangements for the children and the p·hilosophy which underlies them.
"As to the relations of boys and girls, the policy of the Home in this
matter seems to be entirely admirable, and quite in accord with generally
accepted psychological principles. There is ample opportunity for wholesome friendly association between boys and girls, with enough supervision
to insure their protection, but not so much that they need feel repressed,
embarrassed, or insulted by any suggestion of adult suspicion or disapproval
of their friendships. Apparently the young people feel secure in the knowledge of a sympathetic, friendly attitude from the adults in the institution,
and this makes it easy for them to seek and accept advice about such personal problems as their relationship with friends of the opposit'e sex. The
incidents which were described to me of youngsters who needed such
advice were admirably handled. I could offer no criticism of your attitude
towards their problems. The ideal relationship between boys and girls in
an institution is one of free association under kindly and sympathetic
supervision, but with no suggestion of repression or suspicion. This sort
of relationship is obviously the one existing at the Covina Home. The
mingling of the sexes at meals is an excellent plan, as is also the sharing
of social events, such as the dance in progress during my visit. I was

"I do not mean to say that all the children go through their years in
the Home peacefully and without trouble. Each child has his own problems
and trou_bles, ~ut having these problems helps g·r eatly in preparing one for
future d1~culttes. In my own experience it has been so. My houseparents
a,nd superintendent spent much time helping me to learn to control my
temper. As a result I have improved in that' quite a bit.

bo~y 1s. an easy job mixed with fun if one makes use of our tennis court,

improve m their school sports. Building a strong body in this way equips

are not deprive? of those things that other chidlren need and get. Many

them be.l ong to the ·?ebating and other organizations. That is why I think

Field Worker-Miss Catharine Noel has continued to render invaluable
service as a field worker during the past year. Her duties have included:
investi~~tion of applications for admission (aged people and children),
superv1s1on of those on outside relief, keeping in touch with families of
children in the Home, supervision of problem children placed in foster
homes, aiding in after care of children after discharge. We have at the
present time under her supervision 38 children who are being financially assisted in their mother's own homes, and seven children who are being
cared for in foster homes. This extension of our work, developed during
the past ten years, has made it possible to take care of increasing demands
upon the service of the Home without building new buildings or adding to
the size of our Covina plant.
Alumni-The past year has marked an increase in the interest shown
by alumni in the Home. Records of alumni in the Home office have been
made more complete. An alumni newsletter has been issued at semi-annual
intervals, containing news regarding the present' whereabouts and activities of many of the former boys and .girls of the Home. This has enabled
them to get in touch with each other and. to renew old friendships. Alumni
living in and around San Francisco, and those in and around Los Angeles,
have each been brought' together on two occasions in reunion meetings.
We believe that the furtherance of alumni organization has been well
worth the effort.
Visitations-Visiting at the Home by Lodges, and other Masonic
bodies, and by individual Masons, is most desirable when done under
proper conditions. Visitors generally have shown a fine appreciation of
their relationship to the Home and its members, and have deported themselves in such a way as to bring help and inspiration to the chlidren. The
attitude of pity and condescending benevolence is detrimental to the
child's self-respect. He is sensitive about being called an "orphan" or an
"inmate" of an orphanage. He needs rather to be made to feel that he is
the adoptive child of the Masonic fraternity. His developing character is
influenced in an important degree by the ideals of the Masonic institution.
As he grows up in the Home he assimilates a conception of what' Masonry
stands for. This comes to him through his contact with visiting Masons
and through things which he ·hears said about Masonry. He comes to
know himself as a ward and child of the Craft; and to feel that he stands
on a firm and solid foundation, that he possesses a worthy moral heritage.
Akin to the pride of the privately reared child in the honor and good name
of his family, is that of the Masonic Home child in the ancient and honor-

In presenting its annual report, the Endowment Board recognizes the
limitations placed upon such a statement by the lack of time to properly present
alt phases of the program, and of the limited space allocated in the printed
copy of reports of the year. An annual report must of necessity, therefore, be
considered merely a recital of highlights of the program during the year and
must be offered in synopsis form rather than a fully detailed report replete
with every phase of the work in which the committee has dedicated its efforts.
The Board believes, therefore, that the early accountability of the work at
hand should merit the undivided attention of the assembled members and also
warrants the careful perusal of those t o whom the printed repor ts are forwarded. Only in this way may the craft throughout the State be informed of
the progress being made in the Homes Endowment program and of plans
designed to perpetuate this most altruistic and worth-while work.

Included in the gifts received from Lodges are several gifts of money that
were made in lieu of sending flowers to the funeral of a deceased brother.
Donations of this character are increasing year by year, and in the judgment
of your Board this is an appropriate and beautiful way of attesting grief or
respect for a decedent by creating a lasting memorial.
During the year a gift was received from Past Grand Master Crites of one
share of stock of Bakersfield Masonic Temple Association, par value of $1Cl0.
It is estimated that contributions were made by about 5,000 members of the
581 Lodges in this jurisdiction; 323 reported contributions and 258 made no
report other than some of the lodges wrote to the committee that they could
secure no contributions.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Relative to Activities of the Board
Following the established precedent of officially declaring the month
of May as Homes Endowment month, the Board, receiving its authorization from the Grand Master, made plans for carrying on the work of
accepting contributions ,and bequests from members of the craft in the
interests of the aged and orphaned wards of the fraternity. Mindful of
the unsettled financial cooditions of the times and in recognition of unemployment problems prevailing throughout the State, the Board, after
careful consideration, proposed and carried out a new method of obtaining
funds for the maintenance and endowment of the Homes.
In a series of letters mailed out to the Masters of every Lodge in
the jurisdiction, stress was placed on the fact that a sustained drive along
purely business lines would not, in view of the financial conditions prevailing, be received with hospitality by the membership, and that the
success of the program would depend entirely upon those who could afford
to donate to the fund and upon those who felt that the worth of the
program warranted a voluntary sacrifice. The Board consistently held that
a concerted drive for funds would embarrass those members who had
suffered financial reverses and who would absent themselves from their
respective Lodges in the face of well-intentioned but insistent solicitation
from endowment committees.
In addition to the regular flow of correspondence, the Board prepared,
printed and distributed a six-page pamphlet entitled "A Challenge to the
Hearts of California Masons," which, divided into six sections, told of the
history of the Homes and contained informative briefs of the various
phases of the work. Space in the booklet was dedicated to voluntary contributions and bequest forms. Copies of these pamphlets were supplied in
sufficient quantity to subordinate Lodges for distribution to every member
in the jurisdiction, and additional copies were on hand for added distribution upon request.
A pamphlet entitled "The Masonic Homes of California," together
with a voluntary subs.cription blank enclosed therein, was forwarded to
each Master in the jurisdiction equal to the total membership of the respective Lodges, asking the Masters to forward one to each m"e mber of their
Lodge.
One of the most helpful indications of support to the Endowment
Fund has been apparent through the interest shown by members in encouraging bequests to the Fund. Because of the very confidential nature of
such information, it is not possible to know to what· extent the Endowment
Fund is being remembered in wills. However, definite assurance and
inquiries received from time to time cause the Board to be very grateful
for the interest and loyalty being shown by the members of the fraternity.
Response to the letters and pamphlets were immediate. From Lodges
throughout the State contributions poured in and in almost every case an
accompanying letter indicated a satisfaction with, and an appreciation of,
the methods of solicitation. And while it was early apparent to the Board
that receipts for the year would not equal those of the past, · it was
impressed forcibly upon the Board by the tone of the letters received,
that the general membership reacted in a highly favorable manner to a
campaign wholly devoid of high-pressure methods and of embarrassing
situations occasioned by a concerted quota drive.
The Board, in order to express its sincere apptedatfon for contributions to the Fund, has established the practice, upon receipt of a donation
from a Lodge, to issue to the Lodge · a ·receipt for the "tbtal amount, and
then issuing individual receipts to the _members for tht;i.~ contribution.

117

Mailed with the receipt was a letter from the Board thanking said donor
for his part in making the Fund a success, explaining how the money is
expended, and inviting the donor to visit the Homes. To date, 3500 receipts
and letters have been issued and mailed.
The Board feels that herein a goal has been achieved; that criticisms
of the past have been eradicated, and that in face of the general commendation of the plan put into effect this year, the way is clearly shown
for future campaigns in the interests of the Homes. The expressed opinion
of the Board at the beginning of the year, that drives were neither necessary nor desired, and that the mass-warmth of the membership toward
the program of providing life insurance for the youngsters and peace
assurance for the aged, was an integral part of the lives of _the average
member, has been proven true, and that glad fact, coupled with the need
of a campaign of education along these lines, is bound to achieve in the
near future the complete endowment of the Homes program in California.
The Board recommends that the month of May again be designat ed
as Homes Endowment Month and that a program be instituted, with the
idea in mind that the designated month of May serve merely as a calendar
symbol for a year-around observance of, and assistance to, the program
representing the " Heart of California Masonry."
Appropriation
The Board further recommends that an additional allotment of $5,000
be made available to the committee in order that a consistent ·campaign of
education be made throughout the coming year. The Board feels that the
allocation of such a fund designed specifically for acquainting the craft
throughout the jurisdiction with our most cherished program of charity
and of mercy, will, in time, create within the breast of every craftsman,
a deeply rooted sense of partnership with, and in, the benevolent work of
California Masonry. The Board conscientiously believes that the altruistic
factors of true charity lie within the mind and heart of individual Masons,
and that it will require but an occasional reminder from the Grand Lodge,
to direct this charitable benevolence into lines of practical and harmonious
remembrance of the twin responsibilities of our jurisdiction.
In order that your Board may function during the ensuing year, we
therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
"Resolved, that the sum of ($5,000.00) Five Thousand Dollars be and
is hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid_ to
the Masonic Homes Endowment Board for its expenses for the year ending
October 1, 1937."
In closing this report the Board gratefully acknowledges the fine spirit
of Masters secretaries and members, who in cooperating with the work
of the Horr:es, clearly evidenced their belief that "The Soul of F reemasonry
is Charity." The Board commends their splendid spirit of cooperation and
of needed assistance.
In conclusion the Board respectfully suggests that wherever possible,
visitations be made to the Homes at Decoto and Covina by members of
the craft1 for in no other way may the individual clearly understand and
appreciat e the splendid humanitarian work of the fraternity; in no other
way may the individual pilgrim feel the deep and thrilling sense of responsibility and of compensation ; in no other way may he pridefully learn -of
the care and protection offered by HIS fraternity for the more than a
quarter century of humanitarian work among the orphaned, widowed and
aged; and in no other way may he truly envision the solicitude and guar-

118

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
'I • '~"" 'II\\ 'fl

dianship accorded those who have breasted life's tide and of those whose
horizons are still tinctured with the surmise and anticipation of childhood.
Visit these Homes then-and resolve anew that your thoughts' and
your efforts in the future will be dedicated to their perpetuation; realize
that charity, the shining jewel in the crown of human virtue, is alive in
the hearts of your fraternity and that the outpourings of the spiritual
quality of charity exalts and repays itself in the definite materiality of
benefits for our helpless wards.
THIS IS THE CHALLENGE TO THE HEARTS OF CALIFORNIA MASONRY!!
May your Board express the hope that in some not far future date,
when that challenge is accepted, EVERY member of the fraternity in
California can add his epilogue to the annual report of the Homes Endowment Board by saying within his heart, "I have builded a Home,
truly Masonic."

Semrities-(Exhibit B):
Corporate stocks and irrigation bonds have been received by donation
a5 noted. Certain of the bonds, other than irrigation, have been acquired bv
donation and are so marked by the letter "D" under Exhibit B. In the cas~
of donated securities the stated or book value represents the value placed
upon the securities at time of donation. Where the value is uncertain, because of it being an unlisted or a closely held security, entry is made on the
books at a nominal $1.00 value for purposes of record.
Bonds purchased are recorded on the books at cost including premium.
A reserve is set up to measure the amount of premium written off or
amortized. The amount of this reserve is deducted from the total book
Yalue of regular endowment securities, Exhibit B.
Additions through purchase or donation during the current fiscal year
have been listed at the close of Exhibit B, for ready reference; and disposals
have been set in detail in Exhibit C. During the fiscal year total securities
have been purchased in amount $230,479.14, as per Exhibit B; and total
securities have been sold or redeemed in amount $126,542.40, as per Exhibit c.
Total market values obtainable as at July 31, 1936, have been noted in
the Endowment Fund summary at the end of Exhibit B.
The endowment income account shows a total net credit of $28,841.47
arising from interest and dividends received during the current fiscal year,
w!iich has been made available to the Masonic Homes General Fund.
Under Exhibit D is a statement of the "John and Lena Luckenbach
Fund"-a special endowment fund. This statement shows the cash funds
of $28,800.00 according to our prior report plus additional cash received during the current year invested in securities purchased. A separate bank account was opened during the year, Anglo California National Bank No.
24201. According to the terms of the trust the income therefrom is to be
used in the same manner as income from the regular endowment fund.
We certify that the attached statements, in our opinion, set forth the
condition of the Permanent Endowment Fund as at July 31, 1936, with exception as to the stated or book values of securities on hand, and that a
proper accounting has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,

Your Ritual Committee begs leave to submit herewith its report.
A brief statement of the history of the committee and its membership
may be of interest at the present time.
At the communication of Grand Lodge in 1910, the following resolution was adopted:
R <!solved: That the Grand Master be requested to appoint a committee of
three on Ritual, which committee shall include the Grand Lecturer. Said committee shall also be custodian of the esoteric work.
Pursuant to this resolution the first committee appointed consisted of
Past Grand Masters Edmond C. Atkinson and Edward H. Hart, and
Thomas ]. Baker, the Grand Lecturer.
In 1911 Past Grand Master Atkinson died, and after the communication of 1911, Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller was appointed to fill the
vacancy, and the committee so continued until 1917, when Past Grand
Master Hart died, and Past Grand Master William P. Fillmer was appointed in his place. The committee consisted of the same personnel from
that date until the death of Grand Lecturer Thomas J. Baker in 1933.
On the death of Brother Baker, Grand Master Gist, conceiving it to
he of material benefit to the craft, issued an edict appointing Foster G.
Dyer, inspector of the 45th District of San Francisco, as Grand Lecturer,
and three deputies, Brother Leslie E. Wood, inspector of the 22nd District
in Sacramento; Brother Chester H. Warlow, in Fresno, and Brother
Sidney K. Lehman, inspector of the 72nd District in Los Angeles, who
were to teach the ritual to inspectors only, and they in tum to the officers
of the Lodges of their respective districts, and placed the chairman of the
Ritual Committee in direct charge of the work and methods of operation
under the Grand Lecturer and the three deputies.
At the communication of Grand Lodge in 1934, it was decided to continue the plan for a year, in order to observe its efficiency, and to improve
and complete the program. At this communication it was decided to add
one more assistant, thus leaving the Grand Lecturer free to supervise the
work of his assistants in their respective districts.
At the same communication Brother Leslie E. Wood was elected
Grand Lecturer, and Brothers Oscar L. Harris, Lloyd E. Wilson, Chester
H. Warlow and Sidney K. Lehman were named assistants.
At the communication in 1935, it was decided to continue the method
for another year, and it was in operation with the same personnel until
the death of Brother Harris, whereupon Brother Gilbert C. DeForest,
inspector of the 6th District, was appointed assistant in his place.
At the first meeting of the committee it was discovered that certain
small differences existed in the different sections of the state, which were
eliminated, and now, for the first time, there is in each of the four districts
an authority on ritual who is in exact accord with the others.
The Assistant Grand Lecturers .have held numerous schools of instruction for inspectors, which has resulted in more intensive instruction of the
inspectors and consequent increase of their efficiency and assurance.
Too much cannot ·be said in praise of the zeal and unselfishness of the
Grand Lecturer and his assistants, who have given freely of their time,
effort and · service, without compepsation other than that which results
from a proper performance of a duty imposed.
Aside from the saving of the expense of a full time Grand Lecturer,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

we confidently assert that the permanent adoption of the present plan will
prove its efficiency and be of lasting benefit to the fraternity.
A part of the plan is to have the Ritual Committee consist of the Grand
Lecturer and his four assistants, as they will be active in the work, in
constant touch with each other, and thus the element of the frailty of
human memory will be reduced to a minimum.
We, the older members of this committee, will gladly yield our positions as custodians of the esoteric work to these younger men in whom
we have the utmost confidence, and to whom we recommend to you as
being well worthy of your confidence.
We therefore propose the following resolution in lieu of the one
adopted in 1910 creating the Ritual Committee, and recommend its adoption:
Resolved: That the Ritual Committee shall consist of five members, as
follows: The Grand Lecturer and four Assistant Grand Lecturers, who
shall be appointed by the Grand Master, each of whom shall, before entering upon his duties, produce a certificate from the Grand Lecturer that he
is proficient in the work and lectures adopted ·by the Grand Lodge and is
qualified to act as Assistant Grand Lecturer. The committee as so composed from time to time shall be custodian of the esoteric work.
DANA R. WELLER,
WILLIAM P. FILMER,
LESLIE E.

Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SEVENTEENTH ANNUAL
OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Another Public Schools Week has come and gone since the last previous Communication of Grand Lodge. It was another Public Schools
Week, but not just another of those weeks which the American people are
periodically called upon to observe. And we thus commence this report because that was an ever recurrent thought expressed in the editorial comment on our latest observance, and of which the following is typical:
"Public Schools Week which is being observed 1n.... __.................._....,
and throughout the state generally, is more than just another week for
someone to observe. It is a week that concerns the future of mankind.
If ever the eternal problems are solved it will be because our schools
have made better men of future generations than we, ourselves, have
been."
"Special weeks for special interests have grown to be more or less
of a joke. However there are some special weeks we are called upon to
observe which are not only of real importance, but of the greatest importance. One of these is Public Schools Week."
"During the last few years, the fifty-two weeks of the year have
been taken over by all manner of organizations, both public and private,
until there aren't enough of them to go around. But Public Schools
Week in California rolls around each year and steals the show. And
this is as it should be. Any movement to interest the public in the administration of something it is financing is commendable."

139

"Weeks are set apart to various institutions for publicity purposes.
Some of them are well worth while. None of them is more so, nor
more significant, than that which directs the attention of our people
to our public schools.''
The real significance of our observance was admirably pointed out by
Dr. Lewis P. Crutcher, the President of the California State Board of Education in an article written by him for "California Schools" and in which
he said :
"Public Schools Week which was inaugurated by a great fraternal
body has a very definite significance in this time of travail; for it draws
the layman into a more intimate relationship with that great institution
which stands second to none as an exemplification of fundamental democracy which should ever be interpreted in the term 'equal rights to
all with special privileges to none'."
Ours is a lay movement; and therein lies its great value. One of its
primary purposes was the development and maintenance of that intimate
relationship between the public and its schools to which Dr. Crutcher refers; another was to afford an opportunity to the patrons of the schools to
obtain the information they should have of them. And that both these purposes are being effectuated was never more apparent than it was this year.
As has been repeatedly pointed out, it has become literally impossible
in recent years to convey to Grand Lodge, in a report of this character,
anything even remotely approaching a comprehensive idea of the extent
and character of the annual observance of Public Schools Week. To even
indicate, and inadequately, the public interest, the assistance rendered by
the newspapers and the broadcasting stations, the cooperation of civic and
other fraternal organizations, the efforts put forth by the school people, the
nature of the programs presented, and last, but far from least, the loyalty,
ze:il and intelligence with which the Masters and Wardens of our Lodges
engage in this activity of Grand Lodge would necessitate our exceeding the
limitations by which we are bound. And to make special reference to every
local observance well worthy of it would require as many words as are
used in the entire volume of the Annual Proceedings of Grand Lodge.
The marvelous success attending our latest observance is of course
known to the members of Grand Lodge who so materially contributed to
it. Most, if not all, of them have not only personal knowledge of the happenings in their own communities, but through the newspapers and over
the radio learned of the way in which the Week was being observed
throughout the state generally. There are, however, each year, certain
particulars with respect to the observance in general which can be known
only to those who have had an opportunity of reading the reports which
come to our committee and who have the contact our committee has with
not only every lodge in the jurisdiction, but as well also with the cooperating agencies. It is to some of these matters we purpose calling attention
in this report.
There were two noteworthy features of our Seven1:eenth Annual Observance. One was the extent to which the civic organizations in the community were represented on the committee of arrangements and the other
was the impetus in the development of the trend noted last year toward
providing programs that will convey to the public ·d efinite information with
respect to their schools rather than merely provide entertainment.
The following excerpts from a report made by a committee of arrangements are indicative of what appeared in reports from many of our
lodges:

In passing it may be said that not only did those in charge of that observance "carry out the thought of Grand Lodge" in making it a community affair, but it appears that they likewise availed themselves of some
of the suggestions contained in the excerpts from the Superintendents'
Bulletins included in a circular letter sent out by our committee. There is
to us a peculiar significance in this; and for this reason: The Chairman of
the Co~mittee is a man of wide experience and special knowledge. So successful m the past have peen observances arranged and carried out under
his direction that he might well feel that he needed no suggestions from
any sour-ce. But that he was not averse to adopting ideas which he did not
originate evidences his peculiar fitness and, in part at least accounts for
the success of Public Schools Week in that community.
'
In the very early days of our movement and when success was trembling in the balance, nhere was hazarded the assertion that there was no
city, town nor hamlet in the State of California having a public school and
a Masonic lodge in which a successful observance of Public Schools Week
could not be held; and that success was dependent solely on the zeal interest and intelligence with which the arrangements were made and ca;ried
out. Succeeding years furnished evidence of the truth of that statement. And
even now when there is no longer failure to be apprehended but only the
degree of success, the determinative factor is, as it always has been and
probably always will be "The man behind the gun."
A rather striking illustration of this was furnished this year in comparison of the reports from two neighboring lodges. They are about the
same size .a nd are located not only in the same general section of the state,
but in the same county and within twenty-five miles of each other.
'The Master of one of these lodges reported that the success of the
meeting arranged by him "was not as much as usual" ; and the reason given

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

by him Was that it was in part due to the fact that it was the fishing season
and "in part due to lack of endeavor to obtain greater publicity and outside
cooperatiorl,,"
The Ma,ter of the other of these two lodges reported not one meeting
but five. In addition to the observance he had arranged in the community
in which his lodge is located (and where there were two meetings held)
he had likewise arranged for an observance in each of three neighboring
towns. That the programs were as interesting and enjoyable as they appear
to have been was due to the fact, disclosed by the Master's letter, that by
starting preparations early he was "able to obtain the services of some
very prominent and capable speakers." But to us the significant thing is
that the Master went to the trouble of making four typewritten copies of the
printed questionnaire sent him in order that he might make a special report
on each of the meetings. And in addition to this he wrote a supplementary
letter covering the complete observance. It isn't strange that he was able
to say in concluding his letter "I feel that on the whole we had a most successful observance of the week-one of the best, perhaps that we have ever
had."
In passing it may be said that it appears from the reports received by
our Committee that this was not the only lodge which arranged for an
observance in a community other than that where it is located. And too
much commendation can not be given those Masters who with the cooperation of their County Superintendent of Schools arranged a meeting, or
school visits, in a district where otherwise there would have been no observance of Public Schools Week.
It may be well to here digress to say something in general with respect
to reports from our lodges. Much of it will be but a repetition of what from
time to time has been said in the reports made to Grand Lodge by our
Committee. We believe, however, that this repetition is necessary because
of the fact that each year there is a .different group of Masters and Wardens,
many of whom have no knowledge of any report made by our Committee
other than that presented at the Communication at which they are in attendance; and some of whom, we regret to say, do not apparently appreciate the value of the reports they are expected to make of the observances
for which they are responsible.
Our comment on these reports will also furnish an explanation, not,
we think, generally understood, of this factor in the "mechanics" of Public
Schools Week in so far as it is fostered and guided by Grand Lodge; and
in this connection we think we can, as Masons, s,ay with becoming modesty
that although what was in its origin a Masonic event has become a community affair, nevertheless the growth, development and success of the
movement are undoubtedly due to the fact that it is a highly organized
activity of Grand Lodge, and that it is through our Masonic lodges that the
cooperating agencies are ~oordinated.
As is of course known, each year there is sent to the Master of every
lodge in the jurisdiction a form on which his report is to be made, and which
contains a series of questions he is expected to answer'. This is not mailed
until a few days before the date set for the beginning of the observance.
This reduces the likelihood of its being lost or mislaid and it is at hand
when required for use. It is expected; or hoped, that it will receive the
Master's attention immediately after the close of the observance for which
he is responsible; and it is likewise expected that there will be attached to
this form pages of the same size on which will be pasted the newspaper
clippings showing the publicity received. With the .form there is sent an
addressed envelope in which the report is to be returned.
The request for a report from the Lodge comes from the· Grand Master;
and of course it is not deliberately disobeyed nor ignored. But it occasion-

We are . not unmindful of the fact that it sometimes happens that a

his report in the form we, and undoubtedly he also, would like to have it.
But there would appear to be no good reason why the form sent out for the

and there can be no doubt that most failures are due to simple carelessness.
We believe that if the value of these reports were fully realized, a special
effort would be made by those from whom they are expected to forward
them as promptly, and with as much detail, as possible.
:
. Although our Committee n;iaintains contact with City and County Supermtendents of Schools and with the State Department of Education and
also with the parent bodies of the organizations which cooperate in the
observance of Public Schools Week, it is largely through the reports trom
the lodges that information is obtained with respect to the details of the
local observances. It is from these reports also that there· come the suggestions which emanate from our committee. But in some instances they serve
a still more valuable purpose.
Every lodg.e has a file of its own in our records. If we find, as we occasionally do, that some particular observance has not been as successful
in every particular as we believe it should have been, the report from that
commu~ity is carefully analyzed. And if we find, as we usually do, that the
suggestions made by our Committee have not been followed we immediately write the Master of the Lodge while the matter is still fresh in
his mind; not, as we are careful to explain, by way of criticism of anything
done or left undone, but solely with the desire of being helpful and with
the hope that any mistake which possibly may have been made will be
thereafter avoided; and we always ask that our letter be handed to the one
who will be in charge of the observance the next year. And it is gratifying
to be able to report that we have evidence of the fact that this has proved
well worth while.
There were received this year three reports, each of which might in
itself constitute a "handbook" for the proper observance of Public Schools
Week. Every detail of organization was set forth with copies of letters, instructions to subcommittees, bulletins from the Superintendent of Schools
to the Principals with instructions to be by them given to their teachers,
reports giving the number of visitors to each school, details of the programs
and pages and pages of newspaper clippings-all bound in an attractive
cover and carefully indexed.
Mention has been made of the nature of the programs notable this
year as designed to convey information rather than to merely furnish enter-

143

tainment.' There were several manifestations of this both in the type of observance a d in the details of the particular program.
In the rst place not only was there a continuance of the trend toward
making visit to the schools the dominant feature of the observance in
many commu ities, but the care and detail with which the arrangements
for these visits "'ere made evidence the belief in their importance and value.
The arrangements of course varied in different communities; but there was
always apparent ',the one common purpose to have the visitors see and
understand the actual work being done in their schools.
In a large number of instances instead of having special programs presented for them, the visitors saw the pupils engaged in their regular tasks.
The situation which it would appear very generally prevailed is aptly described in the following quotation from a magnificent report received by
our Committee. It appears in the comments of a representative of the Committee's on the observance in a particular school.
"School Week was planned to present a week as ordinary and
everyday as any other normal week in the school year. The Committee
was offered complete cooperation in any program it desired to have
staged; but all arrangements were left entirely to the Principal who as
a result of observances of former weeks desired that all special activity
such as entertainment or specially prepared programs be entirely eliminated in order that parents might observe the exact status of the work
being done whether good or poor."
The arrangements for these visits varied not only in the different school
systems but sometimes even in the same system if in a large city. In some
instances, it would appear from the reports, the visitors were expected to
simply "look and listen"; in some they were encouraged to ask questions
which were answered by either the teacher or, at her request, by some pupil;
and in others printed or multigraphed matter was distributed with information concerning the schools, and sometimes the particular class in which
the visitor happened to be, and in such form as might elicit questions.
We wish we felt warranted in here setting forth at length some at
least of the multigraphed sheets attached to one of the reports received by
our Committee. But all that we may do is to make brief reference to them
with the hope that it may provoke inquiry which will be otherwise answered.
They are in the form of notices addressed to the visitor to whom one was
handed as he entered the classroom. After extending a greeting and announcing the class (with the name of the teacher) and the period, there followed information explaining, among other things, just what the class
was at that time doing, how it was being done, the methods used, which
part of that particular subject the pupils liked best, and which least-and
why; and then certain details under this heading: "What we should like
visitors to observe." There was also an invitation to talk with the teacher.
In connection with what is said about these visits to the schools attention should be called to the fact that in some of the school systems in
which · the observance of Public Schools Week is a factor in school administration, there are sent to the parents of the pupils, and made available to
the public, advance notices, or schedules, showing the time of various classroom activities throughout the week so that visits may be arranged in accordance with the particular interest of the visitor.
It is hardly likely that there will ever come a time when an invitation
to visit a school will be, even to the parents of pupils, as alluring as a ticket
to a movie-to say nothing of a prize fight or ball .g ame. And so it will
probably continue to be, if not necessary certainly advisable to resort to
those methods and practices which have been found effective in stimulating
an interest in these visits.

Madison Lodge No. 23, Grass Valley, California:
Your committee at the last annual communication of Grand Lodge
reported. its approval of the project submitted by this Lodge, whereby a
corporation was to be formed in which the Lodge would be the owner

of all O{ the stock, the purpose being to construct a new Masonic Temple
since th~ former meeting place was destroyed by fire in 1928.
The Lodge, seeking to avoid incorporation, requested permission from
your comrl\ittee to issue its promissory notes for the purpose of financing
the constru'ttion and furnishing of their proposed new Masonic Temple.
Your co\nmittee gave this matter very careful study, and after a personal interview with the committee representing the Lodge .denied their
request for the following reasons:
The Statute~ of 1911, Chapter 572, authorizes and empowers "All unincorporated benevolent or Fraternal Societies or Associations .. . without
incorporation, to purchase, receive, own, hold, mortgage, manage and sell
all such real estate and other properties as may be necessary for its business, purposes and objects of said society . . . subject to the laws and
regulations of said Society ... and the Grand Lodge thereof."
If it is not proposed to borrow money, there would be no objection
to a Lodge taking title in its own name. If, however, it should be necessary to obtain a loan secured by a mortgage or deed of trust there might
be some complications.
Although a mortgage is specifically authorized by the statute, there
yet remains a question arising from the relationship of the Lodge to
Grand Lodge.
It is to be noted that the authority given by the statute is "subject to
the laws and regulations of said Society . . . and of the Grand Lodge
thereof." Under the "laws and regulations" of our Grand Lodge, a Lodge
has no authority to borrow money. And having in mind the control
Grand Lodge exercises over the funds of the constituent Lodges, there
would seem to be good reason for believing a Lodge would not be permitted to contract an indebtedness for the purpose of erecting a building;
because it might happen that not only would the money invested in the
building venture be lost, but there might be a deficit which could only be
met by using Lodge funds which should be preserved for the relief of
its m embers.
It is probable that as the notes matured payment could be promptly
made out of the Lodge funds. If, however, it should happen that a large
number of the notes matured at and about the same time it might not be
so easy to do this. And, if for any reason there should be a default it
would reflect very seriously on not only the Lodge, but on the fraternity
as well. There is also the possibility that every member of the Lodge may
be individually liable on such notes as is a partner.
Your committee has accordingly advised Madison Lodge, which
advice has been cheerfully adopted by said Lodge, and has also adopted
the policy that in future it would be necessary that a corporation be
formed for holding title to and managing the affairs of a building.
Moneta Lodge No. 405, Los Angeles, California:

the purpose of amortizing an indebtedness in excess of $33,000.00 now
existing.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report :
During the past year your Committee has continued to gather new
historical information. Considerable time also has been spent in properly
authenticating material already in our files.
From the start we have recognized that our information must be authentic. Word of mouth reports are often very interesting, but may be lacking in accuracy. There are even instances where printed word which seems
to be reliable may become open to question. An interesting case of this
kind was discovered recently.
An old book which purported to be an official copy of Grand Lodge
proceedings for the year 1856 proved to be quite different from the copy
now regularly recognized in our Grand Lodge files . It contains material
which apparently later was thought inadvisable to be preserved in print.
A deleted edition was printed to take its place. Evidently, an attempt was
made to destroy the original edition . At least one copy seems to have
escaped destruction. It is now in the ·hands of an eastern collector of old
books. We hope that it will be made available to us for a more detailed
study, so that we may determine the real significance of the omissions from
the first original record. Also, we are more hopeful that some one will discover another copy of the first record and place it at the disposal of Grand
Lodge for our archives. Thus-strange as it may seem-there are even
times when our own Grand Lodge records do not tell us all that we may
wish to know I
We deeply appreciate the efforts of Lodges to protect significant relics
and to build up historical material in their own libraries. The Masonic
Library of Southern California at Los Angeles has done a splendid job in
preserving historical material and in making it available to the membership
of that section of the state. We urge all Lodges to develop the historical
sections of existing libraries, or to establish suc:h sections and relic collections where they do not now exist.
We desire to acknowledge our indebtedness to the librarian of the
Masonic Library of Southern California, Brother T. S. Southwick for his
tireless research and the wealth of material furnished us dealing with the
Masonic and personal activities of those interesting characters who have
made up the rank and file of early southern California Masonry.
Some Lodges do not have proper facilities for the proper protection
of their historical material. In such cases your committee will welcome them
as gifts to the Grand Lodge. If preferred, they may be loaned to us for safekeeping until such time as they can be properly cared for by the subordinate Lodge. In no instance should Lodge relics or property be given or left
with private individuals, and thus be subje!:ted to loss, misuse or exploitation.
We have deviated from our usual course, and have only a minor exhibit
at this session of the Grand Lodge. Due to lack of funds most of our more
valuable material has not been put into proper condition for extra handling
without some damage. It is desirable to avoid such damage, so it was
thought better to keep it in our files and ot>her safe places of storage at
this time.
At the present time your Committee is corresponding with the Grand
Lodges of Nevada, Oregon, Arizona and the Phillipines in an endeavor to
perfect our records with respect to history of the Lodges in those jurisdic-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

15.0

tions who were originally chartered by this Grand Lodge and who severed
their relations with the California Jurisdiction _to establish their own Grand
Lodges. Up to date members of the above named states have furnished
your Committee with some interesting and informative material.
We wish again to call attention to the desirability of Lodges keeping
scrap-books containing clippings from local current publications of Masonic
affairs in the several communities and also of the lives and activities of
members of their respective Lodges.
There are many hundred veteran Masons whose fifty years of Masonic
service have entitled them to the 50-Y ear Button. We respectfully request
the officers of the Lodges to obtain the written story of the personal and
Masonic activities of these venerable Brothers and forward same to this
Committee at the earliest possible moment.
Last year your Committee addressed letters to many of the Lodges requesting information with resped to the naming of the Lodges. Many
(Lodges) thus addressed have neglected to furnish your Committee with
the information desired and we respectfully urge them to complete their
replies and forward same to the Committee.
.
During the year 1934 we presented a plan to the membership for the
publication of our history in three volumes. The plan placed no financial
responsibility on Grand Lodge. It depended on the co-operation of the
publisher and· a minimum total of 2000 voluntary subscriptions. Prevailing
conditions caused an insufficient response. The subscriptions which were
received have been refunded and that particular plan of publication has
been abandoned. All of the expense in connection with this plan was borne
by the concern who were to publish the books. Since it was definitely announced that this plan of publication had been abandoned many members
have told us that they had intended to subscribe but had overlooked the
matter at the proper time. There seems to be a general urge to go ahead
with some plan of publication. We feel that a history prepared along proper
lines will be of interest to t-he craft. However, we want this to be done at
the right time and in the proper manner, and advise further study along
these lines by proper committee.
During the past two years the Grand Lodge has appropriated no funds
for this committee. The work has been carried on by members of the committee at their own expense. They have also been ably assisted by a number of brethren who are interested in the work. We hereby express our
appreciation to them, and to the Inspectors, and subordinate Lodge offi·cers who have thus cooperated with us so unselfishly.
In addition to the general recommendations of this report, we recommend that the Grand Lodge continue a Committee on Masonic History
during the ensuing year. No financial appropriation is sought at this time.
We also recommend that the Grand Lodge continue a Committee on
Publication of Masonic History to work in cooperation with this Committee to develop the most feasible and economic means of publication at
the proper time.
LEON 0. WHITSELL,
MARK A. SA WRIE,
DAVID TULLOCK,
RoscoE L. CLARK,
CHAS. R. INGRAM,
THOMAS NORRIS,
CHAS. E. HAAS,

REPORT OF TRUSTEES U. C. BERKELEY CLUB HOUSE
At 4 :SO o'clock Grand Lodge was called off until ten o'clock
Wednesday morning.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club at the University of
California submits to Grand Lodge its annual report of the affairs and
condition of the . institution near the Berkeley campus. The complete report of Norman MacEachen, certified public accountant of San Francisco,
and the estimated budget for the ensuing Masonic year have been handed
to the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge for its consideration, and are
made a part of this report · as though fully set forth at this point. The
audit contains the usual "exhibits," and comprises a complete statement
and analysis of the financial transactions of the Club House Board during
the year, verified by inspection of canceled checks and properly approved
invoices covering the major items of expense. We note with pleasure the
coinment of the auditor that: "The records of the Club continue to be
well maintained."
The estimated budiet for the next year is made up closely of items
and amounts contained in the statement of disbursements for the current
year, except as to the item of depreciation and replacements. For that
item we seek a larger amount. Twelve years ago this month, following
the session of Grand Lodge, M. W. Brother Ar thur Crites, then Grand
Master, dedicated the Club House. The equipment and furnishings, then
just installed, had cost in excess of $10,000. While remarkable care has
been exercised in the use of the place, the item of depreciation and replacements has been steadily increasing for each year for several years last
past. This year's cost-$582.97, shown in the audit-is the largest. Following this summer's inspection and repairs,. the furniture people advise
that the limit has been reached. It will be a sheer waste of money to
attempt any extensive repairs in the future. It will be a case of replacements with new furniture. Since the formation of t he Board of Trustees
there has been in existence in the Board's account a "depreciation and
replacement" fund. This item has been decreased during the present year.
In order that· Grand Lodge may gradually absorb the amount needed for
the replacement of furnishings soon to come, the items in our depreciation
and replacement fund, which also take care of the cost of insurance, should
be materially added to. For that reason, we are asking for a total budget
appropriation of $8,000 at the present communication of Grand Lodge.
The proper amount of insurance, fire and general liability, is carried.

156

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Interest from the banks on unused balances has been received and properly accounted for.
Brethren of Grand Lodge: Nearly fifteen years ago the Masons of
California embarked upon an enterprise which may be correctly likened
to the making of a capital investment. Has the enterprise proven that it
was justified? Your Trustees unhesitatingly affirm that it has. Every
succeeding Grand Master-and each one has visited the Club House and
contacted its work-has enthusiastically subscribed to th.at view. There is
a very homely old saying that "the proof of the pudding is in the eating."
When the Masons of California were liberally subscribing for the erection
of the Club House, the plan was easily "sold" to the members of the craft
by the prophecy of the need and the human interest that the institution
would supply to the men and women, perhaps, more properly speaking,
the boys and girls, the coming men and women, attending the University
of California at Berkeley from Masonic homes. The passage of time has
told the story. Let the testimony of those for whom the house was built
confirm the prophecy. For the present let it suffice to give the testimony
of one witness, called at random from the many who would eagerly appear
to testify. We offer this evidence because it is so typical of the students
who are served, and is so recently given. A young man, on graduating from
the university last May, wrote this letter to the President of the Board:
"Dear Judge Waste:
"I am writing to express, at least in some small degre~, my appreciation for all that the Masonic Club has meant to me. I feel that I
should be guilty of the grossest ingratitude, were I to fail to do this.
"When I entered the University of California, in the fall of 1934,
I was away from home for the first time and practically without friends
until I joined the Club. It is hard, perhaps, for one who has not been
in this situation to realize just how much an organization of this type
may mean. Throughout my career at the university my social life and
my friends have been drawn almost entirely from the Masonic Club.
I shall always look upon the many friendships and associations made
and the many happy hours which I have spent in the Club House as
the bright spots of my college life.
.
"I am sure that I speak for the many members of both the Men's
and Women's Masonic Clubs, as well as for myself, when I extend my
most sincere thanks to you and, indirectly, to the Masons of California, for the wonderful things you have done for us, the Masonically
affiliated students at the university."
Can anyone doubt that that young graduate went out into the world a
better man and citizen because the Masonic Club House was near the
Berkeley campus?
Most Worshipful Grand Master and ·brethren, we submit that the
Masonic Club House at the University of California has proved its case.
Fraternally submitted,
TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC CLUB OF THE
UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA, INC.

By WILLIAM H. WASTE, President.

The report was adopted except the request for funds, which
was referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF DIRECTORS, U. C. LOS ANGELES
CLUB HOUSE
To the M. ', w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Los Angeles fraternally submit their report for the year
ending September 30, 1936.
The year has passed without a change in the personnel of the Board
which is composed of the following brethren : Past Grand Masters: Will
H. Fischer, John Stewart Ross and Dana R. Weller. Brothers: Elmer E.
Beckman, Walter L. Berger, Thos. B. Buchan, Chas. H. Dodds, Wm. S.
McFadden, G. Ellsworth Meyer, Marco R. Newmark, Frank X. Pfaffinger,
C. H. Robison, Clyde C. Shoemaker, Ira F. Thompson and Ben G. Wright.
We were tremendously pleased with the manner in which the students
used the facilities of the Club Houstt during the season of 1934-35, but the
year just closed has surpassed any year in our history. We have had a
total of 26,650 visits by affiliated students and our study room was visited
6,000 times, a 50 per cent increase over the previous year. A total of 114
social functions was held during the year and could you but witness the
pleasure and satisfaction our young people derive from the privileges
afforded, you would agree with us that the effort is well worth the cost.
The organization · of a Masonic Club Alumni Association was completed during the past year arid will, we are sure, prove to be of great
value to both the Alumni and the Club House.
The financial condition is reflected by the report of Brother Reynold
E. Blight, certified public accountant, which is attached hereto and made
a part hereof.
With respect to the budget for the coming year, our estimate aggregates $7,974.29.
Our Club building occupies practically all of our ground space, the
east side being about two feet from the property line. There is a large
vacant lot adjoining us on the east, and as there. are no set back restrictions, we deemed it wise to protect our building by purchasing part of the
lot. In January we bought 22.8 feet, using money on hand in the Building
Fund, which was contributed by the brethren of the jurisdiction for that
purpose.
Each year sees an increase in the enrollment in the university and
likewise an even greater increase in the use of, and interest in, the Club
House. We recommend that such provision be made for support and maintenance during the year 1936-37 as will be adequate for that purpose.
IRA F. THOMPSON, Chairmati.

Adopted as read except that portion requesting funds, which
was referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

Herewith your Committee on Returns pres'ents its annual report.
We find there is a net loss of members. The roll of membership as
of July 31, 1936, being only 127,728. We find the number suspended' for
non-payment of dues greater than the increase of membership by degrees.
But we are not as those without hope.
·
There has been an increasing number of candidates, and there has
been an increase in the number of those restored to membership. Great
as it is there has been a decrease in the numbr of those suspended for
non-pay~ent of dues, and a decrease in the number of those having their
dues remitted. The Grim Reaper takes a yearly increasing toll.
While we cannot say the report is good, it is not so bad as some of
the preceding years. We may say of it as was said of the Curate's egg, it
was good in parts. The gains are increasing, and the losses are diminishing.
Let us hope that in the desire for an increase in the number of candidates there will be no sacrifice of quality.

August 1, 1935 to July 31, 1936

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the M .'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Comm_ittee on Grievances begs leave to report in part as follows:
During the course of the current Masonic year there have been referred to this committee thirty-two trial records arising in Lodges of this
jurisdiction and one petition for reinstatement.
Your committee desires to congratulate the craft, the officers of the
various Lodges in which trials have been held, and the commissioners who
have served in such trials, upon the sincere and earnest manner in which
their several duties have been performed. In a high majority of the cases
handled, · the proceedings appear regular in all respects-or, at least, such
errors as may have occurred were of such trivial importance as not to
affect the disposition of the matter or require special attention by this
Grand Lodge. In some instances, however, your committee finds itself
unable to agree with the dispositions made, and these will be reported to
you separately with our recommendations thereon.
There ar e a few general matters upon ~hich brief comment may be
of value to the craft.
Sections 192 and 192a of our Constitution providing for automatic
expulsion in cases of conviction of a felony, followed by imprisonment
therefor, and where the accused fails to demand a trial, have again been
found most useful in the saving of time, energy and expense. Your committee is confirmed in the view that the . provisions of these two sections
are, at the same time, entirely fair and just to the accused. The procedure
prescribed by these sections should be used whenever the circumstances
are such as to permit of the automatic expulsion proceeding. In one case
covered by this report, the proceedings could well have been under Section
192. In that case, however, formal charges were filed based upon a record
of conviction in the state court, followed by imprisonment. The cause very
properly resulted in expulsion. However, the holding of a meeting for the
election of trial commissioners and the trial thereafter before the commis-

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sioners could welt have been avoided if the proceedings had been brought
under Section 192, as the circumstances permitted.
With respect to the matter of setting forth charges in an accusation,
attention should again be called to the fact that a specification should plead
the commission of the offense and not merely that the accused has been
indicted therefor or has been tried or convicted. It is the commission of
an offense which constitutes unmasonic conduct and not the mere fact that
the accused may have been tried or convicted.
.
Likwise, attention should be called to the fact that under our Constitution a separate vote is required on the guilt or innocence of the accused
under each specification and also a separate vote on the guilt or innocence
of the accused on the general charge of unmasonic conduct. It will not
suffice merely to find the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct without a
vote being taken upon each of the various specifications which appear in
the charges. Nor will it suffice to take a vote upon each of the specifications without a separate vote being taken upon the general charge of
unmasonic conduct.
.
Where vacancies exist in the trial commission at the time of the trial,
same should be filled in the manner provided by the Constitution (Section
200) to the end that a trial commission of the number fixed by vote in
the Lodge may pass upon the charges.
.
Your committee would respectfully recommend that a Master, m
whose Lodge a trial is about to be had, should im.me?iately fa~iliarize
himself with Article IV, of Part VI, of our Constitution (Sections 188
to 207); he should then read the excellent "Manual for the Conduct _of
Masonic Trials" by our late Brother Walter Haas, for many years chairman of this committee; and, if the Master is still in doubt as to the proper
course to pursue in any matter of procedure, he should confer with his
inspector, the Grand Secretary, or some member of the <?rieva~ce Co~­
mittee, all of whom witl gladly and promptly lend their assistance m
the matter.
