At the communication of Grand Lodge in 1935 there was referred to
your Committee on Grievances Trial Record No. 845, from Lodi Lodge
N o. 256. Based upon the record as it then existed this committee recommended to Grand Lodge that a finding of not guilty be changed to guilty
and the penalty be fixed at reprimand, which recommendation was adopted.
Shortly after adjournment of Grand Lodge and before the penalty had
been administered certain facts not appearing in the record were called to
the attention of the Grand Master, which led him to make a personal investigation in the matter. As a result, the infliction of the penalty of reprimand
was held in abeyance. We are convinced that a mistake was then made as
to the accused in this case and we offer the following resolution and move
its adoption:
" Resolved: That the action of Grand Lodge at its communication of
1935 finding the accused guilty and fixing the penalty at reprimand, be and
the same is hereby annulled, vacated and set aside."

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances t o whom was referred Trial Record
No. 875 . from San Pedro Lodge No. 332, begs leave to report as follows :
In this matter, the Lodge attempted to proceed under Section 192 of
our Constitution.
Properly authenticated court records in the fi le show that the accused
had pleaded guilty to a charge founded on Section 288 of our Penal Code
and as a result thereof, was sentenced to San Quentin, the date of th~
commitment being December 19, 1934.
These proceedings were commenced on September 7, 1935-tess than
one year after the date of the commitment to San Quentin.
The notice addressed to the accused was not sent to him a t San Quentin,
but was sent to an address in San Pedro, a recital in the certificate of
service being made that this was "his last known place of address." There
is no showing in the record that the accused had been released from San
Quentin at that time ; and the plain presumption is that he was still confined in prison when this notice was mailed. This would appear evident
from the date on which he was committed to prison.
Grand Lodge has several times reversed expulsions based upon proceedings under Section 192 where the record has disclosed that the notice
given to said accused was sent to his business or residence address when
the accused was in fact in prison at the time. We see no alternative but
to follow fo rmer rulings in this respect.
The form which has been prepared for use in proceedings under Section 192 was not employed in this particular case. In the form which was
used, the accused was merely advised that charges, as set forth in the
judgment and conviction in the Superior Court, were on file in the L odge
and that notice was being given to the accused in compliance with Sectio~
192 of the Constitution. The notice did not advise the accused of his right
to demand a trial, nor require h im to elect, within a period .of sixty days,
whether he chose to have a Masonic Trial. In the opinion of your Committee, the notice was clearly insufficient to conform to the requirement'.s

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of Section 192 of our Constitution. For this further reason, we feel . that
these proceedings must be reversed and commenced anew. Since section
192 provides for a summary method of expulsion in the absence of demand for trial by the accused, all proceedings under said section must
strictly conform to the requirements thereof.
We would further recommend to the Craft that in proceedings under
this section, use be made of the forms which have been prepared for that
purpose. We offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
"Be it resolved: That the proceedings herein resulting in expulsion of
the accused, be and the same hereby are reversed and the matter remanded
to San Pedro Lodge No. 332 for further action."
Your Committee to whom was referred trial record No. 883, from
Mount Davidson No. 481, wherein the trial commission, despite the admission of guilt by the accused, and the uncontradicte-d evidence of his
embezzlements, found the accused not guilty of the charge of unmasonic
conduct, find that from the evidence submitted at the trial as shown by the
record clearly justified a judgment of guilty and we therefore offer the
following resolution:
Resolved, that the finding of the trial commission of not guilty on the
specification and not guilty on the charge of unmasonic conduct, be and
each of them is charged to a finding of guilty, and that the penalty be,
and the same hereby is, fixed at expulsion.

2. That the accused was convicted on August 28, 1930, of violation
of the Wright Act at Tehachapi.
·
The Trial Commission voted: On the first specification: Guilty, 8; not
gu(lty, 0. On the second specification : Guilty, 7; not guilty, 1. On the
charge of ~nmasonic conduct: Guilty., 8; not guilty, 0. On the penalty:
For., expulsion: Aye, 7; no, 1.
\First Specification: The evidence on the allegations of th e first specification was conflicting, and the accused claimed that he had lived in Long
Beaqh for one year prior to the presentation of his petition for degrees to
Alta Loma Lodge on June 1, 1931, but he admitted on cross-examination
that he had not been registered as a voter at Long Beach, and that he
had been registered as a voter at Tehachapi. The accused produced no
other witnesses and offered no other evidence in his behalf.
By their vote of guilty on this specification, the ·c ommissioners found
that the accused was a resident of Tehachapi when he presented his petition to Alta Loma Lodge, and that his petition contained misrepresentations as to his residence.
Section 202 of our Constitution provides that the Trial Commissioners
are the sole judges of the facts proven. Here there was a conflict of evidence; the commissioners had all the witnesses before them; saw their
demeanor and manner of testimony; could judge of their sincerity, accuracy and intelligence; and were fully equipped to decide upon the weight of
the evidence, which is ample to sustain their finding.
No rule of appellate procedure is more firmly settled than that the
weight of evidence is for the Court or jury to decide. Where there is any
substantial conflict of evidence, an appellate court will not pass upon its
weight or preponderance. (2 Cal. Jur., 935). The record shows that there
was such a substantial conflict in the present case, and the action of the
Trial Commissioners on this specification sihould be affirmed.
_
Second Specification: The ac<:used objected to the receipt of evidence in
support of the second specification on the ground tihat the alleged offense
therein set forth had occurred before the accused became a Mason, and
hence the Trial Commission had no jurisdiction." The Master did not rule
on this objection other than to say that he would leave everything to the
Commissioners to determine. (Transcript, p. 5) However, this question
had been definitely settled 65 years ago by Grand Master Leonidas E .
Pratt, in 1870, when be said:
"I have been repeatedly asked, Can a Mason be tried for acts committed before his initiation? There has been no adjudication on this
question in this jurisdiction, and it has been a matter of much sharp
controversy, and various decisions in other Grand Lodges. • * • There
are acts not wrong or immoral in themselves, which are still inhibited
by the Masonic obligation. Such an act, committed before initiation,
could never be the subject of investigation; for it is only by virtue of
having been done in violation of the Masonic obligation that it could
be an offense at all ; and how can one violate an obligation before he
has taken it? But those acts which are in themselves wrong or immoral, though committed before initiation, may be afterwards punished." (Proceedings 1870, _p: 307.)
This ruling was affirmed by Grand Lodge in 1871. (Proceedings 1871,
p. 152.)
The record shows that no evidence whatsoever was offered in support
of the second sp.ecification. The record contains a document which may
be·a copy of the conviction referred ·to in that specification ; but the document was not certified,. and does not purporl to be a copy of any certi_fi~d

The Penalty Affirmed: However, conviction upon one specificatidn is

and in view of the fraud practiced by the accused upon our fraternity,
both by word and deed, we believe that the penalty of expulsion should
be affirmed, as it is amply warranted on the merits of the case.
Violations of Rules of Procedure: The record discloses that two important rules of our trial procedure have been disregarded in this case.
The Transcript (pp. 1 and 2) shows that one of the eight commissioners
was absent at the trial, and that the Master then appointed a brother to
fill this vacancy. An objection was made that the vacancy should be
filled by a brother selected by the commissioners. The Master then stated
that he, as Master, was allowed to appoint a commissioner with the approval of the commissioners. He asked alt the commissioners present if
they objected to this particular brother whom he had appointed, sitting
as a commissioner, and was told by the commissioners that they did not
object. (Transcript, p. 2.) While the subsequent approval by alt the
commissioners removed the invalidity of the original appointment of the
aforesaid commissioner, nevertheless the Master violated an elementary
and fundamental rule of our procedure which has existed for many years.
Section 200 of our Constitution says that if
"there shall be vacancies or a vacancy on the commission, the commissioners may, subject to the approval of the Master, choose properly qualified members or a member of the Lodge to act."
· · This means that to fill a vacancy on the Trial Commission, the commissioners first choose some qualified 'brother, and that after such choice
is approved by the Master, the brother so chosen and approved can act
as a commissioner. The Master has absolutely no power or right to make
the choice or selection of any person to fill such a vacancy. He can only
approve or disapprove the choice of commissioners. This rule is clear,
and is now called to the attention of Grand Lodge because other trial
records coming this year before this committee show that similar violations have been committed by other Masters.
The Master of a Masonic Lodge in this jurisdiction, especially in
matters relating to trial procedure, is strictly a constitutional officer, elected
under and by virtue of a Constitution, deriving his powers from it, and
subjected to its limitations. He has no implied powers, inherent or divine.
(Proceedings, Vol. 1, pp. 220-264.)
Some Masters act as if they believe that they had most of the powers
supposed to have been possessed by King Solomon; and by failing to
seek, find and obey the Masonic Law, they run a grave risk of laying
themselves open to the charge of acting in an arbitrary or unconstitutional
manner.
A Master who finds that charges are about to be preferred in his
Lodge against a brother Mason, should at once confer with his district
inspector, with the Grand Secretary, or with some member of the Grievance Committee, all of whom will gladly and promptly advise the Master
as to the rules of law governing the situation.
Appeal by Accused: On November 14, 1935, the accused was tried
by Tehachapi Lodge, found guilty and sentenced to be expelled. On November 26, 1935, the next stated meeting of Tehachapi Lodge was held;

its Master then announced in open Lodge the result of th e trial and the
same was recorded in the Lodge minutes. On Decemb~r 26, 1935, the
Grand Secretary received the trial record .f~om Tehach~p1 Lodge, an~ on
the same day, in accordance with the prov1s1ons of S.ection 207, he notified
Alt;\. Loma Lodge No. 643, to which Lodge the accused belonged, of ~he
resu\t of the trial. On June 9, 1936, the accused ser".ed on the respect.1ve
Mas[s of Tehachapi and Alta Loma Lodges a notice of appeal, statmg
there n that he had had no knowledge o f the finding and sentence of the
Trial Commission until he was informed of the same on May 19, 1936,
by th Secretary of Tehacha~i Lodge. The a~peal .was served _four months
and t irteen days after the time allowed for its filmg had expired. .
While Section 206 provides that "if the sentence be suspe~s1on ~r
expulsion, it shall go into effect at once, and the Secretary shall 1mmed1ately notify the persons suspended or exp~lled a~d. the ~rand Sec~etary
thereof," this provision does not affect the time w1thm which the notice of
appeal must be filed, to-wit: within 30 da~s ~fter the anno_unce~ent of
the result of the trial in open Lodge, that 1s, m the Lodg~ m w~1ch the
trial was had. If Grand Lodge had intended that the aforesaid requirement
of notification to the accused of the result of the trial should affect the
time within which his notice of appeal should be filed, it would have provided that the thirty days' time should run from the· notification to the accused
of the result of the trial and not from the date of the at11n.ouncement of the
result of the trial in open Lodge. This rule of notice on appeal has sto~d
unchanged and unchallenged for more than half a century, and was originally framed by Grand Master W. C. Belcher, wh? was chairman of our
Jurisprudence Committee from 1864, when he retired as Grand Master,
till his death in 1892.
Section 205 provides that after the commissioners have voted, the
Master shall order the meeting re-opened for the entry of those lawfully
entitled to admission and desirous of attending, and that he shall then and
there read the vote of the commissioners. Whether the M aster -did so
re-open the meeting in the present case does not appear from the record;
but the accused, who attended the trial and who was also represented by
an attorney, could under the provisions of Section 205, have ~en_ianded
that the Master then and there tell him the vote of the comm1ss1oners;
and if the Master then refused to do so, the attorney for the accused,
being a Mason, could have attended the stated meeting of Tehachapi Lodge
on November 26 1935, and he would then and there have learned the result
of the trial. The accused would then have had thirty days' time from
November 26, 1935, within which to appeal. If the accused did not learn
of the outcome of the trial until May 19, 1936, this was because of the
negligence and indifference of himself and his representatives. His dilatory
conduct has permitted the action of the Trial Commission to become absolute and final.
It has always been the policy of this committee, however, to decide
appeals on their merits rather than on points of appellate procedure. We
have followed this policy in this case. There is no merit whatsoever in t~e
appeal and the sentence of the Trial Commission should be affirmed. This
jurisdiction will not countenance or excuse fraud.
We would call attention to the following proposition of law:
Notice of an intended appeal to Grand Lodge must be given by the
appellant, in writing, to the Master of the Lodge within w~ich the trial
was had, within thirty days after the Master's announcement m that Lodge
of the result of the trial, and irrespective of whether or not the appellant
has been notified by the Secretary. o f said trial Lodge of the result of
the trial.

Your committee to which was referred Trial Record No. 899 of Oxnard
Lodge No. 341, respectfully reports as follows:
The accused, ]. S., was evidently proceeded against under the provisions of Section 192 of our Constitution providing for automatic expulsion
upon conviction of a felony and receipt by the a·c cused of the notice set
forth therein.
The only pertinent document in this file consists of a certified copy
of a judgment of conviction of a felony from San Mateo County and the
record of the commitment of the accused to Sii n Quentin Prison.
More than a month ago the Grand Secr~tary called the attention of
the Lodge to the defects in the record but to date they have not been
supplied. There is not·hing whatever to show that the accused was notified
by registered mail as required by Section 192 of the Constitution that the
record of conviction against him had been filed in the Lodge and notifying
him that he had sixty days' time in which to elect, in writing, to have a
trial therein on a charge of unmasonic conduct based on the offense of
which he had been convicted. There is nothing in the record to show that
any notice whatever has ever been given to the accused nor is there anything in the record to show what final disposition was made of the case.
The Master and Secretary of the Lodge evidently believe that the mere
filing of a certified copy of the judgment of ·conviction of a felony with
their Lodge and Grand Lodge automatically expels a member. This of
course is incorrect.
This committee has pointed out on innumerable occasions and been
sustained by Grand Lodge that no valid proceedings can be taken against
any member unless he has received the notice to which he is entitled under
our Constitution.
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:

Resolved, That the action of Oxnard Lodge No. 341 in expelling (as we
assume they did) ]. S., th e accused in Trial Record No. 899, be and the
same is hereby reversed and the case remanded to the Lodge for proper
proceedings under Section 192 of our Constitution.

The resolution was adopted.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

The time assigned to us has again arrived when we give brief but
affectionate attention to those who long bore the burden and heat of the
day but, since we last convened, have forever laid down the working tools
of this life. It may be that many here today have not personally known any
of those me~bers who have passed in this brief annual period, nor yet
known of their labors for Masonry. But be it remembered that each one
of those departed has here today many friends who affectionately recall
his life and works. Thus it is most appropriate for all to join in this brief
service that each may the better perform his <luty either to these who have
now left us or for those friends who may drop from our future activities.
That each one here may feel that he has some small part to play in
paying tribute to the worth of those 173 members of this Grand Lodge who
have passed on since the 1935 communication, will all please rise and join
in a few moments of silent prayer out of respect to those who have
departed.
As we turn our thoughts to the memory of these worthy brethren may
those thoughts be of life continued and not of death as the end of all.' May
we recall with the poet Frink that "The Rose Still Grows Beyond the
Wall":
Near a shady wall a rose once grew,
Budded and blossomed in God's free light,
Watered and fed by morning dew,
Shedding its sweetness day and night.
As it grew and blossomea fair and tall,
Slowly rising to loftier height,
It came to a crevice in the wall,
Through which there shone a beam of light.
Onward it crept with added strength,
With never a thought of fear or pride
It followed the light through the crevice-length
And unfolded itself on the other side.
The light, the dew, the broadening view,
Were found the same as they were before;
And it lost itself in beauties new,
Breathing its fragrance more and more.
Shall claim of death cause us to grieve,
And make our courage faint or fall?
Nay, let us faith and hope receive.The rose still grows beyond the wall.

I

)¥hile not so many of the leaders of this Grand Lodge have been
taken from us during the past year, all too many of those faithful workmen
who 111ade good results possible, have been taken away. There will be but
one gfneral eulogy for all, but special mention must be first given to a few
of more prominence and great activity.
The death of Walter Francis Haas on February 16, 1936, was a severe
loss to this Grand Lodge as he had been the Chairman of its Grievance
Committee since 1925. He was born Nov. 12, 1869, in California, Missouri;
came to Los Angeles May 30, 1884, where he finished high school in 1889.
He studied law and was admitted to the practice in 1891, and followed the
practice of that profession with great credit to the profession and to himself until his death. He was initiated in Palestine Lodge No. 351, January
20, 1903, passed January 27th, raised February 17th, 1903, and became its
master in 1910. He received the Scottish Rite degrees in 1911, was decorated with the Court of Honor in 1915, and received the Thirty-Third degree in 1921. He was knighted in Golden West Commandery No. 43 in
November, 1921. With the exception of the years 1912 to 1914, he was continuously a member of the Grievance Committee from 1911 until his death.
He led an active and useful life in Masonry and in his community and received many civil honors at its hands, for he had been City Attorney of
Los Angeles, Monrovia, Sierra Madre and Alhambra. He was respected
and trusted in his every activity. His loss is keenly felt by every one, but
more especially by his many friends in this Grand Lodge.
Another veteran is mourned in the passing of Eli Broch Trago, on
November 15, 1935, who has been one of the Inspectors of this Grand
Lodge continuously since 1908-twenty-seven years of helpful service.
Brother Trago was born in Cisne, Illinois, October 20, 1868, and came to
Santa Ana in 1886, where he resided until his death. He served the County.
of Orange as its County Treasurer from 1930 until his death, being reelected in 1934 without opposition, a recognition to his worth, and a tribute
to the general esteem in which he was held. He was initiated in Santa
Ana Lodge No. 241, on August 29, 1902, was passed September 19, 1902,
and raised October 22, 1902. He became its Master in 1907, and was appointed lrtspector of the lodges of Orange County in 1908. His passing has
been attended by universal expressions of regret in official, private and
fraternal circles, in all of which he was loved and revered. As an Inspector
his counsel was sought and followed.
Another active Grand Lodge official is mourned in the passing on July
1, 1936, of Oscar Lawrence Harris, Assistant Grand Lecturer for the First
District. Brother Harris was a member of Enterprise Lodge No. 70, located
at Yuba City where he was initiated May 5, 1927, passed May 13th and
raised June 2nd, of the same year. He became its Master in 1933, and
since that time has been enthusiastic and efficient in the service he has
rendered to this Grand Lodge. He was also a past officer in the Chapter,
Council and Commandery of the York Rite bodies. We mourn his loss.
Another face long familiar in this Grand body is missed this year. It
is that of Denman Sully Wagstaff, Chairman of the Library Committee
since 1921. He affiliated with Fairmount Lodge No. 435 in 1913, and was
thereafter active in its Councils. He died December 11, 1935; mourned by

While we have thus appropriately paused to pay our respects to our
departed brethren, we can be assured that within the halls of Freemasonry
they learned much concerning that one God in whom they professed trust,
and in the promise of immortality which that profession implied. Thus,
while we continue their labors here, may we not expect them to continue
their growth in the truth upon another plane? May not the parting be
appropriately expressed in these lines:

My Friend Lives On
I am bidding good-bye to my friend at the dock.
With a shake of his hand in a lingering grip,
I bespeak a God-speed and enjoyable trip;
Every movement I watch as he climbs to the ship.
Standing there among strangers I trouble not of,
Is the one I adore and devotedly love,
With a face so agreeably beaming with light,
And impressing on me an indelible sight.
Tlien I stand on the pier smiling back at my friend.
As the ship that is bearing him steams out to sea,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

I'm aware that his voice would not carry to me,
Though my eyes still behold him affectionately.
As the hull of the vessel sinks out of my sight
I can scan with my eyes-and with all of my mightBut for proof that he's there I am forced to invoke
The fast vanishing evidence, only that smoke.
I no longer can touch him nor hear his voice.
I no longer can .see him in person one jot,
I no longer can meet him in places we sought,
But I know his existence has not come to naught.
While his journeys may be to the places I know,
Or they may take him places I hanker to go,
Yet wherever that vessel be carrying him
Our communion together has no interim.
It is thus I perceive in the presence of death.
Then no more can I clasp my dear friend by the hand
Nor imagine his travels on sea and on land
Any more than can he join our usual band.
May not he be pursuing the pathway he chose,
With a yearning to tell all the things that he knows
Just the same as I long to reveal unto him,
What I'm dreaming of here, be it real or a whim.
I rejoice in the thought that my friend still lives on.
Thus I may not bridge over the chasm between,
To his new ~tate of consciousness here all unseen,
Since my friend carries on into regions serene;
And where his soul may rise to a spiritual plane,
The while my self and senses still earthly remain,
Until I span the chasm with spirit new found,
He will travel ahead by his body unbound.

May we remember and be comforted by these words of that eminent
patron of Freemasonry, St. John, the Evangelist:

I. John, 3:
1. Behold what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us,
that we should be called the sons of God ! therefore the world
knoweth us not, be.cause it knew him not.
2. Beloved, now are we the sons of God; and it doth not yet appear
what we shall be; but we know that, when he shall appear, we
shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
3. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself,
even as he is pure.

Eulogy
By Lloyd E. Wilson.
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of Grand Lodge:
It is entirely appropriate that there should be a Memorial Service
for.the departed breth~en at the annual communication of a great fraternity
which demands of all its members a confession of their belief in God and
which teaches the immortality of the soul. Because of our steadfast ~elief
in these fundamental principles, we approach this Memorial Service not
as those who weep and mourn but rather as those who rejoice that these
our brethren, who have gone the way which no man may avoid have don '
so with faith and hope and that they now are happy in th:ir Father'~
house, "where God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes-where there
shall ~e neither ~ourning no~ weeping, for the former things are passed
away. If there is any mourning on such an occasion as this, we weep as
men who weep for themselves, because in times past, as we have faced the
death of our friends, our faith in God and our belief in the immortality of
the soul have been shaken, and we have not always rebounded with the
strength of soul and conviction of the mind that would leave us facin
our own inevitable end with the faith and hope that all Masons should ha g
as they look toward "that undiscovered country from whose bourne :;
traveler returns."
We c~me, therefore, not only to honor our departed members, but
to re-examine ourselves, because not only have they gone into the Unseen
World, but we too have a rendevous with death and will disappear.
. The age-old question: "If a man die, shall he live again?" is still
without a conclusive answer in terms of positive proof and as men h
f d h" . .
,
ave
~ce t 1~ 1~timate problem they have tried many solutions. Some have
simply d1sm1ssed the whole matter by saying, "death is the end f II
r£ ,, S
h
b
o a
.1 e.
ome ave een nonchalant and have put on the attitude of taking
it all for granted; others have tried what they choose to call the common
s.ense attitude. and have said: "What must be, must be," and that what
hes beyond, hes beyond-that it will take care of itself and whatever it
~s, we can't change it. Others have said: "We don't know anything about
it, ~nd "".e can't know anything about it, and since we can't, one world at
~ time i_s enough for me." Others have believed in God and in the
immortality of the soul because in all ages and in all places men have had
the same q~estioning and the same longing for eternal life and they have
felt that this call of the finite to the infinite would not go unanswered b
a just and merciful God.
Y
M?st of our difficulty, my brethren, lies in the imagination rather than
.
m the intellect. We can't picture immortality-we can't build for ourselves
a picture in which all of the parts fit perfectly. Because we disappear into
~he u~se~n and ca.n not visualize that which lies beyond, we find difficulty
in believing anything. The trouble is in our habit of seeing only with the
eye: "Seeing is ?elieving" we say, and what we can't see we can't believe.
This effort to. picture somet~ing in order that we may believe something
~as resulted in such fantastic conceptions of the hereafter that we are
h~ely to throw the whole thing overboard, and if we as Masons were to do
this there would be no occasion for a Memorial Service for these, our

189

brethren, who have gone "to that blissful lodge which no time can close."
I want to suggest that the fact is that since immortal life is an unseen
world, as Dr. Harry Emerson Fosdick has pointed out, the first step in
understanding it is to realize that we now live in an unseen world. "We
endure as seeing Him who is invisible." There should be no real difficulty
here when we stop to consider the reality of the invisible. We, ourselves,
are invisible. Our bodies, it is true, are visible and easily seen, but our
personalities, our powers of intellect, whatever genius we have, and our
capacity for brotherly love and affection are all invisible. The effects and
the results of these are seen, but we ourselves are unseen. Again the
creative powers of love, of the mind, of the will and of right motivation are
invisible and only the results are seen. The hope, the vision, the skill, the
real force that is back of the results are all visible. Again ideas with all
of their tremendous power are invisible. The results may be seen with
the eye. An idea, plus canvas, plus paint-and we have a Madonna! An
idea, plus paper, plus ink-and we have a symphony! An idea, plus marble,
plus a chisel-and we have a great statue! These results are all visible,
but the real force-the creative idea back of it all-the vision which saw it
in the mind's eye-all these are invisible!
Again, hope is invisible! No man ever saw it, but no man ever lived
long or effectively without it. It is the silver lining in the cloud, it is the
rainbow in the storm, and in the hour of deepest trouble hope sustains and
leads us on. No man ever saw love-love of ho~e, love of family, love of
fellows, love of God, but no man ever lived well without it. And so it is
with hope, with faith and with love-with all the grander, finer things of
life. They are all invisible, but they are the realest things in all the world;
they are lasting, enduring-not only from generation to generation, but
from age to age; in all times and places they are the real elements which
drive us forward, which make us what we are and which make life real
and livable to us.
And so again "we endure as seeing Him who is invisible," and just as
science does not stop with the visible but always has something out beyond
which is the final mathematical relation of the universe-something which
is unseen but very real, so do we who have faith in God "understand that
worlds have been framed by the word of God so that that which is seen
hath not been made out of things which do appear" and the real worldthe invisible world-becomes very real to us, "while we look not upon the
things which are seen but upon the things which a.re not seen, for the
things which are seen are but temporal, while the things which are not
seen are eternal."
And thus in this world, in the midst of much of which the eye may
behold, we really live in the unseen, invisible part of it, and it is there that
we live and move and have our being, and when we go, and when our
friends go into the invisible, they go to "that house not made with hands,
eternal in the Heavens," trustingly, hopefully, perfectly in proportion as
they have lived here in the unseen world. These, our brethren have passed
away, men who in their lifetime as Masons exemplified in their lives the
finest teachings of this noble brotherhood, who lived their profession of
brotherly love, relief and truth and who are not only missed in this
gathering today but whose absence makes it seem imperfect, We shall
delight to remember them over the years in a score of ways, even though
they have gone on into that invisible world to form another golden link
in the chain which binds us forever to the unseen world, where all who
have acted by the plumb, meet upon the level to part no more.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as follows:
As reported in previous submissions, one of the worst offenders against
the sovereign jurisdiction of our California Grand Lodge has been the
Mexican "Supremo Gran Oriente del Rito Nacional Mejicano" of Mexico
City. It hel~ a chartered. group of twenty-one Lodges and chapters composed exclusively of Mexican men and women in California. Adverse conditions, however, reduced this number to negligibility and for a time we
thought ourselves free of this incubus.
. However, now we find with restored prosperity and as a result of
having re.tained. intact t~~ nuclus of these inert Lodges that many of them
ha~e again revived activity although only spasmodic and casually. It is
cla1m~d n?.w that there are again twenty Lodges in existence in California
of this Rite, but your committee has reason to doubt the existence or
·
activity of this number of organizations.
.we find that during the past year the Grand Lodge of this Rito
Nac1onal ':"~s rent by a quarrel which resulted in one faction withdrawing
and organizing a separate supreme body calling itself the "Muy Respectabl~ Benemerito Gran Logia. Rito Nacional Mejicano" and elected one Jorge
Villada as Grand Master with headquarters at No. 47 Avenida Francisco y
Mader~ in ~exico Cit~. T·his. faction appointed Rafael Ulloa Grand Deputy
for California. a.nd he 1.mme.d1ately . began activity in attempting to revivify
the few re.maining Cahforn1a Mexican Lodges. He did succeed in getting
the following Lodges chartered by his group:

While the disorganization and decay of the Mexican Lodges was going
on it seems that a Mexican Grand Lodge was organized in the city of
Laredo, Texas. This was formed of three Mexican Lodges which had been
operative in the Texas city. They adopted -the name of "Gran Logia Mejicano del Estados de Texas del Rito Escoses Antiguo Y Accepto." This
Grand Lodge rapidly organized in various parts of Texas, a.nd through the
kindness of Most Worshipful Jewel P. Lightfoot, Past Grand Master of
the Grand Lodge of Texas, we are given the information that this Clandestine Texas Grand Lodge now numbers two thousand members distributed
over thirty subordinate Lodges. This clandestine outfit sent an organizer
here named Mateo F. Flores and he found groups of Mexican Masons who
had formerly belonged to four Mexican subordinate Lodges of the "Grand
Lodge Benito Juarez" of Torreon, Coahuilla, which were known as:
Nirvana No. 8, being the last one; Hiram No. 45, San Bernardino;
Caballeros de Oriente No. 41, San Pedro; Minerva No. 30, Los Angeles.
This organizer succeeded in organizing and chartering this group of
unorganized Mexican pseudo Masons in two Lodges in the south, Dante
No. 34, meeting at 764 Amethyst Street, Los Angeles, and Caballeros de
Occidente No. 6, P. 0. Box 737, Fresno, Calif.; and in the north in the
Bay District, Portola No. 29 with fourteen members and chartered January
10, 1936, and meeting at 57 Rich Street, Ferman Bernal, Master. They
have other Lodges in the state but we have not contacted them.
We are informed through the careful survey and e~orts of our brother,
Orla A. Pratt, that there are no Lodges of this Texas Grand Lodge formed
or operating in the Imperial Valley or in San Diego County. It seems that
some of the Mexican Masons who formerly met under authority of the
Rito Nacional have joined a Grand Lodge organized in the northern district
of Baja, Calif., and this Grand Lodge meets in Tijuana and owes allegiance
to the Grand Lodge "Valle de Mejico."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We have perhaps gone with greater particularity than was necessary
into the matter of these Mexican irregular organizations, but we felt it
worth while to review the situation clearly at this time as we expect important developments in the near future. They seem to have the impression
that by forcing the maintenance of an organization in California that they
can ultimately coerce our Grand Lodge into extending recognition to them.
They will continue to follow this policy until they are thoroughly disillusioned as were the leaders of t·he Grand L odge Benito Juarez. There is
a circumstance which is working for the continuance of these Mexican
clandestine organizations in California and it is this: When the leaders of
these irregular Lodges fail to get recognition here, they go back to Mexico,
even temporarily, and join a Mexican Lodge which holds recognition of
the Scottish Rite of Mexico and once a member of such a Lodge they
immediately apply for and take and· receive the Scottish Rite degrees which
enables them to come back to California and American cities and visit regular Scottish Rite bodies here, and so they are immediately thrown into
fraternal intercourse with regular California Masons. This happens repeatedly. in San Diego, in the cities of Imperial County and in Los Angeles.
Mexican Masons who could not visit a Blue Lodge in either of these cities
are able to visit the Scottish Rite bodies and to there fraternize with the
Masons with whom they could hold no converse in the Blue Lodges. Some
remedy should be found for this.
Filipino Organizations
The situation with respect to the three Filipino Grand bodies, ".Caballeros de Dimas-Alang," "Gran Oriente Filipino" and "Legionarios de!
Trabajo," remains about the same. We are informed that the Dimas Alang
has moved its headquarters from 839 Kearny Street, San Francisco, to
26 Weller Street, Los Angeles.
There seems to be more activity in Filipino Lodges at the present
time around the city of Los Angeles and in fact in' southern California
generally. There is .o ne in El Centro and perhaps another at Calexico.
Brother Orla A. Pratt, member of our committee, discovered that their
Rite resembles the ceremony of the Scotti.sh Rite, that it consists of thirtythree degrees, including of course the first three Craft degrees. In San
Diego County the Dimas Alang has four lodges, three of these being in
San Diego and one in Escondido. Their office is said to be at times at 641
Sixth Avenue, San Diego.
The "Gran Oriente Filipino" has at least one and possibly three
Lodges in San Diego County, two of which we think are in San Diego
city. We have endeavored diligently to get more information regarding
these Filipino Masonic organizations, but the task is extremely difficult.
For the most part the members are suspicious. Many times the same individual is known by several names, one which he uses among his fraternal
associates, another which he may use in business or where he is employed
and a third ·for his social contacts. We feel, however, that the Filipinos are
devoted to .their fraternal organizations whether Masonic or otherwise and
that while extortion is undoubtedly practiced on their membership it is
not oppressive and is not resented. The members appea r to be very loyal
to their officers, which makes information more difficult to obtain.
In a previous communication we reported that a Lodge had been
formed on the Island of Kauai at Lihue, H awaiian I slands, by the Gran
Oriente Filipino. Brother C. H. Shepherd, Inspector of the 102nd Masonic
District at Hilo, was kind enough to investigate the entire situation of
Filipino Masonry there and we have his report that this spurious character
of Masonry is dead in the islands.

Negro Organizations
The situation with respect to fhe negro Lodges, Grand and subordinate, is practically unchanged. The Prince Hall organization of colored
Masons was known as the Most Worshipful Sovereign Grand Lodge of
F. & A. M. has in certain districts consolidated some of their Lodges
notably in the Imperial Valley and this is probably for pecuniary reasons;
generally this Rite is pursuing the even tenor of its way.
We hear very little of Hiram of Tyre Lodges (colored). We reported
last year that the number of their active subordinate Lodges throughout
California was nine and that these were further reduced by internal dis·
sension which resulted in litigation. We do not believe that there are now
more than six subordinate Lodges remaining of this Rite.
Occasionally we hear of negro bodies belonging to an or.g anization
known as "Most Worshipful King Solomon Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted York Masons National Compact." This appears to be a national
organization. The National Grand Master is said to be S. S. Simmons,
955 \V'ashington Place S. W., Atlanta, Georgia; the National Grand Secretary is said to be R. ]. Simmons, 724 East Third Street, Duluth, Minn.
Some of the state Grand officers are said to be John H . Ralls who is the
State Grand Secretary, P. 0. Box 2316, San Francisco, Calif.; Grand General Warden of the state is the Rev. W . S. Woods, 539 York Street Pittsburg, Calif.; Grand Chaplin of the state seems to be the Rev. D.
Knox,
1430 East Adams, Los Angeles, Calif. ; State Grand Treasurer is B. M.
Johnson, P . 0 . Box 911, Corcoran, Calif. We are anxious to continue the
search of Lodges and officers of this organization if it is independent of
the negro organizations which we know to exist in the state.
Co-Masonic Organizations
There seems to be nothing new along the line of co-Masonry, although
we believe their Lodges are active and apparently in better financial condition than last year. We also notice a .g reater feminine curiosity concerning ceremonies and rituals of Masonic Lodges. We have .discovered, for
instance, that in Los Angeles there exists a school for the instruction of
women in the symbology, philosophy, and esoteric meaning of Masonic
Rites and ceremonies. This school was organized and promoted some
twenty years ago by Dr. Harriet L. Henderson, a native of Columbus, Ohio.
She was a great traveler, and in her visit to France she came in contact
with some of the great French occults and Masons, particularly one Dr."
Girard Encausse known also as "Papus." He was the head of the "Martinistes" or "Order of Elus Cohens" founded by Martines de Pasqually.
This organization was sometimes known as the French " Illumines." This
Rite consisted of seven degrees with a capitular one of Rose Croix.
In 1915 she incorporated in California the "Women's Order of Esoteric
Masonry." This corporation carried on its work in the city of Los Angeles
largely and it consisted of personal and class instruction in the meaning
ritual and philosophy of the three Craft degrees of Masonry. W ome~
only are admitted to the classes which are held daily at 1511 Reid Street
?om~times also known as Menlo Avenue. They make no attempt to organize mto Lodges but content themselves with attempting to explain the
deeper significance of the Ritual ; although their objects as stated in their
charter are:
"To establish, promote, maintain, supervise, ·instruct, control, and regulate branch orders, organizations, associations and classes under the
supervision of this corporation."
There is no concealment about their work as there is a significa~t sign
over t~e door of the building at 1511 Reid Street, "Women's Order of
E soteric Masonry."

The co-Masonry which we have in this state is a part of a national
organization called the Order of Human Rights and is a part of an international organization called the Order of Universal Co-Masonry which
admits both men and women. We are informed that in England there are
three main co-Masonic organizations, viz: "The Order of Universal CoMasonry," "The Honorable Fraternity of Ancient, Free Masonry," admitting women but which welcomes men Masons as visitors, and "The Honorable Fraternity of Ancient, Free Masonry" which admits only women
but which allows no men in the Lodge rooms either during degrees or at
other times.
The Intrusion of Clandestine White Masonry
Your committee from time to time is in receipt of information that
other than colored and feminine Masonic bodies are operating in California. ·
We have some reason to believe that an organization known as the Grand
Consistory of Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of the Valley of Boston,
chartered March 31 , 1884, is operating not only in Massachusetts and New
York but we believe has established one or more Lodges in California. We
have no direct evidence of this, but this alleged Scottish Rite body claims
jurisdiction over the Craft degrees and over the entire territory of the
United States of America, its territories and dependencies. Its Grand
Orient is in New York City and the Grand Secretary is Hugh F. Miller,
58 Cedar Road, Medford, Mass. We do know that this organization has
taken up the cudgels for John F. Furniss in Ohio and is undoubtedly backing the attempt of Furniss to maintain a spurious Grand Lodge in Ohio.
Sometime ago there was handed to us from Hollister, Calif., through
the kindness of Brother O'Bannon, a 32° Scottish Rite Patent issued by
an organization known as "The United Supreme Council of 33rd Degree
for the Southern and Western Masonic Jurisdiction of the United Stat~s
of America, Its Territories and Dependencies." It is in blank, is signed
by men with such Anglo-Saxon names as Thomas F. Harper, 33°; Rufus
Williams, 33°; Austin Fitzroy, 33°, Secretary General; G. 0. Williams, 33°,
Sov. Gr. Com.; John L. Gorden, 33°, Lt. Gr. Com. This patent was shown
to a teacher in a junior high school with the request that he inscribe his
· name upon it. The teacher brought it to Brother· O'Bannon. We believe
that this is some clandestine Scottish Rite organization claiming jurisdiction over the first three Craft degrees and probably chartering and working
a number of subordinate Lodges in the state of California. We intend to
pursue this inquiry.
Y-0ur committee has been extremely active throughout the year in
attempting to ferret out the existence of clandestinism in this state. We
are, however, enormously handicapped in our efforts by the fact that it is
impossible or inconvenient for the members of the committee to get together at the communications of Grand Lodge. There is so much to be
discussed, so much to be considered, so many specific plans to be laid and
such great difficulty in effecting this cooperation by mail that we feel that
this committee should be made a permanent committee of Grand Lodge
and mileage provided to and from Grand Lodge for its members.
In any event we feel that clandestinism is not dead in California. On
the contrary, we may now be confronted with the activities of white American Masonic irregular organizations seeking to break into the exclusive
jurisdiction of our Grand Lodge. We would, therefore, respectfully recommend that the Committee on Clandestine Masonry and its work be continued, that an amendment be formulated and adopted at this communication
of Grand Lodge amending Sections 27 and 71 of the Constitution of Grand
Lodge of California so as to .constitute the Committee on Clandestine
Masonry to be a standing Constitutional Committee under the provisions

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of Section 27 and that its members be entitled to their mileage to and from
Grand Lodge under and by virtue of the provisions of Section 71 as
amended.
Fraternally submitted,
WILLIAM A. SCHREIDER,
JOHN ALPERS,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS

Your Committee on By-Laws has reviewed and considered the resolutions of the various Lodges increasing fees, decreasing fees, increasing dues,
·decreasing dues, fixing affiliation fees, decreasing affiliation fees, eliminating affiliation fees, changing time of stated meetings, excepting holidays as
stated meeting nights, and providing for change of meeting place.
We have found these resolutions to be in order; they have been approved by the Grand Master and we recommend their approval by Grand
Lodge.
It is pleasing to note that there ·is now a tendency to increase as well
as to decrease fees and dues, which indicates that our constitutent Lodges
are endeavoring to select a sound financial basis upon which to operate.
The wording of the amendments shows careful reference to the uniform
code of by-laws upon which we commend the Masters and Secretaries of
the Lodges submitting amendments.
We move the adoption of this report approving said amendments.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Control is pleased to submit the annual report of its
activfries during -the Masonk year.
It wishes to call to the attention of the Grand Lodge again the earnest
support and friendly cooperation of the Boards of Relief and the individual Lodges.
It· is recognized that one of the principal objects of the Board of
Control is to serve the Boards of Relief and individual Lodges by furnishing information and advice when desired during the year, and particularly
during Grand Lodge, and it is glad to lend its services in working out
unusual problems which may present themselves. The result has been a
very close understanding between the Board of Control Boards of Relief
and Lodges. This has been generally beneficial and h;s also resulted in
financial saving to the Grand Lodge of California.

Grand Lodge Meeting
During this Grand Lodge session the usual annual conference was held
by the Board of Control and the representatives of the various Boards of
Relief and Employment. It was most enthusiastic and educational.
Various important matters for the benefit of Boards of Relief and
Employment were discussed freely by' those present. ·It appeared to be the
consensus of opinion that much had been gained by thi·s conferen~e.
Boards of Relief
During the year your Board of Control has had for consideration the
requests of certain Lodges that they be permitted to withdrawn from the
local Board of Relief. Such requests come to this' board under Section 83
of the Constitution. We shall not here discuss the specific cases but
merely the principle involved.
·
Whether a Lodge is within or without the same city limits; whether
there may be Lodges in two adjacent cities where no boundary lines may
easily appear is not so much the question. There is mutual interest in the
common welfare of the fraternity in a given area to be con~idered. If a
somewhat detached or remote Lodge decides that it can save money by
not paying per capita tax to a Board of Relief it may not realize Its own
responsibility to its sister Lodges and it may be unaware of the actual
service now being rendered by the Board of Relief in return for the
money paid in.
·
Your Board of Control is convinced that two things should be done in
such instances. First the local Board of Relief should constantly maintain
active contact with all its supporting Lodges, that the officers and members
may know the nature and extent of the Relief and Employment work
being .done, and second that before taking action to withdraw from a
Board of Relief the Lodge should carefully consider its own responsibility
to the other Lodges and Masons in that area and give this equal or greater
weight than the financial obligation involved. Officers and ·past officers
of such a Lodge can properly take an active part in Board of Relief work
and develop a better appreciation of such work and respo_nsib!lity.

You will note that the average cost per placement is lower each succeeding year. Also that the TOTAL cost the last three years is actually
less than in either 1932 or 1933. As the service improves the question is
sometimes asked "Are we becoming too commercial?" The members of the
craft engaged in this splendid work believe that to get a brother a job is
the best possible way to express true fraternalism. The only way to do this
is to have a job for th e man.
Your Board of Control believes that up-to-date business-like methods
must be used in operating our Employment Service. W e do not need to
neglect or lose sight of the fraternal obligations to do this. Employers,
whether Masons or not must be convinced that the Service is the be~t for
them. At this point we want to present some forther figures for your consideration. We offer these figures to show how our results look when measured by the usual commercial yard stick.
In the Annual Statistical Reports for the Employment Service this
question is asked, "If your office made the same charge for jobs as a fee. paying agency, i. e., 10 per cent for all temporary jobs, and 25 per cent of
the first month's salary for all permanent jobs, what would your office have
earned during the past year?" Three of the six offices reported that on this
basis a total gross income of $92,809.68 would have been received. The
total cost of operating these three offices was $15,675.39. These figures
speak for themselves.
Appropriations for Employment
In considering requests for an appropriation of Grand Lodge funds to
assist in the work of the Employment Service your Board of Control has
given thoughtful consideration to the needs of the Masonic community;
the record of expense and placements in previous years; the interest and
activity of the brethren engaged in directing the work and perhaps most of
all have we considered the manner in which proper encouragement and
operation of the Employment Service is actually reducing the demands for
relief. The requests from the six (6) offices this year exceed the amount
appropriated in any previous year. In each case the officers of the Local
Employment Service have appeared before this Board and given substantial reasons for their requests. They have presented their problems frankly
and fairly. In some cases emergencies exist a nd the amount asked is likely
to be less next year. We believe this splendid work of the Employment

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the M.'. W.'. Gra1id Lodge of California:
With reference to the resolution offered by Brother Mallachowitz to
fix the salary of the Grand Secretary at five thousand dollars ($5,000.00)
per annum for all services, your committee is of the opinion that this
amount is not adequate, considering the character and importance of those
services.
In addition to the usual services of the Grand Secretary for Grand
Lodge and as Secretary of the Masonic Homes of California, he has a
.multitude of duties, among which are correspondence with foreign jurisdictions, receiving and entertaining visiting brethren, etc., all of which involves the expenditure of time and money. He is, in fact, the contact man
between this Grand J urisdiction and Masons throughout the world and
therein performs a valua·ble service in gathering information as to conditions and activities of many foreign jurisdictions. The calls upon his time
and energy are numerous and time-consuming. By reason of his definite
location, access to records and data and familiarity with the history and
activities of Grand Lodge, as well as the constituent Lodges, he is a source
of information which is particularly helpful to the Grand Master and other
Grand Officers, as well as to individual brethren. He is almost daily interviewed by members of the jurisdiction as to innumerable questions which
he is able to answer readily, thus economizing the time of many officers
and members.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that the resolution offered by
Brother Mallachowitz be not adopted.

Adopted.

Masonic Club Houses of the University of California at Berkeley and
. Los Angeles
/
Your committee has revie~ed with great interest the re/orts of the
Trustees of the two club houses and has analyzed the statejl1ents of the
public accountants made in connection with these reports. 1As in former
years, we are convinced that both Boards of Trustees are / exercising the
greatest care in the management of these i!)stitutions. Tl)~ continued interest of men of the high type represented by the membership of these
Boards is highly gratifying to ·this Grand Lodge.
The increasing use of the facilities of the clu·b houses and participation
in their attendant activities indicate that the club houses form a very important and worthwhile activity of Grand Lodge and merit our continued
support.
·
·
In reviewing the reports for the past few ·years, we are convinced that
the Trustees of both club houses have cut their expenses to the minimum,
but we feel that during these lean ye.a rs, more stress has been laid on
economy of operation and less emphasis has been placed on making proper
allowances for depreciation. Of course this was largely due to economic
pressure and the necessity of reducirtg expenses in ·Grand Lodge, and not
to lack of foresight on the part of the Trustees.
The budgets for both Club Hous es, as presented, contain provisions
for depreciation, but ·as the furniture in the Club House at Berkeley is
older, it is likely that· the depreciation aHowance will have to · be used for
replacement, while the Trustees at -Los· Angeles will continue their policy
of setting aside depreciation in cash.
In approving these budgets we urge upon the Boards of Trustees and
future Finance Committees of Grand Lodge the importance of making
proper provision for' depreciation, and of setting it aside in cash, or its
equivalent, so that, when necessary, replacements may ·be made without
additional -strain on the finances of Grand Lodge. We, therefore, offer the foHowing resolution and fl10Ve its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $16,000~ 00 be appropriated from the funds
of Grand Lodge for the support of the Masonic Club Houses, $8000.00 to
be paid to the Trustees of . the Masonic Club House at Berkeley · and
$8000,00 to be paid to the Directors of the Masonic Club House at Los
Ang-el es.

Adopted.

·· Your Committee has reviewed ·tlie ·repo.r t of t.he ·Masonic Homes Endowment Board for the year just past, and notes with gratification the

craft our responsibility in the Masonic Homes of California, and the need

Lodge.

Grand Lodge Per Capita
The Constitution pr~vides for the levying of a per capita of SO'c to provide for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various committees. As will
be noted by the Budget, which is being submitted hereafter in this report,
the revenue derived from this source, together with other revenues coming
to Grand Lodge, will not be sufficient to provide for Gr:\nd Lodge activities for this coming year. About $15,000.00 short of providing for these
expenses and activities. Our conclusions on this excess expense is more
fully set out in our report on the Budget. It is probably sufficient to say
now that the money is already in the bank to care for this additional expense. It is there, due to the "calling" of some of the investments of Grand
Lodge which have been accumulated in previous years. The committee believes that it can see, within the reasonably near future, and probably this
coming year, where not only this excess expense can be cared for but some
small additional reserve laid aside, without increasing the per capita levy
on subordinate Lodges. We therefore are not recommending the levying
of any greater per capita assessments than that provided by the Constitution, that is a per capita of SOc.
The Constitution also provides for a per capita levy of SOc for the
Building Fund of the Masonic Homes. In addition to this Building Fund,
and the other revenues coming to the Homes, the Homes Trustees have
recommended the levying of an additional per capita of 75c for the maintenance of our two Homes. Your committee is in accord with this request. This will leave the total per capita levy of Grand Lodge the same
as it has been the past two years. Your committee offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That a per capita levy of 75c per member be levied, and
when paid, shall be paid by the Grand Secretary to the Trustees of the
Homes, for the operation and maintenance expenses of the Homes.

find their financial condition such that they can not pay Grand Lodge dues
has not only decreased, but has been entirely eliminated. One such Lodge,
being Concord Lodge No. 117, is reported by the Grand Secretary to be
delinquent in this year's dues. We are assured by the representative of this

remitted in the very near future. This will make all Lodges up in their dues
to Grand Lodge for the current year. Concord Lodge has paid the $200.00
remaining unpaid on its dues for the year 1933-34.

recommended an appropriation of $150.00 to pay for the portrait of the

recommended for this purpose for many years. In looking over the portraits ~urnished in recent years, your committee is satisfied that a proper

unless proper portraits can be obtained, that Past Grand Masters, as well
as succeeding Grand Masters, will be hesitant to have their portraits
painted. From the best information we have been able to ol:>tain, it wouid
seem that if this appropriation be increased to $250.00, much better, if not
completely satisfactory results, should be obtained.

Budget
In analyzing the report of the Grand Secretary on receipts and disbursements for the· year ending July 31, 1936, your Committee finds that
the income received was approximately that set out in the budget and that
the total disbursements are $1100.00 less than the budget. This is a very
splendid showing. The total expenses for the year exceeded the total income for the year by $9440.00. This is the second year that expenses have
exceeded income, the previous year showing a deficit of $8500.00. In estimating the income and expenses for this coming year it would seem that
there will be a further shortage of approximately $15,000.00, or for three
years, $32,900.00, all of which has been paid out of reserves built up by
Grand Lodge in past years. There can be no question in the m inds of your
committee that the continued incurring of deficits, and thereby the using
up of surpluses, is bad practice and cannot be continued indefinitely. I t
does appear to your committe, however, that the finances of Grand Lodge
are improving and that this is particularly true of the finances of the
Homes. In discussing the Homes affairs with the Trustees, they assure us
that the per capita requirement for the maintenance of the H omes for the
year succeeding this one can be materially decreased. This of course is
based on the conclusion that this coming year will show the same proportion of improvement that the year just closed has made. It would therefore
seem to your Committee that for the year 1937-38 the budget can be
balanced and some amount be added to the reserve and an act ual decrease
in per capita assessment be made to the constituent Lodges.
There are some items in the budget, particularly the it em of relief,
that are difficult to estimate. Consideration, however , must be given to
these items and therefore the amounts set after several of the items herein

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California :
Past Grand Master Hervey, chairman, submitted the following reports:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
matters submitted for its consideration and makes the following reports
thereon :
Correspondence Report
The Grand Master in his annual communication suggested the propriety of having a Correspondence Committee report prepared and pub!is·hed for the information of the brethren. The committee wholeheartedly
joins in that recommendation, and recommends that a correspondence
report be prepared and published, and that the matter of cost to be referred
to the Finance Committee. I move the adoption of the report of the
committee.

Adopted.
Gambling
The Grand ' Master, in a very logical and impressive way, called our
attention to a vice or abuse that has disturbed this grand jurisdiction for
a number of years. It has to do with the matter of gambling by Master
Masons who are attached to or cmi'n ected with or a<:ting for other organizations. The Grand Master has full plenary power over every Lodge in
the state and every Master Mason in the state. These activities, however,
are conducted, or have been conducted, by institutions outside of our Grand
Lodge, institutions in which no man can hold membership unless he is a
Master Mason. There has been no affirmative law in our Constitution
covering the case. Your committee has carefully considered his remarks and
also the resolution introduced by Brothers Harry Carlson, Past Master of
Indian Rock ; Roy H. Parkinson, Past Master of East Bay; John W.
Lawton, Past Master of Hillcrest Lodge, and is of the opinion that this
Grand Lodge should establish as its policy that gambling in the name of
or for the benefit of any Masonic institution or concordant order by Master
Masons is a Masonic offense; and the committee therefore recommends as
the policy of this Grand Lodge that gambling by Master Masons be prohibited in Lodges or on behalf of Masonry or in institutions connected
with Masonry.
Now, brethren, we think you have very wisely adopted a policy for
Grand Lodge.. In order to ca rry that policy into effect it requires legislation amending our Constitution, and the Jurisprudence Committee has
prepared suitable legislation to carry your policy into effect, and it will
present that legislation.

; Adopted.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

223

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

222

Power of Lodge Trustees
The Grand Master reported that two questions had been asked him
concerning the power of boards of trustees of Lodges to receive funds in
trust for certain purposes. I need not read it; you read his message and
you heard it. Under the civil law a Lodge of Masons has no capacity to
act as trustee, and it would be a very unwise policy on the part of Grand
Lodge to consent to members of a Lodge acting for the Lodge as trustee
of an express trust for an individual or any beneficiary other than the
Lodge thereof. It is the recommendation of the committee that the.opinion
of the Grand Master that the Lodges cannot act as trustees of trust funds
be approved.

Adopted.
Eligibility of Bartenders
The Grand Master reported the reply he had made to the Secretary of
a Lodge regarding the eligibility for degrees of two candidates. The first
of these candidates works in a local lunch room where meals are served,
and the other is a bartender on a cross-channel steamer. The Grand
Master's comments on this matter raise the whole liquor question, which
has been a troublesome question in this Grand Lodge for many years.
Prior to the adoption of the eighteenth amendment we had a statute making
a man engaged in the serving of liquors as a bartender or the running of
a saloon ineligible for the degrees. That legislation was repealed after the
passage of the eighteenth amendment, in the disappointed thought that
the United States Government would have more power in regulating liquor
than Masonry had.
After the repeal of the eighteenth amendment the people of this state
turned over the control of the liquor traffic to the Board of Equalization,
and provided that there could be no saloons. If there are no saloons there
are probably no bartenders. We are of the opinion that cocktail lounges
and cocktail bars and other doggeries, no matter how euphonious their
names, are nothing more nor less than saloons, and that the only difference
between the new saloon and the old saloon is that men sometimes find
difficulty in getting a place at the bar because of th~ women customers.
The remarks of the Grand Master were logical and fully in accord
with Masonic policy and principles; but your committe thinks that, in view
of the pending legislation which is to be voted on by the people within
thirty days, that the entire liquor situation in the State of California may
be modified, and the present deplorable situation be remedied to a considerable extent, and the problem presented during the coming year may be
a different problem from that now presented to us. For that reason, it is
the opinion of the committee that legislation in addition to that now on
our statute book on this subject be not passed at this communication of
Grand Lodge.

Adopted.
Physical Qualifications
The East Bay Masters and Wardens Association proposes a resolution
reading:
Resolved, That it is the sense of the Grand Lodge that Section 94 of
the Constitution should be so construed and interpreted that the decision
of the Lodge, made in accordance with the provisfons of said section, as
to the physical sufficiency of a candidate, be allowed to stand.
If this resolution is reduced to its ultimate . terms, it means that a
certain law of the Grand Lodge must be interpreted according to its terms.
The law is very plain. We see no reason why any Grand Master should be
told to interpret the law according to its terms. If we legislate that a

Grand Master should interpret the law as he finds it in the Constitution,
he would probably interpret it as he finds it i~ the Constituti?n.
.
The resolution is directed to the law relative to the physical qualifications of a petitioner. Formerly the law required that a candidate be able
to literally comply with the requirement~ of the degrees. :'-fter ye~rs of
discussion the law was "Changed to a reqmrement of substantial compliance.
After the Master has advised his Lodge of the nature of the physical defe~ts
of a candidate, the Lodge by vote can exerci.se a discretion and d~term~ne
whether or not the candidate can substantially comply. The d1scret10n
vested in the Lodge must be a reasonable discretion. If the Lodge is
unreasonable in the exercise of its discretion, then the Grand Master has
the right and the power, as the final arbiter, to determine whether the discretion vested in the Lodge has been abused.
Finding that there is no need for a change of the law, and that no
good purpose would be served by adoption of the resolution, your committee recommends that it be not adopted.

Adopted.

Date of Annual Elections
Brother Winthrop L. Keen of Loyalton Lodge, and other brethren
from the northeast section of our grand jurisdiction, appeared before your
committee asking the right to hold the stated meeting for the election of
officers in certain Lodges in that area in the month of November instead
of the month of December. They represented that the Lodges are in the
mountains and that travel in December is dangerous, or prohibitive, because
of the snows ; that many of the brethren are virtually snowed in at the time
required by our Constitution for the annual election; that many members
reside at a ·considerable distance from the Lodge and, because of that fact,
are prohibited from attending the annual meeting.
Your committee recommends that the Constitution be amended to
permit Loyalton Lodge, and other Lodges so circumstanced, to hold the
annual meeting in November instead of December.

Adopted, and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Presentation to Retiring Masters
York Lodge No. 423 proposes an amendment to Section 88 prohibiting
the practice of subordinate Lodges presenting retiring Masters with Past
Master's jewels, and as a substitute for such testimonials proposes that
Grand Lodge issue a life membership certificate to each retiring Master.
As a matter of fact, every Past Master is a life member of the Grand ·
Lodge of California so long as he is in good standing in his Lodge. The
same is true of his rank in his own Lodge. We see no purpose or point" in
having such a certificate. Moreover, we are of the opinion that we should
not interfere with Lodges in this matter of jewels. We therefore recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Adopted.

A Shorter Roll Call
At the 1935. annual communication the Grand Secretary proposed a
Constitutional amendment to shorten the roll call at Grand Lodge sessions.
He would amend Section 22 to read as follows :
"Each Lodge represented by a Master, Warden, Past Master or
Representative duly elected shall be entitled to one vote."
The committee believed that there would be no infringement of the
rights and prerogatives of any Lodge by having the brethren get together
and cast their vote through the Master or principal representative present;
that it would save quite a lot of time. We therefore recommend the adoption of this amendment.

Grand Lodge concurred in the report, and the resolution was
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence. On the coming in
of that committee's report, the proposed amendment failed of
adoption.
·
Propriety of Purchase of a Building in Which Liquor Is Sold
The Grand Master in his message stated that he had been asked by
one of the Lodges as to. the propriety of its purchase of a building for a
meeting place, a portion of the building being used for a poolroom and the
sale of liquor being operated in a lawful manner and licensed, and so forth.
The Lodge wanted to know as to the propriety of purchasing the building
under those conditions. The tenant had a lease on it, probably to run for
some time. The Grand Master said that, in his opinion, the propriety of
purchasing a building for a Masonic meeting place under those conditions
was very questionable, and he advised that it be not done. That section of
his message was referred to our committee, and we recommend that the
opinion stated by the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.
Pictures of Past Masters
It seems that at the last communication Grand Lodge authorized the
purchase with Lodge funds of pictures of Past Masters. That authorization was made in a case where the pictures were to be placed in a fireproof
safe to be used in the event the originals were lost. The Grand Master
was asked whether it was now permissible to use Lodge .funds to purchase
the pictures of Past Masters to be hung in the anteroom of the Lodge. He
replied to them that there was no distinction between having them for
safe keeping in the vault and having them for safe keeping in the anteroom
of a Lodge room ; that if it was proper in one case it was proper in the
other. The committee recommends that the opinion of the Grand Master
be approved.

Adopted.

Life Membership· Funds
Brother Charles R. Cooper, Past Master of Presidio Lodge No. 354,
has presented a resolution relating to life membership funds, and Brother
Somers of Military Service Lodge No. 571 has also presented a resolution
on that subject. Both resolutions propose legislation to the end that the
life membership funds should not be perpetual, but 'Could be withdrawn in
whole or in pa,rt by the Lodge for its expenses when it needs funds. In
other words, the proposals are to destroy the requirements now in our law
that life membership funds are perpetual funds and cannot be used for any
purpose except to earn income for the Lodge. The committee is of the
opinion that those funds are not earned by a Lodge at the time the life
membership is taken out, nor are they earned by the Lodge at any time
during the member's life. Those funds are to pay a member's dues. They
do not ordinarily realize to the Lodge an income that is as large as the
dues; there is a loss to the Lodge in dues every year.. That loss is made
up by the fact that the fund is permanent and no part is paid out at the
time of death of a life member. It is not an earned fund; it is earning
money for the Lodge every year and is a trust fund and should not be
dissipated. We recommend that the resolutions be not adopted.

Grand Lodge concurred.
Brother Leo Bruck proposes that Section 87 of the Constitution, beginning with "all investments of funds" to and inclusive of " reputable bank or
banks" be repealed and the following be substituted: "All investments of
funds (except life membership funds, the investment of which is prescribed
by Section 129) by a Lodge shall be through trustees elected by the
Lodge, who shall invest such funds in securities or property to best of
their judgment, with the consent of the Lodge."
The present law requires that the investments be made by deposit in
bank or in securities which are legal investments for savings banks in
California or Hawaii. Brother Bruck proposes that investments of funds
be left to the sound discretion of the trustees of the Lodge. Your committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.
Brother Bruck proposes that Section 129 be repealed-that has to do
with the investment of life membership funds-and substitute the following: "All amounts paid for life membership shall be deposited in some
reputable bank, or invested in first class securities according to the best
judgment of the trustees with the consent of the Lodge, and only the
income thereof shall be used by the Lodge, the original amounts to be
forever kept and maintained as and for a permanent life membership fund."
The committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.

Clandestine Masonry
Brother Schreider of the Committee on Clandestine Masonry proposes
that the Special Committee on Clandestine Masonry be changed to a standing committee, a constitutional committee; and we recommend that as a
matter of policy the committee be made a standing committee and the
matter be referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for legislation. The proposed amendments are as follows:
Sec. 27. The following standing committees shall be appointed by the
Grand Master at each annual communication just before the close, viz.: On
Finances, On Accounts, On Grievances, On Correspondence, on Returns,
On Pay of Members, On Credentials, On Library, On By-Laws, On
Charters, On Clandestine Masonry, On Grand Lodge Week Activities, to
consist of five members each; On General Policy and Purposes, and On
Jurisprudence, to consist of seven members each; the duties of which committees shall continue during the year thereafter, and shall cease at the
close of the next succeeding annual communication.
Sec. 71. The Past Grand Masters, appointed Grand Officers, chairmen
of standing committees, and the members of the Jurisprudence, Policy and
General Purposes, Grievances, Finance, Credentials, Pay of Members,
Charters, Clandestine Masonry and By-Laws Committees shall receive payment for their necessary expenditures for transportation to and from each ,
annual communication of the Grand Lodge, in the same manner as ordered
for the officers or representatives of Lodges; but no Grand Officer, Past
Grand Master, chairman or member of a committee, or officer or representative of a Lodge shall receive such payment in more than one of those
capacities, nor shall he receive it unless he shall have been in attendance at
such communication from the first to the last day thereof, inclusive, unless
excused by the Grand Lodge.

Report adopted, referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence,
by which committee Sections 27 and 71 were recommended to be
amended by adding therein the Committee on Clandestine Masonry, and adopted by unanimous vote.
