around the bay viewing the San Francisco Bay bridges and the 1939
Exposition site. Six hundred feet of 16 m.m. motion pictures were taken
of this trip and prints can be purchased for $25 each, or they may be
rented. Arrangements in either case should be made through the Grand
Secretary's office. It has been suggested that similar pictures of Grand
Lodge Week activities be taken at each subsequent communication of
Grand Lodge under the direction of the activities committee, and a duplicate print to be placed in the archives of Grand Lodge.
The get-together dinner Tuesday night, October 13th, was attended
by 947 brelthren. We feel that we should at this time acknowledge our
special thanks to Past Grand Master Will Fischer for the excellent manner in which he discharged the important duties of toastmaster.
The trip to the Masonic Home at Decoto on Wednesday October 14th
was enjoyed by approximately 800 delegates and friends.' The hundred
automobiles were counted in at the entrance to the Masonic Home 1 of
which 137 were supplied through the courtesy of East Bay brethren, and
to them we extend our hearty appreciation. All enjoyed the delightful
ei:itertainment rendered at the Home through the courtesy of the residents. The arrangements at the Home, including the entertainment, were
made through the courtesy of our genial Superintendent, Brother Frank B.
Hartman.
May the committee on behalf of the Masons and the constituent
Lodges of the East Bay district express regret that, through circumstances
over which none of us had any control, we were not only unable to have
this communication meet in Oakland, but several of the matters which we
had arranged for your entertainment were of necessity cancelled. These
included a dinner for the visiting ladies at the Masonic Club House
University of California at Berkeley, and that splendid Masonic drama'
"Spirit of Hiram," the latter of which was to have been produced through
the courtesy of the Scottish Rite Players of Oakland.
We have attached to this report, which is in duplicate, a copy of all
form letters, circulars and programs. We ask leave to be allowed to file
at a later date a financial report with the Grand Master for his approval
. which shall contain a detailed statement of receipts and disbursements. At

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
To the M.". W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
decisions of the Grand Master as reported in his Message and finds · that
all of said decisions are in accordance with the law and recommends
their approval with the exception of decisions IV, X, XV, upon which
separate reports will be made.

Report adopted.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to whom was referred Decision
No. IV of the Most Worshipful Grand Master respectfully report as
follows:
This decision refers to the power of a Lodge or Trustees of a Lodge
to receive funds and securities in trust for certain purposes. While the
provisions of Section 88 of our Constitution clearly contemplate the
acceptance of funds "in trust for any proper specific purpose," we approve
the decision of the Most Worshipful Grand Master that the purposes of
the proposed trusts referred to in the ruling are not such as are intended
by the provision above quoted.
We, therefore, recommend that the decision be approved.

Report adopted.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which was referred decisions
of the Grand Master set forth in his Message, reports as follows upon
Decision No. X:
Said decision is approved upon the assumption that the authority
exercised by the trustees is within the scope of the powers granted to
the trustees by the standing resolution adopted by the Lodge. Section 87
of the Co1istitution specifically requires that the Lodge must retain control
of its funds and property, and that although title or other authority is
vested in trustees provided for in a standing resolution, the trustees
nevertheless shall always be under the control of the Lodge and that
investments and reinvestments shall be subject to direction of the Lodge.
The section further provides that no money shall be drawn without ex-

235

press consent of the Lodge appearing in its records, and the only authorization for withdrawal of funds by action or through the officers of the
trustees must therefore derive its authority from affirmative action of
the Lodge, either specific or general.

Adopted.
Regarding Decision No. 15, without concurring entirely with the
reasoning set forth by the Grand Master in the first paragraph of his
ruling as reported therein, your committee believes that the conclusion
announced in the second paragraph thereof is proper and should be
affirmed. We therefore recommend that the conclusion be approved.

Adopted.
Your committee has carefully considered the proposed resolution to
amend Section 22 of the Constitution, relating to voting in Grand Lodge
and we are of the opinion that any change in this section will involve
various chanegs in the Constitution and we therefore report the matter
back to Grand Lodge for its determination.

The proposed amendment failed of adoption.
There has also been referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence a
proposed amendment to the Constitution relating to gambling enterprises.
We approve the proposed addition to the Constitution, reading as follows,
and recommend its adoption:
Sec. 166A. No Lodge or individual Mason shall, directly or indirectly,
give or attempt to give aid or countenance of Masonry to any raffle, lottery
or other gambling enterprise forbidden' by law. Nor shall any Mason
participate in the conduct or promotion of any such raffle, lottery or other
gambling enterprise conducted in the name of, or directly or indirectly
for the pecuniary benefit of, any Lodge or of any organization a prerequisite of membership wherein is that the persGn be a Master Mason. No
Lodge shall accept any of the proceeds or profits of any raffle, lottery or
other gambling enterprise.
Whenever it shall appear to the Grand Master that any such raffle,
lottery or other gambling enterprise is being conducted, or is about to be
conducted in the name of, or for the benefit of any Lodge, or of any
organization a prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a
Master Mason, or in the name of or for the benefit of 'any committee or
subordinate body thereof, he shall cause to be personally served on any
Mason appearing to be engaged in the conduct or promotion of said enterprise, a notice requiring said Mason immediately to abandon and discontinue his participation in said enterprise. If the Grand Master shall find
after investigation and hearing, of which the accused shall have due and
timely notice and at which he shall be entitled to appear, that such Mason
has engaged in such enterprise and has failed to abandon and discontinue
his participation therein after having received the aforementioned notice
to desist, the Grand Master shall suspend such Mason from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry. Each such suspension, together with the
reasons therefor, shall be presented to Grand Lodge at its next succeeding
annual communication, and shall remain in full force and effect unless
otherwise ordered by Grand Lodge.

The report was adopted and Section 166A was added · to the
Constitution by unanimous vote.
There has also been referred to your committee the resolution of
Loyalton Lodge No. 359, to amend Section 135 of the Constitution so as to
permit Lodges in the mountain sections to hold their annual election of
officers in November. We can readily understand that climatic conditions

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

236

237

'PROCEEDINGS OF THE

in December in some parts of the jurisdiction render it practically impossible
to hold Lodge meetings in December, but it will be impossible to make
exceptions in behalf of any particular Lodge. We therefore recommend that
Section 135 of the Constitution be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 135. The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secre:tary of each
Lodge shall be elected annually, by ballot, at the stated meeting next
preceding the anniversary of Saint John the Evangelist, and a majority of
the votes cast shall be necessary to ·elect. Provided, however, that a Lodge
may by a standing resol.ution adopted after notice in writing to every
member of the Lodge, approved by the Grand Master, and effective six
months subsequent to such approval, provide that the annual election
may be had at the stated meeting in November each year. (1936.) They
shall be installed as soon as practicable thereafter, and shall hold their
respective offices until their successors shall have been duly elected and
installed. Installations may be either public or private.

Adopted, and Section 135 was amended as set out above by
unanimous vote.
There was submitted to this committee the resolution of Silver Gate
Lodge No. 296, providing that the form of <limit be revised to include

the respective dates, name and place, all upon the face of the <limit. We
see no objection to this proposed change and recommend that the words
above set out be included in F orms 243 and 244, relating to certificates of
withdrawal.

The report was adopted.

The annual election of officers was now held, the result being
as follows :
The R.'. W.'. Rollie W. Miller of Sunset Lodge No. 352 was
elected Grand Master.

was elected Deputy Grand Master.

No. 260 was reelected Grand Treasurer.
rhe V.". W.". John Whicher of King David's Lodge No. 209
was reelected Grand Secretary.

was reelected Grand Lecturer.

ROLLIE WEBSTER MILLER
Grand Ma•ler
1956

In 1807, just one hundred years before the seventieth Grand Master came
to California, his ·great grandfather, John Miller, finding the State of North
Carolina too thickly settled, decided that he would seek his fortune in the new
state of Kentucky. His father, a soldier of the Revolutionary war had passed
away and with his widowed mother left for his new home. He served through
the war of 1812 and was in the ·battle of New Orleans.
Brother Rollie Webster Miller was horn at Smithland, Kentucky, October
17, 1884. His father Rev. J. Sam Miller, a retired Baptist minister is now
living at Los Angeles, in his 87th yea·r . His mother's maiden name was Martha
Z. Hooks, a daughter of James R. Hooks, who came to Kentucky from North
Carolina and was the first Knight Templar in the western part of Kentucky.
Shortly after coming to Los Angeles in 1907, Brother Miller became connected with the Los Angeles College of Osteopathy and later became its
Secretary and General Manager. He now is the oldest special agent in point
of service in California connected with the New England Mutual Life Insurance
Company.
In February, 1911, Rollie Webster Miller petitioned Sunset Lodge No. 352,
F. & A. M. for the degrees of Masonry, which were conferred upon him the
following month. He was initiated March 7, 1911; passed, March 14, 1911, and
made a Master Mason March 31, 1911. His ability was soon recognized by the
members of his Lodge, as it has been in every line of activity in fihich he has
been engaged. The following year he was elected Treasurer of the Lodge, and
so served until 1915, when he was elected Junior Warden. He was Master of
Sunset Lodge in 1918, and in 1923 he was appointed Inspector. Soon after he
recognized the value of the district officers meetings, and those held under his
jurisdiction were pointed out as examples to be followed by other districts of
the State. He was soon known throughout the jurisdiction and we find him
elected Junior Grand Warden in October, 1933. At the next communication
of Grand Lodge he was elected Senior Grand Warden; 1935, Deputy Grand
Master; 1936, Grand Master.
Brother Miller is a member of the Los Angeles 'bodies of the Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite, Al Ma!ikah Temple of the Shrine, South Gate Chapter
R. A. M., and is Past President of the Southern California Past Masters'
Association.
Brother Miller was married in 1917 to Miss Catherine Brown, whose
charm and personality have added to the many deep and lasting friendships,
which this couple have gained.
.
Rollie, as he is known throughout this jurisdiction, has been successful in
his every effort. However that success has been won, as success always is, by
hard work and strict attention to every duty to which he has been assigned. He
has put forth his best efforts and has conscientiously endeavored to maintain
the same degree of efficiency in every assignment, from that of a member of
his first committee to that of Grand Master,

DEVOTIONAL SERVICE

The fear of the Lord maketh a merry heart, and giveth joy, and gladness, and
a long life.
Whoso feareth the Lord, it shall go well with him at the last, and he shall find
favor in the day of his death.
To fear the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: and it was created with the
faithful in the womb.
She hath built an everlasting foundation with men, and she shall continue with
their seed.
To fear the lord is fulness of wisdom, and filleth men with her fruits.
She filleth all their house with things desirable, and the garners with her
increase.
The fear of the Lord is a crown of wisdom, making peace and perfect health
to flourish; both which are the gifts of God: and it enlargeth their rejoicing that love him.
·
Wisdom raineth down skill and knowledge of understanding, and exalteth them
to honour that hold her fast.
The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and· the branches thereof are long life.
The fear of the Lord driveth away sins: and where it is present it turneth
away wrath.
A furious man cannot be justified; for the sway of ·his fury shall be his destruction.
A patient man will bear for a time, and afterward joy shall spring up unto him.
He will hide his words for a time, and the lips of many shall declare his
wisdom.
The parables of knowledge are in the treasures of wisdom: but godliness is
an abomination to a sinner.
If thou desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord shall give her
unto thee.
For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction: and faith and meekness
are his delight.

Conducted by Reynold E. Blight, Acting Grand Chaplain
Bass Solo--"Bless This House" - - - Oliver Jones
The Scripture reading is taken from the first chapter of Ecclesiasticus:
All wisdom cometh from the Lord, and is with him forever.
vYho can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of
eternity?
Who can find out the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the
deep, and wisdom?
.
Wisdom has been created before all things, and the understandmg of prudence
from everlasting.
The word of God most high is the fountain of wisdom; and her ways are
everlasting commandments.
1 0 whom hath the root of wisdom been revealed? and who hath known her
wise counsels?
.
(Under whom hath the knowledge of wisdom been made mamfest? and who
hath understood her great experience?)
There is one wise and greatly to be feared, the Lord sitting upon his throne.
He created her, and saw her, and numbered her, and poured her out upon all
his works.
She is with all flesh, according to his gift, and he hath given her to them that
love him.
The fear of the Lord Is honour, and glory, and gladness, and a crown of
rejoicing.

The Meditation
It is highly appropriate that we open the communication of Grand Lodge
with devotional exercises. That Freemasonry is not a religion but is profoundly
religious is a trite saying, and yet it is significant. When Freemasonry ceases
to be religious it ceases to be Freemasonry. The consistent policy of the United
Grand Lodge of England, that source of Masonic regularity throughout the
world, in refusing recognition to institutions calling themselves Masonic but
which have deleted from the r itual all allusion to the Deity and to spiritual
realities, follow a true, deep instinct. Religion-that is, faith in God and the
authority of moral truth-is the Rock upon which Freemasonry stands secure.
~
Let us therefore, for a brief space, climb the Mount of Meditation. While
we may not hope that our hillside will become a Mount of Transfiguration
we can, at least, pray that it may become a Mount of Vision, that for a time
we may breathe the pure air of the higher altitudes and come back refreshed,
our minds clarified, our hearts purified, by a brief sojourn on the mountain-top.
'The religion of Freemasonry cannot be interpreted in the terms of dogma
and doctrine. Theology, no matter how conventional or orthodox, would be
out of place in this presence. Rather we would express religion as faith, that
unshakable confidence that lies deep in the heart of man, born of profound
intuition, confirmed by experience, the one unique possession of man, that
which differentiates him from the animal creation. Faith is the key that unlocks the riddle of the universe. Faith is the clew that leads us through confusion and defeat to the true significance of life.

of man, and teaching the brotherly life. Its aim is to aid its sons to win a
clearer conception of their duty to God and man, to develop their spiritual
faculties, to refine and exalt their lives in fellowship and service, leaving each
one to add to its profound and simple faith such elaborations and embellishments as may seem to him to be true and beautiful and good, with due respect
for and appreciation of the thought and faith and dream of his Brothers and
Fellows."-(The Religion of Masonry by Joseph Fort Newton, p. 17.)
Whittier, the good Quaker poet, might have been writing a Masonic hymn
when he sang :
0 brother man, fold to thy heart thy brother, .
Where pity dwells, the peace of God Is there;
To worship right1y ·1s to love each other, ·
Each smile a hymn, each kindly deed a prayer.

It is in this spirit that this august assemblage is convened; in this spirit
God grant we pursue our deliberations. In words of holy prayer we invoke
His blessing on this communication. Bright-gleaming over the Master's chair
shines forth the letter "G", which shall splendidly symbolize for us the noble
ideals of our ancient craft: Divinity, justite, kindliness, charity, fraternity,
faith. In Divine fellowship of love and service Freemasonry leads its sons
tu the very footstool of .God. In charity it renders homage to God who is our
Father. This is true religion, through which the sincere and earnest soul is admitted to the Holy of Holies where the light of the mystic Shekinah sheds
its heavenly radiance, the enduring symbol of the presence of Deity.
Again I quote Dr. Newton: "Religions are many, but Religion is one:
to do justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly with God. Toward this great and
simple religion-greater than all sects, yet the basis of each-the world is
now moving. Forms of faith build and unbuild themselves like summer clouds,
but the substance of faith abides. T heologies are but sky-tents where the
soul of man rests for a day or an age in its journey from faith to faith. That
religion which is the fellowsh ip of man with God is to the passing forms of
faith as the sunlight to the clouds, as the sea to the ships that float upon its
bosom. Beyond the clouds is the sky. Below the ships is the sea. The clouds
will turn to rain and -then to mist again, and the ships will pass on out of
sight. But the sky remains, and the sea ebbs and flows, symbols of those deeps
which call to deeps in our fellowship with Him who inhabiteth Eternity. In the
primal sanctuary of the soul, where man is alone with God, faith abides in
uni~y and power."-(The Eternal Christ, by Joseph Fort Newton, p. 79.)

The Invocation
Our Heavhily Father; Great Architect of the Universe:
. Once more 'ii~- ~-eet 'in this accustom'ed place.. ;md . in the ancient adoring
habit of our venerable craft we pause at the beginning. 'o f our deliberations to
ask Thy blessing on our assembling. At this altar of prayer we lift hands of
worship and beseech Thy benediction on our work. We are well aware that
without Thee we cannot please Thee, so we come to Thee as naturally as
flowers turn their faces to the sun, as rivers seek their freedom in the sea,
as little children find comfort in their mother's arms, pleading that Thy Light
shall shine upon us, Thy Love enfold us.
0 Eternal Father, we uphold in the arms of sincere love the guests of
our beloved craft in this jurisdiction. Vouchsafe Thy benediction upon the
aged folks who have sought and found, in the loving protection of our F raternity, sanctuary from the buffetings of an unkind and thoughtless world.
Grant to them a gentle serenity. Fill their lives with peace, and as their paths
dip down into the Valley of the Shadow may they realize the fulfilment of
the promise : at eventide it shall be light. Let there be a "bridge of sunset
into the Eternal Day."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Bless, too, 0 Father-Mother God, the children, who so early in life have
fallen under the shadow of bereavement and have turned to their Father's
Lodge for succor and support. We are happy that we are permitted to dry
the tears of sorrow from baby faces, that we can lift the burdens that would
weigh too crushingly on little shoulders and little hearts, that we may guide the
tottering footsteps until the tiny feet are strong enough to tread life's pathway
alone. Give these little ones, for a time confided to our love and care, health of
body, purity of heart, smiles to brighten the hours, and the glory of the lighted
mind.
Our hearts are very tender, 0 God, as we think of the brethren who have
been called from us since last we met in this place. The vacant places in our
circle of friendship bring a sadness to this hour of meeting; but we rejoice
that Thou didst grant to us the privilege of their companionship, and for all
the happinesses and inspirations of their comradeship, we thank Thee.
We remember with deep affection our brethren of the mystic tie withersoever dispersed around the globe, and bless Thee for that profouud sympathy that
binds us together, men of every race, of every tongue, of every religion, comrades of the divine adventure in search of truth, pilgrims along a dusty highway
travelling towards a Heavenly Jerusalem. We rejoice in the heroic story of
our qrethren of other years who have gone before, men, who through the loug
centuries, have fought valiantly and suffered bravely to redeem mankind from
ignorance, superstition and tyranny. May we, in our time, prove ourselves
worthy of their example. And particularly do we pray for our brethren in
other lands who today are grievously persecuted because of their loyalty to high
ideals of freedom, enlightenment and human progress. Give them courage and a
great hope. Even in the dark hour of their agony may their hearts be illumined
and strengthened with the assurance of ultimate victory, when righteousness
shall triumph over wickedness, liberty over despotism and love over crnelty.
May we now pray for our country. Through the long and troublous years
Thy hand, 0 Lord, hath protected us. We believe we are fulfilling a divine
destiny, that we, under Thy guidance, are working out a noble purpose, and
that through us all nations shall be blessed. In this strangely tangled time,
grant us wisdom. Amid the bafflements and confusions let us not lose sight of
the splendid dream that gleamed in the souls of the Fathers, a vision of a land
where liberty, justice, equality, fraternity, should prevail and peace rest like a
continuing loveliness upon a happy and contented people.
And the peace that we ask for our own land, we ask for the world. 0
Compassionate One, look with mercy upon a race torn with hatreds and conflicts, given up to sordid ambitions and cruel purposes. Confound the machinations of tyrants and taskmasters, who, drunk with arrogance and lustful for
power, would plunge the nations into fratricidal and brutal strife. Defeat their
foul designs and re.move this hideous shadow of threatening war from our
homes and meeting places, and may the spirit of concord and amity animate
the hearts of men. May the time soon come when the consciousness of human
brotherhood shall shine like a glorious radiance in the minds of men, destroying
all suspicions and antagonisms, and wrapping the globe in a realization of
divine familyhood.
Now we turn to the business of the day: we entreat Thee, 0 Great Archi-.
tect of the Universe, grant us guidance that we may legislate wisely. May no
unworthy motive prompt our actions: Let no unkind word pass our lips.
Save us from dissension and controversy, and may the spirit of fraternity and
understanding create and maintain an unruffled harmony in all our gatherings.
May all we do redound to the honor of our beloved craft, to the service of
our fellows, and to the glory of Thy Great Name. Amen

Masonic History
Your Committee on Masonic History, under the direction of Leon 0.
Whitsell, Seniot Grand Warden, has gathered a large amount of important
data and information which will be of priceless use to the Masonic historian
of the future, and which should be . available to the Masons of this generation.
Obviousl:y, this valuable historical matter should be published, and this Grand
Lodge should give consideration to the ways and means necessary to accomplish this result. I recommend the continuance of the Committee on Masonic
History and a proper appropriation for its use.
Masonic Education
For the past twenty years each incumbent Grand Master has endeavored
to stress the need of our brethren and our Lodges for additional information
and education, particularly on the subject of the spirit, purposes, philanthropy,
history and philosophy of Masonry ; but the best method or means of research
and teaching have always been subjects of a widespread diversity of opinion.
Our reports teem with the comments of Grand Masters and of Grand Lodge
committees, but not yet has a satisfactory means been devised to meet what
every one of us recognizes as a real need.
At the beginning of the year I appointed a Committee on Masonic Education and am pleased to report that this committee has made an exhaustive
and careful study of the matter of Masonic Education. It has examined the
~thods heretofore pursued in this jurisdiction, as well as those followed in
other jurisdictions. As the result of their efforts the committee has arrived
at the conclusion that the Lodge system of Masonic education adopted and used
in several sister jurisdictions is better adapted to our purposes than any other.
I have given consideration to the plan as outlined by your Committee on
Education and I am in full accord with its conclusions and commend to your
most careful consideration its report to be hereafter given to this Grand
Lodge.
Visitations
The grand jurisdiction of California embraces a vast territory. Our
southernmost Lodge in California is almost a thousand miles from our northernmost Lodge, while our Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands are at a distance of
two thousand miles. In the brief span of a single year it is impossible for a
Grand Master to meet with all tqe Lodges, or even to meet with all the districts. I have .gi:ven the larger part of my time during the past year .to the
pleasurable and stimulating task of visiting as many of the districts and
Lodges as possible. These visitations in no instance imposed a hardship, and
never for a moment have I begrudged the necessary time or travel to meet
with my brethren. I shall always treasure pleasant memories of the numerous
happy occasions, on all of which I was uniformly received with the respect due
to my high office, and treated with the utmost friendliness and fraternal courtesy. My heart is filled with gratitude to my brethren who have been more
"than kind to me, and I wish that I could have served them and our honorable
cause far more than my strength and mind would permit. I sincerely wish
that the time had permitted an opportunity to visit all the Lodges in the
jurisdiction. My obligations to my brethren and the Lodges are far too numer-

Hawaiian Islands
On the occasion of my visit to the Hawaiian Islands I was accompanied
by Judge Frank M. Smith, chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board, and our reception in the islands was charmingly cordial. The hospitality
of our brethren in this most distant part of our jurisdiction has become proverbial, and the delights of a visit to them has lured many of my predecessors
to make the long journey. Every hour of our stay was gladdened by fraternal
courtesies and an outpouring of friendliness. This visit made a deep and lasting impression on me which will always be a fond and cherished memory.
The progress of the Lodges and the fine Ma,sonic spirit of the membership was
apparent on every side and quickly won my admiration, which I was pleased
to express to them in words of commendation and praise.

Masonic Homes
In my visitations and inspections of our Homes at Decoto and Covina I
have found them to ·be economically managed, with fairness to the residents
therein and also to the craft, and take this opportunity on behalf of the brethren to express appreciation for the loyal and efficient services of the T rust ees
who_are carrying on our most important task, and performing it with great
credit to themselves. I have long had a deep personal interest in all matters
having .to do with these important institutions and I am very grateful and
proud that this Grand Lodge is translating into splendid practice the charitable
tenets of our Institution. The Homes are a visible evidence to every Mason
of the tender solicitude of the craft for the unfortunate and the orphan. I have
no criticism to offer regarding the H omes, or the management. They have
my full commendation. I bespeak your earnest attention to the report which
will be given to you by the Trustees.

Grand Lodge of 'Scotland
The Grand Master was invited to be the guest of the Grand Lodge of
Scotland in November and December, 1936, at its bicentenary celebration
of the organization of that Grand Lodge on December 2d, 1736. Not being
able to leave my -duties for the time required to make the visitation, I had
reluctantly to forego the pleasure and privilege of accepting the invitation. I
appointed Past Grand Master William Rhodes Hervey the representative of
this Grand Lodge to attend the celebration, which duty he assumed and discharged with his usual efficiency and to the credit of Grand Lodge. He was
cordially received and hospitably entertained. One of the interesting features
of the occasion was the installation of the present King of England as Grand
Master Mason of Scotland. Later in the session I shall call for a report from
Brother Hervey.
Masonic Club Houses
The maintenance of the Masonic club houses at the University of California (Berkeley) and at the University of California at Los Angeles is one
of our important activities. On many and frequent occasions I have had the
pleasure to receive the hearty and personal endorsement of that work by many
people. This reflects the able supervision of the respective Board of Trustees
and the prominent place taken by the club houses in the student activities of
the universities. Many students avail themselves of the privileges provided
for them and the daily attendance at both club houses is large. From my personal observation I believe that our cooperation and generous support should
be extended to this worthy enterprise. I feel that I express the thought of the
entire craft when I say in this respect that all of us most certainly have a
splendid opportunity to participate in laying such foundation as will ' instill
into the hearts of the younger generation those great principles of Masonry
which will in a measure lighten the burdens of the splendid youth of our nation
who will be called upon to take up· the tasks where we leave off.
Conference of Grand Masters
Your Grand Master attended the annual conference of Grand Masters in
the city of Washington. and participated. in the important work of this conference. I came away with the feeling that the· conference cements close personal
relations among the Grand Masters of many jurisdictions, which redound to
the benefit of their respective Grand Lodges. While there is no thought of a
general Grand Lodge, many matters relative to uniformity, cooperation, charitable activities and inter-jurisdictional relations are profitably discussed. The
exchange of views and recitals of ,failures and successes were interesting and
helpful.

Masonic Homes Endowment Board
The ~asonic Homes Endow~ent Board is cha rged w.ith an important
duty relating to the Homes and is carrying out the work assigned to them with
diligence and intelligence. The activities of the Board have borne good fruit
~nd a wide field of usefulness, stretching through the years, lies before it. This
1s a work in which I will ever be continually active, and I hope that increasing
numbers of our members will dedicate themselves more fully to this unselfish
and noble task. The Board should continue to have the sincere, whole-hearted
~uppo:t ?f the ~dges. As better condit ions generally prevail throughout the
iunsd1ct1on, the improvement should be reflected in more substantial contributions to this most worthy cause.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Special Committees
At the last communication of Grand Lodge a resolution was adopted directing the Grand Master to appoint a committee to evolve a suitable plan to
put the policy of Grand Lodge relative to subversive activities into effect. I
appointed such a committee consisting of Past Grand Master Benjamin F.
Bledsoe, Past Grand Master George L. Jones and Past Grand Master Randolph V. Whiting.
At the same communication a resolution was adopted for the appointment
of a special committee to investigate the matter of erecting, maintaining and
carrying on twq Masonic hospitals-<>ne in San Francisco and one in Los
Angeles-and the Grand Master was directed to appoint such a committee to
report at this annual communication on the feasibility of establishing such
hospitals or establishing Masonic wards in existing hospitals. Pursuant to
said resolution, I appointed a committee which consists of Past Grand Master
Charles M. Wollenberg, Roy Parkinson and Halcott B. Thomas.
I respectfully ask your thoughtful consideration of the reports of these
committees when the same are brought to your attention during this communication.
Flood Relief
During the devastating floods of last winter I directed the Grand Secretary
to communicate with all the Masonic jurisdictions in the flooded areas, making
inquiry as to their needs for assistance. Returns were received from all of
them to the effect that, while the losses were appalling, no ·Masonic aid was
needed and that the Red Cross Aid would prove sufficient. One jurisdiction,
however, was so sadly stricken that in February I ordered $500 to be sent to
the Masonic Flood Relief Committee at Louisville and a like amount to the
American Red Cross.
Social Security
Since the advent of the Federal Social Security Act, so far as it is applicable to employes' and employers' taxes, also . the excise or unemployment
tax on employers under the Social Security Act, and the further unemployment tax levied by the State of . California, there has been considerable confusion and much doubt has been expressed by Maste.rs and secretaries of our
Lodges regarding liability of the Lodge under the act.
It is my information t.hat the Commissioner of Internal Revenue has
specifically and definitely ruled that M.asonic Lodges are not exempt. In fact,
any Lodge that pays one or more employes comes under the act, and I am
further informed that it has been ruled by the department at Washington,
D. C., that the Grand Lodge and its subordinate Lodges are employers within
'
the meaning of the act.
The brethren of course will realize th~t . it is practically impossible to fully
and completely set out the features of this act in detail here, and the interpretation and rulings thus far given in the many phases already questioned in the
operation of the act, and I merely state th~se general major features which
are applicable; of course having in mind that this matter will no doubt be
taken up in due course for such action as the brethren may deem advisable.
Consolidation of Lodges
During the year El Centro Lodge No. 384 and Oasis Lodge No. 664 presented proceedings for consolidation and, after making an adequate examination
of the matter, it was my opinion that such consolidation was conducive to
the best interest of the two Lodges and to the best interest of Masonry and,
therefore, I gave my approval to such consolidation.

~uring the ye.a r two Lodges applied to me for dispensations to hold special

Insurance
. . J?uri?g the year I was asked whether or not a Lodge could procure public
!tab1hty insurance through a group policy issued in favor of a Master and
Wardens' association and I held that a Master and Wardens' association is
not a proper medium through which such insurance could be placed. I believe,
however, that many of the Lodges should have this type of protection and
therefore respectfully submit that the Grand Secretary be authorized to provide
for group insurance ,through a reputable company.
Masonic Publications
The Grand Lodge of California does not publish or distribute any
magazine or periodical, nor is any such magazine or periodical published
in this jurisdiction under the sponsorship of, or as the official or approved
medium of, this Grand I.edge. There are several so-called Masonic publications issued and distributed in California, and during the year many
complaints have been made to the Grand Master relative to some of these
publications. Such complaints are mostly directed at the methods used
to obtain advertising, and for example I will cite a single instance: A
complaint against a San Francisco magazine was made on the ground that
the solicitor of the publication stated that the funds received for advertising were going to help <lefray the expenses of this Grand Lodge. If such
a statement was made it was a false representation. It is common knowledge that some reputable merchants regard so-called Masonic advertising
as a racket.
I believe that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not bring this
rnatter to the attention of Grand Lodge, because misrepresentations and illadvised acts on . the part of publications denominated by their publi$hers
as "Masonic," or by .the solicito.rs of SU\:h publications, bring discredit ·to
Masonry.
· ·
Constitution of the United States
Each and all of us are indeed proud of the active part the era.ft has played
in celebrating the sesquicentennial of the adoption of the Constitution of the
United States, and of course have been vitally interested in the series of programs inaugurated commencing September 17th, 1937. Our history shows
that through the one hundred and fifty years following the adoption of the Constitution, we of the craft have supported and defended that immortal document
and the priceless heritage handed down to us through the generations.
The Constitution, being the very foundation upon which the superstructure
of our American government is erected, is the bulwark which guarantees to
every citizen his individual liberty.
I deem it fitting and proper that this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
California, and all Lodges within the jurisdiction, should take sorrie active
part in the celebration, and with this in view I am directing that during this
session of this Grand Lodge at least one hour be set aside and devoted to the
purpose of commemorating this .historic event. To the end that all Masons be
given an opportunity to join in this national celebration I suggest that, during

the year, the Lodges of the jurisdiction set aside some day or evening for a
similar purpose.
May we forever be guided by the proclamation of our ~orefat?~rs, expressing the ideals of America, and with the traditional American spmt, keep
forever inviolate the immunities and rights and privileges that have through
these generations constituted the :very soul of our nation. As many of us h~ve
so labored and have come to the Shadow of Life, God grant that as we give
our accounting to those who take up the task we will have given over, untarnished, that which we have striven so hard to retain.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY

Correction of Error
At the last communication of Grand Lodge an error was committed, due
to the confusion and hurry at the end of a busy session, in the adoption of
the resolution relative to the appointment of a standing committee on clandestine Masonry. This resolution proposed an amendment to Section
of the
Constitution which, by inadvertence and mistake, repealed the prov!Slons of
said Section 27, providing for the appointment of a Master and a Warden on
each of the standing committees. I recommend that one of the first acts of
. the present communication be to amend said Section 27 of the Constitution to
restore thereto the provision that at least one Master and one Warden shall
be appointed on each of the standing committees. Prompt action in this matter
is suggested so that the appointment of Masters and :v'fardens to sery~ on
committees may be made forthwith and that such appointees may part1c1pate
in all the business of the committees during this annual communication.

2?.

Conclusion
I am fully cognizant of the fact that any measure of success during the
term that I am just completing is due to the unselfish devotion and sacrifice
of the brethren, and I express my earnest appreciation of the splendid assistance of the Grand Lecturer, and for the aid that he and his associates have
given me, and I am grateful for the opportunity presented through which I
have benefited by the counsel and advice given by Deputy Grand Master James
T. Fraser, Senior Grand Warden Leon 0. Whitsell, and Junior Grand Warden
William H. Waste.
The invaluable aid and assistance of Grand Secretary John Whicher has
immeasurably lightened the duties of your Grand Master, and it is my earnest
prayer that he be spared to us for many years to come and that he may continue
to serve us as he has so ably and earnestly done for many years.
With all of the pleasures I have experienced in the honors that have come
to me I have been ever mindful of the sanctity of the office which you have
conferred upon me, and again acknowledge my sincere appreciation, and I
trust that those who step into this honored place will, throughout their respective
terms, be extended the wonderful help and cordial cooperation that I have
enjoyed the past year.
Cordially and Fraternally,
ROLLIE W. MILLER,
Grand Master.

Registration of Grand Lodge
At the last annual communication the chairman of the Committee on
Clandestine Masonry introduced a resolution (which was adopted ) directing
the Grand Secretary to cause to be registered with the Secretary of State the
full and proper title and designation of our Grand Lodge and its constituent
Lodges, together with its seal and the jewel of the Grand Master as the
insignia of the Grand Lodge: and to register also the square, compass and
the letter G as the insignia of the Lodges, all as provided by chapter 409 of
the statutes of 1933 of California for the registration of names, designations
and insignia of fraternal societies.
The Act provides that "No fraternal society shall be permitted to register
any name or insignia similar to or so nearly resembling another name or
insignia already registered as may be apt to deceive." It further provides
that "Any person who wilfully wears, exhibits or uses for any purpose a
name or insignia registered hereunder, unless he or she shall be entitled to

fraternal society registering the same, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and
upon conviction thereof shall be punished by a fine of not to exceed one
hundred dollars or by imprisonment in the county jail for a period not to exceed
sixty days."
I complied with the terms of the resolution, and hold the receipt of the
Secretary of State, certifying, under date of November 4, 1936, that the "Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State .of California and its subordinate Lodges" .are duly registered.

Report of Auditors
To the Finance Committee, Grand Lodge:
· In accordance with your instructions, we have completed an audit of the
books of account of the Grand Lodge, F . & A. M. of California for the fiscal
year ended July 31, 1937. The following statements are submitted herewith:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's report of cash receipts and disbursementsgeneral fund.
Exhibit B : Grand Secretary's analysis of cash received for the account
of Maso~ic Homes of California.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's report of cash receipts and disbursementsgeneral fund.
Exhibit D : Grand Treasurer's report of assets on hand July 31, 1937.
The scope of our examination included a verification' of total cash funds
received during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1937 from the annual returns
covering the fiscal year 1935-36. Funds received and on hand held in suspense
based upon the annual returns for 1936-37 were not included in our examination. Total receipts due from Lodges as per individual annual returns were
found to be in proof by total number of membership, classification of source
of revenue, and total "amount of gross revenue received, as evidenced by the
recapitulation record of all Lodges. Total of all receipts were found accounted
for and the cash received therefrom deposited in bank ·accounts. Bank accounts
were reconciled and verified, and sufficient examination of detailed vouc;hers
was made as to satisfy ourselves as to the correctness of the accounting.

The following amounts due Grand Lodge are entered in the books and
covered by notes:
(a) Unpaid dues from annual returns:

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodg_e of California:
Again I am privileged to make a report of my activities as Grand Lecturer during the past year. It has been my pleasure to visit many of the Lodges
on different occasions, where I have been courteously received by the officers
and brethren.
I accepted invitations from twenty-nine of the Lodges to install the officers
and attended many meetings of the Masters and Wardens as well as Officers'
Associations. At these meetings I have stressed the necessity of devoting the
time to a study of the Constitution and the Digest of Decisions. Schools of
Instruction are held by the Inspectors to perfect the officers in the ritual and
the time should not be taken from the Association meetings for that purpose,
when a thorough knowledge of the laws and regulations of Grand Lodge is so
vitally necessary to the proper functioning of the Lodges. An officer's position,
and particularly that of Master, is one of dignity, importance and responsibility,
and a wrong decision on his part might easily destroy the peace and harmony
of the Lod!\'e. Ignorance of the laws of Masonry is inexcusable when a little
application to a study of the subject will prepare a Master to meet most any
difficulty as it arises.

Comer Stone Ceremonies
At the request of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, I convened Grand
Lodge ai: the city of Courtland on May 8 and proceeded to the city of Clarksburg, where, with the able assistance of the officers and ·Past Masters of
Franklin Lodge No. 143, I laid the corner stone of the Clarksburg Community
Church.
On May 20 I again convened Grand ;Lodge in the city of Sacramento for
the purpose of laying the corner stone of the C. K. McClatchy High School.
Both affairs were well attended and I acknowledge with deep appreciation the
splendid manner in which the 'committee on arrangements discharged their
duties.
Assistant Grand Lecturers
The Ritual Committee has held five two-day sessions during the past year
for the purpose of studying the Ritual and discussing such matters · as have
been brought before it.
The Assistant Grand Lecturers have held lodges of instruction throughout
the jurisdiction at regular intervals, and i:he attendance records turned in by
the Inspectors show that this work has been passed along to the officers of
the several Lodges. Greater uniformity in the ritual has been the result.
Reports From Inspectors
It has been gratifying to receive the reports from the Inspectorr,. In no
instance has any difficulty of importance been related to me, but on the contrary, these reP<>rts show a healthy and harmonious condition in the Lodges.
This is due in no small measure to the splendid work of the hspectors, Whose
untiring and unselfish devotion to thefr duties have greatly simplified and
lightened the work of the Assistant Grand Lecturers and myselt Working in
their dual capacity of Assistant Grand Masters and Assistant Grand Lecturers,
the Inspectors have met and solved many problems for the Lodges, which
would otherwise have been placed before the Grand Master or Grand Lecturer,
according to their nature. Too much praise cannot be given this fine body of
men, who year after year carry on much of the :burdens and responsibility of

for their important work in this Grand Lodge.

normal conditions an officer so appointed might well continue in his travel to
the East, :but where an appointive officer shows his inabilt iy t o discharge the
duties of . his office, I can see no reasonable excuse for elevating him to the next
higher station and subsequently electing him Master, just to avoid hurting his
feelings, when the harmony and usefulness of his Lodge are at stake. Some
Lodges go even further and make the position of Chief Coach the starting
point which adds another year to the line. In many cases this custom works
out well, but in just as many instances it fails. To make a hard and fast rule,
as some Lodges have done, that any brother who has spent a year in coaching
candidates is entitled to start through the chairs and in the course of seven
or eight years become its Master, may be doing an injury, not only to the
brother in question but also to the Lodge. A man may be a good teacher and
peculiarly fitted to instruct candidates and be not in the least qualified for t he
important position of Master, and by the same token he may be a complete
failure at the job of coaching, yet possess unusual executive ability which would
equip him for the office of Master to the ultimate good of all concerned. This
matter is not, I realize, one to be legislated by Grand Lodge, but must be handled by each Lodge in its own way. I do, however, offer the following suggestion: that the appointive offices from Junior Steward up to and including Junior
Deacon be considered as provipg grounds, and that the Master when filling
these stations, make it clear to the appointees that they fill their offices at his
pleasure, for one year only, so far as he is concerned. N o Master ~hould presume to speak for his successor and every Master has a perfect right to fill
the appointive offices with new faces if he deems it advisable. In this way,
junior officers who have proven they are well qualified to serve the Lodge may
be appointed by the next Master to a higher station, and those who have
failed to show the required ability could be dropped from the line without the
feelings Qf anyone being hurt. I offer this suggestion with a feeling that, if
adopted, the next few years will witness a great improvement in the government of some of our Lodges.

Ritual For Stated Meetings
Numerous requests have been made for a revision of the Ritual for the
conduct of Stated Meetings. The subject has been discussed at the meetings of
the Ritual Committee with the result that the committee feels ·a marked improvement could be made by eliminating some of the needless repetitions and
by simplifying and clarifying the entire procedure. I therefore recommend that
the Ritual for the conduct of Stated Meetings be referred to the Ritual Committee for revision, to be reported on at the communication.
The Apron
So much has been asked about the proper wearing of the apron and so
many requests have 1been made for rulings, that while I do not think it advisable or necessary to make any definite ruling, still ·it is entirely appropriate
that I make mention of the subject in this report.
For many years it has been customary to wear the apron outside the coat
when attending the communications of the Grand Lodge and when on processions. At other times many of the brethren choose to wear it under the coat.
I have learned that in some jurisdictions the apron is worn outside the coat
on all occasions, but so far as I can determine this ruling has never been made
in California. To clarify the situation, let me say that Grand Lodge communications and processions of the Lodges are looked upon as formal in nature
and at such times the apron should be worn outside the coat. No harm is done·
in wearing it beneath the coat at Lodge meetings, if the brethren choose to do
so, and there can be no question but that a brother is properly clothed when it
is thus worn, providing it can be easily seen. This custom has existed for
so long that I am of the opinion Grand Lodge has, by its acceptance, shown
its approval.
Funeral Services
Several Lodges have asked if they could use the old funeral service instead
of the new, giving different reasons for their preference. One Master claimed
authorization from the Inspector of the District. He quoted the Inspector as
saying, "That if the Master liked the old service better than the new, it would
be all right for him to use it." I can only say that the funeral service as now
printed, and distributed through the office of the Grand Secretary, has been
submitted to and approved by this Grand Lodge and that neither the Grand
Lecturer, the Inspectors nor any other person has authority to change it without the consent of Grand Lodge.
Lodge Officers
While I believe that a survey of the officers in the Lodges of this jurisdiction would prove them to be men of integrity and ability, above the average
and well qualified to discharge the duties imposed upon them, I am sorry to
report that many cases have been brought to my attention showing some Masters
to 1be entirely unfitted, both mentally and temperamentally to guide the destinies
of their Lodges. Discord, confusion and inharmony have been the inevitable
result. In all cases trouble could have been avoided if the Masters had consulted the Inspector of the district or had taken the time and pains to refer
to the Book of Constitutions of this Grand Lodge. I do not take issue with the
well established rule of our fraternity, that any member of a Lodge in good
standing is eligible to any office in the Lodge, but I am of the opinion that the
custom has 1been allowed to grow among the Lodges, wherein a brother is
appointed Junior Steward and is permitted to believe that in seven years he

Conclusion
It would be a mark of ingratitude on my part if I were to close this report
without expressing my deep appreciation to the Most W orshipful Grand Master
for his many acts of kindness and cooperation during the ' past year. Working
with him has been a pleasure that I shall not soon forget.
To Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller, the Assistant Grand Lecturers,
the Very W orshipful Grand Secretary, the Inspectors and Lodge officers,
I offer my sincere thanks for their kind and sympathetic assistance, which has
done much to fill the year with pleasant memories•
Respectfully submitted,
LESLIE E.

wOOD,

Grand Lecturer.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ANNUAL ORATION
By WILLIAM B. OGDEN
Grand Orator

Our Heritage
To the M." · W.". Grand Lodge of Califomia:
The office of Grand Orator ought to inspire one to high ideals and lofty
planes. Annually for nearly a century my predecessors have stood on the dais
of Grand Lodge and delivered words of wisdom, hope and inspiration in
tones that stirred their hearers beyond conception. Not all can attain the heights,
not all can paint the lily or tint the sunset sky to a new loveliness-<>ne can
only bring to you such gifts as one possesses; the task is mine, the award is
yours.
It is the duty of the Grand Orator at each Annual Communication to
deliver an address to Grand Lodge upon matters appertaining to the Craft, and
the topic "Our Heritage" has been chosen for the subject of the address today.
Heritage may be defined as something inherited; something handed down
to us by our fathers ; something possessed; or it may be defined as something
cherished not for its intrinsic value but because of whence it came or for some
inherent quality; and it is in the latter sense that ·I propose to discuss it. We
should also bear in mind that we live in America and practice American ·
Masonry. For what then do we, as Americans and as Masons cherish Masonry?
That we might have divergent views as to what constitutes this great heritage
is not difficult to conceive.
Some might cherish Masonry for its antiquity. It is said to have existed
from time immemorial. There are those wh0 refer to the Magi of Egypt as
our Fathers in Masonry; and with some reason, for at a time 3,000 years
before the present era, in a coµntry ·bowed down under idolatry, they worshipped one unseen, omnipotent, omniscient God, admitted their members
by three steps, and taught their precepts by the use of the tools of architects
and builders as symbols. There are others who sincerely :believe, and accordingly
cherish Masopry because its origin and civilization are thought by them to have
been concomitant. Others will tell you of the Ancient Mysteries or the Dionysian Artificers or the Roman Collegia or the Comacine Masters, and each
will sincerely believe that there was the origin of Masonry or the means
whereby it was transmitted to us of today.
But he who cherishes Masonry for its antiquity need not refy upon similarities or myths or legends for the basis of his appreciation. Among the
treasures of the British Museum are sixty-four ancient Masonic manuscripts
the oldest of which is the Regius or Hallowell Manuscript; sometimes called
the former because it was found in the King's Library, and sometimes called
the latter in honor of its discoverer.
This ancient document is written ·by hand on. vellum or parchment and in
a scr.ipt and langu~e as foreign to the eye today as Greek itself, yet, it is
English, and from its form and phraseology those who have made a study of
such things tell us it was written sometime between 1315 and 1390, and by the
document itself we learn that even then Masonry was honored for its antiquity.
Each of you has made the computation and will agree with me that that
was 600 years ago. But can you visualize, can your mind conceive, the time
that has elapsed since the hand of man penned or brushed its pages. Let us
assume the year 1315, then

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

339

It was:·
Two centuries before the Reformation.
Two hundred years before the word "Protestant" took on its present
signification, and Martin Luther was not to see the light of day for 175
years, nor would Columbus petition Queen Isabella for a like period.
One-third of all the land in England belonged to the P ope at Rome, and
The revenue of the Pope from England was greater than that received
by England's King.
Edward II was King of England, and it was but a year after the
Battle of Bannockburn, the greatest defeat ever suffered by English arms.
The Hundred Years' War had not yet started.
Gunpowder had never been used in warfare.
Land transport was by foot and saddle, roads were mere trails and
parties traveled from town to town under protection of armed guards.
Roger Bacon was in prison because he had sought to teach a new
philosophy which he had brought back from his travels in Egypt and India.
Marco Polo had just returned from China and had been excommunicated bec;ause he presumed to teach geometry and the sciences which he
had learned on his travels.
Jacques de Malay, the Grand Master of Knights Templar, had been
shortly before this time, burned at the stake by order of the French King
and at the behest of P ope Clementine.
The Black Death which was to take a toll of more than one-half of
all England, had not yet devastated that fair land.
Chaucer, the first English poet, was not yet born, and Sir John Mandeville, the first English prose writer of note, still lived.
The Magna Carta had been extorted from King John at Runnymede
but a hundred years before, and there were Englishmen still living who
had witnessed the assembling of the first House of Commons.
And the first page to be taken from a printing press would not be
seen by Gutenberg for a century to come.
,
There is the picture I The space of 600 years can be realized only when
measured in progress of events, rather than in time, and by such a picture for
comparison.
It was a land of the high and the low, the rich and the poor, the noble
and the serf, the priest and the illiterate. Yet Masonry lived, and had lived f~r
centuries, for so many centuries, in fact, that even then its past was lost m
tradition and legend, and yet "the attentive ear received the sound from the
instructive tongue and the mysteries of Masonry were safely lodged in the
repository of faithful breasts."
· · Shall we not say, then, that those who cherish Masonry for its antiquity
are somewhat justified in their appreciation? And yet if age alone were all that
Masonry had to offer, would it justify its existence, or our labors in its behalf?
It is at least debatable.
·Then there are others who cherish Masonry for its practice of teaching
by $ymbols. This is probably the most ancient of all methods of instruction
and communication. Macaulay said, "Logicians may reason about abstractions,
•b ut the great mass of men must have images." It is true that the letters we use
in writing and the figures of the accountant are symbols, but they are abstract.
One may be educated, learned, and therefore able to decipher the meaning of
the writer or ascertain the results computed by the accountant, but the uneducated, no matter how intelligent he may be, is unable to gather a single thought
or idea of the' meaning of the writer from the written figure or letter.

340

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Not so, however, with the method of teaching by symbols. Intelligence is all
that method requires, and the degree of intelligence determines only the extent
to which the lesson or philosophical thought may be carried by the recipient.
I may say to you that we stand upon the level. For one ii means simply that
our elevation is equal, but for another it would take hours to express all the
philosophy of life embraced within that symbol. Thus each according to his
capacity participates to the uttermost in the lesson to be taught.
Science teaches that an idea is conveyed seven times more quickly through
the eye than through the ear. A scene once viewed remains indelibly upon the
memory, while a description by word of mouth may quickly fade.
Shall we not say, then, that those who cherish Masonry for its method of
teaching are somewhat justified in their appreciation. Yet there are other
methods and means of teaching, and it may be debated whether they are not
better. Certainly we must seek some other justification for our existence.
Again, there are those of us who cherish Masonry for its teachings. But
every precept of Masonry comes from that Holy Book which is the rule and
guide of our Faith, and no thought is expressed in the teachings of Masonry
which could not be equally well and as appropriately expressed in the chapel,
church, synagogue, mosque, temple, or cathedral of any of the several religious
faiths.
It may be this religious touch to our ceremonies which attracts many of
our members who have no other connection with the Word of God, and if so,
shall we not say that they, too, are somewhat justified in their appreciation of
Masonry 1because of this characteristic? And yet if this alone is to be considered,
I fear it does not justify our existence, for such appreciation could be as well
or better fostered amid the faithful of any religious sect under the direction of
a leadership devoted to the worship of the Great Creator.
Then there are those who cherish Masonry for its accomplishments. I do
not speak of our charities which, although numerous and of considerable magnitude, are 'by Masonic law restricted to our own members and their dependents.
Many, indeed, may question that Masonry has any accomplishment to its credit
aside from these charities, and may greatly deplore the fact that we are not as
an institution in the forefront of great civic movements, or the leader in economic and political propaganda.
By Masonic law, Lodges do not memorialize Congress, nor advocate the
passage of laws, nor the election of men, nor promote a particular religion,
nor prefer one political party above another. Such is not Masonry's method or
means of accomplishing its ends, nor ever has been.
As early as 1723 we find the rule stated in Anderson's reprint of the Old
Constitution, as follows:
"Therefore no private piques or quarrels must be brought within the door
of the Lodge .. . . far less any quarrels about religion, or nations, or state
policy . . . . (for we) are resolved against all politics as what never yet conduced to the welfare of the Lodge, nor ever will." (Art. 6, subd. 2, Anderson's
Old Constitutions, ed. 1723.)
Masonry in America from the earliest days has adhered strictly to this
!aw~this landmark, if you pleas~and no Grand Lodge has departed from
the rule. When, if ever, American Masonry steps out of its character as a society for the promotion of the moral and social virtues, and engages itself in
controversial matters, that day will Masonry enter upon a course fraught with
grave danger.
Perhaps even in this Grand Lodge there have been times when ardent,
faith fut members eager to 'be up and doing have noted with keen regret · that
our Committee on Policy and General Purposes had, conformably to this law,
reported adverseJy on resolutions which to those members seemed admirable in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

341

every respect, resolutions which other organizations were adopting by acclamation and for which they seemed to receive the approbation of all right-thinking
people. But such is not the way in Masonry, and .because it is not the way it
has been done, there must be a reason, and a good reason, or it would be otherwise.
In civil· life, majorities, when aroused are all powerful and intolerant, and
would if permitted utterly crush all opposition; utterly annihilate all opponents. Such is the course of history; such had been the experience of the
Colonists who migrated to America to escape intolerance. So in government we
have written laws, a constitution, and a Bill of Rights, and courts are set up
as an independent arm of government to administer them for the protection of
the rights of the minority.
On the other hand, Masonry is and always ha·s been tolerant of all sincere
beliefs. By that ancient law the opinion of a majority can never by mere force
of majority resolve be made the opinion of the minority. Force cannot change
a belief, nor law control an opinion. Samuel Gompers wisely said: "One fact
stands out in bold relief in the history of men's attempts for betterment. That
is, that when compulsion is used, only resentment is aroused and the end is
not gained. Only through moral suasion and appeal to men's reason can a movement succeed." Hence Masonry has this ancient law for the protection of the
minority, and the belief or opinion of the minority, however small, is, and ought
to be respected and tolerated so long as it does not violate the moral and philosophical tenets of Masonry. Moreover it is conducive of harmony, and "harmony is the strength and support of all societies, especially of ours."
So, if this has been the rule of conduct on the part of Masonry from a tittle
whereof the memory of man runneth not to the contrary, then that l;ule must
be the safe rule and the rule consistent with its character as a moral and philosophical institution. How then does Masonry accomplish its purposes?
Masonry promises nothing to the novitiate; as an institution it obligates
itself to nothing. The obligations of Masons are mutual and reciprocal, ·b ut
the institution nowhere assumes any obligation for or to its members. Masonry
is not socialistic. It is not communistic. It is not collectivistic. It has no feature
of its teachings · or workings that bears any resemblance to a combination of
efforts, or a community of interest in the results. It is merely a manner or way
of life. It is purely personal and individualistic.
There is not a man in this Grand Lodge who has not stated that he freely
and voluntarily, unbiased by friends and uninfluenced by mercenary motives,
offered himself as a candidate for the degrees of Masonry. He himself arrived
at that conclusion. It was his own personal and individual desire that brought
him to the point of petitioning for the degrees.
It is equally true that he petitioned as an individual ; was investigated as an
individual ; was balloted upon and took the several degrees as an individual.
With ea~h degree he received a charge. In those charges were set forth
certain duties he, himself, persona!ly and individually owed to his Creator, to
his country, to his neighbor, and to himself, and it became his duty and he was
obligated to go forth and exemplify in his everyday life those Masonic virtues
which were epitomized in the charges. And if Masonry is highly esteemed in the
community in which he lives and in the circle of his acquaintances, it is because
he, himself, personally and individually has been obedient to the precepts of
Masonry, and if Masonry is ·11ot esteemed in his community or in the circle of
his acquaintances, it is because he, himself, or some other individual Mason
has fallen short of being a true Mason. I ts honor, its reputation and its usefulness are in the hands of the individual Masons of the community. Thus
through the individual does Masonry accomplish its ends, and to the lives and
works of our members must we look to ascertain the accomplishments of
Masonry.

the basis of Masonic teachings.

signal for rebe.llion (p. ~40) ... Freemasonry cannot deny the outstanding

Masons. Thes~ Co~gresse~ were imbued with the purest Masonic spirit as
proved by their action which was expressed in the Declaration of Independence." (Freemasonry and Revolution, pp. 240, 241.)
Yet notwithstanding the distinctly Masonic character of the movement and
the preponderance of Masons engaged, careful and long continued research
has not developed a single record of a Masonic Lodge Grand or Subordinate
that can ..be said to !ndicate that Masonry as an organiz~tion had taken any sid~
or P.art 1.n the. conflict; those Masons who participated were courageous enough
to nsk hfe, liberty and fortune without involving the institution or seeking to
have it stand at their back, and every crisis in the affairs of men has and will

c?urageous enough to go forth alone, unaided by the reputation of any institut10n, ~nd make the fight for. Truth and Light and Liberty. That is Masonry's
f~ncbon and reason for bemg and it must ever continue to inspire men to
higher and better and more worthwhile accomplishment.
Nor is it surprising to find that American Masonry in the year 1802, while
m~y were .yet alive .who participated in those stirring events, witnessing the
rapid d~plet.10n of their ranks at the hand of the Grim Reaper, and desiring, as

guarded by the Tiler's Sword.
As the Great Creator set a cloud by day and pillar of fire by night to lead
the chosen people in their wanderings in the wilderness so I have reason to
belie_ve, our Masonic forefa~hers gave us this emblem as' a beacon to guide us,
lest m the days to come amid all the phantasies of the theorists in the wilderness of politics, we should turn aside to worship a molten calf. '
This Union of States, this government of law and not of men this Con~tit~tion of 0e United States based upon the Masonic principles 'of liberty,

~erhaps the editor of the Los Angeles Times had something of this idea
m mmd when he wrote on May 17, 1917, in a long editorial on the 200th anniversary of the founding of the Grand Lodge of England, this paragraph: "One
of the watchwords of Masonry is the watchword of the loyal American people

But sometimes I fear that Pershing was right. Sometimes it seems that
indifference pervades our ranks ; sometimes it seems that the Lodge is at refreshment and that the Tiler's Sword is sheathed and hangs in the locker with
the discarded regalia. Beyond question it was not so in those former times.
Our forefathers were alive to their duties as Masons and their lives and their
actions will live through the ages as examples for "all who go this way.''
Their works and their inspiration will beckon us as a cloud by day and a pillar

The rights of the people, and of the individual, obedience to law and constituted authority, and the obligation upon the individual to subordinate himself and his own pleasure and profit to the good of the community, are all
principles embraced within the tenets of Masonry, and the duty to actively uphold them is clearly placed upon the shoulders of every individual Mason in the
charges delivered at his initiation, passing and raising. Wh~n we are in the
midst of domestic tranquility, when progress and prosperity move forward as
upon lubricated rails, it is easy to forget those principles which safeguard our
rights as Free Men and whi~h Free Masons have been obligated to uphold.
Our Brother, General John Pershing in an address several years ago
remarked that "the greatest danger faced by the American people today is indifference." All those things which in former days were held in high regard:
the church, the community house, the affairs of government, the rights of the
people, and of the individual, are today, to too many of our citizens, more or
less matters of indifference in their 'busy lives. We are prone to give little or
no concern to those things which do not immediately and directly affect our
purse or our person.
There was a time in this country when its citizens were deeply religious,
when they took an active part in the discussion of public affairs, when the
family was a matter of concern on the part of its head, when the thought and
activities of the young were guided with a strong hand; strict observance was
the order of the day, and our forefathers in Masonry were strict observers of
the tenets of Masonry.
When the wrongs committed by a distant and autocratic government could
no longer be borne, Masons as individuals ,became active, memorials were sent
to the King, and all edicts of the King and Acts of Parliament were debated
throughout the colonies; the Committee of Safety appeared; the Sons of
Liberty organized ; the Committee of Correspondence sprang into existence ; the
American colonies were a forum wherein appeared such men as Otis, Dickinson,
Hancock, Warren, Livingston, Patrick Henry, Hamilton.. Madison, Jefferson,
Franklin, with hundreds of other Masonic leaders who in those stirring times
at the risk of their individual lives, liberty and fortune, stood forth and proclaimed those Masonic principles of liberty, justice, equality, and individual
responsibility. I need not recite the deeds of our forefathers in Masonry which
led up to the establishment of an independent government for this country of
ours, for their record is known to all of you. I would but mention one of their
accomplishments-the making and adoption of the Constitution of the United
States and the initiation of a national government thereunder.
It has been said that !'too much of our thinking is an emotional glorification.
of the past rather than a dynamic realization of the present." At the risk of
being indicted for such an offense, I recall to your minds that a majority of
the delegates actively engaged in the work of the convention were Masons ;
that our illustrious Brother George Washington presided, and that Franklin,
Hamilton, Madison, Dickinson, the two Pinckneys, Ellsworth, the two Morrises,
Wilson, Sherman, Mason, Randolph, Rutledge, and Livingston led the debates;
that after its adoption and the election of George Washington as the first
President we find him at his inauguration taking the oath of office on a Bible
brought f~om the Grand Lodge of New York, while Chancellor Livingston, the
then Grand Master of Masons in New York, administered the oath ; nor is it
surprising to find the cabinet of Washington composed of Masons, ·md that
the appointees to the Supreme Court of the United States were likewise
Masons. Need we go further?

ANNUAL REPORT OF TRUSTEES
To the M. '.W." .Grand Lodge of California:
We present herewith the annual report of your Board of Trustees who are
charged with the administration of the Masonic Homes. This includes a statement of all receipts and disbursements for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1937,
and a roster of residents of the two Homes as of August 31, 1937. We also
include the amount of funds collected since July 31, to September 30, 1937.
Immediately after the close of Grand Lodge last October, the Board selected
officers for the ensuing year as follows :
President, Charles M. Wollenberg (whose term will expire October,
1938).
Vice-President, James B. Gist (1939).
By the requi'l'ements of section 36 of the Constitution, the Grand Treasurer
is the Treasurer of the Homes, and the Grand Secretary is the Secretary of
the Board of Trustees and of the Homes.

Meetings
Four general meetings attended ·by all the members of the Board were held
in the year, and weekly meetings were held by committees of the Board at
San Francisco and Los Angeles. By reason of these frequent committee meetings there has never been any delay in passing upon applications for admission.
Admissions ·
Last year, from September 1, 1935, to August 31, 1936, · 61 applications for
admission to the Home for adults were approved. During the same period of
time 23 boys and g irls were admitted to the Home for children.
This year the admissions to the Home for adults numbered 53 and 24 boys
and girls were admitted to the Home for children.
Children Graduates
In June of this year eight boys and nine girls were graduated from the
Covina High School and honorably dismissed from the H ome. One boy was
honorably dismissed to the Lodge from which he came because he had reached
the age of eighteen years. The problem, what to do with and for these dismissed boys and girls, immediately presents itself. It is a matter of vital concern to the children and to the Lodges whose wards they are. We believe that
the Masonic Home of California for i:hildren is the ·best institution of its kind
in the United States. The chief aim of the Trustees, ably and intelligently
carried out by the Superintendent and his staff of house fathers and house
mothers, has .been to give to the little ones consigned to our care a real home
life, as nearly approximating a good natural home as possible. But it must be
obvious to all the Lodges that the Superintendent and the members of the
Board of Trustees cannot undertake the task of finding places of employment
for these iboys and girls after they leave our care. Sad to relate, too often
Lodges lose interest in their wards after they have been admitted to the Home.
For many years it has been the custom of the Secretary of the Homes each
spring to write to all Lodges having children to be graduated in Jµne, advising

of the fact that dismissal will follow graduation, and asking that the Lodge
make plans for employment. Too often these appeals are ignored. It sh~uld
not be so. The problem, in our judgment, could largely be solved 'b?' ~e a~pomt­
