Summer Camp at Balboa
We have had to meet an assessment of some $3,200 for seawall and dredging this year. This expenditure will be made out of entertainment funds contributed by the various Lodges and friends of the Home at Christmas time.
The "Masonic Camp" at Balboa is the summer playground of our children
where, away from the heat of the valley, they enjoy some three months
annually, life on the beach, swimming, boating and fishing, and return to
Covina about the first of September in the best of health.
While we have a considerable investment in this camp, it is all gift money,
and the lots purchased for $100.00 each with the "John Tucker" gift of seventeen years ago, are now quoted at from $800 to $1,000.

Trends in Child Care
This last summer our Superintendent, John M. Downen, of the Covina
Home, attended the Masonic Executives' Conference at Minneapolis, and we
quote from his report:
"One important fact that was brought out at this Conference was that
institutional populations, both children and aged, are dropping in number
throughout the nation. The general tendency is to transfer charity burdens from
private to public shoulders, and public relief generally is not being given through
institutions. The depression brought the necessity for emergency relief on a
scale so large that only the government could take care of it; and now it appears
that government is going on taking care of much that a few years ago would
not have been thought a proper charge on public agencies.
"Those who are engaged in caring for children by the institutional method
must be challenged by the present-day undoubted tendency toward other modes
of care, either relatives' homes or in foster homes.
"In considering this trend with reference to our own institution and its
set-up, there is one factor which I believe differentiates our Home from the
ordinary institution. The child in our care, even though a full orphan, has a
consciousness of "belonging." He early becomes aware of the significance of
the Masonic background of the Home. He feels that he is a member of the
family of Masons in California; he often speaks of 'my Lodge.' This feeling
of security and of being wanted is reinforced by his many contacts with
Masonic visitors, whom he often meets personally. In some cases, like the
privately reared child, he even becomes 'spoiled.'
"I am convinced that in all this there is a something which differentiates
our Home from children's institutions generally. This difference is due not
alone to our special way of handling the children, but even more to the Masonic
foundation upon which it rests, and which endows it with a quality that I have
not seen in any institution otherwise founded.
"In spite of all this, when we observe the unmistakable trend away from
the institution, we cannot but be put on notice. It behooves us to 1be aware of
what is going on. It seems not unlikely that we are entering an era that will
witness sweeping changes in social and charitable practices. We should not be
the last to perceive these coming- changes, but rather among the first."
Earning System for Children
Some years ago we realized that the savings accounts did not answer the
need of boys and girls, especially during adolescence, to have a practical experience. with money. A savings account does not move; if it does it is not a
savings account. It is not sufficient to tell a fifteen year old child: "Save all
your money, and it will be useful to you after you leave the Home." The

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

child cannot learn about money unless it is coming into and going out of his
hands. Four things he should learn about it: earning, spending, savings, giving.
He can learn these only by practice.
At the age of approximately thirteen the child moves into a Senior building and :becomes a member of a Senior group. He then 1becomes eligible to be
paid for work he does in the various departments of the Home, and at the
same time is required to begin to pay for his clothing, school supplies, toilet
articles, recreations and luxuries. In fact he must pay for almost everything
_except food, shelter and medical care. If he breaks or damages property, he
is charged for it.
Paid jobs include farm work, caring for chickens, orchard work, care of
grounds, janitor work, painting, repair work, kitchen and dining room work,
office work. The pay is scaled according to the age of the worker and the
quality of the work, and is so arranged that with reasonable industry and
utilization of work-opportunities the ·boy or girl can "make ends meet." If he
is above average as a worker he will have money to spend on luxuries, such as
a radio or a bicycle, or can make deposits in his savings account, which is quite
often done. On July 31 ,t he boys had an average credit balance of $19.03; the
gjrls' average was $3.89. Two boys were in debt, as· compared with eleven
girls. The poorer financial condition of the girls is due to two factors, the
higher cost of their clothing and their weaker ambition for financial inde-

We think there is no doubt of the practical training value of this financial
system. The cost of maintaining and operating it is considerable, due to the
clerica,l work involved, and the fact that extra industrious boys and girls will
earn a surplus to spend in luxuries or place in their savings. Any system of this
kind is bound to have imperfections, just as do all fiscal systems of grown
people. On the whole, however, we believe it is of great benefit, and is worth
more than it costs.

Savings System
Forty-five children or about one-third of our whole number, at present
have individual savings accounts in the Bank of America at Covina. One of
these is that of a girl who was discharged from our care in 1930, but who has
chosen to carry her account here since that date, the present balance in her
account being $363.01. The average 1bala:nce in the forty-five accounts is
$36.92. Checks on these accounts must be signed jointly by the child depositor
.and the Superintendent of the Home.
These accounts have various origins, the most common one being the savings of a small child brought to the Home when the child enters. Sums of
money given to children by their Lodges or by relatives and which are not
needed for any immediate purpose, are often diverted into the savings accounts;
in fact, accounts are often started in that way. Accruals to accounts come
through gifts made for the purpose; and after the children are old enough
to be earning money, by deposits which they voluntarily make from money
which they earn in excess of their immediate needs.
It is the general understanding that withdrawals from the savings accounts
w:ill not be made. until after the child leaves the Home, the purpose of them
being to provide for the needs of the child during his adjustment period after
discharge. Rarely a withdrawal is permitted for some special reason while the
child is still in the Home; but in most cases the savings are held intact until
·discharge.· At that time usually the account is closed, and the credit balance is
remitted to the <boy or girl, or to the parent or guardian, according to circumstances.

Old Age Security
We now come to our immediate concern, the influence of the California Old
Age Security Act on the Decoto Home. The Legislature passed and the Governor signed Assembly Bill No. 1, which gives persons residing in homes for
the aged pensions up to $35.00 monthly under certain conditions. Of our present
population of 352, probably 200 can qualify for these pensions. A number of
our residents at Decoto have already contacted the State Department of Social
Welfare and the Department in turn has discussed with your Trustees the
granting of pensions to certain residents of the Home.
We call to attention of Grand Lodge at this time the fact that acceptance of
payments from guests on the large scale which would be involved will constitute a new 'practice in the conduct of the Home. Heretofore we have had
in force a ruling requiring children of residents to pay toward their maintenance
if those children were able; however but few payments from this source have
been received.
In the present instance, however, the payments would be made by the
majority of those in our care, and it is estimated that such payments would reduce the annual net operating cost of the Decato Home by some $60,000.00. We
are taxpayers and our Home comes under the law. Our people are entitled to the
same treatment from the State as those in other institutions.
If we do not accept this aid, we have but two alternatives: to turn these
people out of our Home and bid them seek aid from the State; or continue to
operate as at present, letting the members of the craft absorb the expense which
the State stands ready to pay.
We believe the Decoto Home, regardless of where the money comes from
to pay its expenses, is rendering a priceless service to its residents. It gives
them a haven of security, a congenial atmosphere with the company of others
of their own age and outlook on life. While there are those who will prefer
to remain outside the Home if they can receive $35.00 a month from the State,
there are many others to whom the privilege of ending their days within its
gates will mean safety, freedom from worry, the enjoyment of congenial companionship, and assurance that when sickness comes they will have the best of
medical care and nursing.
Thirty-five dollars a month at best will provide but indifferent food and poor
housing and will give no opportunity to lay up a reserve for medicine or to meet
other expenses of illness. If the recipient of old age pension should elect to remain in the Home, paying such charg~s as we ip.ay designate, he not only gets
substantial diet, good housing, but has his medical needs and hospitalization provided for ; besides many other advantages.
We, therefore, recommend that the Trustees be instructed to permit recipients of Old Age pensions to remain in the Masonic Home.

a member of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, who already had given us $90,000.00
and a deed to his home in Beverly Hills. His gift this year was in the sum of
$72,651.23. This gift, however, was on the condition that we pay an annuity
of $1,000.00 yearly to aged relatives of Brother Flint, or to the survivor of
them.
We also received a generous gift of $25,000.00 from Brother George H.
Wadleigh, Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, and his wife Harriett; likewise subject
to the payment of an annuity of $1,625.00 yearly.
We know the members of Grand Lodge join us in thanking Brothers Flint
and Wadleigh, and trust they and their good wives will live long to enjoy the
knowledge of the happiness they are bringing to others.
Amended Articles of Incorporation
To enable us to comply with the conditions of these gifts it became necessary to amend our articles of incorporation to obtain authority to receive transfers of property conditioned upon an agreement to pay an annuity to the
transferor or his nominee.

Responsibilities of Lodges
In other years we have had occasion to call attention to the responsibility
of Lodges for the care of their distressed members who are not in fact fairly
a charge upon the whole fraternity. Last May a petition for admission to our
Home for adults was received from one of the Lodges of this jurisdiction,

351

Rules for Admission
From the beginning of the Homes it has been the rule to allow each Lodge
two residents at the Home for adults without charge, and one additional resident
for each three hundred members or fraction thereof in excess of three hundred.
For each resident in excess of the quota allowed, a charge is made in an amount
fixed from time to time by the Board of Trustees. No charge has heretofore
.been levied against Lodges for account of members who received cash relief
outside the Home.
Believing that this rule was inequita·ble, the Board in April of this year,
amended the last sentence of the last paragraph of the rules governing admission to the Home for adults, as it appears at page 440 of the Proceedings
for 1935, to read as follows :
"For each additional applicant (in excess of the quota) admitted to the
Home, or to whom outside aid is given, a charge will be made in an amount
to be fixed from time to time by the Board of Trustees."
Repairs and Replacements
On account of economic conditions, all repairs and replacements which
could .be postponed without detriment to our buildings have for several years
past been delayed. This year certain repairs were imperative. At Covina the
steam and hot water systems have been completely overhauled at a cost of
approxiqiately $4,000.00. We face the replacement of a mangle in our laundry
in the near future, as well as a further development of a satisfactory water
supply.
.
Replacement of carpets and other furniture at both Covina and Decoto
have caused considerable outlay.
We look forward to increased costs for this year due to the upward trend
of all commodities, and in this connection present the following tables showing
the increased cost in various departments of both Homes, as compared with the
average of two previous years:

To the Board of _Trustees:
In submitting my twenty-eighth annual report as Superintendent of the
Decoto Home, I am pleased to state that the general conditions are satisfactory.
Tihere has been the usual routine in the management of the Home, without any
· special change during the year.
Last year the membership of the Home was 352; 191 men and 161 women.
Since then, 53 have ·been admitted; 50 have passed away; also, there have been
3 departures; .leaving a present membership of 352; 201 men and 151 women.
The average age is 74 years. Of the men and women, 26 are married couples.
The health conditions of the Home have been fairly good, considering the
age of our members. An average of 45 men and women are being cared for
in our hospital department.
The services rendered by our men and women in the several departments
and on the grounds have been of material benefit to the Home, and is greatly
appreciated.
There has .been no change in the management of the farm. A large part of
the ranch has :been leased on shares or on cash rental. Our share of the hay
crop has been more than sufficient for the needs of the farm department. The
surplus being sold in the local market.
The orchards have supplied plenty of fruit, figs, and nuts for table use;
the surplus was sent to the drier and stored for future use. The vegetable
garden has furnished a variety of vegetables, berries and greens ; and the
poultry yard has supplied eggs for taible use.
Our water supply has been more than equal to the demands made for household, lawns, fire, and irrigation purposes. Our reservoirs have been full at all
times.
The social life of the Home has been greatly enriched by literary and
musical programs, made possible by generous volunteers from Lodges, Eastern
Star Chapters, and friends assisted by residents of the Home. These entertainments are given in our Assembly Hall, and often close with dancing.
The members of the Home often prepare programs, consisting of vocal
and instrumental music, community singing, readings, stage sketches, card
games and dancing-music being furnished by the Home orchestra. Tuesday
evenings are devoted to cards; Friday evenings to chorus practice. Every

366

Thursday evening we have Sound'Moving Pictures in the Assembly hall, whiclt
are welt attended by the members of the Home. The moving pictur~s are
furnished by the San Francisco Film Board of Trade. The Moving Picture
Operators Union No. 169 of Oakland, send one of their members to operate
the picture machines in our projection room. These pictures and operators to
run them, are furnished at no ex·pense to the Home. Brother Warren G. Bailey
of · Balder Lodge No. 393, San Francisco, who donated the moving picture
equipment last year, has made another donation which has improved the acoustics
of the hall, by having the rear wait covered, which greatly improved the sound
effect in the Assembly Hall.
Our chorus now consists of twelve men and women residents of the Home.
They take part in our Sunday services, and lead in community singing and
home programs.
Radios are installed in the club rooms and social halls, where alt can enjoy
the radio programs.
All holidays have been observed 'with appropriate exercises. The croquet
grounds are well patronized.
In addition to our own pictures, many members of the Home have, from
time to time, enjoyed visiting moving picture theaters in the vicinity of the
Home; also, opportunity to make . trips to Oakland and San Francisco, and to
occasionally visit a Lodge or Eastern Star Chapter.
During the year, alt necessary repairs have been made. Many rooms,
outside doors, cornices, windows and door frames, screens, .fences and benches
have been painted.
Our paint and carpenter shops have repaired and varnished all dressers,
tables, etc., also, all repairs to doors, locks, windows, etc. This service has
been done entirely by members of the Home.
Many books have been donated during the year, and have been placed on
the shelves of our main library and branches ; in the club rooms and social
halls. A large number of newspapers and magazines are regularly received,
and greatly contribute to the enjoyment of the patrons of the library and reading rooms.
The Alameda County Free Library maintained at the Home, is· also
greatly enjoyed.
Masonic degrees, at times, are conferred in our Temple by visiting Lodges
for the benefit of the brethren of the Home.
During the year, the officers .of the Grand Lodge and a large number of
brethren from various Lodges have made many visits to the Home.
I am pleased to again extend my appreciation of the services rendered by
the officers and employes 'throughout the year, and to express my sincere
gratitude to the members of the Board of Trustees for the assistance they
have, at all times, given me.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Report of Superintendent-Covina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
A few months ago I finished ten years of work at the Covina Home.
During that time 295 children have come to us and 294 young people have
P'l:ssed fro~ our do?rs out into the world. It has been a great privilege to
witness this procession of children coming to us in the time of their need
weakness, and often bitter misfortune; to have seen them grow and develo~
da;: by day until they were able in most cases to stand alone and go out on
their o':"n power .. Truly the Covina · Home, founded and sustained by the
generosity of California Masonry, has profoundly influenced the lives and
destinies of many a future man and woman.

remaining eleven have secured employment. This employment was secured in
many cases through the activity of officers of the Lodges or through the
Masonic Employment services.
What Graduates are Doing-In the five years ending in 1936 there
were graduated from the Home sixty boys and girls, averaging eighteen years
of age. Their present occupations are as _follows:
Students .................................................................-........................... 9
Secretarial W4)rk.............................................................................. 9
Telephone. QPt;rator~::-·····- ..................................,.................... ,...... 4
Other business pos1bons................................ _.............................. 9
Nurses, graduate...............................................................-......-...... 3
Mechanical tradet............................... ~.............................................. 7
Cosmetologists ............................................................................... _. 2
Housewives ........................................................................................ 12
Not lmown..................................... ~ .................................. ~................. 5
A number of these are already attaining marked success in their chosen
occupations. At least three of the boys are forging ahead toward executive
positions in business. The girls who have married are succeeding in that job,
showing that their life with us was good training for homemaking. None of
these young people, so far as we know, have been in trouble with the law, or
on relief. In other words they are taking their places successfuJ.ly in the
difficult conditions of modern life, despite the handicaps which surrounded
their early childhood. May we not believe that the Home has been instrumental
in helping them overcome these handicaps?
Getting Started-No matter how excellent their training while in the
Home, it is inevitable that there shall be a period of adjustment when they
step out into the world. The word we get from them after they have lived
under actual conditions outside is: "We never realized what we had in the
Home. You soon find out that the outside world is different, and much harder."
We feel that this is as it should be. If our young people go forth with a
plentiful supply of enthusiasm, vitality, and self confidence, they will ·be able
to survive the trials which they are bound to undergo in the process of getting
adjusted to the outside world.
The Individual vs. the Group-In the conduct of the Home it is our
constant aim to place the interests of the individual child first at all times. We
must ·be more concerned with the child's welfare than in the functioning of
the Home as a smooth running machine. However, i£ the individual in his
conduct goes too much counter to the general social patterns that are wholesome for the group, the best interests of the greater number may require his
removal, not as punishment, but as a matter of better adjustment, both for
him and the others. While occasionally there is a child who seems unable to
make progress in a large group, we believe that in most cases membership in
the larger number is a stimulus to the development of many desirable traits.
Children learn much from each other, and under proper conditions much that
is good. Comparison and competition are strong spurs to effort.
Variety of Methods-Ideally, a child-caring agency should have at its
command a sufficient variety of resources and expedients that it can meet the
needs of every child consigned to its care. We use the institutional home as
the :basis for our treatment, and we believe this serves best the requirements
of the greatest number; however, the use of outside care in mothers' own
homes, in foster homes, and in a few cases in hospitals, has certainly enlarged
the usefulness of our service to children .
Outside Care--In a number of instances a child who was not doing
well in the Home has been placed in a private foster home and there has
gotten along nicely. The success of this arrangement \lepends upon the care

As the Older Child Sees It-Recently when I was talking with some
of the older boys and girls, they made various expressions of what they
thoug.ht had. been the effect of life in the Home upon them. What they said
wa~. interesting, so . much so that I asked them to put their expressions in
writing. The following are quoted from what they wrote:
"Your life is changed when you come to the Home. You learn to
cooperate with others, to live harmoniously, and to do things for yourself."
"There is always a sense of security and safety that many private
homes lack. We also take part in the governing of the Home. It has
changed my lifd in many ways. My ideals have been raised very high."
"We are not burdened with the thought of where our next meal is
com.ing from, but ':"e're taught to be economical and not extravagant. The
Semor boys and girls are given a chance to earn money, to keep it on an
account, and draw from it when necessary to buy their clothes and other
things. It gives us good experience with money, for we can have no
more than wd earn. It gives us a personal pride, for we know , that the
clothes we wear and the things we have are really ours because we have
earned them."
"In showing visitors through the Home I have often found that they
were surprised because they expected something different. The things
that surprised them the most were : that we did not wear uniforms; that
the boys and girls eat together; that we go to public schools; that we are
happy. They often say 'Why, this is not like an institution; this is more
like a real home.' "
"One of the important
features of the Home is the choice to be our01
selves. I don't feel as though I were a wheel in some machine. I feel as
though whatever I want to do and be, I can do with me the boss. True,
there are rules and regulations-there must be some pattern to follow.
But almost every thought we get is our own. None is ever forced upon
us. I feel that the things I do are mine. I have all the freedom I need to
be the person I would most like to be."
From Dependency to Self Support-The main purpose of the Home is

~o take dependent children and change them by nurture and training into

independent men and momen. When they are little they must be completely
cared. for ; with each year of their growth they gain something in ability to
sustain themselves. The real test of what we are doing for them is to be
found in their success in self support, and in their usefulness to society after
they leave us. Measured iby this standard we feel that those who have left us
from year to year in the past have given a good account of their preparation
for life.
. Last June. seven.teen young people, nine girls and eight boys, were graduated
from the Covma High School ·and were returned either to relatives or to their
Lodges. Of these, six are attending business college or university; while the

385

386

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

with which the .placement is made and supervised after it is made. Recently
we had the case of a boy who got the "big head,'' as many boys do. In his case
the attack was so violent that he became a detriment and stumbling block to
others. He was placed on a dairy and poultry ranch, where there were no other
boys to show off to, and where there was plenty of hard work which he could
not escape. He stayed there a year and made good; now he is •back with us,
most appreciative of his opportunities in the Home and setting a fine example
to others.
At present we have under supervision of our social worker nine children in
foster homes, 26 children in their mothers' homes, and one child in an outside
hospital.
Vocational Guidance-During the past year for the first time we have
made use of expert advice in vocational guidance and counseling for our
students about to graduate. We secured the services, at moderate cost, of an
expert in this line. Under his direction a number of tests were given, the results
of which he studied and then personally advised each student as to the lines
they seemed best fitted to pursue successfully. We believe that advice of this
kind will tend to decrease the number of square pegs in round holes, of those
who select their vocation by the process of drifting.
Interested · Friends-Again this year as in the past the children in the
Home have been made to feel in many ways the warm friendship of "the
Masons," to them a vast body of men who stand for right and justice, and
who are their friends. Visitations of Lodges are always events of interest to
the children and generally speaking these contacts are decidedly .beneficial to
them.
Particular mention should be made of the annual Christm~s party which
has been given for the children for the past fifteen years by the Masonic
Lodges of Monrovia; Monrovia Lodge No. 308 and Sojournei: Lodge No. 607.
This party is always held during the week before Christmas. The plans for it
are so carefully made and well carried out that it has become one of the principal events in the children's year. At the party held last December there was
present one boy (later graduated . and discharged) who had attended every one
of these fifteen Monrovia Christmas parties.
Mount Olive Lodge No. 506, whose membership is made up largely of men
connected with the motion picture industry, is another Lodge which during t.he
past several years has maintained a specially active and very generous interest
in the welfare and happiness of the children. They made a most interesting
motion picture depicting life in the Home, which picture has had circulation
among many Lodges. They presented the Home with a modern projection
machine for sound pictures. For several years they have maintained a Covina
Home Recreation Fund, and have encouraged us to draw upon it for special
pleasures and recreational features which could not be paid for from other
sources. During the past summer they gave the children at the summer camp a
fine new sail•boat, also a canoe of the best construction.
Perhaps the best feature of the generosity of the aibove mentioned Lodges
is the spirit which they have put into their giving, the fine friendliness a,nd
cordial goodwill which has accompanied it.
The Chris.tmas Fund-Mention should be made of the Christmas and
Entertainment Fund, made up this year of contributions from 269 Lodges and
86 other Masonic organizations and individuals. This fund has enabled us not
only to provide generously for the children at Christmas time, .but also to
furnish throughout the year many special pleasures and treats that otherwise
would be impossible. Notably, from this fund are paid all the expenses of the
camp at Balboa, where the children spend two months in Summer.
JOHN M. DowNEN, Superintendent

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the M.'

.w: .Grand Lodge of California:

Your Board herewith presents its Fifth Annual . Report, being for the
period between August 1, 1936, and September .~y}~~(,

Reynold E. Blight, Secretary
One Million Dollars
In presenting the annual report of the Masonic Homes Endowment program, it is the great privilege of the Chairman to announce that the Permanent
Endowment Fund now exceeds a total of ONE MILLION DOLLARS 111 1
This long desired goal, imbedded for decades in the hearts and minds of
the great pioneers of the Home movement-now an accomplished fact, is
praiseworthy, not only because of the size of the fund, .but because of the sum
total of human regard and sacrifice it so adequately represents. It is the firm
belief of the Board tliat Masons of the jurisdiction wi!I look upon the accumulated amount specified here in our report, as a secondary factor, despite its
magnitude, to the testimony it offers· of sacrifice, of protracted concern and of
a clear-cut evidence of brotherly love extended to those whose lives and
happiness are dependent upon the charitable interest of the entire Fraternity.
This fact and not the aggregate amount attained, is the basis for the pride
the Board takes in offering its annual report, because at no time during the
past months has the Board permitted any semblance of a specifie.d quota drive
for funds to enter into the educational program outlined at the Annual Communication of last year. The Board has been content to present in a simple
and unassuming manner the simple story of the Homes of California Masonry,
and any success achieved during the period just ended rightfully belongs, not
to the Board, but to the vast majority of average Masons of the jurisdiction,
who have caught the vision of the privilege of service and have rendered it,
gladly and willingly, in the interest of our children and elders at Covina and
Decoto.
Educational Program
In carrying out the program for 1936-37, the Board has kept its promise,
voluntarily made a year ago, that under no circumstance would a quota drive
for funds be attempted in the face of uncertain and unstable financial conditions created by unemployment and readjustment, but that a program predicated
on a non-aggressive and purely fraternal plan of education would be carried
out among the members of the Craft. The Board believed then, and it believes
now, that such a program offers the only means of logical approach to a me1?bership already interested and aware of the existence and needs of our twm
institutions of mercy. On this premise and in keeping with the fundamentals

403

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

402

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of Masonry, the program for the year was planned and put into effect with
heartening results equally obtained from a spiritual acceptance of the Homes
program, as well as a material evidence of regard from brethren scattered
throughou~ the entire jurisdiction. The Board found, among the brethren,
an eager interest to learn more about the Homes, its history, its growth, and
data on the lives and activities of the elders and children, and was much encouraged to note this widespread desire on the part of Craftsmen to enlarge
their understanding of Home matters.
Pamphlets--Correspondence
Acceding to this demand and to encourage the infiltration of Home lcnowle~ge among members of the Craft, the Board caused to be prepared fifteen
different types of pamphlets and folders containing information on every phase
• of the Homes program. These pamphlets, distributed mainly through Masters,
Secretaries and Homes Endowment Chairmen of Lodges, reached a total of
290,000 printed pieces, and undoubtedly contributed greatly to whatever success
the program has enjoyed during the current year. The Board believes that
through the distribution of these pamphlets, Masons of the jurisdiction are per·haps better informed upon the vital subject of the Homes project than at any
time in the history of the institutions, and by virtue of this mass knowledge,
have demonstrated their interest and care in a practical and concrete way.
Contributions to the fund were more numerous during the period just closed
than that of any other year since the inception of the Homes ideal, and while
individually smaller than those of less stringent times, the aggregate total, as
well as the aggregate interest involved, proved highly encouraging to Board
members who had advocated an educational campaign rather than one carried
out for purely financial results.
Further evidence of the renewed interest manifested in the program was
the fact that numerous letters containing requests for information, Home data
and pamphlets, were received by the Board, which, in answering these letters
and furthering the general program, sent out many pieces of correspondence
·
during the year.
Work of Homes Endowment Fund Chairmen
The Board, while making no definite effort to decentralize the correspondence and contact activities of the program, tried, through the medium of
Homes Endowment chairmen in each subordinate Lodge, to render a more
personal liaison than that permitted by Board correspondence, between those
seeking information and those able to provide it. In connection with the activities of the Homes Endowment chairmen appointed in the majority of Lodges,
the Board has only words of praise. Their work among the members in distributing informative pamphlets, making talks before their respective Lodges,
contacting personally many non-attending Lodge members, together with their
constant contact and co-operation with the Board, aided the program immeasurably and contributed greatly to the high level of knowledge of Home
affairs that now pertains throughout the jurisdiction. Three hundred and eighty
of these chairmen were appointed in as many Lodges at the request of the
Board, and individually and collectively functioned in a meritorious manner
throughout the year. Their constructive efforts were of such outstanding good
to the general program that it is a matter of keen regret to the Board to
announce that some Masters of Lodges saw fit, despite repeated requests, to
withhold such appointments within their respective Lodges, thereby retarding
the proper dissemination of information to which the members were rightly
entitled. The Board recommends to incoming Masters the immediate appointment of Endowment chairmen in such Lodges, and suggests, wherever possible,

the reappointment of those chairmen, who, by .virtue of past experience, are
best qualified to carry on the work to be undertaken during the coming year.
These brethren, whose worth in the program has been certified by splendid
results, undoubtedly will want to continue their work of charity, and needless
to say, the Board earnestly bespeaks for them the consideration of new Masters
when appointments for the new year are being made.
Financial Report

In announcing the financial returns for· the year, the Board calls attention
to the splendid response registered from the Lodges in the California jurisdiction. This generous spirit, manifested by mass approval and multiplied giving,
is a cheering thing to every Master Mason interested in preserving and safegarding the institutions dedicated in our name, and symbolizes richer divi. dends for charity and mercy in the days to come.
Appended tci this report will be found the report of the auditors, authorized
by the Finance Committee to audit the accounts of the Permanent Endowment
Fund of the Masonic Homes, showing a full and complete statement of the
condition of said fund as of July 31, 1937, with additions to August 31, 1937.
An appropriation of $5,000 was made at the last communication for the
expenses of your Endowment Board, and the whole of said sum has been
expended as shown by the following account:

From the Auditor's report it seems a clearly established fact that interest
among members is keener than ever before, and is distributed over a greater
number of donors than at any time in the history of the Homes program. For
this encouraging fact, the Board is grateful and proud; grateful for the individual loyalty given the program by so many of the brethren, who took unto
themselves and passed on the messages sent out by the Board, and who became
a valuable part of the program throughout the years; proud, because in the
face of economic uncertainty, members of the Craft upheld the financial necessities of the program by a consistent display of sacrifice and thoughtfulness,
giving whole-heartedly in the interest of those dependent on the charitable
heart of the Fraternity. For this, and of this, we are indeed g rateful and
appreciative.

Wills and Bequests
It" is also a matter of pride to the Board to point out the number as well
as the amounts made available to the fund through the creation of wills and
beqm:sts. These sizable sums, caused to be executed in the main by members
of the Fraternity, will be used in swelling the Permanent Endowment Fund of
the Homes program, and, apart from the never-ending good to be accomplished
by the administration of such funds, will live throughout the years as a living
monu~ent t~ the charity and the love of the individual donors. May we say
here, in paying our respects to those who have named the Endowment Fund
as beneficiary to their .ennobling motives of human compassion, that no words
c;if ours, however much they may be filled with the warmth of approbation and
u.nderstanding, ~ould po~sibly equal the actions of thanks, and the glorified
sign~ls of happiness and contentment on. the faces of our helpless wards, now
and m the ~ears to come. One may not purchase, as a commodity, either happiness for ch1ldhood, nor peace and contentment for old age but in ·the Masonic
catalogue of charity an avenue has been created for the ~rovision of a background where these qualities naturally apply and develop, and fortunate indeed
are. those whose hearts feel, and whose eyes lead them to the gates, beyond
which dwell the God-given virtues of brotherly-love and benevolence. The
number of bequests this year offers definite proof that there live among us
brethren whose hearts are attuned to the needs of our wards and whose
deter!11ination .to carry oi:i to the. best of their individual abilities, are signalized
as milestones in the charitable history of the Fraternity.
Everlasting Monuments
In connection with that part of the program dealing with wills and bequests, it may b~ mentioi:ied that this phase offers a fertile fiel<i, as yet almost
u~touch~, d~sp1t~ the sizable amounts contributed during the past years. A
wider dissemination of factual information, as well as · a recitation of the
bene~olent aspects of this portion of the Homes project, is of prime necessity
and importance. The Board believes that were the matter brought consistently
to the attention of those making wills and testaments, that a large percentage
woul~ gladly take advantage of the opportunity extended of making their
donati~ns count th.e ~ost. in permanency and administrative good. Throughout
the entire fie!~ of insbtut1onal care, there is none greater than that represented
by the Masonic. H?mes program of California and Hawaii. This fact is general~y known within the bounds of the organization, and, to a certain extent,
outside, as many social and welfare agencies thrqughout the State after
making exhaustive investigations of Home life at Decato and Covin~ have
voluntarily written reports of commendation regarding general conditions
existing there. Back of the entire plan of the Homes program is the ideal first
envisioned by the early · pioneers of the movement, of creating a Home {n the
truest sense of the word, where fatherless and motherless children of tender
age could be enfolded in the love of a great Fraternity, and where the elders
after a life-time spent · in active Masonry, could retire to their Home for th~
~unset of their lives. This institution-this Home-this ideal-presents a glor1ous .and unsurpassed. opportunity to those blessed with the world's goods, of
erecting an everlasting monument, dedicated in their names and endowed
throughout the coming years with the exalted virtues of devou~ understanding
and sympathy.
Attorney Members of the Craft
The Board desires to record its thanks to attorney members of the Fraternity, whose interest and assistance in the prepa.ration of wills and bequests
has been an outstanding contribution to progress made in this sphere of activ-

405

ities during the past year. The Board, realizing the need of an authentic
directory of facts regarding the Homes, as well as an instrument of assistance
in planning the legal disposition and properties, prepared and distributed such
a booklet to Masters and attorneys throughout the jurisdiction, and· the remarkable response from members of the bar has been one of the highlights of the
year's program. The brochure, under the title of "Homes, Truly Masonic," we
feel will continue to serve the double purpose of acting .as a constant reminder
and assistance to attorneys preparing wills, as well as presenting properly any
claims the Homes may have as a possible beneficiary in the legacies of those
desirous of writing a remembrance therein.
Home Visitations
Concrete proof of the keener interest displayed in the Homes program was
the constantly increasing visitations made during the current year. This evidence of solicitude and interest in the welfare of our Home guests has been
a very heartening factor in the sum total of the year's efforts, and has added
materially to the contributions, gifts and remembrances accorded the g!!neral
program. The Board has consistently advocated visitations, both for the individual member, and for group visits from constituent Lodges, and it is interesting
to note that those Lodges making such visits have been in the forefront in size
and number of contributions. The reason for this is readily understandable.
The member who pays a visit to either of the two Homes sees for himself the
magnitude of the project,-the splendid home-like atmosphere that prevails,the smoothly conducted business management ;-the total lack of disciplined
restraint, and the natural home-life of the children; he sees the elders at
Decato living in a congenial atmosphere of cordiality and friendship, impossible
to associate with institutionalized charity; he meets the superintendents of the
Homes, John M. Downen at Covina and Frank B. Hartman at Decato, and
is impressed with the fitness of these outstanding men for the task they have
undertaken and are pursuing, capably, sincerely, and with that vital something
which in time of war would be called meritorious service-over and beyond
the call of duty. He sees all these things and more, and is impressed, not so
much with the scope and power of this magnificent thing his Fraternity has
created, as with the thrilling thought that HE is a part of it; that HE is
one of the builders; that here his strength of correlated effort is embodied
in a mountain of constructive service, and that he is further empowered by his
affiliation to enlarge and to prolong this structure, emblematic of Masonic
tradition. HIS HORIZON HAS BEEN LIFTED and he now sees with the
clarity of nearness the Home program in its true perspective, no longer
remote and visionary, but proximate and real.
Open Invitation to Visitors
For the many reasons enumerated, the Board urges the continuance of
visits from those who have done so in the past, and suggests a closer association
from those who have not taken advantage of the open invitation extended by
the management and our Home guests. A · closer, more cordial relationship,
beneficial to both members and family, is 'bound to result. The Homes appreciate the interest shown; the children and eiders like to feel that they are truly
in the hearts and minds of the members, and the members themselves :are
infinitely bettered by a wider understanding of Home affairs and by the warmth
of human contact with those less fortunate than themselves.
In this connection, however, the Board suggests that when a pilgrimage is
planned, the Sl.lperintendent be notified prior to the date of visitation in order
that proper preparations be made for the visiting delegation. It is likewise
advisable that group visits also be announced beforehand, as certain hours

are set aside for the uninterrupted association of Home members and brethren,
which, if ascertained in advance, will make the visit far more enjoyable than
one undertaken in a haphazard manner. The Board again extends a cordial and
continual invitation to every member of the jurisdiction to visit the Homes at
the earliest opportunity and learn, first hand, of the life and activities of our
Home family.
General Program-Trips
During th~ year just closed, it was a source of great pride and thankfulnes·s
to the Board to observe the splendid performances of so many brethren who,
desirous of advancing the ideals and practical purposes of the general program,
served in the vanguard in many ways. Without the sustaining help of these
sincere and capable brethren, the Board would have found the task a difficult,
if not an impossible one. With them the load was eased, the way made clearer
and the results more far-reaching and lasting than it could possibly have been
without their hard work and general support. Too numerous to mention indivi~ual!y, the Board must regretfully, therefore, record its thanks anonymously,
with the hope that each and every contributing member throughout the State
will realize that his efforts and his constructive assistance are registered, if not
in this report, certainly in the hearts of those to whom his efforts were
dedicated.
Included in these efforts were the thousands of man-miles covered, the
innumerable talks, the countless contacts, and the preparation of material concerning the Homes program. In each of these fields, the Board did not suffer
from a lack of willing workers, but found an ever-ready interest and a keen
desire on the part of many brethren, to render understanding service to the
cause of charity. If there could be a highlight to this year's program, already
replete with instances of self-sacrifice and long hours of hard work this voluntary service co1,1ld be rightly termed the epitome of the year's efforts. For
this service 'll!'e are indeed grateful and are highly optimistic regarding the
future safety and well-being of our beloved institutions. In so many hands of
concern, they cannot fail.
Thanks to Officials
To the Board of Trustees of the Homes, who throughout the year worked
in complete harmony with the Endowment Board and who, individually and
collectively, contributed much in time and effort, the Board is deeply grateful.
To the Inspectors we are desirous of according our thanks for the transmission of messages; for the constant contacts maintained throughout the
respective districts, and for adding a cordial note of co-operation and assistance
to the general program. Their efforts were of the highest caliber and rightfully
deserve the thanks of the entire jurisdiction.
The work of the various Masters and Secretaries was but another evidence of the Homes-mindedness of the vast majority of Lodge officials throughout the State. With a seeming lack of concern for their own private affairs,
these brethren worked early and late in carrying out the necessities of the
program, and were instrumental in creating and maintaining a high level of
interest in the general program. Their constructive labors are registered in
renewed regard for our institutions and in the increased number and size of
donations, gifts and bequests made to the fund.
Leadership of the Grand Master
The work of the Grand Master has been an inspiring demonstration of
exalted effort during the whole of the period just closed. His keen knowledge
of the Homes Endowment program; his ready conversance with every detail

connected with the management of the institutions, together with his intensity
of purpose in furthering the educational program, has been an exemplar for
all to see, to admire, and to follow. It has been the "good fortune of the Chairman, as well as other members of the Board, to travel with the Grand Master
and to learn at first-hand of his constant thought and solicitude for those he
has so aptly termed "Our Home Guests." His interest in their welfare is so
great that in numerous addresses made before constituent Lodges he has never
failed to mention the definite obligation placed upon the entire jurisdiction by
the appeal of their combined love and trust. With all the powers at his command the Grand Master has aided and furthered the program to the utmost
of his ability and care. He has labored diligently in the vineyards of charity,
and the program has been immeasurably bettered because of his keen. perception of Home affairs, and because of his constant solicitude for ·the welfare
of our wards. The Board could express no greater thanks to our Grand Master
for his outstanding services, than to assure him of the continued regard of
those who have had the rare privilege of working with him, and of certifying
the esteem and genuine affection in which he is held at Decoto and Covina.
Visit to Hawaii
In June of this year it was the pleasure of the Chairman to make a trip
to the Hawaiian Islands in the company of the Grand Master. The hospitality,
the genial fellowship and the innate courtesy of our island brethren made the
short sojourn one of unadulterated enjoyment and one long to be remembered.
Your Chairman was impressed with the many outstanding achievements of the
various Lodges, but was wholly unprepared to receive the evidence, everywhere,
of an intimate knowledge of Home affairs, as well as a remarkable 'response
consistently accorded the general Homes program. Here, in this island empire,
3000 miles removed from the mainland, was a keen understanding of Home
problems, a strong determination to be a vital and necessary part of the program, with a resultant flow of contributions to the fund, equalling, and in some
cases, exceeding those received from California Lodges, numerically larger and
financially stronger. In each of the Hawaiian Lodges we found proverbial
Hawaiian hospitality and charity allied with the benevo-lent traditions of
Masonry, which in· expression eradicated the miles between and became a vital
an<I- indispensable part of the jurisdiction's Home Endowment program. T he
Board gladly records its awareness of the consideration giveri the program
by: the Hawaiian brethren and expresses its deep appreciation for general
co-ordination and support.
Contribute Any Time
During the year the Board has essayed by personal contacts and letters
to eradicate the fairly prevalent idea that only during the month of May are
contributions acceptable. This attempt has met with some degree of success, but
greater efforts to remove this erroneous impression must be continued if members are to be properly informed on the subject of year-round donations.
Standing as it does merely as a calendar symbol rather than a period in which
donations are to be made, the month of May should be considered as a culminating and reckoning interval in the year's work of remembrance, because,
just as the demands made by the Homes are constant and perplexing, just in
even ratio should the combined. care of the Craft be registered in day-by-day,
week-by-week, and month-by-month solicitude and regard. We cannot avoid,
nor do we care to avoid, this ever-present responsibility to our Family; we
cannot "fulfill the law of charity" by an occasional gift or thought, but must,
with unswerving watchfulness, meet the trust with every-day devotion. To
those blest with a sufficiency of the world's goods, and for whom sizable

408

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

409

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

contributions will not constitute sacrifices, the Board earnestly requests periodic
donations throughout the year without regard to the calendar period selected
annually as a summation of 'the year's efforts. To those (to quote the Grand
Master) "whose hearts are as great as their purses are small" the Board
suggests a budgetary system of allocating their donations regularly throughout
the year, rather than making a large annual contribution, which would, perhaps,
entail too great a personal sacrifice. By following this suggestion those with
limited funds, by judiciously prorating their donations without impairing their
own home and personal necessities, may keep the faith and preserve their
privileges of co-operation to the ideal represented by the Homes. While it is
true that those donations are nobler when accompanied by self-denial and
sacrifice, the Board has, in no wise, advocated nor requested contributions from
brethren whose financial conditions forbade it. The Board believes, however,
that the ultimate dream of a complete and adequate endowment for all time,
can only be achieved by the active and regular participation of every Craftsman
in the jurisdiction.
Recommendations
For the coming year the Board has few recommendations. Beiieving that
the educational program has proven worthy and meritorious, its continuation
is strongly urged; and, in order that the plan may be exercised to the fullest
extent, we solicit the creation 'o f a working fund consistent with the amplitude
of the work at hand. We recommend the continuation of the relationship built
up during the current year between Lodges and Homes; and lastly, we strongly
suggest that attorney members of the Craft enlarge their activities among
clients desirous of leaving their worldly goods to a cause, humanitarian, benevolent and lasting.
In order that your Board may function during the ensuing year, we therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :
"Resolved, that the sum of six thousand dollars be and is hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board for its expenses for the year ending October 1, 1938."
It has been the happy privilege of the Board to serve the jurisdiction
during the past year in this constructive program of brotherly love and charity.
Under the inspirational leadership of the Grand Master, furthered by innumerable instances of co-operation and. support from officials and members, the
work has been made less arduous, our efforts less difficult. Crowned with some
degree of success, the Board, in reviewing the endeavors of the past year,.
acknowledges the honor of representing this major program and records its
pride in the heartening results of material and spiritual benefits for those
placed under the shield of Masonic protection.
The Heritage of Fraternalism
Our wards at Decoto and Covina, in reposing their trust in the traditional
benevolence of Masonry, have presented a magnificent challenge to the ideals
of the Craft. Otherwise homeless and friendless were it not for the shelter
provided by the altruistic faith of the Fraternity, our charges are more than a
material responsibility. Representing, as they do, those who have given a
life-time of service to the cause of Masonry, and who, through no fault of
their own, were brought face to face with disillusionment, neglect and despair,
representing, as they do, the innocents, who through the mysterious ways of
Divine Providence, were deprived of the support, the strength and the love of
parents; representing as they do the opening and closing chapters of life's
book-the children and the elders-the magnificent endeavors of the Masonic
Homes program transcends the material and soars into the spiritual. And it 1s
this spiritual appeal that offers challenge to the best within us. We must answer

that challenge; we must provide that bulwark of material protection. We must
maintain that spiritual panacea for the lonely and the orphane~, so th~t when
we open the Book of Life for the children, we may do so with the JOY and
pride of promise, and when the last chapter is .read and the book reverently
closed, we may justly say: We have kept the faith, for these are the, precepts
of Masonry, these are the Homes, truly Masonic.
Fraternally submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Auditor's Report-Endowment Fund

To ·the Endowment Fund Committee, Masonic Homes of Cali/or~:
In accordance · with the authorization of the Finance Committee, we have
audited the accounts of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic
Homes of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1937. The following
statements are presented herewith:
Exhibit A : Summary Statement of Endowment Fund Assets.
Exhibit B : Statement of Endowment Income and Capital Account.
Exhibit C: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements.
Exhibit D : Statement of "John and Lena Luckenbach Fund."
Schedule A-1: Lists of Regular Endowment Fund Securities Acquired
Prior to July 31, 1936.
Schedule A-2: Lists of Regular Endowment Fund Securities, Additions
to Fund 1936-37.
Schedule A-3 : Statement of Securities Redeemed and Sold.
Securities-(Schedules A-1 and A-2):
Corporate stocks and irrigation bonds have been received by donation as
noted. Certain of the bonds, other than irrigation, have been acquired by donation and are so marked by the letter "D'' under Schedule A-1. In the case of
donated securities the stated or book value represents the value placed upon
the securities at time of donation. Where the value is uncertain, because of it
· being an unlisted or a closely held security, entry is . made on the books at a
nominal $1.00 value for purposes of record. Insurance policies are listed at a
nominal value of $1.00 for conservative purposes.
Bonds purchased are recorded on the books at cost, including premium.
A reserve is set up to measure the amount of premium written off or amortized.
The amount of this reserve is deducted from the total book value of regular
endowment securities, Exhibit A.
Detailed lists of additions through purchase or donation as well as sales of
securities and redemption of bonds have been set out at the end of the regular
lists of securities and are marked Schedule A-2 and A-3 for readr reference.
Total market values of bonds, stocks, -etc., are by compa,rison with book
values. as follows :

the curricula and methods of instruction in our public schools. With the knowledge thus acquired they were better able to appreciate the programs presented
in the schools and at the public meetings.
It is extremely gratifying to be able to report that there was a very general compliance this year with the suggestion we have been making that not only
the public addresses, but as well the programs presented by the pupils of the •
schools, should be designed for the dissemination of information rather than for
mere entertainment. At many of the public meetings, and over the radio, the
speakers dealt with the problems of modern education, and of the methods
adopted for their solution. They pointed out that the real purpose of our
public schools is to qualify all the children of all the people to make their
regpective contributions, according to their native talents and abilities, to that
enlightened citizenship which is dependent upon the proper and appropriate
education of the individual citizen; and that to attain this objective, there have
been devised and developed curricula of various types and content suited to the
interests, needs and capabilities of the individual pupil.
The radio publicity was no less effective than was tliat furnished by the
rural and urban press. In addition to the courtesies extended us by the State
Chamber of Commerce, the State Department of Education, Parent-Teacher
Associations, Womens Clubs and other organizations which have regular allotments of radio time, the broadcasting stations were exceedingly generous in
their cooperation. It is more than probable that hundreds, perhaps thousands of
our people who for one reason or another could not, or would not, make a
visit to the schools or attend a public meeting, but who "listened in" to some
speaker, got a new slant on the modern school.
Without the public press and the broadcasting stations, Public Schools
Week would never have become what it now is; but valuable as are these media
for the dissemination of information, we cannot too often reiterate that what
the schools are actually doing can best be learned by personal visits and through
the programs furnished by the pupils with exhibits of ·school work.
As is of course well known, our committee in these reports studiously
refrains from mentioning any Lodge, or community, either in praise or criticism; because, as has been frequently explained, it would be obviously impossible to give praise to all who deserve it, and we believe no good purpose would
be served ·by publicly calling attention to those who do not. But we canno~
forbear from here expressing our gratification in the fact that this year the
Masons in Honolulu observed Public Schools Week.
For some years the Lodges in Honolulu, for reasons which seemed to
them good and sufficient, had made no effort to sponsor an obser vance. This
year, however, they joined in holding a public meeting with a program which
must have been exceedingly interesting. The significance of public schools in
America formed the theme which ran through a series of talks climaxed .by the
address of the Superintendent of Public Instruction whose subject was "The
Public School-America's Best Gift to Civilization." There were also short
tafks by students who capably expressed their appreciation of what the publi~
schools mean to them.
We feel that it should be stated, lest a wrong inference may be drawn,
that Lodge Maui consistently continued to observe the "Week" even during
those years when no attempt to do so was :being made elsewhere in the Territory. This year it was properly, and very appropriately, tied in with the annual
observance of May Day which is there known as "Lei Day" and also as
"Child Health Day."
There were again this year, as there always are, many local observances
to which special attention might well be called because of the excellence of the
programs and the introduction of novel features. Limitations of time and space,

4,32

PROGEEDINGS OF THE

how~ver, will- permit extended reference to ·b ut one of these; and first we

mention another mat~er to which it is hoped due heed will be given.

In the report of an observance for which no apology need have been made;
the Master'.s comment was that it was "not the success that such an important
and well established project deserved to be. As Master I feel that I failed to
• catch the full significance and importance of the observance until it was over.
Because of this I think that some well directed reminder to the Master early
in, the year would serve to bring the duty to his attention in time to allow for
a definite and carefully planned program."
Now the fact of the matter is that there had been, as there always is, a
i·eminder to the Masters o( al!' our Lodges "early in the year." In January a
notice from our Committee was sent to the Secretary of every Lodge. It was
sent to the Secretary because the names of the Masters were then. not yet
availa'ble. It was, however, addressed to the Master; and on the envelope was
a notation that it was for the Master and should be handed him immediately.
This early notice is sent out ~ith the hope that an immediate start will
be · made with the arrangements for the observance by the appointment of a
committee and a conference with the school authorities. Mention may here be
made ·o f the fact that there are several Lodges in which there is a permanent
committee of arrangements with only one or two new appointees each year,
This_ idea might well be considered by other Lodges in the jurisdiction, because
there can be no question that an experienced committee functions more smoothly
a·n d efficiently than one composed of members who are r.ot familiar with the
"mechanics" of the observance. ·
In connection with the foregoing, we again refer to a· rather anomalous
condition with which we have be.en confronted dur,ing the last two or three
years; So successful have been the observances that the Masters of our Lodges
in · s'ome communities feel that no special effort is required of them. And we
desire to here repeat the .warning contained in one of our reports a _few years
ago, :when referring to the fine cooperation receive·d from the school people
we said, ,
"Now, _desirable as this in itself is, we must have in mind the possibility
of its developing into a situation which would defeat the end we have fo
view; and it will not have been the fault of the school people, but of those
upon whom Grand Lodge has a right to rely for the furtherance of the
movement it originated and continues to foster.

0

"In our recognition of the advisability, indeed necessity, of securing
the co-ordinated action of the community, it was never intended of course,
that the Masters of our. Lodges should ,be reiieved of the responsibility
primarily devolving upon them. And it must 1be alw;:ys remembered that
the great value of Public Schools Week is in the fact that it is fostered
not by .the school people, 'but by laymen. It is essentially a lay movement.
To have it understood· as only' an activity carried on by the school people
would be no less objectionable than it would be to have it regarded as an
event in which only Masons are concerned."

Although the observance has become, as .it should be, a community affair
and not a Masonic event, and although the civic organizations of the community
and -the school people should be. represented on the committee of arrangements,
the Lodge should be the nucleus of the organization created for the observance
whiCh. is fostered arid supported by the Fraternity. We have a duty to ourselves as well as to the community; and Public Schools Week must not be
permitted to h_ecome other than_what it was intended to be. Up to the present
time there have been no untoward happenings; but we must continue to be
vigilant in guarding against that i>ossibility.

-In addition to the booths demonstrating modern procedures in the education

The exposition was continued for two days from 1 :00 to 6 :00 in the
afternoon and from 7 :00 to 10 :00 in the evening, and was supplemented by a
spectacular pageant portraying four phases in the life of youth and which was
the concluding event of an observance of Public Schools Week which will ·be

The mention of adult education in connection with the observance to
which reference has just been made suggests the thought that Public Schools
Week furnished an opportunity for bringing home to -the people of many com,
munities a realization of the fact that California is not content to educate. only
the youth, but is providing an opportunity for those long past school age to
acquire an education which they may have ·been denied in their youth, or to
acquire arts and skills for which there came a desire only with maturing years.
The night classes and continuation schools providing education for adults
attracted a large number of visitors ; and in one of the largest of our cities
there was a public meeting sponsored by the County Council of the American
Legion which was devoted exclusively to adult education. Through brief talks,
supplemented by exhibits, live presentations and .typical class work, various
phases of adult education were called to the attention of an audience which
filled the large hall to overflowing.
It would appear that there is no phase of public education that was not
brought to the attention of the people during Public Schools Week; and it is
not strange that in a public statement the President of the California State
Chamber of Commerce said, "It is obvious that since the first observance of
Public Schools Week in 1920, citizens and business people especially, have
developed a greater confidence in our free American schools and a more profound realization of their importance to our American ideals of liberty and
democracy."
Visits to the schools continue to be apparently .the most popular feature
of the observance, as they are undoubtedly the most valuable; and in a report
received from the Superintendent of Schools in one of our larger cities, and
which included comments and suggestions received from school principals
appears the following significant statement: "We think that the visitors this
year seemed more interested in the school in general than they did in their
individual children-a hopeful sign. Their questions also were more intelligent
and showed a genuine desire for information."

"The inauguration of this movement (Public Schools Week) was
attended with a considerable doubt of its 'success, even on the part of

There was much criticism, frequently severe in tone, from the outside. The
Masonic press was not convinced that such an enlargement of Craft labor
was in accord with the plan and purpose of Masonry. We were solemnly
told that such effort was 'political,' the use of which word by any ignoramus had beforetime effectually damned every generous proposal and
frightened off timid brothers from labor directed to practical and profitable
ends.
"But year after year the week of observance has attracted ever more
friends and ardent supporters. The objectors were silenced when it was
found that harmony still prevailed, and that a great and lasting benefit was
' being registered by the communiti\!S because of presentation and discussion
of school problems, demonstration of educational methods, and the discovering of existing needs. Other jurisdictions, noting what of good had been
accomplished, have followed it also in making the observance a fully community affair, with Masons taking their place among the general body of
the citizenry in considering the most important of all public institutions.
"There are now few if any to openly criticize. Experience is the best
and surest of teachers, and unqualified success of the California experiment
has convinced erstwhile doubters and i;ritics, where argument had failed. As
a consequence it is widely accepted among American Masons that the
·public school~ are to be at all times championed by the Craft. This is as
it should be-the children of today will be the citizens of tomorrow. Upon
their shoulders will rest the weighty responsibilities of community, state
and national life. Huge affairs of the time to come, already shaping dimly
upon the horizons of thought, will demand far more from the men and ·
women of another generation than is required from ourselves, even though
to us the puzzles of existence are baffling and the situation appears as filled
with perils. For .such reasons Masons, in common with all good citizens,
should strive mightily tci <1-dvance and keep at highest level the cause of
popular edu~ation, and to insist that the public schools shall be fitted in all
things for their gigantic tasks."
All of which is respectfully submitted.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
HOSP~TALS

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to whom was referred the resolution of Angeles Mesa
Lodge No. ·625, "to investigate a matter of erecting, maintaining and carrying
on two Masonic hospitals, one in San Francisco and one in Los Angeles, and
the feasibility of establishing such hospitals or the establishment of Masonic
wards in existing hospitals," beg leave to report as follows :
We have communicated with the several grand jurisdictions of the United
States and find that at the present time there is no hospital maintained for or
by Masons, recognized by or under the authority of any Grand Lodge, and
although we have heard of Masonic hospital associations, we have been unable
to find any that were not in every sense o·f the word private corporations and
not recognized in any way by the Masonic authorities of their respective communities.
In the course of our investigation, we found that the grand jurisdiction
of New York had built a very magnificent memorial hospital on the grounds
of the Masonic H ome at Utica, New York, with funds collected just before
the conclusion of the World War for war relief purposes. A member of this
committee was informed by the superintendent some years ago on his visit
to this hospital that it had been the intention to allow Masons from any part
of the state to use this hospital, but that this was found to be impracticable,
and it was then and is now, only used by the residents of the Home.
Incidentally, this hospital has a capacity of somewhere around 200, represents a $1,000,000 investment for the building and several hundred thousand
dollars for equipment, the latter being donated in a large part by the various
Lodges of the state.
There is one, and as far as we know, only one hospital maintained by a
Masonic jurisdiction for the brethren generally, and that is the hospital at
Melbourne, Aust ralia, just recently completed under the Grand Lodge of Victoria. We quote:
"The intention of the Board of Control was to provide general hospital care for all members of the craft wishing to avail themselves of
this facility, and to extend a helping hand in sickness to those town or
country members who could not afford private or intermediate hospital
rates in other institutions, or employ the services of specialists,"
In pursuance of this plan a hospital has just been completed with a capacity of sixty beds, which will be used for general surgical and medical
purposes, but will not take care of children or obstetrical cases. It has been
so designed and land acquired, so that it can be developed when funds permit to
an ultimate capacity of 250 beds. It is interesting to note that the cost, at
the present time, for this sixty-bed hospital, exclusive of land, has been $344,028.
At the time of writing thii report, the hospital not having been open a sufficient length of time, we have been unable to ascertain anything regarding
their success or the difficulties encountered, as well as the cost of hospital
maintenance of this institution.
Your committee recognizes the problems confronting the average man
today when hospital care is needed. We know the cost of such care and we
have carefully gone over the report of the Committee on Medical Care, headed
by Ray Lyman Wilbur of Stanford University, some few years ago ; we have
read the report of the Julius Rosenwald Fund, issued this year, and a large
part of the "Hospital Survey of New York," as well as the reports of New

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

438

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

York City and other communities where hospital group insurance maintains,
and we have come to the conclusion first, that the buildh1g of hospitals by the
Grand Lodge of California in Los Angeles and San Francisco would mean
the outlay for capital expended of at least $2,000,000. Second, establishment
of Masonic hospital wards in existing hospitals by Grand Lodge would give
those living in the vicinity of these two cities an advantage over the membership in rural districts; third, the incident of illness is personal and the membership at large cannot be taxed to meet the expense of either method suggested.
We find that from 28 to 33 per cent of existing hospital beds are unoccupied and that hospitals generally are running in the red due to this fact.
In the last few years the voluntary hospitals of over sixty cities have
developed "group insurance," whereby a group in a particular industry can
provide in advance for hospital care.
We have a feeling that within the next two years this group hospital
insurance is going to be available in most communities where hospital facilities are available. We realize that the individual cannot take advantage of
the low rates afforded by such insurance unless he belongs to a group as
represented by a craft, or a commercial establishment, or a lodge. We. believe
that a law should be developed that would enable the Masonic Lodges of this
state to set up an organization which would enable its members to take advantage of the low rates established by this insurance.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that the construction and maintenance of the two Masonic hospitals, one in San Francisco and one in Los
Angeles, or the establishment of Masonic wards in existing hospitals, as
suggested in the resolution creating this committee, not be carried out.
Respectfully submitted,
C. M. WOLLENBERG,
Roy PARKINSON,
HALCOTT H. THOMAS,
