To the M.'.

w:. GrOAUJ Lodge of California:

It is fitting that this Grand Lodge should take time during its annual
communication to observe the Sesquicentennial of the Constitution of ' the
United States. It would be fitting for any body of men thus assembled to
properly observe an event of such importance but it is especially appropriate
for a company of Masons to pay a proper tri~ute to the instrument of govern-·
ment under which they live.
The part which Masons had in the events preceding the Declaration of
Independence is well known e.nd likewise we are all familiar with their participation in the drafting of that important document. Suffice it say that twentr~
nine of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were Masons, numbeting in that group such important men as Samuel Adams, Benjamin Frankljn,
Thomas Jefferson, Robert Morris, Roger Sherman and others. It is not surprising in view of the general participation of Masons in the events leading up
to the Revolution that we should find them active in the actual warfare. From
the Commander-i~-Chief, Brother George Washington down to the privates in
the ranks, we find Colonels, Majors, Captains, Lieutenants and the backbone of
the army, common · soldiers, Master Masons. Such outstanding _heroes of. the
War for Independence as Alexander Hamilton, John Marshall, James Madison_.
General Greene, G~neral Lee, General Sullivan, Lord Sterling, La FaY,ette,
General Steuben, Montgomery, Jackson, Gist, Knox and Ethan Allen w.e re inen
who had distinguished themselves not only as soldiers and patriots · but as,
Masons.
It is interesting however that well known as is. the participation of Masons
in th.e events prior to 1787, there is not the same general knowledge and app,reciation of the part played by Masons in the drafting of the Constitution of the
United States and the struggle for its i:atification. This may perhaps be due
to the general failure of all men everywhere to fully appreciate the significance
of what took place in that constitutional convention and the difficultie~ which
beset it. ·Important as was the Declaration of Independence and vital as . was
the Revolution, both would have succeeded of themselves and failed of the
final objective if the Constitutional Convention had failed to . achieve the result
which has come to be known as the greatest document ever struck off ·by the
mind and purposes of man at a g.iven time. There is perhaps no more false
statement ·that could be made about the Constitution than that it was·' strtic~

442

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

off at a given time ·by a body of men inspired by th~ occasion and consciously
guided by a beneficent Providence.
In order to fully understand what happened in the historic hall in the City
of Philadelphia from May 14 to May 17, 1787, it is necessary to go back an
view again the circumstances which gave rise to the meeting and the backgroun
against which the drama was to be played. When the Revolution started n
1776 with the shot that was heard round the world, the thirteen colonies w e
by no manner or means united in the cause which was soon to test thJ ir
strength. As the war progressed it became evident that they must unite or fall
and the very good prospect of failure became a uniting force rather than .the
sense or awareness of a common cause. We need only to remind ourselves of
the difficulties which beset Washington to recall that there was no strong
central government capable of winning support for the cause or strong enough
to demand financial support for the army. Had there been any responsible
body in control of the affairs of the colonies, the sinews of war, food, clothing, equipment and money with which to pay the troops, would have been
forthcoming. More than once the enemy was on the verge of a decisive
victory against inadequately equipped regiments, only to be cheated of that
victory by the strategy of leaders who did not dare to risk the issue. The war
could have been brought to a much earlier conclusion had there been a strong
central governing body that had the confidence of all the colonies.
The need for such a government became apparent long ·before the close
of the war and the Second Continental Congress, in an effort to establish
such a government, drafted the Articles of Confederation. This instrument
was presented to the colonies for their approval in order that it might be
put into operation, but it is interesting to note that it was not adopted by
enough of the thirteen to make it operative until 1781. This failure of this
government could easily be anticipated and may ·best be illustrated by the fact
that during one period the government sent out a call for taxes totaling
$8,000,000 and received less than $400,000.
This, then, was the form of government under which the colonies were
when the peace was finally signed that made them forever independent from
Great Britain, and by the same act launched them on their own among the
nations of the world. Faced immediately by all the problems of international
intercourse, the need of paying the debts incurred by the war, the urgent
necessity of establishing foreign trade and getting as rapidly as possible upon
friendly terms with the other countries, it was inevitable that the colonies
should at once begin to feather their own nests and promote only those
enterprises or alliances which were most likely to benefit themselves.
With such an attitude prevalent among the separate states it was inevitable that, with the growing problems of commerce and industry, the individualism of each of the colonies should be developed to such a high pitch that
there was no opportunity for united action. Indeed it soon became evident that
there was no hope for a united country and the Articles of Confederation
became almost useless as an instrument of general government. The situation
which faced the young country was not promising. There was a population
of only about three million people, widely scattered over a great area, and
broken up into four major parts, each with distinct interests.
In the New England states, Massachusetts {including Maine), New
Hampshire, Rhode Island and Connecticut, there were about 900,000 inhabitants. Here was the village form of government binding together people with
·something of a common background and a common religion. They formulated
the doctrine of government later expressed in the Declaration of Independence,
that government must rest upon the consent of the governed.
The second main section was that which we might describe as the Atlantic
coast plain. Here the plantation system was in vogue in the states of Delaware,

\

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

443

Maryland, Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. The population was about
l,20e,OOO, of whom half were slaves.
The Middle States was the region between the plantation country and
ew England, consisting largely of three great river valleys, the Hudson, the
usquehanna, and the Delaware, which ran into the three gi;-eat ba~s, and near
ose mouths stood the important cities of New York, Ph1ladelph1a and Balo re. The population was about 700,000.
The last major division of the country was that great moui:itain r.egion from
ce tral Pennsylvania to northern Georgia, a belt about 150 miles w1?e and 700
mil s long. This was the frontier of the day and had a population of not
to ~ceed 150,000.
1such a wide diversity of interests would have been difficult to compromise
1
under a strong central government, but it was ~ext to i~possible ~nde! the
Artitles of Confederation. The air was filled with rebellion and dissatisfaction. Two hundred former soldiers of Washington's ar?1Y m~rched on Cong~ess,
assembled in Philadelphia, and so menacing was their attitude that by. night
Con~ress stole away to Princeton and later to New -york to hold their ses.
sions. A group of Washington's former officers devise~ a pl.an to secr~tly
overthrow the government, and had not a copy of their notice fallen mto
Washington's hands it is likely that they would have succeeded. The masses,
fired to a frenzy by their own suffering, revolted in M.assac~us~tts, under the
leadership of an old soldier named Shays, a?~ so ;ap1dly did 1t spr.ead ~hat
one-fifth of all the citizens of Massachusetts iomed m the revolt and 1t gamed
a following in other states. When this rebellion was finally suppressed the
only person punished was the Governor of Massachusetts, whom the peop~e
refused to reelect because he had used force to carry out the oath of his
office in doing his duty.
This then, was the general state of disunion and discord which prevailed
ih 1786 ~hen the Governor of Virginia invited all the states to send delegates
to a convention to be held at Annapolis in September, 1786, to consider how
far the states could agree upon common regulations of commerce. When the
date of the meeting arrived there were too few delegates present to take any
action and so they contented themselves with issuing another call for a convention to be held in Philadelphia on the second. Monday in May, 1.787, "to
take into consideration the situation of the United States, to devise sue~
further provisions as should appear to them necessary to render the Constitution of the Federal Government adequate to the exigencies of the Union."
This suggestion was finally approved by the dying Congress, on January
21 1787 but with the proviso that the convention "be for the sole purpose

The difficulties which beset the convention and the slight progress made

Time does not permit nor does wisdom dictate that we should here spend
our time in an exhaustive analysis of what took place in the four hundred
hours of debate on the plans and proposals that finally produced the ultimate
,Prixlu.ct. Suffice it to say that the convention which met to amend the Articles
pf Confederation quickly discovered that it could not successfully sew new cloth
to .old and make a sound garment and consequently turned almost at once to
the task of framing an entirely new instrument of government.

'm

While we might like to think that the final draft of the Constitution
was ilP ipspired document that fell from the hands of the delegates at a given
.ti~e .and jn .a given form, yet it was far from that and was in fact a series of
~ornpromises. Thre~ _great cqmpromises were made without which the conventiop. must have .adjourned without accomplishing anything. The first was between · the large and small states by which all states were to have equal rep re- •
sentation in the Senate and proportionate representation in the lower house.
The second chiefly affected the Atlantic plain and southern states with the
plantation system and provided that in computing taxes and determining representation, only three fifths of the slaves were to be counted. A clau,se was
inserted whereby the slave trade was not to be prohibited prior to 1808. The
final compromise disposed of a conflict between the northern commercial states
and the southern agricultural states whereby Congress was given control of

445

commerce, both interstate and foreign, but was prohibited from levying taxes
n exports.
On September 8, the hardest labor had been completed and the work was
t med over to a Committee on Style with instructions to draft the final form.
T· e committee reported on September 12 and the following day the printed
dr ft was ready. The next three days were spent in carefully comparing each
art cle and section of the final draft and on September 15 the work was consid ed completed, adopted and ordered to be engrossed for signing. The net
res t consisted of about four thousand words, 0 nly eighty-nine sentences and
abou one hundred and forty distinct provisions. Never before nor since has
such a brief document laid down such principles and rules on so vast a range
of m tters of the highest importance and complexity.
n September 17 the convention met for the last time. The document had
been engrossed and was laid before the members for signing. Of the fi ftyfive who had been present when the convention opened, only forty-two remained at the close and of these some were unwilling to sign the final draft
as individuals. It was at this point that Benjamin Franklin rendered the greatest service to the cause by making an eloquent plea in which he freely stated
that he did not approve all that had 1been done but that he had discovered in his
long years that the older he grew the more apt he was to doubt his own
judgment and pay more respect to the judgment of others. He concluded by
saying, "On the whole, sir, I cannot help expressing a wish that every mem'ber of the convention who may still have objections to it, would with me,
doubt a little of his own infallibility-and to make manifest our unanimity put
his name to this instrument." Franklin then moved that the Constitution
when signed be attested as "done in convention by the unanimous consent
of the States represented." This latter wise suggestion made it possible for
the document to be presented to the Congress and to the legslatures as one
having the united support of all who were present. Of the twenty-eight Masons
who were elected delegates, only eighteen remained throughout and finally
signed the Constitution, but numbered among them were some of the strongest
and ablest, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, Rufus King, James Madison, Robert Morris, Charles Pinckney, Roger Sherman and George Washington, to name but a few.
These men were equally prominent in the great struggle for ratification
for it soon became evident that the leading men of the various states did not
regard the instrument as even workable, much less a great piece of masterful
planning for government. The first state to ratify was Delaware on December
7, with New Jersey, Georgia and Connecticut following in rapid succession.
The real struggle began in Pennsylvania and extended into Massachusetts,
'New York and Virginia. The latter two states did not finally ratify until
after the ninth state, New Hampshire, had accepted the Constitution thus
insuring its trial, and Rhode Island held out until the last, the Constitution
winning in that state by only two votes. The pivotal struggle had been in
Pennsylvania, and had the Constitution failed there, it is unlikely that it could
have been adopted. Upon so slender a thread had hung the destinies of the
United States, that if eighteen men had voted differently, ratification would
have been defeated. If ten delegates in Massachusetts, six in Virginia and two
in New York had changed their votes there would have been no "more perfect
union" and the United States would not have come into existence at that
time, at least.
Such was the situation in which a new fo rm of government was launched
with all the misgivings and dire forebodings that could be assembled about
one enterprise. That the form of government set up under the Constitution
has endured is attributable to three main factors; first, the early return of
p·rosperity with new confidence in the future of the country, second, the per-

I

sonality of George Washington and the utter confidence which everyone had
in his honesty both of intention and act, and lastly the administrative genius
of Alexander Hamilton who had done all he could to write a different sort o
constitution and, failing in that~ had turned with equal fervor to the task
making the accepted one work. It is to these three factors together with t e
willingness of the American people to live under the form of government wh· h
they had adopted and the sound interpretations of that governing docu nt
by successive presidents and judges, that we owe the unprecedented gro th
of the United States and the happiness of its people,
It is a little short of amazing that a Constitution written one hundre and
fifty years ago and designed for the government of thirteen relatively mall
's tates with a population of only 3,000,000 people should have survived th tremendous development that has taken place since that time. Not only h~s the
country grown to forty-eight states, 3,000,000 square miles and 128,000,000
people, but the problems of such a nation have grown beyond the physical bortlers. The development 1of · rapid transportation, even more· rapid communication and the involvments of interstate, intrastate and foreign commerce have
pre;ented to each subsequent generation problems of which the founders never
dreamed and could they have foreseen them, it is entirely probable that they
would have considered it utterly impossible to draft a Constitution that could
meet such situations. Nevertheless the problems have confrdnted the nation and
we have come to this day through as amazing a development as any people
have ever witnessed and the Constitution with its relatively few amendments
has proved adequate to every difficulty.
We are not to infer from this progress and the adaptability of the Constitution that it has all been without a struggle. In every generation with its
growing difficulties there has been a small or larger group ready to demand
'change in both Constitution and form of government. There are always with us
those to whom the old is unacceptable and who cry for change, and there are
likewise those who would not hesitate to change both language and form if
need be, to accomplish their purposes.
This is not confined to any one person or set of persons any more than it
is confined to any one age. We have those today who tell us that the Consti.tution is outmoded, that it can no longer meet the changing needs of current
times,. and that our form of government as established by the Constitution is
fast breaking down. These people would have us believe that if only the country
would adopt the constitutional changes they suggest, or scrap it altogether for
some other form of government, that all our worries and cares would drop
away like flies in cold winter and that the gates of an earthly paradise would
be thrown open to a weary people. We are told that we now have but one
choice; either that of Communism or Fascism, both forms of dictatorship, the
one of the masses and the other of the classes represented by one person as
dictator. Admittedly, there is always danger of the overthrow of government,
especially when you have accepted the principle that that government derives
its just powers from the consent of the governed and when any party in government holds human rights and life lightly, it is to be expected that aroused
groups of people will likewise hold life and property lightly, ·b ut I do not
concede that we have only the choices already referred to.
There is another choice that is ours and one which we 'have so far elected
to continue and that is the preservation of the American system of representative government, known as democracy. My brethren, there is a danger to that
system today but the greatest danger is not from the comparatively small
group of Communists nor is it from the even smaller group of Fascists. It is
from that group of elected representatives of the people who take their responsibilities lightly and who have forsaken both their own principles and the
principles of the representative government by their willingness to take the pro-

1

447

gram of those who would dictate for all. When the elected representatives of
he people become content to take program and no longer assemble to make
. rogram for America then, my brethren, democracy is on the way out, ~d ~e
ill turn to some other form of government and you may be sure that 1t will
b one that promises much and delivers little and that little under a despotism
th t makes life miserable for those who love freedom, life, liberty and the pursui of happiness.
The success of the United States up to this day has been due to a basically
sou form of government and the willingness of the people to submit to that
gove nment. The best governmental system in the world will not wor~ if there
is no on the part of the governed a spirit of obedience and cooperation. If we
want to preserve for ourselves and our posterity the government under which
we h ve enjoyed the fruits of our labors, under which we have been free to
enjoy life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness there must be a re~e~ication
of ourselves to the principles of representative government and a w11lmgness
to be bound by those things which mean the greatest good for the. g:eatest
number. There must be a new dedication to obedience to law and an ms1stence
upon the application of that law to all alike, which implies a willingness to
have the law applied to ourselves.
The Constitution of the United St ates does not need to be scrapped or made
over but many unsound ideas of government do need to be scrapped and many
people do need to be made over. This country needs a new bi~th .o f t~at sense
of personal responsibility that characterized the fo~nders and 1t hkew1~e needs
something of the old reverence for those things which have proved their worth
over the years.
We need as citizens and as Masons, to look back and see from what we
have been d;livered by our form of government under · the Constitution and
ask ourselves if we would have been better off without it.
We need to look back over a century and a half of history, see the tremendous changes which have taken place under the Constitution and ask ourselves if it is likely that any change can occur in the future that will be so
great that that same Constitution cannot find the way under law to preserve
the welfare of the nation .
We need to look at all those things which we hold dear in family, home
and country and ask ourselves again if any other nation in all the world enjoys
what we accept so carelessly.
We need to look about us in the world and see the misery that follows in
the wake of revolution the destruction of life and liberty that characterizes.
tyranny of any form a~q ask ourselves if we want that in the United States.
We need, as Masons, to bring ourselves to a fuller knowledge of th.e
blessings that surround us, to a greater appreciation of the beneficent for~ .of.
government under which we live, and as we love our homes and our families
and as we cherish the freedom which we have to worship God as we see fit, we
need to cherish and revere that which stands between us and tyrants-THE
CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES.

Supreme Grand Master, Whom we approach with the tenderest words we
know upon our lips : Father, mother, love; now at this hour of sorrow we c me
to Thee. We are remembering with overflowing hearts the good men and rue
who so short a time ago formed part of our mystic circle, but who walk wi h us
no more. Even though our hearts are sad we refuse to believe that the goodness, unselfish devotion, and all the excellencies of mind and soul that c~arac­
terized our lost companions have perished forever. The very remembraqce of
them is a benediction, and just as the flower sprouts from the seed, atlld the
glorious blossom of beauty and fragrance bursts from the bud, we are sure
these souls are finding larger and more splendid fulfillment in fairer realms.
Goodness and beauty, truth and love are immortal, because they partake of
Thy Divine nature.
'
We thank Thee that we were permitted the inspiration of their companionship, and rejoice in the blessedness of their memory. "Eternal rest grant them,
0 Lord, and may Perpetual Light shine upon them." Comfort the loved ones
left behind, and may they feel beneath them the Everlasting Arms.
"O Lord, support us all the day long, until the shadows lengthen, and
the evening comes, and the busy world is hushed, and the fever of life is
over, and our work is done; then, in Thy Great Mercy, grant us a safe
lodging, and a holy rest, and peace at the last." Amen.

To the M.'. w:. Grand' Lodge of California:
From the beginning of time men have gathered in one manner or another
to take note of their friends' departure from the activities of this world. This
custom has been adopted as an essential part of Masonry. It is altogether
fitting and proper that we do this because from these occasions are drawn
many useful lessons of life. Each one erects his own monument in his character and deeds. From a review of the deeds of our friends we may learn to
emulate his good qualities and avoid the pitfalls that temporarily ensnared
him. Thus we improve conditions for ourselves and others.
While we may not here review the good deeds of each of those whose
passing we note, and while each one knows only too few of those listed, yet
each one present may take part in this ceremony in realizing that every one
named in this list was for one or more years the Master of his Lodge and
the director of its activities in the community. He had many friends who
placed him in that position and recognized his sterling qualities. They mourn
his loss as a friend and we may well, in this short ceremony, recognize his
service to Masonry.
As we turn our thoughts to those one hundred and ninety-seven brethren
of this Grand Lodge, who have passed to the great beyond during the last
year, may we contemplate the great labors they have performed in our
vineyard and increase our resolve to improve the world by our lives.

By this appropriate pause to pay our respects to the departed members
of this Grand L-odge, let us be reminded that the greatest tribute to a friend
is to give him of our time and counsel while he is here. On the other side
he works along without us. Here we can at least share his burdens and cheer
him along the way. His path may be easy or it may be hard but whichever it
is true friendship should never be lacking. This spirit of friend.s hip has been.
so well expressed by our late dearly loved P. G. M. David J. Reese that his
words are again recalled to you here.
'Tis only a half truth the poet has sung,
Of the house ·by the side of the way;
Our Master-.,had neither a house nor a home,
But He walked with the crowd day by day,
And I think when I read of the poet's desire,
That a house by the road would be good;
But service is found in its tenderest form,
When we walk with the crowd in the road.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

457

So I say, let me walk with the men in the road,
Let me seek out the burdens that crush;
Let me speak a kind word of good cheer to the weak
Who are falling behind in the rush.
There are wounds to be healed, there are breaks we must mend.
There's a cup of cold water to give;
And the man in the road by the side of his friend
Is the man who has learned how to live.
Then tell me no more of the house by the road·
There's only one place I can live :
'
It's there with the men who are toiling along
Who are needing the cheer I can give.
It is pleasant to live in the house ·by the way
And befriend, as the poet has said
But the Master is bidding us, "Bear ye their load,
For your rest waiteth yonder ahead."
I could not remain in the house by the road,
And watch as the toilers go on,
Their faces beclouded with pain and with sin,
So burdened their strength nearly gone.
I'll go to their side, I'll speak in good cheer,
I'll help them to carry their load,
And I'll smile at the man in the house by the way
As I walk with the crowd in the road.

Out there in the road that goes by the house,
When the poet is singing his song,
I'll walk and I'll work, midst the heat of the day
And I'll help falling brothers along;
'
Too :busy to live in the house by the way,
Too happy for such an abode.
And my heart sings its praise to the Master above
Who is helping me serve in the road.
Respectfully submitted,

By CHAS. M. WOLLENBERG

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Brother Leonard Sumner Leavy was born in San Francisco March 5, 1876.
He was educated in the public schools of San Francisco, and graduated from
the University of California in 1898 with high honors. Later he was graduated
from the School of Pharmacy. In 1899 he entered the service of the City and
County of San Francisco and continued in its employ in many different
capacities, ·until the time of his death on June 11, 1937.
In 1923, under some new amendments to the city charter, he was placed
at the head of the purchasing department, a most important position, and in
which he not only obtained local, but national recognition. From that time on
he played a most important role in the administration of the affairs of this
city. In 1932 a new charter was adopted creating the office of controller. He
was placed in this most important position on January 8, 1932, and served in
the capacity of controller until his death. In this capacity he became the most
important cog in our municipal administration.
Fearless and honest, yet kindly, he knew how to refuse and not only built
up a budget that was lived up to, but placed our city in the forefront of municipalities financially.
In Masonry, he was initiated December 2, 1916, passed to the degree of
Fellowcraft on December 11, 1916, and raised to the Sublime Degree of Master
Mason on December 22, 1916, in Paul Revere Lodge No. 462. He serv~d
that Lodge as Master in 1921. On May 14, 1926, he dimitted to become a
charter member of Veritas Lodge No. 640, where he remained a valued member until his death. He served this Grand Lodge as Inspector of the 4lst
Masonic District from 1923 to 1935. In the latter year he was appointed a
member of the special committee on Financing Building Projects, which he
occupied to the end. He was a meinber of the Scottish Rite for twenty years,
where he served as .Wise Master of the Rose Croix. In the Rite his worth
was recognized by the conferring of the honorary distinction of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor.
A week before his passing, in apparent perfect health, he remarked, itJ
discussing a funeral he had attended that day, "that he wanted a simple Ma~
sonic funeral, and his friend, the speaker, if living to conduct it."
Death came to this, our brother, without a moment's warning, on the
evening of June 11th. Walking home in company with his son-in-law he staggered and fell to the street; death was instantaneous.
I quote from the daily press: "Neither the hurried newspaper pieces,
written with fingers still stiffened by shock, nor the funeral-born eulogies
of his fellow officials, can begin to tell the story of what the death of Leonard
Leavy means to San Francisco, or what his life has meant to the people of
the city." And so his remains lay in state under the dome of the City Halt,
where he had served these many years and his multitude of friends listened
· to the Mayor and other public officials give tribute to his worth and probity.
He was buried from this hall on June 16th. The craft services were
under the auspices of Veritas Lodge No. 640, of which the deceased was a
founder and Past Master. For this occasion the regular officers gave .way
to others. Past Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg acted as Master, with

In Memoriam
IRA FRANCIS THOMPSON
By ELLSWORTH MEYER

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Since the last communication of this Grand Lodge the Supreme Architect of the Universe has raised many of our brethren to the Celestial Lodge
above. It is fitting that we should note their passing and add our humble words
of tribute to their memory.
Among those who have gone to the Lodge Eternal is Worshipful Brother
Ira Francis Thompson, late Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of California, who for many years was an active and beloved member of · the Grand
Lodge.
Brother Thompson was born on a farm in Crawford County, Wisconsin,
on June 20, 1885. He was orphaned by the passing of both his father and
mother while he was still a baby. His childhood, therefore, was largely spent
behind the plow and in the performance of the other arduous tasks incident
to farm life. At the age of fifteen he came to Eureka, California, where he
secured his high school education. He then enrolled at the University of California at Berkeley and not only earned his own way, but by prodigious effort,
typical of him, he completed the · usual six year course of undergraduate
and law studies in four years. He was thereupon admitted to the practice of
law in 1909 and after one year in one of the leading firms in Oakland, he
moved to Los Angeles where he engaged in general practice until 1923. In
that year his ability and reputation brought him an appointment as a judge
of the Superior Court of that county. The three years he spent on that bench
brought recognition of his talents and his availability for higher office.
In 1926 he was elevated to the DistriCt Court of. Appeal. He soon disclosed that he was well equipped for appellate court work and his elevation,
in 1932, to the Supreme Court of California was received by the bench, bar
and public with the highest approbation. In fact, he had come to be regarded
as such an able and seasoned jurist, surprise would have been caused by calling
attention to the fact that he had reached the highest tribunal of this state less
than ten years after his first judicial appointment, and at the early age of
forty-seven years. His professional career was remarkable and this brief chronicle of his advancement of itself would indicate that he possessed rare talents,
a sterling character and was living proof that under the American system of
government even the freckle-faced boy behind the plow can reach the stars.
This account of his professional career would indicate a life full of activity, and"yet Judge Thompson found time and energy for many other activities and avenues of service to his fellow man. Since we cannot hope to trace
his manifold contributions we shall limit ourselves to an account of his Masonic
career.
He received the three degrees in Elysian Lodge No. 418._at Los Angeles
in 1916, and served as Master in 1921. He was president of the fall class of
1923 in the Los Angeles bodies of the Scottish Rite and, being a remarkably
good ritualist, was soon portraying leading roles in those degrees. As a consequence of his work he was decorated a Knight Commander of the Court of
Honor in 1931.
Shortly prior to 1924 a movement was begun, having for its purpose the
establishment of a Masonic clubhouse near the campus of the University of

GRAND . LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

461.

California at Los Angeles. The initial group of interested parties turned to
him for leadership and as the plan evolved · he became chairman of the board
of directors, which position he still held at his passing. He derived particular
pleasure from his connection with the Clubhouse 'and always entertained the
keenest interest and affection for the young people there, sentiments which
they heartily reciprocated toward him. To do justice to his labors for the
clubhouse alone would require more than our allotted time, but it may truly
be said that he, more than any other one person, was responsible for the magnificent edifice which stands near the southern campus, a ,mpnument to Masonry
and a man.
In 1929, as the new community of Westwood Hills began its phenomenal
growth, it became apparent that a Masonic Lodge should be established there:
Several groups began but they naturally gravitated into one, with the· result
that Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677 was instituted in 1930, with Brother Thompson, already a Past Master, as its first Master, and i:he father of ·itS plan of
Masonic research. He was reelected and served throughout 1931 a!So.
For many years he served the Grand Lodge in varying capacities. In·addition to his thirteen years as chairman of the Board of Directors of the club"·
house, he for several years was a member of the Committee on Ma.s onic Education; during 1934 he was on the Grievance Committee, and in 1935 was Grand
Orator. Many present tQday will recall the stirring and masterful grand oration which he delivered from this platform at that communic?.tion.
His honors, civic and fraternal, were mariy and varied, but in the hea'rts
of his friends he received his greatest recognition. He possessed a character
which was never questioned and even in his greatest triumphs he was ever
mindful of his early struggles and always helping some one up the path of
life. He adored his Creator, he was an uncompromiSing ·patriot, a devoted
husband and father, a true and trusty friend, a benefactor of his fellow man,
a man and a Mason.
His passing on August 4, 1937, a.t the age of fifty-two years, se.ems all
too soon ; yet
As today we him revere,
And his farewell we seem to hear,
As he puts out to sea, sailing toward eternity,
Uplifted high in heart and hope are we,
·
Until we doubt not for one so true
There must be other nobler· work to do.

In Memoriam
THOMAS FLINT
By DANA R. WELLER
To the M.'. W.'. Gra11d Lodge of California:

Thomas Flint, born May 19, 1858, at San Juan Bautista, and died November 18, 1936, at Hollister, aged 78 years.
He was married December 2, 1896, to Anna May Fisk, at Woodstock,
Vermont, who bore him five children, all of whom survive him.
After receiving preliminary schooling in California he attended Dartmouth
College, graduating in 1880 with the degree of A. B., and received the A. M.
degree from the same college in 1883.
Initiated in Texas Lodge No. 46, at San Juan Bautista, on March 12, 1881,
and raised April 23, 1881; served as Senior Warden in 1883-4, and· as Master
in · 1884 ahd in 1892.
In Grand Lodge he was appointed Grand Sword Bearer in 1893, and in
1894 was elected Junior Grand Warden; 1895 Senior Grand Warden; 1896
Deputy Grand Master: and in 1897 was elected and installed Grand Master.
All these positions he filled with credit and honor.
In 1895-6 he served as Grand High Priest of Royal Arch Masons.
In 1894-5 as Grand Patron of the Order of Eastern Star.
His fraternal activity was not confined to Masonry alone.
In 1891-2 he was Grand President of the Native Sons of the Golden West.
He was a charter member and Past Exalted Ruler of Hollister Lodge
No. 1436, B. P. 0. E.
In reporting upon his address as Grand Master the committee stated :
"He has wielded the emblem of authority with which you invested him unsullied by any act unworthy 0£ our noble fraternity, and in such a manner as to
reflect honor upon himself."'
·
His activity in Grand Lodge did not cease on his retirement as Grand
Master. He was constant in his attendance at our communications, always
ready and willing to assume any task imposed upon him.
In 1908 he was appointed a Trustee of the Masonic Homes, serving until
1917. His services to the Homes were of incalculable benefit. His soundness
of judgment, the wisdom of his counsel, and his invariable kindness and courtesy endeared him to all with whom he came in contact, and aided materially
in paving the way to the present high state of efficiency in the management Of
our institutions.
"
In civic affairs his career was no less notable and honorable. Elected to
the State Senate in 1889, he served four terms, or until 1905, the last ten years
as President pro tern, a position he filled with great distinction.
Perhaps the greatest eulogy which could be pronounced upon the life of
this truly distinguished man and Mason is that contained in an editorial printed
in the local paper at Hollister shortly after his death, which is quoted in part:
"Thomas Flint is dead. But the stories of his hatred of political skullduggery, the stories of his love of fair play and honesty in dealing with his
fellow man, and the stories of his devotion as a husband and a father, will
not die with him.

man who passed up the governorship because he refused to bow to the dictates
of a 'political boss' he mistrusted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC .HISTORY
To the M:. w:, Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History has made no rare or dramatic disi:overies du.ring_ .the past year, but we are able to report a research that has
added definit~ irifo_rmation concernin~ our Grand Lodge history for the first
five years of its existence. The facts, briefly, are as follows:
The f).rst volume of our recognized Proceedings covers the records of Grand
Lodg11 from its formation in 1850 to the year 1854 inclusive. A foreword in
that volume states that the proceedings were reprinted in 1856 by order of the
~r~nd Lodge, because of the lack of sufficient copies then existing. Records
ind1~ate that 250 co~ies had originally .been printed for each Grand Lodge
sess1oq of the preceding five years. It has always seemed' strange that out of
that total of 1250 copies none seemed to 'have escaped the ravages of time.
There were vague reports that copies did exist in far away places. Meanwhile
a popular story had grown to the effect that all of the original copies had been
purposely dest.roy~d to conce.al certain unpleasant happenings that they were
supposed to contain, and· which had been omitted from the reprinted edition.
The story_ seen:ed. plaustble because there is definite knowledge that certain
!roubles. did exist in those years, and which does not appear in the Proceedings which we now have.
Under these circumstances we were fortunate this year in locating a set
of the Proceedings as originally printed for the Constitutional Convention of
1850, and for the Grand Lodge sessions for .t he years 1850, 1851, 1852, 1853
and 1854. These were kindly placed in our hands for examination and for
comparison with the Proceedings that we now recognize as official. The work
was som~":'hat laborio~s, because there had been considerable rearrangement
of the original Proceedings for each year. Transactions for one day were often
transposed to another to provide a different order or sequence. Notes were
carefully prepared, and ph0tostatic copies made in some instances, from which
a thorough report is being made for our files.
.
· It was disappointing not to have found the story that those original Proceedings were supposed to contain, but we can now definitely refute the tradition that it occurs in those original records. In short, the greater part of the
report of Grand Master Hyam for that year is miss ing, In the first page
of his address we find this note: "The subject referred to by the Grand Master
in connection with the late difficulties in this state, commencing here and
ending on the 57th page of his address, are left out by mutual consent of' him?elf and Gra~a .Lodge." We would certainly like to know just what appeared
in those 56 missing pages ! From other sources, however, we have some documentary evidence of some of the things that must have been discussed in the
missing parts of his address, but like our brethren of 1852, we have decided
·
to omit that information from this printed report.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

465

During the year we have prepared an index with cross reference; of the
Proceedings of Grand Lodges since its organization. This painstaking work
of several months on the forty-four volumes of our Proceedings has opened
a storehouse of valuable Masonic information, and made it available and usable.
It is our purpose to enlarge the scope of this index to cover other historical
sources.
On August 20th of this year we addressed a letter to the secretaries of
our jurisdiction asking for copies of Lodge bulletins and publications for
reports on the compilation of the histories of their fifty-year Masons, and
whether Lodges had fireproof safes or vaults for their records. The prompt
and generous response of the secretaries overwhelmed us to such an extei;it
that we have not been able to express individual thanks, and must take this
means of expressing our appreciation for their wonderful cooperation.
The number of bulletins has overtaxed our capacity for display, but we
are showing as many .as possible in our exhibit. Replies to our question indicated that Lodges are taking a greater interest in preparing histories of their
fifty-year Masons, and are making a splendid job of this. feature. Some Lodges
are now even securing the history of each member.
There has been a gratifying increase in the number of Lodges that now
have fireproof facilities and reports show that many others are making plans
for suitable protection for their records and relics. In a trip which members
of our committee made with the Grand Master among Lodges of the Mother
Lode we were particularly impressed with the vaults that had been constructed
at Hornitos, Dutch Flat and Georgetown. These small mountain Lodges
have set examples worthy of all imitation.
Here are a few records of unusual years of service that have been given
by faithful brethren to some of the subordinate Lodges:
One brother served Bear Mountain Lodge No. 76 as its Master for twenty
consecutive years.
Brother William Bull Meek was Master of Gravel Range Lodge No. 59
for 28 years. These were not consecutive.
Forbestown Lodge No. 50 had Brother William Schultze as Master for
28 years and four months.
The record as Master seems to go to Brother William Adams, who was
installed as Master of ,Hornitos Lodge No. 98 for thirty consecutive years.
Ione Lodge No. 80 had a Senior Steward who occupied the same position
for thirty-three years.
George W. Pennington was Secretary of Pacific Lodge No. 136 for
thirty-five years.
Yolo Lodge No. 81 had the same Secretary for forty-three years.
Brother Joel Wilder was installed as Tiler of Union Lodge No. 58 for
fifty-three years.
Brother John · Fisher has been a member of Hiram Lodge No. 43 for
sixty-seven years. He has served as an officer for sixty-six of those years,
with twenty-three years in the Master's chair.
We are informed that one Lodge appears to have carried the name of a
woman on its rolls for many years. We wish to stress the fact that they carried the name only. It appears that she belonged to the Eastern Star an.d simply
signed the wrong roll book upon initiation due to the fact that a brother s_erved
as secretary for both organizations and picked up the wrong book. The mistake
was not discovered until recently.

Last night you had an exhibition of lantern slides, depicting certain phases
of Grand Lodge history. The serious pictures were made from material in our
historical files, and are the qeginning of what we hope will some day be a
complete set of lantern slides that may be loaned for entertainment and education in subordinate Lodges. The pictures of Saschel Woods, who brought
the first charter to California, and of Past Grand Master Hyam, were obtained
only recently after a search of five or six years. This will give you some idea
of the difficulty of building up · the complete collection that we hope to secure.

done that they unanimously elected Brother William H. Taylor as their first
Grand Master, and Brother Quezon as the Deputy Grand Master. They adopted
as unwritten law that there should be rotation thereafter, and since that time
the office of Grand Master has been regularly alternated between an American
and a native of the Philippines.
The first act of Brother Taylor ilS Grand Master was to appoint Brother
Buencamino as the Grand Bible Bearer of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands. A few days later there was a public parade of the fraternity, which
was something unknown there before that time. It was a proud day for all,
but particularly for the Grand Bible Bearer. With the sacred Book open to
the world before him he passed down streets that were lined. with thousands
of awestruck natives. To many of them a new light was dawning. Here and
th.ere among those who watched the procession pass he saw the bright faces of
many to whom he had read the Holy Word in secret places in those days
before Masonry was brought into the open as it was by the actions of American Masons and our California brethren in particular. We hope to give you
more of the interesting story of the Philippine Lodges at some later date.
Again we would like to remind Lodges of the desirability of maintaining
scrap books of Lodge activities. Lodge bulletins, newspaper clippings, and
pictures will do much to inform new members of your traditions and landmarks. Many Lodges are doing splendid work along these lines and find it
stimulating to the membership at large.
As in several past years the work of your committee is being carried on
by voluntary workers and without appropriation from Grand Lodge. We wish
to express appreciation to those many individuals who have done their bit in
this work and to invite others to join with us. You will find it interesting and
helpful at the same time.
We recommend that a Committee on Masonic History be continued. We
ask for no appropriation at this time.

466

The Grand Lodge of California has a peculiar interest in the Grand Lodge
of the 'Philippine Islands, and we are indebted to Brother William H. Taylor
of this city for an outstanding research on the history of Masonry in those
· islands. We can only give a brief hint in this report of the interesting story
that will be available to you at a later time.
The first attempt to introduce Masonry in the Philippines was in 1756and since that time the fraternity has suffered from bitter intolerance, persecutions and even executions. American Masonry was taken there by our soldiers at the time of the Spanish-American war, but the 'first Lodge under the
jurisdiction of California was not chartered until October 10, 1901. Two other
California Lodges were chartered in the following ten years. In 1912 these
three Lodges, with the encouragement of the Grand Lodge of California,
formed the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands., It is interesting to note
that when they drafted their Constitution they took the Constitution of the
Mother Grand Lodge of California, and simply substituted the "Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands" wherever the California name appeared. The next
step was to amalgamate the other twenty-seven Masonic Lodges which held
charters from various far flung jurisdictions, but the consolidation did not
occur until 1917.
Those other Lodges had passed through bitter trials because of the antagonisms of the officials of the dominating church, and the subservient public
officials: The same house was seldom used more than once for a meeting place.
Wh,ile a Masonic meeting was being held it was customary to invite the young
sons and daughters of the members to make merry with song and dance as an
excuse for the gathering. Meanwhile the faithful brethren met in the most
secluded parts of the building. Secret · hiding places were provided for paraphernalia, and Lodge furniture could be ingeniously converted into innocent
appearing household objects.
On one occasion the civil 'authorities unexpectedly arrived to raid such a
meeting. The young folks hushed their singing and the dance ceased. The
brethren opened their doors to the officers, who rushed in and found a group
of substantial men engaged in that game of chance known as "monte." The
part of the banker was being played by the Lodge Master. After the fruitless
raid was over the brother was congratulated for his foresight in coming to
the meeting with a deck of playing cards and the equipment of a gambler.
·
Natives had been forbidden to read or own the King James version of
the Bible! bu~ for years Brother Felipe Buencamino, Sr., would gather natives
around him m caves and secret meeting places and read to them from the
sacred Book. On one occasion, near Manila, the church authorities secured a
motion picture, which was then quite a novelty, and charged one Bible as the
price of admission to the show. The Bibles thus collected were burned in the
public square.
When fusion of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines was completed with
the Regional Grand Lodge of the natives, our American brethren were outnumbered nine to one in the voting representation. Naturally it was presumed
that the Philippine brethren would elect their leader, Brother Manuel Quezon,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Masonic Education beg leave to submit the following
report:
Your committee began the year's work with a new chairm.a n and six new
members. We were of the opinion that we should first make a survey of the
act.ivities of Grand Lodge since 1915 along Masonic educational lines. We,
therefore, carefully read those portions of the official Proceedings of the annual commu11ications of this Grand Lodge during the twenty-one years last
past which related to Masonic education. This study included the ~eports of
previous committees on Masonic education, extracts from the messages of
Grand Masters and Grand Orators, recommendations of the Committee on
Finance and of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and the action
of Grand Lodge thereon. We found that while it was proper Masonic education, yet the means to be adopted and the educational lines to be followed,
have been subjects of widespread diversity of opinion. In other words, the
problem was one of method.
Our study then was directed to cull out of these proceedings accepted,
principles underlying a program of Masonic education. We found there were
three, viz. :

1. That Masonic education should be confined to Masonry subjects;
2. That Masonic education should be directed to the candidate, and
3. That Masonic education should not be compulsory.
Since these three principles are the residuum of our experience and apparently have met with the approval of this Grand Lodge, they were adopted
as the basis of our program of Masonic education for the year.
We then turned our attention to other Grand Lodges. We found fhat some
thirty Grand Lodges of the United States have been experimenting with the
problem. From this study we finally concluded that the best method to be
adopted was a Lodge system of Masonic education.
This system is simple, direct,' and costs but little money. The Worshipful
Master of a constituent Lodge appoints a committee of three, five or seven
members.. The candidates meet with the Lodge committee four times-once
before taking the first degree and once after each degree, including the third.
The candidate has nothing to read, nothing to study and no examination
to pass. He only listens while a member of the committee explains something
of the history of Masonry, of the organization of the Lodge and of Grand
Lodge, of a Mason's financial obligations, of the proper attitude of a Mason
to politics and religion, as well as a little of the symbols, rituals, ideals and
purposes of Masonry.
Our Grand Lodge committee suggested ten subjects of discussion for each
of the four meetings, making forty in all. We have appended to this report
a list· of these forty subjects.
We decided to experiment with this system ·in about half a dozen Lodges
of the jurisdiction. But the plan seemed to be so well received that perhaps
thirty Lodges tried it out and found that it worked successfully.
However, we early learned that there was one obstacle to be overcome.
We had no authentic printed information upon these various subjects and we
had no money to publish or buy any. So we communicated with the Board of
General Activities of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of New York. This
board kindly forwarded several copies of its "committee papers." These papers

GRAND LODGE O_F CALIFORNIA

469

comprise a booklet of 138 pages. Your committee read the booklet very carefully and, save for minor changes to conform to California work, we foWld
it to be readable, practical and authentic. We passed copies of this booklet ~o
several Lodge committees and are advised that the booklet meets with their
approval.
This booklet contains a chapter upon each of the. forty suggested subjects
referred to above. We believe that if the booklet could be rewritten so as to
conform to our work it would fill a great need in this jurisdiction. As a
matter of fact, o.u r committee has already prepared a list of the necessary
changes.
We communicated with the New York committee and asked whether, if
duly authorized, we would be permitted to use their pamphlet by copying a
part, word for word, and rewriting the rest, of course giving New York due
recognition. New York graciously replied, in part, "Indeed you may use the
·
material in any way you wish."
We are informed by a reliable California publishing concern that 10,000
copies of the booklet, as so rewritten, could be furnished this Grand Lodge at a
total cost of $987. That cost is .less than ten cents a copy.
Permit us to add that during the twenty-one years this Grand Lodge has
been experimenting with Masonic education our constituent Lodges have raised
121 561 candidates in Masonry. If each of those Masons had been told somethi~g about Masonry what a well informed body of Masons we would today
have in this jurisdiction.
Based upon our study and experience this Masonic year your committee
makes the following recommendations:

1. Tnat the Committee on Masonic Education be continued next year, its
members to be appointed by the incoming Grand Master.
2. That the above outlined Lodge system of Masonic education be used
next year among such Lodges as· agree thereto.
3. That the committee be directed to re-write the booklet above referred
to and known as "Committee Mem~rs' Papers," so it may conform with the
requirements of this jurisdiction.
4. That when approved by the Grand Master as to contents the Grand
Secretary be directed to print 10,000 copies of the booklet as rewritten, and
to distribute the same as he may determine.
5. That the sum of $1200 be appropriated to pay the cost of such publication and for incidental expenses of the committee.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California: .
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry. begs leave to report as follows:
Clandestine activity among the pseudo-Masonic Lodges of California has
been confined to the irregular and spasmodic functioning of their subordinate
bodies during the past year. In ~eneral they have maintained their several
existences as set forth in our report at the last communication of Grand
Lodge. Some of the irregular bodies, though, have shown some real activity,
probably due to racial rather than purely Masonic stimuli. For instance, N egro
bodies: Brother Roullard of · our committee ceports that the N egro Hiram of
Tyre Grand Lodge, which was split wide open in 1935, carrying their differences into the courts revived sufficiently to hold its 27th general communication
in Fresno from June 20-23, 1937, when one L. P. Lea of Los Angeles was
elected Grand Master. The local F resno Lodge is named Raisin City No. 5, of
which Joe Farley is Master. It seems that the members of the Negro Eastern
Star Grand Chapter meet together with the masculine Masons. There is very
definite antagonism of this group toward the Prince Hall bodies and Masons.
The other Negro Grand Lodge which was known as Most Worshipful Sov~
ereign Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons has changed its name to
"Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Free and ·Accepted Masons of
California Jurisdiction." The annual Communication of 1936 re-elected T heodore Moss as Grand Master. Their bodies were to hold their 1937 communication in Portland, July 19.
Mexican Masonry
There is little change in the organizations of the Mexican Masonic groups
in the state. The two factions-to-wit, Benemerito Rito Nacional and the
original Rito Nacional which resulted from a refusal of the Grand Master
Ramirez in Mexico City to divide his authority with consulting ' groups-have
maintained their individual Lodges. •rhe efforts. of the Mexican Grahd Lodge
of Texas through its deputy Mateo F. F lores to wean away the local Lodges.
of the older Rite does not seem to have been successful. Very few have· deserted
the original Rito Nacional or the Benemerito Rito.
··

Filipino Masonry during the past year. In several cities of California invitations'
to public installation of officers ceremonies", public dances and social functions···
have been widely distributed.

General Luna Lodge No. 8, on March 27, 1937, in Music A rts H all, 233 South

and our Grand Master seems to have been handed an invitation though after the
festive event.

.The work of this committee has indirectly resulted in the publicizing the existence and activities of the Clandestine bodies. Our members have been made

many of the individual members of these clandestine bodies and some of the
responsible officers and representatives to seek for their organizations affiliation
with our Grand Lodge or recognition by our Grand Lodge. Many Mexican members of the Rito Nacional have sought ways and means by which they could be
affiliated with or join some regular Masonic Lodge or even to have their Lodges
taken in bodily by our Grand Lddge. Especially an effort was made by the
Deputy Grand Master of a Filipino Grand Lodge called Sov. Grand Lodge of
the Filipino Archipellago-operative in Califomia and not recognized by the
regular Grand Lodge· of the Philippine Islands which we recognize-to obtain
recognition for his body and his Lodges. He wrote a letter to our Grand
Secretary which was referred to your committee for investigation and report.
We contacted this individual and informed him that he had no Masonic standing
in California, that neither he nor his members could be admitted as visitors or
affiliates in our Lodges, that his organization had neither fraternal nor legal
Masonic standing in California and that it could probably be enjoined from using
the Masonic name under Chapter 409 of the Statutes of California of 1933. The
exclusive and sovereign character of our statewide jurisdiction was explained
to him and that he could receive no recognition from any American or English
Grand Lodge. He informed the Chairman of this committee that this Grand
Lodge of the Filipino Archipellago was chartered in 1916 by the Grand Orient
of Spain and in 1925 was released by that Sovereign Grand Body and was
formed into a Grand Lodge with a rite of 33 degrees modeled after the Scottish
Rite but conferring only up to the 18th degree in California.

not more than one Grand Lodge of Masons can have recognition and reiUlar

REPORT OF THE MASONC CLUB
UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA, BERKELEY

~II of the va rious groups functioned splendidly, and one new group was
organized, known as Omega Delta Mu, with its membership made up of De
Molays, active, inactive or majority members. These young men have been
most helpful whenever opportunity offered.

William H. Waste, President cif the Board of Directors, presented the auditor's report of the financial condition of the club,
and requested an appropriation for the support of the club for
the ensuing year. Referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF THE MASONC CLUB
UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA, LOS ANGELES
To the M." . w: .. Grand Lodge of California:
Your board of directors of the Masonic Club of the University of California
at Los Angeles fraternally submit their report for the year ending September
30, 1937.
We were stunned, as you all were, by the sudden passing of our chairman,
Brother Ira F. Thompson. Our work, our fraternity and our state have suffered an irreparable loss. The memory of his calm judgment and wise decisio~s
will ever be before us, serving as a guide and counselor in our meetings yet
to be held.
·
The following resolution was adopted by our Board at a meeting held September 30, 1937, and is made a part of this report:
Whereas, since the last meeting of the Board of Directors of the Masonic
Clubhouse at the University of California at Los Angeles, our beloved chairman,
the Hon. Ira F. Thompson, has been called from the scenes of his earthly
activities after having served as chairman of this board from its inception in
1924 until his passing on August 4, 1937; and
Whereas, he had guided the clubhouse project through the manifold problems of financing and constructing the beautiful structure in such an able manner
as to permit the presentation of the completed edifice to the Grand Lodge of
California not only without expense to that body, but with a substantial reserve
·remaining in the construction budget; and
Whereas, under his wise and friendly counsel the clubhouse and its activities
have been established on a sound financial basis and have become a great and
good influence in the campus and community life at Westwood; and
Whereas our late brother by his personal character and conduct earned and
enjoyed the ~onfidence, respect and affection of each member of this board;
now, therefore,
Be it resolved, that in the passing of Judge Thompson this board has suffered the irreparable loss of an able and conscientious leader and a devoted
friend and companion to whom we hereby acknowledge our gratitude and affection and to whose widow and family we express our deep sympathy in their
hour of trial, and
Be it further resolved, that the secretary be, and is hereby, directed to
spread this resolution upcin the minutes of this board and to transmit a copy
· of the same to the Thompson family.
·
The usefulness of the clubhouse continues to increase and no doubt such
will be .the case from year to year as each year brings an increase in the enrollment at- the University.

489

The Masonic Affiliate Council which supervises the activities of the club?ouse held 17 meetings. The social affairs were many and vari~, including 26
mformal dances held on Wednesday afternoons with an average attendance of
over 300. A ver?' successful play entitled "Wits End" was presented by the
Drama Club, which held _a total of 31 meetings, parties and teas by the Areme
Alu!11nae Group, a carnival sponsored by the Masonic Affiliate Council 27
affairs by the Areme Actives, including a Mothers' dinner and a Fathers' di~ner
~ormal parties, a fash~on show, and a benefit to provide funds for Thanksgiv.~
mg baskets to be furmshed under-privileged 'families.
The _Grand Matron and her suite were received and tea was served by the·

Arem~ girls.

T~e Board of _Directors entertained the clubhouse undergraduates and
Alumni at a dance with nearly 1,000 in attendance. The outstanding affair of the
year was a re~eption to our Most Worshipful Grand Master, Rollie W. Miller,
tendered by this board. In addition to our Grand Master and Mrs. Miller seven
Grand Lodge officers and their wives were present with a total of approxlmately
1,000.
Masonic affiliated students visited the clubhouse nearly 30 000 times upward
of 5,000 visits being to the study room.
'

Blight, Certi?ed Public Accountant, which is attached hereto and made a part
hereof. It will be noted that another 5% dividend has been received from the
United States National Bank, making a total recovery of 75%.

G.R OUP HOSPITAL . INSURANCE

SALE OF LIQUOR

The of.ficers of Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625 presented the
following:

J. W. Eddy, Past Master of Paso Robles Lodge N 286
pfreshented th~ f~llowing proposed substitute for Section oi29-A
o t e Constitution:

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

The undersigned, being members of this Grand Lodge, beg leave to present the following resolution:
Whereas, There exists in our minds a belief that further study is needed
on the subject of hospitalization for Masons; and
Whereas, As there is a definite statement of like mind by the Special
Committee on Hospitalization, embodied in their report, read before and ac. cepted by this Grand Lodge, on Tuesday, October 12, 1937; and
Whereas, There is in operation at the present time, in certain corporations, crafts and fraternities a plan wholly supported by the individual employe, craftsman, or member thereof, such plan being known as " Hospital
Group Insurance" ; and
Whereas, No less an authority on the costs and operation of hospitals than
Past Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg informed the undersigned that
all hospitals in the city of San Francisco, with one exception, are now admitting patients under the "Hospital Group Insurance Plan"; and
Whereas, Brother Wollenberg also stated that in the light of his experience he believed that some plan of "Hospital Group Insurance" might be
used by individual Masons of this jurisdiction, after due permission and authorization of this Grand Lodge; and
Whereas, Inasmuch as the premiums of "Hospital Group Insurance" are
:borne by the individual who may expect to benefit therefrom, and not by
his employer or fraternity, and are of amounts less than one dollar per month;
and
Whereas, according to the opinion of Bro. Chas. M. Wollenberg, permission from Grand Lodge is necessary to enai,>le the Masonic Lodges of this
jurisdiction to set up organizations which would enable its members to take
advantage of this low rate hospital insurance.
Therefore, be it resolved: That the Grand Master be instructed to appoint
a special committee to investigate the plan of Group Hospital Insurance and
to frame the necessary legislation enabling Masonic Lodges in this Jurisdiction
to set up an organization which would enable its members to take advantage of
the low rates established by this "Grnup Hospital Insurance," and to report
back at the next annual communication of this Grand Lodge.
JOHN

E. ROBERTS, W.M.

CLAUDE R. Cox, S.W.

w ALTER R. GENTRY, P.M.
JOHN J. HUMBLE, P.M.

Referred to the Committee on PoliCy and General Purpose\\

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California: ·
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to submit the following report :
Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the firm of
Ruckstell and Land, Certified Public Accounta.nts, to examine the books and
rec~rds ~f the. Grand Treasurer, the Grand $ecretary, the Masonic Homes of
~a!tforma and the Endowment Fund. The reports of Brother Webb's examina- ,
t10n .of al~ these records have been filed with your committee and have had its
cons1d~ra~1on. These reports are now on file with the records of Grand Lodge.
They md1cate that all records are correct and in proper shape and all. receipts
properly accounted for and all expenditures properly made.
. Brot~er W~bb is entitled to the commendation of this committee for the
time, the attention and the personal interest he has given to this examination.
It exc~eds t~e amount of remuneration which Grand Lodge has been making
f?r this service. Brother Webb feels that he is entitled to additfonal compensation. Heretofore, we have paid him for all the work that he has done for the
Ho~es as we!! . as for Grand Lodge a sum of $450.00. We feel that he is
entitled to additional compensation and have agreed with him on an additional
fee o~ $250.00. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption.
·
Resolved, That an additional compensation of $250.00 be allowed the firm
of Ruckstell & Land for the auditing done this past year and that the same
be charged against the general expenses of Grand Lodge.
Grand Lodge Week Activities
The report of the committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities fully sets
forth what has been done for the entertainment of the members who are
att<;nding' this Grand Lodge which report has been adopted by this Grand Lodge.
It 1s to be noted from the report of this committee that the amount expended
exceeds the amount allowed by approximately $1,200.00. While the committee
is relucta~t to see the amount of any appropriation exceeded, yet it feels that
the committee has done a very splendid job; that the entertainment Tuesday
night was high class and most enjoyable and also, that the trip to the Masonic
Home by the members of Grand Lajge was more than worth the while. This
latter item very largely accounts for the increase of the amount expended over
the amount previously appropriated to cover the expenses of this committee.
Your committee has approved of all of these expenditures and offers the .following resolution and recommends its adoption :
Resolved, That ~he sum of $3,200.00 or so much thereof as may be necessary

Custodian for Western Star Lodge
Your committee has for consideration the resolution of Brother Carl H .
Seamans, providing for the employment of a full-time custodian of the Masonic
relics and records, which are housed in the Masonic Temple at Old Shasta,
Tehama County, and making an appropriation therefor.
These valuable relics of early California Masonry, collected by Western
Star Lodge No. 2, are now being kept in a fire-proof vault which was constructed in 1928 by Grand Lodge at a cost of $3,000.00. They are, therefore,
being preserved from loss or deterioration.
Undoubtedly, these relics would bf/ of great interest to visiting Masons
and their friends and, although it would be gratifying to exhibit them as historical evidence of our long and honorable Masonic record in this state, your
committee is of the opinion that the present state of the finances of Grand Lodge
does not warrant the incurring of such expense. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
"Resolved, That the proposal to employ a full-time custodian of records
at the Masonic Temple at Old Shasta and making an appropriation therefor,
be and the same is hereby disapproved."

Your committee has for consideration the following resolution presented
by Brother Chas. R. Cooper.
"Resolved that the Finance Committee be authorized to make a suitable
appropriation for the publication of the manual for Blue Lodge Stated Meetings,

The proceedings of the 1936 Annual Communication on this subject reads as
follows : (Report of Committee on Policy.) If there is a real demand for a
manual it should be prepared and published. The committee recommends that the
Grand Secretary prepare such a manual if, in his judgment, there is a demand
for it and it is needed, and that the matter be referred to the Finance Committee for an appropriation for such publication, if in the future the Grand Secretary desires to publish it.
Your committee is of the opinion that, if the Grand Secretary believes
such a manual is needed and prepares the same for publication, the expenses
of publication not exceeding $200.00 should be authorized.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:

of Stated Meetings is needed, and if he prepares such a manual for publication,
he be authorized with the approval of the Grand Master to expend the sum of
$200.00 or as much thereof as may be necessary for the publication thereof."

The important and arduous duties of the office of Grand Secretary and the

than it was three years ago, is fully justified by the service rendered and should
·
remain unchanged.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved, That the resolution fixing the salary of the Grand Secretary at
$5,000.00 per annum be disapproved and that the salary of the office remain
unchanged.

Portrait of Grand Master
For many years it has been the policy of this Grand Lodge to appropriate
$150.00 for the portrait cif the retiring Grand Master. Last year, your committee raised this appropriation to $250.00 due to a belief that for the previous
sum appropriated: that is, $150.00, satisfactory portraits could not be obtained.
Your committee is still of the.same opinion. Your committee, therefore, recommends that our retiring Grand Master- the M.".W.".Rollie W. Miller-have
his portrait painted and present the bill . to the Grand Secretary, in an amount
not to exceed $250.00, who is authorized to pay the same and, when the portrait has been painted to be hung in the gallery of the Past Grand Masters.
Portraits of Preceding Grand Masters

lack of presence of the portraits of the following Past Grand Masters: William
Rhodes Hervey, William A. Sherman, Will H. Fischer, and George L. Jones.

portraits. We are still of the opinion that these Past Grand Masters should
have their portraits painted. Your committee, therefore, recommends that the

Grand Lodge Per Capita.
The Constitution provides for the levying of a per capita of 50 cents to
provide for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various committees. As will be
noted by the Budget, which is being submitted hereafter in this repo:t, the
revenue derived from this source, together with other revenues commg to
Grand Lodge, will not be sufficient to pay the oper~ting expens~s . of Gr~nd
Lodge during the coming year and care for the various appropriations bemg
made in this report. This is more fully explained in that portion of this report
hereinafter submitted dealing with the budget. This does not mean, however,
that the funds are not on hand to care for all Grand Lodge expenses for the
coming. year together with all appropriations recommended. This, however,: is
not due to the monies provided by the per capita collected but to funds which
have come into Grand Lodge Treasury through the calling of securities and
which funds have not yet been reinvested. These funds and securities have
been accumulated in previous years as a reserve against the time when they
might be needed. The budget has not been balanced for thre~ yeai:s, the exact
deficit amounting to approximately $30,000.00. Your committee 1s firmly of
the opinion that this deficit should not be permitted to further accrue; in other
words that the budget should be balanced this year. We are, therefore, recommendi~g that, in addition to the per capita of 50 cents provided by the Con~ti­
tution an additional per capita of 15 cents be levied to care for the operating
expen~es of Grand Lodge and the various appropriations made in this reporl
The Constitution also provides for a per capita levy of 50 cents for the
Building Fund of the Masonic Homes. In addition to this Building Fund, ~nd
the other revenues coming to the Homes, the trustees have suggested the levying
of an additional per capita of 75 cents for maintenance of our two homes. In
discussing their report with the Homes Trustees, it appears to your committee
and is agreed to by the trustees that a per capita levy of 50 cents will be sufficient to cover the needs of the Homes. Your committee, therefore, offers the
following resolution and recommends its adoption :
Resolved, That a per capita levy of 50 cents per member be levied, and
when paid, shall be paid by the Grand Secretary to the Trustees of t~e Homes
for the operation and maintenance expenses of the · Homes and be 1t further
Resolved That a per capita levy of 15 cents per member be levied for the payment of Grand Lodge expenses and for its various Masonic activities.
