BOARD OF CONTROL REPORT
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Control is pleased to submit the annual report of its
activities during the Masonic year.
Our Grand Master has been unusually helpful· in his assistance and
advice during the entire period.
It has been another year of hearty co-operation of the Boards of Relief
and individual Lodges with the Board of Control.
Due to the systematic handling of cases at the present time by Boards of
Relief and Lodges, there is a decided decrease in the calls upon our Board
of Control to collect from Lodges of other jurisdictions.
Our work however, has grown in the direction of consultations and
advice on many problems that arise during the year and we believe the
results are the avoidance of errors in policy and growth in uniformity of
the work of the Boards of Relief and Lodges.
Meetings
.
It has been necessary to hold one special meeting during the fiscal year.
Correspondence however, .has been continuous.
A committee of the Board consisting of Robert F. Calender and Frank
M. Wise visited the San Diego Board of Relief in relation to problems which
that Board desired us to consider. The result of that conference was a
meeting during this Grand Lodge of a large representation of the San Diego
District with the Board of Control. The conference was highly successful in
its results and an even closer bond established.
A dinner meeting was held October 13th for general information and
discussion. There were seventy-four present. The meeting was very enthusiastic and we believe beneficial to all concerned.

Your committee has received and recomm_ends the approval of the
following:
1. The application of Seal Beach Lodge No. 616 for permission to
change the name thereof to "R. E. Dolley Lodge."

Recoveries
The Board of Control has recovered for Grand Lodge $200.00 and also
$63.00 for a local Lodge as reimbursements.

2. The application of Canby's Cross Lodge No. 679 to Canby Cross Lodge
No. 679.

Total ................................,...:....,................,.........,..............$680.Qj)
Again, Brethren, we are happy to report a decrease in the requests. for
reimbursement, although last year we expressed the thought that we · had
reached an irreducible minimum. We belive, however, that further reductions
cannot be expected.
It is true that the calls for relief have been less during the past year
owing to the many relief agencies functioning, which have in a measure, lessened our burden. Notwithstanding this fact, however, our Boards of Relief
alone have dispensed the sum of $S4,293.00 during the past year for the relief
of brethren of our own and other jurisdictions.

The. Employment Service
We are modest when we tell you again that the Masonic Employment Service in this jurisdiction continues to make an outstanding contribution to Masonry.
Its growth in efficiency and number of placements is a credit to the enthusiasm
of the men behind this splendid constructive work. The opportunity for service
in this field is unlimited. The Masters and Wardens of our Lodges should
interest themselves in employment by urging employers to use the service, and
by the appointment of active Employment Committees to function within the
Lodges.
We shall not burden you with statistics except to say that the six employment offices continue to make progress, each in its own way. In some there are
real problems involved, and your Board of Control has been asked to advise and
counsel with the local officers, to the end that better results will be possible.
A comparative Financial and Statistical Report is submitted herewith (opposite page), and made a part of this report. It is worth your while to study it.

Respectfully submitted,

REPORTS OF GRIEVANCE COMMITTEE
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
There have been referred to your Committe on Grievances the trial
records and petitions for restoration set forth in the report of the Grand
Secretary.
Before reporting on these several matters, your committee desires to make
a few general observations and recommendations to the craft.
Sixteen proceedings referred to this committee were brought under Section 192 of our Constitution. This section, as you will recall, permits of automatic expulsion when the accused has been convicted of a crime classified ·as
a felony, imprisoned pursuant to such conviction, and upon notice of intended
action, fails to demand a trial before the Lodge. The experience of the past
several years has demonstrated the wisdom of that section. We would again
recommend that in proceedings under Section 192 the prepared forms be used
in order that no question may arise as to the sufficiency of the several acts
required in such a proceeding. Great care should be exercised in the giving
of the required notice. It should be sent to the last known place of address
and not necessarily to the address appearing on the Lodge records. If, at the
time of the giving of the required notice, the accused is in prison, such notice
must be sent to him at the place of imprisonll)ent.
It is interesting to note that in three instances which are covered by this
report, the accused demanded trials before trial commissions, and in each of
these three cases such trials resulted in acquittals, even though the accused
in each case had been convicted in courts of the land and imprisoned pursuant
to such conviction. Your committee is in hearty and unanimous accord with
.
the results in each of these three matters.
Two other cases have been presented in which demands for trials were
made and were later withdrawn by the accused. In each case the Lodge proceeded to declare the expulsion as though no demand for trial had been made.
.This was the proper procedure and your committee is in entire accord therewith.
.
Section 205 of our · Constitution provides in part that the result of the
trial shall be announced to the Lodge in the presence of its members only,
at the next stated meeting after termination of the trial, and that such result
shall be recorded by the Secretary as the judgment of the Lodge. The minutes showing this action should be incorporated in the record transmitted to
the Grand Lodge. Failure to include a copy of the minutes showing such

During the past year the question has arisen as to whether a Lodge may
be relieved from furnishing to the Grand Lodge a transcript of the testimony
before the trial commission. The request is usually based upon the desire of
the Lodge to avoid the expense incident to the preparation of such transcript.
· Section 207 of the Constitution would seem to answer· the question. That
section reads in part as follows :
"In all cases, whether appealed or not, the Master shall cause the Secretary
to prepare a transcript of the record of trial, and immediately transmit it to
the Grand Secretary; together with information of the appeal intended, if any
there be."
It will be noted that the preparation of this trial record and its transmission to the Grand Secretary must be done in all cases. A formal ruling
of Grand Lodge in 1925, "Ross Diges.t ,'' paragraph 461, holds that the provisions of Section 207 are mandatory.
We would also call to your attention that the quoted portion of Section 207
provides that the transcript of the record of the trial shall be "immediately"
transmitted to the Grand Secretary. We mention this particularly because of
the fact that in a number of instances there has been considerable delay in
the preparation and transmission of these trial records. This has sometimes
resulted in the review o·f the trial record by Grand Lodge a year later than
would have ·been the case if the record had been promptly prepared and transmitted to the Grand Secretary, as .the Constitution requires.
It has also come to the attention of your commit~ee that in some instances
there has been great and unusual delay on the part of some Lodges in taking
further action on retrials where matters have been reversed by Grand Lodge
and remanded for retrial. For example: We have before us this year a
record (No. 921) in which the accused was expelled by his Lodge September
11 1933 by proceedings had under Section 192 of the Constitution. At its
co:nmunlcation in 1934 Grand Lodge reversed this expulsion, holdin'g that
Section 192 was not applicable because the accused had not been imprisoned,
as is required · before proceedings may be had under that section. At the .same
time Grand Lodge directed the Lodge to cause proper charges to be preferred
and a trial thereon had in proper manner. No further action was taken
thereon until June of 1937, a lapse of two and one-half years after Grand
Lodge had given its direction. While no specific time is ordinarily contained
in any such direction by Grand Lodge, we may respectfully suggest that all
directions by Grand Lodge to subordinate Lodges should be complied with expeditiously. In this same connection it may not be amiss to point out that any
such direction by Grand Lodge to retry case is mandatory and must be treated
as such by the Lodges. Where specific directions are given to a Lodge by
Grand Lodge as to a retrial, it is not within the discretion of the Lodge to
' disregard such instructions.
These several matters are called to the attention of Grand Lodge merely
by way of comment on the part of your committee, and we see no necessity
for any formal action there.on by this body.
We now proceed to report our recommendations upon the various trial
records.
Your committee has carefully reviewed each and all of the hereinafter
enumerated trial records. We beg leave to report that in each of these cases
your committee finds no irregularities of any importance ; the rights of the
accused appear to have been properly safeguarded and substantial justice
seems to have been done.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record No.
914, from Livingston Lodge No. 658, find that in this case the accused presented a petition for the degrees of Masonry to Tehachapi Lodge No. 313 on
November 29, 1932. At a subsequent Stated Meeting of the Lodge the accused
was rejected and notified thereof, and his fee returned. On August 29, 1935,
the accused presented a petition for the degrees to Livingston Lodge No. 658,
and in answer to the question No. 8, "Have you ever presented a petition to
any Masonic Lodge? If so, when and to what Lodge?" he replied "No." In
answer to question No. 9, "Have you ever been rejected by any Masonic Lodge?
If so, when and by what Lodge?" He replied, "No." In answer to question No.
14, "Have you read all the questions contained in the foregoing petition and
are all of the answers thereto in your own handwriting? And do you, upon
your honor, declare the foregoing statements to be true?" he replied "Yes." At
the trial the accused stated that he did not know that he had been rejected. Notwithstanding serious charges of perjury against the accused, the trial commission found him not· guilty. The records show unmistakably that the finding of
not guilty is unsupported by the evidence ; that suspension is the least punishment that should be administered under the facts disclosed. Your committee
therefore offers the following resolution and moves its adoption:
Resolved, That the action of Livingston Lodge No. 658 in acquitting the
accused of unmasonic conduct be and the same is hereby modified; that accused be, and he is hereby found guilty on the charge with which he was
accused, and that the punishment ·be fixed at suspension.

Report adopted.

Relief
At_ the last ~nnual communication Brother Wesley Kergan presented a
resolut.1on proposing amendments to Section 90 and 163 of the c n t't t'
and this matter .was postpon~d to this communication to offer time f~/ ~ ~t~~n,
by your Co~m1ttee on Policy and General Purposes of the general subi'ecyt
matter of relief.
We h~ve not be~n able to frame a fo;mula on the subject satisfactor to

t~e c~mm1ttee, and instead of presenting an unsatisfactory formula we t~ink

t at r amendment to Sections 90 and 163 a substantial improvement can ·be
m~de m our la~, that the result intended ·by the resolution of Brother K

will be accomplished.

ergan

The said se:tio~s. gr~w out of decisions by Grand Masters which were
more all-~mbracm~ in. their verbiage than was probably necessary or intended
The charitable obligations of Masons are carefully restricted so that an un~

519

reasonable and overly burdensome requirement need not be met. The Lodge
in matters of relief is the agent or almoner of the members, doing on their
behalf those acts of kindness that cannot be done by a member, or that is
more conveniently and satisfactorily performed by the Lodge, acting for and
in behalf of its members collectively. No good reason appears for requiring
a higher and more extensive duty of the Lodge than is required of its members.
Yet Section 90, ·b y its terms, demands of a Lodge an extraordinary sacrifice
on its part if calls for relief exhaust all its resources. During the "depressions" many Lodges would have become ·b ankrupt had it seen to it that "all
the needy brethren of its own membership and neighborhood are not supposed
to want, or to be made a burden to others." Section 163 purports to give to a
Master Mason, his widow and orphans, when in distress, the right to ask
for "and receive" relief from .the Lodge, without qualification as to the ability
of the Lodge, the merits of the case, or the extent of demands ·being made on
the Lodge by others for its succor and help.
Your committee is of the opinion that the drastic requirements of those
sections, in themselves, m.illify the force of the law, and that the sections
should be amended to state a just, generous and reasonable rule. It therefore
recommends, as a matter of policy, that the requirements of Section 90 he
modified by amendment to provide that "Each Lodge, according to its circumstances and ability, shall see to it that the needy brethren of its own membership and neighborhood are not suffered to want or to be made a burden to
others." And that Section 163 be amended to provide that relief asked of a
Lodge be given by the Lodge in accordance with its ability.
Your committee further recommends that this matter be referred to the
Jurisprudence Committee to formulate and present to Grand Lodge proper
amendments to Sections 90 and 163, embodying said policy.

Grand Lodge approved the report. It was then referred t o
the Committee on Jurisprudence, which reported back recommending that Section 90 be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 90. Each Lodge shall see to it according to its circumstances and
ability that the needy brethren of its own membership and neighborhood are
not suffered to want or to be made a burden to others. It shall refund to
any Masonic Lodge in whose behalf the relief is granted all moneys expended
for its own needy members, not to exceed twenty-five dollars in any one case,
unless the excess ·be authorized by the Master of the Lodge or Board of
Relief in the jurisdiction. It must relieve its own members, their widows and
orphans, when in distress, regardless of their place of residence.

Grand Lodge concurred in the report and Section 90 w as
accordingly amended as above set out by unanimous vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence also reported back Section
163, recommending the amendment prop.o sed by the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes be approved and Section 163 of
the Constitution was amended, by unanimous vote, to read:
Sec. 163. Every Master Mason in good standing, his widow and orphans,
when in distress, has and have the right to ask for and receive relief from
the Lodge of which such Master Mason is, or was a member, or from the
Lodge within whose jurisdiction he is, or they, or any of them may be, in
accordance with its ability, or from any Master Mason able to bestow the
same.

Social Security
The Grand Master in his annual message directed our attention to the fact
that the Commissioner of Internal Revenue has ruled that Masonic Lodges
are not exempt from the provisions of the Federal Social Security Act.
An effort is being made in many quarters to secure an exemption for fraternal organizations from the burdens imposed by this Act. And if such efforts
are successful we will accept the law and regulations as the proper rule for
our Lodges and this Grand Lodge to follow.
It may be that we would be misguided in any effort to escape the taxation
required by the Act, and thereby deprive our employees from the benefit of the
Act. W e think that many older deserving Masons are employed by our Lodges,
and that it would be beneficial to some of them if they had the protection of
the Act in their old age, or during a period of unemployment.
The Grand Master makes no specific recommendation, and this comment by
us is made because of the reference of the subject matter to this committee.

Report adopted.
Masonic Publications
The Grand Master in his annual message very pertinently commented on
certain abuses that had come to his attention, arising out of the commercial
aspects and practices of those who publish Masonic periodicals.
Your committee is advised that this is no new subject, and that complaints
have been made from time to time that the methods of obtaining advertising
were in some cases of a questionable nature. None of these publications have
the sponsorship of this Grand Lodge, and none of them are under the control,
directly or indirectly, of th e Grand Master or the Grand Lodge. T he warning
note sounded in the Grand Master's message should be ample notice to all persons using the word "Masonic" in their commercial enterprises that a continuation of abuses and complaints will certainly result in affirmative action being
taken by this Grand Lodge to correct them. Advertisers do rtot always know
that a publication is a purely private commercial enterprise, independent of
the Grand Lodge or of the Lodges. Masonry should not be discredited by anyone
because of the unwise or unethical acts of al} individual operating outside and
beyond the scope of its authority and responsibility. However, the Masonic
institution owes it to itself to maintain its dignity and its reputation, and if
the necessity arises it will not be remiss in checking abuses and practices that
are to its detriment.

Report adopted.

Life Membership Funds
Charles R. Cooper has introduced a resolution proposing amendments to
Sections 42 and 129 of the Constitution to authorize the withdrawal from the
Life Membership Fund upon the death of a Life Member of the amount paid
into the fund by him, which authorization would be retroactive in its operation ;
and, provided further, that in the event of the dissolution of a Lodge the assets
of the Life Membership Fund of such Lodge should be disposed of by Grand
Lodge in accordance with the pro rata interest of the living Life· Members, and
that the interest in said fund of each living Life Member shall be applied by
Grand Lodge toward the payment of Life Membership in the Lodge with which
he affiliates, or toward the payment of dues therein, as he may direct. In the
event of the failure of a Life Member to affiliate within six months, his pro
rata interest in said fund shall revert to and be retained by Grand Lodge.
The resolution providing that on the death of a Life Member that "the
amount standing against his name in the Life Membership Fund shall revert to
the general funds of the Lodge," is a subject matter that was before us at the
Annual Communication of 1936. At that time we reported: "That the committee
is of the opinion that Life Membership Funds are not earned by a Lodge at the
time the Life Membership is taken out, nor are they earned by the Lodge at any
time during the member's life. Those funds are to pay a member's dues. They do
not ordinarily realize to the Lodge an income that is as large as the dues· there
is a loss to the Lodge in dues every year. That loss is made up by the fa~t that
the fund is permanent, and no part is paid out at the time of the death of
a Life Member. It is not an earned fund; it is earning money for the Lodge
every year, and is a trust fund which should not be dissipated." The amendment
was not adopted by Grand Lodge.
Upon further consideration of the subject matter, your committee is still
of the opinion that no part of the principal of the Life Membership Fund should
be withdrawn, but that the same should be kept in perpetuity for the benefit of
the Lodge.
Your committee has given careful consideration to the resolution, the purpose of which is to protect Life Members in the event of the dissolution of. the
Lodge in which they hold such membership, and is in full sympathy and accord
with the proposers of the resolution as to the propriety of protecting Life Members of a Lodge whose charter has been suspended, forfeited or revoked. Your
committee, however, does not approve of the method proposed for the accomplishment of this purpose.
That this matter may have the proper consideration by this Grand Lodge,
your committee offers the following resolution:
Resolved, That Section 129 of the Constitution be amended by adding
thereto the following :
"In the event of the dissolution of the Lodge the assets in the Life Membership Fund of such Lodge, if any, shall be delivered to the Grand Treasurer,
who shall hold the same as a trust fund pending the disposition thereof. The
Grand Lodge shall determine the interest of each living Life Member in said
fund, and the interest of Grand Lodge therein, on a just and equitable basis,
and such determination when made shall be final and conclusive. The Grand
Treasurer shall distribute said fund, or the proceeds of a sale thereof, in
accordance with the determination of Grand Lodge."
And, be it further resolved, That Section 42 of the Constitution be amended
to read as follows :
"In case of the dissolution of a Lodge the Grand Secretary or some
brother by him duly authorized, shall at once proceed to receive its funds on
hand, except its Life Membership Fund, collect its outstanding dues, dispose

523

of its jewels, furniture and other property of every kind in such manner as
shall seem to him most judieious; and he shall place the proceeds thereof, after
the payment of all just debts and necessary expenses, among the funds of
the Grand Lodge."
Be it further resolved, That Section 38 of the Constitution be amended
by adding thereto the following : "4th. From that part of the Life Membership
Funds of a dissolved Lodge as may be allocated to it, pursuant to the provisions
of Section 129 . . ."
Be it further resolved, That Section 134 of the Constitution be amended
to read as follows :
"The surrender or forfeiture of the Charter of a Lodge, when declared by
the Grand Lodge, shall be conclusive upon the Lodge and its members, and
all its funds, jewels, furniture, dues and property of every kind, except its Life
Membership Fund, shall be disposed of as provided in Section 42, and its Life
Membership Fund, if any, shall be disposed of as provided in Section 129."
Your committee respectfully recommends that the resolution by Brother
Cooper be not adopted. Your committee further recommends that as a matter
of policy the Life Membership Funds of a dissolved. Lodge shall not revert in
whole to this Grand Lodge, but shall be distributed in a just and equitable manner among the living Life Members and this Grand Lodge. Your committee
further recommends that the resolutions offered by it, proposing to amend
Sections 38, 42, 129 and 134 of the Constitution, be referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence.

The report was adopted and referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence, w hich reported back recommending the adoption
of the proposed amendment as set out above; and Sections 38,
42, 129 and 134 of the Constitution were thereupon amended by
a five-sixth vote.
Remission of Dues
Bro. Henry K. Friedberg, of Traver Lodge No. 294, proposes an amendment to Section 128 of the Constitution, by adding after the word "them" at
the end of the fourth sentence, the following: " . . . . or having attained the age
of seventy years."
The purpose of the amendment is to place members having attained the age
of seventy years in the same position with reference to advance remission of
dues as members who have been in good standing in this jurisdiction for forty
years or more. The remission in both cases to be in the sound judgment of the
Lodge, and granted by reason of misfortune, inability, or other good cause.
Your committee on Jurisprudence has signified its approval of the form
of the amendment as proposed, and your committee recommends the adoption
of the resolution.
The report was adopted and Section 128 was accordingly amended by a
five-sixth vote, to read as follows :
Section 128. No Lodge shall charge or collect as its annual dues from
members less than nine dollars. The only receipt for dues to be used by the
Lodge shall be a uniform one prepared by the Grand Secretary and sold by
him. Dues shall commence with the first day of the month next following the
conferring of the third degree, or the election to meinbership in the case of
affiliation where the <limit is filed with the application, or in the event that the
<limit is filed following election to membership by affiliation, then with the first
day of the month next following such filing. No Lodge shall remit the dues

of its members or any of them for any stated period or in advance; but it may
annually remit the accrued dues of those of its members who render special

that by special resolution, applicable only to the particular member involved, a
Lodge may, in advance or otherwise, remit the dues of any member who shall
have been a member in good standing in this jurisdiction for forty years or
more, or having attained the age of seventy years, and who in. the sound judgment of the Lodge, should, by reason of some misfortune, inability or other
good cause, be exempt from the payment of dues. No Lodge shall levy any
extra assessment on its members.
Liquor
Brother J. W. Eddy, Past Master of Paso Robles Lodge No. 286, proposes
a substitute for Section 129-A of the Constitution, to provide that no Lodge
shall receive a petition for degrees of Masonry from one who is engaged as
principal or agent in the business of manufacturing, wholesaling or retailing
liquor of any alcoholic content whatever as a beverage, and providing further
that a Mason who hereafter engages in such practice ·or business shall "ipso
facto stand expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry."
Your committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Report adopted.
Hospital Group Insurance
Brother John E. Roberts, Master of Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625, and
other members of said Lodge, have proposed a resolution relative to the subject
of hospitalization for Masons, and have asked that a special committee of this
Grand Lodge be appointed to make a study of the subject.
It is the opinion of your committee that the individual members of a Lodge,
or of a group of Lodges, could form a hospital insurance group, and thereby
secure all the benefits that would accrue from having this Grand Lodge, or any
of its subordinates, sponsor and operate such a plan. If an insurance group is
formed it should not use .the word "Masonic" as a part of its name or designation. This being the case, there is no need for the committee asked for by this
resolution. Therefore, we recommend that it be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Report adopted.
Old Age Security
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California in their
annual report called the attention of this Grand Lodge to the fact that under
the law of California many persons residing in the homes are entitled to old
age pensions.
They further call our attention to the fact that the acceptance of payment
from guests in the home would constitute a new. practice in the conduct of
the home. Ueretofore we have cared far those who were dependent. If old

525

age pensions are paid, many · of our guests in the home would not be wholly
dependent, and in many cases might be independent.
The Trustees recommend that this Grand Lodge instruCt them to permit
recipients of old age pensions to remain in the Masonic home.
Since this matter will require discrimination and discretion in each individual case, it is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that the Trustees of the Masonic homes be authorized in their sound discretion
to permit such recipients of old age pensions ~s· may desite to remain in the
homes, to do so; and we recommend the adoption of such a policy.

Report adopted.
Accounts
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the resolutions introduced by the Committee on Accounts, to amend Sections 37-E and
·
•
37-K of the Constitution.
The sections provide that the accounts of the Board of Control and of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board be approved by the Grand Master. The
reason for the exceptions in the matter of accounting made in connection with
these two Boards is that an appropriation is I!4lde by Grand Lodge for their
respective needs, and the amounts thereof are turned over to· the Boards in ·a
lump sum through a warrant drawn by the Grand Master· and Grand Secretary
on the Grand Treasurer. The Committee on Accounts audit the payment by
Grand Lodge, and determine whether the same is made in accordance with the
authority given by Grand Lodge. When these funds have been received by the
respective Boards they are expended, subject to the approval of the Grand
Master, and in the annual reports of the Boards, an accounting is given to the
Grand Lodge, and submitted for its approval or rejection.
,'
Your committee is of the opinion that in the tw.o cases specified it ·is not
improper for Grand Lodge to make an exception from its salutary general rule
submitting the propriety of expenditures to the Committee on Accounts for
approval.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
The report of the committee failed of adoption:; and the mat~

ter was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which
committee reported, recommending the adoption of the proposed amendment. They failed however to receive the necessary five-sixth vote and the amendment did not prevail.
A Proposed Prohibitory Regulation
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration the resolution submitted by Riverside Lodge No. 635, requesting Grand
Lodge "to adopt a regulation prohibiting the use of Masonic temples or any
part thereof for meetings of either employers or employees, striking or otherwise, for the discussion of matters growing out of or calculated to lead to
strikes, lockouts or other like political, industrial or labor disputes."
Your committee believes that the action requested by the resolution is
unnecessary and of doubtful wisdom. The sub-letting of Masonic temples or
halls for meetings of outside groups of any character is a matter properly within
the control of Lodges and temple associations, whose knowledge of local conditions and whose prudence should be the safest guides.
·
Your committee, there.fore, .recommends that the resolution of Riverside
Lodge No. 635 be not adopted.

Report adopted.

System of Teaching the Ritual
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration a resolution submitted by Whittier Lodge No. 323, and Greenleaf Lodge
No. 670, both of Whittier, and Paso Robles Lodge No. 286 reciting that in the
judgment of their officers and members "the present system of teaching the
ritual has not proved satisfactory." The resolution requests Grand Lodge to
"restore the old system of a full time Grand Lecturer with an adequate salary.''
Such tests as have been made of sentiment among constituent Lodges with
respect to the relative merits of the two systems have been inconclusive. The
so-called new system was adopted after the death of Bro. Thomas J. Baker of
blessed memory, and has been continued from year to year on an experimental
ba~s. Its sponsors and adherents believe that, in general, it is working more
satisfactorily than the old system. They recommend that it be continued in
operation for another year. Your committee believes that this recommenda~ion
should be accepted, but offers, on its own part, the suggestion that at its annual
communication in 1938 Grand Lodge should definitely determine under which
syst.em it prefers to proceed.
Your committee therefore recommends that no action be taken on the
resolution of these Lodges at this annual communication, and that the so-called
new system remain in effect for the coming Grand Lodge year.

Report was adopted.
Peace Day
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration a resolution submitted by Arcadia Lodge No, 547, proposing "that October
8th of each year be set aside and designated 'Peace Day' and used for the
purpose of promoting peace, throughout the world." The resolution states a
belief "that if each Masonic Lodge throughout the world put forth greater
effort in keeping with the ideal of world peace, such ideal would be attained."
Your committee is, of course, in full accord with the ideal of world peace,
11n ideal to which all of us are devoted, but doubts the efficacy of this proposal.
Masonry has been destroyed by the Communist governments of Russia and
Spain, the Fascist government of Italy, and the Nazi government of Germany,
and is without appreciable influence in China and Japan. Its foothold under the
radical government in France is insecure. These are the countries, with England,
now most prominent upon the theatre of events which may make for peace or
war. The issue in these circumstances, and probably in future circumstances,
will be decided through the play of forces in no wise controllable by our con. stituent Lodges or by this Grand Lndge.
Your committee sees no objection to such peace ·observances as individual
Lodges may from time to time wish to hold, but is persuaded that the setting
apart of a day to be formally observed annually by all Lodges in this Grand
.JurisdiC:tion is unnecessary.
We therefore recommend that the proposal contained in the resolution of
Arcadia Lodge No. 547 be not adopted.

Master.

full hearing by the Grand Master. His case was closed by the act!on of the
Grand Lodge in sustaining the action of the Grand Master and m not reinstating. the Master to his office from which the Grand Master had suspended
him.
'We, therefore, recommend that his request be denied.

MORNING SESSION
Friday, October 15, 1937.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 :00 o'clock, the Grand Master presiding.

SUBVERSIVE ACTIVITIES
Freemasonry's asserted and practiced aim in the world has been the practice, exaltation, and achievement of Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth. It ~as
never ceased to incite men to a support and adoption of these all-embracing
appeals for a betterment of the status of mankind.
In other words: Freemasonry, throughout its ever glorious histor:i:, pas
endeavored to instill into the minds of its members a realization, apprec1atmn,
and acceptance of those moral virtues which must live. and grow if. civili~ation
is to live and grow. It has ever relied upon its world-wide members~1p, wh1thersoever dispersed, to practice those virtues in order that its teachings may be
wrought into actual accomplishment. It has never, to our knowl~d.ge, attem~ted
to set up some form of organized machinery whereby some particular proJect
might be advanced, or some menacing movement might be put down. It e:rer
fights its battles in the hearts of men, by suasion; never on the fields of action,
by show of force.
Every Mason in California loves his country ~nd her in~titutions and
wants to see them retained and built up for added service to mankmd. In recognition as well as in demonstration of this fact, he should ever conduct himself,
in private thought and in public conduct, as if he felt that the salvation ~f
that country and the success of those institutions, actually depended upon his
own individual effort-upon his loyalty, his ability, his foresight, his abhorrence
of wrong, his unyielding support of truth and right, as he is ena~led indi~idu~lly
to sense those qualities. In this wise, he should demonstrate his Americanism
and justify his Freemasonry. This will mean that every Masonic heart is a
citadel of enduring strength for those things best calculated to serve democracy
and civilization· ever fearlessly engaged in persistent combat with all the foes
of righteousnes~-with all the forces engaged, directly or indirectly, in activities
that, unresisted, would destroy America, her aims, her achievements, her
hoped-for destiny.
As individuals, we the members of the Grand Lodge of California here and
now and as long as life shall last, announce ourselves in militant opposition to
all forms of activities that seem to challenge America's future or offer menace
to America's present.
Upon this rock we build our faith; upon this enduring rock we shall ever
strive to sustain and support Home, Country, and Freemasonry.

The above was adopted by unanimous vote.

Senior Grand Steward, Paul Save, of America Lodge No.

ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS
The annual election of officers was now held, the result
being as follows :
The R.". W :·. James Thomas Fraser of Humboldt Lodge
No. 79 was elected Grand Master.
The R. ·. W. ·. Leon 0. Whitsell of Orange Grove Lodge
No. 293 was elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R.". W.". William H. Waste of Durant Lodge No. 268
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
The W.". William B. Ogden of Hollywood Lodge No. 355
was elected Junior Grand Warden.
The V.". W.". William P. Filmer of .King Solomon's Lodge
No. 260 was re-elected Grand Treasurer.
The V.". w:. John Whicher of King David's Lodge No.
209 was re-elected Grand Secretary.
The V.". W.". Leslie E. Wood of Provident Lodge No. 600
was re-elected Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master-elect caused to be read the names of the
appointive officers, as follows:
Grand Chaplain, A. Harry Severson, of Arroyo Lodge No.
274.

442.

Grand Orator, Warren E. Libby, of Blackmer Lodge No.
.

Assistant Grand Secretary, Frank G. Hobbs, of Alexandria
Lodge No. 531.
Grand Marshal, John Alpers, of Seaport Lodge No. 550.
Grand Standard Bearer, Alexander D. Potts of le Progres
de l'Oceanie Lodge No. 371.
Grand Sword Bearer, Fred A. Kelsey, of Mount Olive
Lodge No. 506.
Grand Bible Bearer, Louis Persons, of Humboldt. Lodge
No'. 79.
Senior Grand Deacon, Thomas Anderson, of Pacific Lodge
No. 136.
Junior Grand Deacon, Leo Bruck, of Jewel Lodge No. 374.

475.
Junior Grand Steward, John Gries, of Ferndale Lodge No.

193.
Grand Pursuivant, Russell C. Horstqiann, of Fruitvale
Lodge No. 336.
Grand Organist, Chas. E. Anderson, of Jewel Lodge No.
374.
Grand Tiler, Frank G. Watson, of Presidio Lodge No. 354.
He also announced the appointment of Chas. Albert Adams
to be a member of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California, vice self, term expired.
The M.". W.". Dana R. Weller was appointed Master of
Ceremonies and the officers elect and appointed, excepting the
Grand Treasu.r er and the Senior Grand Steward, were installed
by the retiring Grand Master in due and .ancient form.
The newly installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a Past Grand Master's lapel button, in which was
set a beautiful diamond; and also invested him with the apron
of a Past Grand Master. The Chas. Albert Adams insignia was
transferred from the retiring to the encumbent Grand Master;
and the other chair officers exchanged the lapel pins.
Victor Egan, Master of Humboldt Lodge No. 79, in behalf
of his Lodge, presented to the Grand Master a brief case.
Past Grand Master Weller, then in behalf of Grand Lodge,
presented to Past Grand Master Miller a rich oriental rug.
At 2 :10 o'clock, all business be~ng completed, Grand Lodge
was closed in Ample Form.
J. T: FRASER,
Grand Master.
JOHN WHICHER,
Grand Secretary.

October, 1937
BY JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my Fourteenth Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee. As in past years, the Report has been the
work of the Chairman, and the views expressed under the various topics
are, of course, his individual ideas. While it might be of interest and of
value to embody in this report all that occurred in the Masonic world
during the three years the Committee was "on vacation," space prevents
such treatment.
The topics covered are, therefore, those that we believe have merit,
as considered by Grand Lodges, their Officers and the various Committees
on Correspondence and embodied in the Proceedings received since our
last Annual session.
Some topics or conditions that are of general interest finding space
in the various Proceedings, but which are not treated at length in the
general body of this Report, may be briefly summarized as follows:
WHO'S WHO IN CHINA: The Far East now occupies the attention of the world and what the result will be it is impossible ,to prophesy. The Grand Lodge of England entered China Masonically in 1844;
the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1863; the Grand Lodge of Scotland
in 1864 and the Grand Lodge of Ireland in 1919. China, of course, has no
Grand Lodge and under the recognized rules of Masonic procedure is
therefore open Territory.
On October 28, 1930, the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands
issued a dispensation for the formation of Amity Lodge at Shanghai,
China. The above mentioned Grand Lodges assumed the attitude that by
reason of this action there would be danger to the general interests of
Freemasonry in China and suspended relations with the Grand Lodge of
the Philippine Islands. Similar action was taken by a few Grand Lodges
in Australia and the United States. Most of the Jurisdictions, however,
held to the generally accepted view that as China was open Territory the
Grand Lodge of the Philippines was well within its rights. After the
establishment of Amity Lodge No. 106, four other dispensations were
issued.

By members referred to as "for!!ign" are meant all who are racially
non-Chinese. Among those classed as "Chinese" are a proportionately
large number of American and British nationality, born and bred abroad.
Classified according to nationality, the percentage of "foreign" members
would be about equal to that of the purely Chinese members. The District
includes 225 members; but 26 duplications, owing to dual-membership in
one or more Lodges, brings the total up to 256 for both classes of members.

A recent report states that at a meeting held July 22, the Grand Committee of the Grand Lodge of Scotland reported the draft of a ·p roposed
agreement by the Advisory Council for China between the Grand Lodges
of England, Ireland, Scotland, Massachusetts, and the Grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands. It was reported that the agreement had been signed
by the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, with
the expectation that his act would be confirmed at the next ailllual meeting of that Grand Lodge. The other Grand Lodges having approved, the
Grand Committee recommended that relations of amity between the Grand
Lodge of Scotland and the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, suspended some time ago, be restored so soon as the latter Grand Lodge
confirms the agreement.
From this it would appear that at least in Masonic circles there will
be peace and harnwny in China.
BETTER A NEIGHBOR THAT IS NEAR THAN A BROTHER
FAR OFF: The National Federated Crafts, an organization restricted to
Masons who are employees of the Federal government, advertised that
they would hold their annual meeting in Dallas, Texas, in September, 1936.
The Grand Lodge of that Jurisdiction has a regulation that organizations,
having as a requirement membership in the Masonic Fraternity, may not
operate there unless specifically "recognized'; by it. The then Grand
Master issued an Edict, against the National Federated Crafts and other
Organizations that had not secured such recognition, in part as ·follows:
. "This is to advise you that such organizations are forbidden by the
Grand Lodge of Texas, and that all persons engaged in organizing such
bodies, and all Masons who join the same are committing a Masonic offense,
which, if persisted in, will subject them to trial.
"You are hereby instructed to diligently canvass the membership of
your Lodge, as to the activities of any of its members in such forbidden
organizations, and to request such members to desist therefrom and to
sever their connections with such organizations, and in the event they shall
fail to do so to have proper ·charges preferred against them and presented
for. speedy trial."
The Officers of the National Federated Crafts answered with good
grace that they were Masons, and had no desire whatever to infringe upon
the prerogatives of the Grand Lodge, and accordingly ordered all "Crafts"
in Texas dissolved and their charters returned.
Covered by this Edict also was National Sojourners, Inc., composed
of past and present commissioned officers of the uniformed forces of the
United States Government, who are Master Masons. In 1924 its first
chapter was established in San Antonio, and together with eight other
Chapters had been in continuous existence after that time. ' The purposes
of the National Sojourners are as follows:
"Cultivating Masonic ideals.
"Supporting all patriotic aims and activities in Masonry.
"Developing true patriotism and Americanism throughout the Nation.

The Grand Master of Nebraska recommended the appointment of a

in the British Empire. They are not issued in cipher form, and the
Fraternity in those Jurisdictions do not seem to· be any worse for their

WHICH SYSTEM IS BEST?: The Gr'and Secretary of the Royal
Arch Masons in speaking before the Grand Lodge of Texas (1937), while
not answering directly the popular question, "What have they got that
we haven't got?" presented the following:
·
There are two distinct ideas. One is to make it easy to acquire
membership in the Masonic bodies, and another is to make it harder to
acquire membership. With the first, easy to get in, and harder to stay
in. With the other, harder to get in, and easier to stay in.
This is from our Grand Recorder Hamersly o{ the Grand Encampment of the United States. He has just finished a tour of the Masonic
bodies of Europe England and Scotland, and I want to give you his
observation. He is making ~ comparison between the Masonic bodies of
England and the Masonic bodies of the United States, and he takes those
seven years which we learned to call the period of depression, from 1928
to 1935, as a comparison on that much of his report. I will read to .you.
In 1928 the English Lodges numbered 4,400. The number of subordinate
Lodges in England was 4,400 in 1928. In 1935, seven years later, there
were 4,900 Lodges in England. You see the increase, nearly 100 a year.
500, to be exact, for the seven years.
The membership in England in 1928 was 250,000. In 1935 it was
380,000. Do you notice the increase during those seven years? Now,
listen to the statistics of the United States. In the United States in 1928
there were 16,000 Lodges. In ·1935 there were 15,400 Lodges, or a loss 'of
600 Lodges in our country in that seven years, while there was a gain of
500 in England during the same seven years. The membership in the
United States in 1928 was 3,300,000, while in 1935 it had dropped to
2,500,000.
LET THERE BE LIGHT: There are almost as many ideas upon
this subject as there are Jurisdictions. A large amount of time and money
has been expended we believe without results in attempting to devise a workable program that will appeal to Masons generally. One Grand Master very
plainly stated that the average Mason did not want to be educted. Perhaps
he was justified from the results in a large number of Jurisdictions. A plan
that is producing satisfactory results in various Jurisdictions is educating the
candidate in Masonic lines during the time he was elected until he becomes

Mason. . For the Masonic student and those having an. interest
history, perhaps the best method so far has been by the establishment m

The following from the Grand Master (1936) of the Philippine Islands
presents one of the finest pieces of work it has been our good fortune to read:
"I appointed a Special Committee to make recommendations on the .
organization by the subordinate Lodges of classes for illiterate persons;. ~y
idea was to have each Lodge hire the necessary teacher, or teachers, whose
services could no doubt have been secured at nominal charge, as many of
our Brethren belong to the teaching profession, and organize evening classes
to be held in one of the rooms of the Lodge hall or in some other suitable
place. This humane and patriotic labor in behalf of persons who have not
had those opportunities which we consider the birthright of every person,
would no· doubt have redounded to the credit of the Fraternity in these
Islands. Unfortunately, however, the Committee made its report only a few
days ago and it was for this reason impossible to adopt a definite plan. In
spite of this several Lodges have organized and are conducting such classes
for the illiterate, and in view of the interest shown, I recommend to the
incoming Grand Master that he appoint a Committee to continue the work
of organizing classes for the illiterate and I urge our Brethren to take an
interest in this constructive activity of Masonry."

THE HORSE AND BUGGY DAYS: The airplane, the automobile
and the radio have eliminated the barrier between the "city slicker" and the
"rube," and the "hick town" and the "industrial center." Henry J. Allen,
Grand Orator of Kansas, in an oration very fittingly presented what Masonry
in the past stood for to a large proportion of our members:
"My mind goes back to a building which I knew in Manhattan, Kansas,
forty years ago. Above a central window of the second story facing Main
Street, on certain nights a transparent sign bore the legend 'A. F. & A. M.,' ·
and below, the square and compasses. The whole community knew it as
the Lodge room of the Masonic Order. ·
·
"To that building one night in my young manhood, with a spirit of utter
devotion, I went to ·receive my Entered Appr~ntice degree. I think l rec;ill
that night as I recall nothing else in all my life. In equally poign•nt mood
I recall the inspiring symbolism which led me entranced through th.e. th.ree
solemn journeys that brought me to my citizenship in the d'e gree of a Master
Mason.
" I was a young business man with a wife and baby, and an ambition to
live the normal life of a useful free citizen. Times were bitter, although I did
not know it then. Those were the only times I had ever tried to do busin.e ss
in. I thought they were regular times. We were emerging from the depression of the early nineties and getting ready for the great political contest of
1896.
"Many of my neighbors I did not know. I knew my competitor by
sight, and deemed him a man undesirable in all ways. But when, after the
elevation my thought and spirit had experienced through the degrees, I came
to receive the congratulations of these neighbors and fellow citizens upon my

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

602

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

entrance into full fellowship as a craftsman, I detected in them a new dignity.
Manhattan became to me a new sort of place because these older men had
made me a brother to themselves, and had interested me with them in their
dreams of individual behavior and a better social order. A new mein sat
upon them and upon the town.
'
"And today when I think of the physical manifestations of Masonry,
I do not visualize the beautiful temples our Order has builded. When I
think of Masonry, I am back in a modest rectangUlar lodge room above a
store in Manhattan, where the bankers, the merchants, the lawyers, the
teachers, and the farmers gave me the sign, pass word, and grip of a fellow
craftsman, and made me Master of those gentle mysteries which set apart
in a sacred chamber of my life a new chapter of resolutions and a new sense
of human obligations.
· "To me all these ordinary men of my daily life with their straight and
simple faiths, took on a new nobility. I see them now as I stand before you
at this formal instant, and through them I see Masonry. . . ."
MASONRY REGARDS NO MAN FOR HIS WORLDLY
WEALTH OR HONORS: The able Chairman of the Correspondence
Committee of North Carolina states that this phrase should be classified
with the Dodo, which is intended to be a stronger statement than the one
about "horse and buggy days," if you have not seen a Dodo..
Some one has truly said that "Fame is vapor, riches take wings, and
the only earthly certainty is oblivion." "Public opinion is very fickle.
Popularity is a vapor which passes with the changing of the breezes of
public judging. One is a hero of today and an anathema tomorrow--and is
the same person aside from 'worldly wealth or honors' both times. If in
our Masonic estimation of a man we think of him in connection with honors,
externals, popularity, the public whim, we sow the wind and have no reason
to do other than expect to reap the whirlwind. Public persons are none
less than human. It is their human presons whom we make Masons. If
perchance they are projected into greatly changed conditions, their relation
thereto changes. Change the window-dressing into what the candid camera
sees, and you debunk the subject to what he really is. Put him on the spot,
as sooner or later must happen, and you have a different person (for the
public gaze) from him in the midst of brass bands and parades and hat
throwing. What we are saying is, that the tendency of Masonry to esteem
some Masons in terms of their worldly honors and distinction, also is a
tendency toward fickleness. Away back in 1933, much laud was given to the
President of the United States because he had made a special trip to New
York to be present for the raising of his son. Then in the early part of
1936, that chorus of praise changed to a veritable anvil chorus of knocks by
those who were disgruntled, or who 'viewed with alarm' or who knocked
in camoufiage--they said he had fired Masons from offices by devious means
and put in their places others who were supposed to be hostile to Masonry.
Other charges may have been advanced, but this one we heard most frequently.
"When the Prince of Wales was Empire Salesman he was the world's
most popular Mason. Times changed. Things came on the boards, of which
it is not needful to write here. Result: Masonry has in far too many Masons'
mouths become too uncharitable to the last degree. Edward, Duke of
Windsor, has paid the price of being in the public eye and being human
withal. Masonry regarded him not as human but in the habiliments of
prominence. It's as hard to regard him as human now, as before he was
required to make his Great Choice.

603

"We repeat as we began: what we need is more of respect and love for
the individuals who are Masonry, shorn of incidental or accidental matters
fore~ to Masonry itself. Can we not make the ritual mean what it says'Masc;mry regards no man for his worldly wealth or honors'?"

"Free~asonry is not a political institution. It knows nothing of kingdoms
republics or empires or states. I~ deals with men only as children of a comn Father and has nothing to do with political controversies that distract

low~ (1935):

(Chairman C01'respotu1ence Committee): The Jurisprudence Committee of
Missouri went a few steps further in reviewing the Grand Master's decision
(supra) when they stated that nothing must be done by rhese brethren iliat

(Chairman Correspotuience Committee): The Grand Master of Missouri
answered .t he question, "Does the Masonic Law prevent its members from
forming an American Legion Post composed exclusively of Freemasons, where
no ¥~sonic Lodge is sponsoring the Legion Post?" then answering the succeeding question :
Ai:iswer: No. Our members as ind\yidual Masons, may form such a post, if
they wish.
No. 5. Question : Can such a Legion Post, composed exclusively of
Masons, use a Masonic name for their pos.t?
Answer : Yes. This answer is qilalified with the statement that the Legion
Post must do nothing which would tend to bring disrepute to the Masonic
Fraternity.
.
The Masonic Fraternity in effect has a property right in its nomenclature
and has a just right to regulate the use of Masonic names by members of the
fraternity, and to forbid the use of Masonic names by outsiders. To date, the
Grand Lodge has only restricted the use of Masonic· names "for commercial or
otper business enterprises." This section has been interpreted many .times. ·
The Law itself and all of the decisions go to the question of using Masonic
terms for commercial purposes. The American Legion professes high ideals and
it cannot be said that its purposes are commercial.
• I am not attempting to pass on the American Legion question as to whether·
or not the requirement of Masonic affiliations violates its constitution. The
American Legion's only requirements for eligibility for membership is· that an
applicant shall have an honorable discharge from one of certain branches of the
military establishment, from service rendered during a particular period of
time. The Preamble to the Constitution of the American Legion is as follows :
"For God and Country, we associate ourselves together, for the following
purposes: To uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States of
America; to maintain law and order; to foster and perpetuate a one hundred
per cent Americanism; to preserve the memories and ·incidents of our association in the Great War; to inculcate a sense of individual obligation to the
community, state and nation; to combat the autocracy of both the class.es and
the masses ; to make right the master of might; to promote peace and good will
on earth; to safeguard and transmit to posterity the principles of justice, freedom and democracy; to consecrate and sanctify our comradeship by our devotion to mutual helpfulness."
' American Legion Posts are prohibited from entering into political controversies.

During the past years the absence of degree work has furnished an
opportunity for leadership in the Worshipful Master and his officers. The
Ritual has ceased to become attractive, even when handled in the most
correct manner. Only when exemplified by a visiting team or accompanied
with some other attraction will it interest the members to such an extent
that they will attend. In a number of cases during the past few years we
have seen from five to ten members besides the Officers present at the
conferring of the degree, but when an interesting speaker followed the
same brought into the Lodge room from fifty to seventy-five members, who
found more pleasure and entertainment in the ante room during the conferring of the degree than witnessing the same. It is a condition and not
a theory.

Ohio (1936):
(Committee on Masonic Service): If the future welfare of Lodges is to
be assured, we must disseminate light and information and give Masonry that
perennial freshness which will hold ~he ll:ctive interest of its ~embers throughout the generations. As to how this might be best accomplished has been a
matter of much earnest thought by the Committee throughout the year. The
conclusion has been reached that Freemasonry, being a voluntary o:ganizati?n,
we cannot hope to force education on its members, but correct mformat10n
can be disseminated through Lodge programs in such a way as to leave on the
mind an imprint that will have a salutary effect upon the Craft.
The kind of program that would be adapted to the needs of the greatest
number of Lodges is, of course, greatly to be desired. It was finally determi~ed
to select fifteen subjects, have a working synopsis of each, a suggested out11?e
of a program for the meeting, have these printed in booklet form and distributed free to our Lodges. The Master and his Committee can then work out
complete a selected program on the theory that greater interest will be had wi~h
such personal touch, as well as the development of that great local talent m
all Lodges and which should be utilized.

South Australia (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee:) The Grand Master of Maine
made a novel innovation in Freemasonry by issuing a proclamation calling upon
Officers and Brethren of each Lodge to assemble in special Communication in
October, 1935, and partkipate in a ceremony of Re-obligation and Re-consecra.tion to Freemasonry. As part of the program the proclamation was read, the
Brethren were to stand and take upon themselves anew the obligation of our
third degrees, and the message from the Grand Master which was sent to every
Lodge was read.
The purpose of these meetings was that early in the activities of the
Masonic year, the members of our Lodges should gather about their altars
and there renew in their hearts the obligations and lessons of Freemasonry to
the end that each might become a better Mason and a better citizen. What a
fine idea!

DEATH IS SO PERMANENT
Since the commencement of the gasoline age approximately 1500 different makes of potential death and destruction have been placed in the
hands of experienced and inexperienced operators, of all classes from young
people in their non-age to old people in their dotage. When you consider
that during 1936 there were 36,000 deaths caused by automobiles, a greater
number of deaths than was suffered by the American Army in France, the
gravity of the situation is better exemplified than by preachments.
Be tolerant to the pedestrian; he has his faults, but they are not crimes
punishable by death.

West Virginia (1936):
( Grnnd Master): Several requests for dispensations to confer degrees in a
shorter time than Stated Communications have also ~been denied. I have just
lately returned from the conferences of Grand Masters of the United States
where this subject was discussed at length. It was the unanimous opinion that
our ritual and catechisms constitute the foundation stones of our Fraternity
and except in extreme cases like war or military service no candidate should be
considered greater than our Constitution, Laws, and Usages. Masonry has a
right to the reputation of being a difficult organization in which to gain
admittance. and an easy one to get out of. It horiors every man whom it accepts
into membership but no man, no matter what his position, power or intluence,
honors Masonry by becoming a member except by his daily living as an upright,
just, useful, reputable and patriotic citizen.

LEAVES BEFORE THE STORM ·
Originally Communism had a real meaning, but the term is now generally used to designate one who has progressive ideas or does not agree
with his opponent. Considering it in its original sense, as well as emphasizing other "isms" of a like character, our Country is faced with a rising
tide of lawlessness which must cause grave concern. Our organization
must play its part, not by the mere passing of resolutions or lip service,
but action.
The United States today needs leaders with the stamina of General
John A. Dix, who at the outbreak of the Civil War ordered, "If any man
attempts to haul down the American Flag shoot him on the spot." Those
who are most active in attempting to undermine our Government, when
met with opposition, are the first to appeal to law and order.
Arkansas ( 1936):
(Grand Master): I see the necessity of every Mason not only in this but in
every Grand Jurisdiction, living true to the ideals of the Fraternity. We are
in the era of changing governments in the world. We know that a democracy
under the control of good men is the greatest form of government on earth, but
it is the most dangerous when under the control of bad men and it is not only
our privilege, but it is our duty to be informed in our principles and ideals and
then to exercise in behalf of the general welfare of all our American people.
We must not countenance a practice of the nullification of good laws and edicts
which safeguard the moral fibre of the institution of Freemasonry. A law that
is a good law ought to be obeyed, and if it is not obeyed punishment ought to
bl! inflicted. But if there be bad laws in our code then they ought to be repealed
and not nullified.

"5. The communists are now organized in the United States to take over

"6. That there is a Commonwealth College at Mena, Arkansas, supported

REFLECTED GLORY
Organizations which have as a requirement membership in the Masonic
Fraternity have assumed a grave responsibility, because to the general
public they represent Masonry and their sins of both omission and commission are viewed as a part of the system. In our educational system we
have the Public School, Junior ColleKe and the University, each serving a
worthy purpose, and so perhaps do the coordinate bodies of Masonry.
We are charKed that we owe a duty to our neiKhbor, and when we
consider the Shriners' Hospitals for Crippled Children, the Knights Templar
Educational Loan Fund, the Scottish Rite's efforts on behalf of the Public
Schools, the Sciots' Foundation for Convalescent and Undernourished
Children, the work of the Order of DeMolay, the Rainbow Girls and Job's
Daughters, and other activities in support of Masonry, as well as helping the
other fellow, perhaps we can be tolerant of some of the regrettable actions
complained of. They can be remedied by constructive action rather than
criticism.
District of Columbia (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It is a rare case nowadays when
a Grand Lodge gives permission for a Lodge to sponsor such organizations as
the DeMolay and Boy Scouts. Not that they do any particular harm to the
sponsoring body, and no doubt they do much good in their fields, but this
writer has always believed it was bad policy to give any such organizations
even a tentative connection with the Craft. With organizations composed of
Masons it is somewhat different, although there have been many times when
these organizations made a plague of themselves, and brought down upon themselves censure and discipline. But the tendency among Grand Lodges continues
to em!}hasize their own supremacy in matters Masonic, and it is gradually coming to the knowledge of the brethren that they are responsible to the Grand
Lodge for their conduct first, last, and all the time.

Illinois (1935):
(Grand Master): With the internal affairs of these organizations Masonry
does not care to interfere. Supervision or regulation of their management,
ritual, ceremonies, meetings, or social activities is neither practical nor desirable. Masonry, however, has the right to insist and must insist that these
organizations and their members shall not violate the fundamentals of Masonry,
the ancient landmarks, the long established principles and practices, and those
regulations of modem times adopted in deference to prevailing public opinion
in matters religious, moral, or social in order that Masonry might continue to
hold the res.pect and good opinion of mankind. Illustrative of the l~tter, I cite,
the prohibition against Masons appearing in public drinking saloons in Masonic
clothing and the Masonic rule of Sunday observance.
Iowa (1935):
(Grand Master): I do not believe that there was ever a time in the history
of Masonry when it was as essential that the various bodies and organizations
of Masonry should be as closely connected and work as close in harmony as
at the present time. And with this in mind, the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch
Ma·sons in Iowa is sponsoring a movement for the closer co-operation, and a
closer association between the various Masonic bodies, the Blue Lodge and the
York Rite and the Scottish Rite because if it should ever come to a time when
we should have in this country some of the trouble that they have had in
'foreign countries, it would be very necessary that Masonry be on a very firm
foundation. We are asking the Royal Arch Chapters to do everything in their

Oregon (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): On numerous occasions during
the past year, as recorded in their messages, Grand Masters- have had occasion
to bring every pressure to bear to restrain a certain organization from indulging
in practices, unlawful in character and detrimental to the reputation of the
Craft. In one instance drastic punishment wa·s meted out to a group of misguiped individuals who flaunted the authority of the Grand LOdge. Time was,
when a Grand Master raised his voice in protest over the antics of some of
these bodies, that abuse, vituperations and threats were rained upon him. Times
have changed. The concept in the past was crystalized into a conviction. The
Grand Lodge, wlth the Grand Master as its head, backed by its Code of Laws,
is supreme in all things Masonic. All other bodies, so long as they predicate
their membership on a Masonic affiliation, must conduct their affairs in a
manner that will not bring discredit on the parent body, weaken the moral fibre
of its members, nor annul that great precept that enjoins us to obey the laws
of the country in which we live.
Pennsylvania (1935):
(Grand Master): The attention of the Grand Master has been repeatedly
called to practices by the members of these appendant organizations which are
un-Masonic in character. Technically, this is beyond the control of the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge, and for that reason it might be said that it fa not
our concern. These organizations are regarded by the public at large, however,
as being Masonic, inasmuch as they are made up exclusively of Masons; and,
as the public is not aware of the lack of control by Grand Lodge over these
organizations, they rightly look to the proper Masonic authorities to correct
these evils.

619

Grand Lodge should not take the responsibiJ.ity of supervising or regulating

insist that these organizations and their members do not violate the fundamental principles and practices .of Freemasonry, and we must also insist that
the individual conduct of their members shall be such that · the good opinion

Texas (1935):
(Grand Master): This Grand Lodge has on many occasions taken the position that it is not responsible for . any of these pseudo-Masonic organizations,
and that none of them form any part of Ancient Craft Masonry. The stubborn fact remains that by reason of the widespread use of the word "Masonic"
in connection with such organizations, and because their memberships are
made up exclusively of Masons~and in certain cases, the families of Masonsthe public is led to believe that they are in fact Masonic. Indeed, the general
public seems to recognize some of these organizations as being the very highest
round in the Masonic ladder. We have a responsibilitY to the public and to
ourselves in this matter, and it seems high time that we concern ourselves with
its discharge.
Ancient Craft Masonry seems to function very well for quite some time
without any of these appendages. Then some enthusiastic brethren seem to have
conceived the idea of other organizations with "side degrees" for us~ther
organizations for our wives-still others for our son~thers yet for our
daughters-and so forth and so on. We find no fault with the purposes of
these organizations. As a .rule, they are doing worthwhile work, and should
continue to do so in their proper sphere. Some of them function as they
should-but others do not always do so in every respect. I raise no question
whatever about the right of any or all of these organizations to exist and
function as the sort and character of organizations which they really are.

As I understand it, the missfon of Masonry includes the promotion of
brotherly love and friendship among its members, the alleviation of human ills,
the erection and perfection of a moral edifice as the similitude of a just and
upright Mason, and other aims and purposes well known to all of us. The
outer world recognizes Masons by their acts as well as by their professions.
With such aims and with such responsibility, Masonry is necessarily stringent
in its regulations and jealous of their infractions.

(Grand Master): Previous Grand Masters, in this and other Grand Jurisdictions, have viewed with positive alarm the multiplication of mushroom
bodies, all clamoring for recognition and for an opportunity to meet in our halls.

621

Some of these societies are occupying our sacred temples as guests, yet

We would fiercely resent invasion of our homes by strangers, yet we tolerate

occupy our stations, use our altars, pry into preparation rooms and in other

I trust I may live to see the day when our temples shall be closed to all who

which we once felt when we first found ourselves within the hal1owed precincts
of our Masonic Lodge.

men love to join and which try to promote fellowship and mutual help, but so
long as its membership is made up exclusively of Masons, it must exp~ct to
conform to Masonic law and principles.
SERMONS IN STONES
As stated by the Chairman' of the Correspondence Committee of Missouri, perhaps the desire to garner votes, as well as realizing the desire to
be a part of the ·passing parade, influences invitations to participate in the
laying of cornerstones. To this might also be added the viewpoint of
those having charge of the building being erected, whether from a political
angle or otherwise.
We read in the Proceedings of New Mexico that at the laying of the
cornerstone of the Post Office at Carlsbad there was read a letter from
Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, and a Brother present was
the personal representative of Postmaster General Farley.
District of Columbia (1936):
(Grand Master): 0 f the public activities of our Grand Lodge during the
period under <;onsideration, the laying of cornerstones with Masonic ceremonies
takes a prominent place. A compilation of these events shows that the cornerstones of 27 buildings were so laid. These included churches, Lodge halls, schooI
and college buildings, the new National Educational Association building and
the buildings of the Department of Labor and the Interstate CommeTce Com.
mission. At several of these ceremonies, prominent officials of the United
States Government were present and spoke, among them being Presidents William H. Taft and Herbert Hoover, Vice-President Thomas .Riley Marshall;· and
the then Assistant Secretary of the Navy, and now President Franklin D.
Roosevelt.
'Special mention should be made of the un~ual and unique ceremony performed at the laying of the cornerstones of the new buildings of the ·

622

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Department of Labor and the Interstate Commerce Commission. These ceremonies were held on the same date and at the same hour, simultaneously,
although the two buildings are located two city blocks from each other. Grand
Master Reuben A. Bagley officiated at the Labor Department building, and a
group of brethren, headed by Past Grand Master Gratz E. Dunkum, were
appointed and deputized to officiate at the Interstate Commerce Commission
building. By means of loud speakers, electrically controlled, the ceremony was
synchronized so that the brethren who were deputized to act at the Interstate
Commerce Commission building were able to follow the ceremony at the Labor
Department building and enact the visual portions of it. The propriety of this
course may give rise to question, but there is what we regard as ample authority
for it. lti May, 1932, our Mother Grand Lodge of England laid the
"Dedication Stone" of the Freemason's Ho,spital at Ravenscourt Park, the
ceremony actually being conducted in Olympia, London, miles away from
the hospital.
In leaving this subject of laying cornerstones, it will not be amiss to make
record of the fact -that, in 'the earlier days of our Republic, most of the public
buildings of Washington were laid by our Grand Lodge. I cite, as exam.pies, the
United States Capitol, the Smithsonian Institution, the Washington Monument,
the War College, even the cornerstone of the District of Columbia. It is much
to ,be regretted that modern and present day officials do not see fit to invite our
Grand Lodge to participate in the erection of government buildings by conducting this ancient and time-honored ceremony. It is beautiful in its symbolism
and impressive in its rendition.
Missouri (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Notwithstanding the increased
number of buildings being erected by public funds in recent years, there is a
growing decrease in the number of cornerstones which are laid with Masonic
rites and ceremonies. Again, the reviewer has his own opinions as to why. We
have purposely made a study of the number of cornerstones laid in the United
States during· the past year and find that the number is largc!ly dependent
upon the weakness or strength of the fraternity in the community in which
the building is being erected. In other words, if there are Masonic votes to be
secured, the ·probabilities are the project will secure favorable consideration.

Massachusetts (1935):
(Grand Master): The principles inherent in our institution should set us
apart from any other in our charitable consideration for a temporarily embarrassed member. The ordinary bill for dues, followed up with a . coldly impersonal letter, and the subsequent more or less perfunctory demand for money,
such as would be deemed sufficient in an ordinary club, certainly does not
suffice.
In determining the Lodge's responsibility, the first thing to be learned
is the individual's Masonic interest. Next,. his ability to pay, which must reveal
his circumstances to a point which will uncover his personal story so that the
Worshipful Master, before recommending suspension for non-payment of
dues, can decide whether he is merely removing from the membership list a
man who is not interested in Masonry or whether he is depriving a worthy
brother of a moral and spiritual support which his Lodge can give him in
his time of trouble.
One conspicuous instance has been noted of a Mason in good standing for
thirty-one years, reported to Grand Lodge and suspended for non-payment of
dues at a time when he was suffering the loss of his business through no
fault of his own. Harassed beyond measure by his sudden reversal of circumstances, from affluence to poverty, mentally disturbed and sick with it all, he
had ceased to open any of his mail, and so did not even read the notice of his
pending suspension. Had a careful inquiry been made of his circumstances,
balanced against his long period of membership, it is unthinkable that the
Lodge would not have protected his membership.
The perplexing problem of unresponsive delinquents can, in a great many
cases, be solved through the assistance of service committees. Delegating investigations to a tactful, carefully selected group will result in uncovering
the reason for many cases of non-payment of dues, and save the Lodge
from unfair action at a time when some brother needs the moral support of
his Lodge to help ltim over a difficult period. Through this investigation many
members can be influenced to reduce their indebtedness in part, if not entirely,
thus making a practical contribution toward the solution of the problems.
At a time when a member is struggling hard to meet various obligations,
and feeling himself losing ground, be will often become bewildered to a point
which warps his judgment and prevents his communicating with officers of his
Lodge. The tragic results of withdrawing that friendship, and brotherly love,
which can be so helpful through such a trying experience, are too apparent
to need emphasis.
