New York (1936):
(Grand Lodge): A by-law which provides for a classification of candidates by age for the sole purpose of determining the amount of the initiation
fee to be paid by each class is not unconstitutional or contrary to the regulations of Grand Lodge or of the principles of Masonry.
Ore&"on (1935):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A few years ago Masonry
throughout the world was suffering from obesity. It had just put on a superabundance of useless fatty tissue about the waist line and had lost its trim
fighting figure. Old Dr. Dep.ression prescribed a reducing diet which has
caused quite a reduction in membership poundage and a resultant toning up of
the entire structure.
Ore&"on (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A very unusual affair developed
in one of the (Nebraska) Lodges. The Secretary of the Lodge received a phone
call from the wife of one of its members, who was in arrears for dues, in
which she requested him to tell her how much it would cost to put her husband
in good standing again. The Secretary obliging told her and the next morning
received ai check in the mail for the full amount. Later on he learn.ed that the
delinquent brother had suffered a stroke of apoplexy, that had rendered him
unconscious, all of which occurred previous to his telephone conversation with
the wife of the member. All might have been well had not the illness of the
member proved fatal, for with that the astute wife requested that the Lodge
bury her husband and pay the funeral expenses.
The Grand . Master ruled that inasmuch as the brother was unconscious
from the beginning of the attack he could not pay or cause to be paid, and
therefore he had not been reinstated by his wife presenting the money. To
avoid future situations of this kind the Grand Master recommended that a ballot
be taken on reinstatements in the future.
Texas (1934):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): There being so many Masons in
name only, willing to ride through on free passl!s, enjoying the rights and
privileges of the fraternity while loyal and true Freemasons pay their passage
both in dues and personal service. These "free rides" are the same who ultimately furnish the list of those who go out by way of suspension for nonpayment of dues.

To the writer this is an announcement of a new doctrine. We have always
understood that Masonry did not interfere with a man's religious or political
opinions. We have understood that it was req,uired of a member of the Order
that he should believe in the existence of God, and observe as a rule and
standard of his life morality coupled with this belief in the Supreme Being.
This old Brother was of course a member of the Masonic Lodge or the
question would not have arisen as to his burial. The War has been over
seventy years and doubtless in his youth he was as conscientious in his convictions when a young man and in the army as he was afterwards in his belief
and practices as a member of the Masonic Order.
If the doctrine stricti juris should .be applied to the old Brother after his
death, should it not have been applied to the Lodge while he was a member
and before his death. If the Lodge had harbored a disloyal member and permitted an unworthy brother to remain a member therein, wasn't it a little late
to say after his death that just because he asked for an emblem or a souvenir
to .be placed upon his casket that the privilege should be denied him. As the
old lawyers used to say, "Isn't this sticking in the bark," when his life was
before them as a member of the order.
As far back as 1872, Horace Greeley said : "The masses of our countrymen, north and south, are eager to clasp hands across the bloody chasm which
has so long divided us."

SHALL WE TREAD THE SAME PATH?
We wish space would allow us to present the excellent review of the
Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of the Grand Lodge of Missouri, which sets forth at length existing conditions in different localities
other than English speaking Jurisdictions. Just as Masonry in the United
States was stronger after the persecution during the Morgan episode, so
perhaps those Grand Lodges now under the ban <>f Dictators will in time
resume their place in the life of their respective nations.

THE JOURNEY'S END

Grand Master of Illinois in taking drastic action, which resulted in the
suspension and expulsion of a number of members who took part in this
form of amusement, marks the high water point in the treatment of this
activity.
In a number of cases the glowing promises and the activities of the
paid Promoters operating the campaigns have but added to the objections
to such form of financing. Like other vexing problems, which have arisen
from time to time, the Powers that Be "have landed and have the situation
well in hand.''

This subject is continually before various Grand Lodges, not only as
to the revision of the Ritual but also suggestions as to the manner of its
rendition. The Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of Utah summarizes the matter as follows:
"The Committee (Kentucky) charged with the duty of revising the
funeral ritual, presented its report and a copy of the ritual, which is
printed. The committee stated that .this revision .is 'proposed in order to
make the service more practical and brief, and consequently more desirable.'
As printed, this ritual has the virtue of brevity, at all events.
"The present writer can hark back to a time when a Masonic funeral
service was almost intolerable, on account of its character, its coldnessnot a suggestion of a sympathetic human touch-and the manner in which
its parts were usually rendered by tho~e in charge was excruciating. In
more recent years we have noticed a marked improvement in the rituals
presented. We have also observed a growing tendency to shorten this
Service and to hasten and have it over with as quickly as possible. We
endeavor to keep in mind the fact that we live in the age of the automobile,
the stream-lined train and the air ship, and that the tempo of our movements in general has been greatly accelerated, but it does seem to us that
the demand for haste, for speed, might stop short of the ceremonies in
which we pay our last tribute of respect to the memory of a departed
Brother. Sometimes we almost wonder if we will reach a point where we
will stop long enough
" ' * * * to wrap the draperies of our couch about us,
and lie down to pleasant dreams.'
"We may be in too much of a hurry to pay attention to the 'draperies'
and to the 'couch' but there can be no doubt about our reaching the point
at·which 'life's fitful fever will subside.' "

*

*

*

"The Grand Master of Kentuc'ky discussed the matter of Masonic
funerals and called attention to the fact that often members of the Craft
were not buried by their Brethren, in deference to the wishes of the
families. He remarked on certain features of the Kentucky service-out of
harmony with present-day usage and custom, as possibly being responsible
for the disinclination of families to have a Masonic funeral. One characteristic of not a few Masonic funerals the present writer has attended
was not mentioned by the Grand Master. That is the unfavorable impression left by the manner of rendering the ritual. It doesn't follow that
because a Brother has been elected Master of his Lodge, that he is a fit
person to conduct such aservice. Often, the reading of the ritual is
execrable; given in a monotone; no expression or regard for the sense
of the passages; words mispronounced and generally bungled. It is hardly
occasion for surprise that families should and do avoid such service."

THE GHOSTS OF CHANCE
There are two subjects in the Grand Lodge Proceedings, the excerpts
from each of which if set forth at length would embrace all of the pages
of the average Correspondence Report. One of them is the endeavor to
finance propositions by taking advantage of the weakness of the human
individual to take a chance.
Some Grand Lodges have passed drastic legislation which will undoubtedly eliminate the condition complained of. The example of the

Colorado (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Lodge (Illinois) has
the power to determine the qualifications of its members and the conditions
upon which they shall remain members, even to the extent of arbitrarily denying them the privilege of joining other organizations.
Masonry has the right to insist and must insist that these organizations and
their members shall not violate the fundamentals of Masonry and prevent,
through the simple device of assuming another name, the creation of a class of
Masons independent of or superior to the principles, practices, and regulations
of ancient Craft Masonry.
Setting up or promoting a lottery, sale of lottery tickets, or the possession
of them with intent to sell are criminal offenses in Illinois. The use of the
mails and interstate transportation of tickets, literature, and other matters in
aid of lotteries is denied by Federal Law.
The Potentate of the Shrine was advised that the fund-raising campaign
was a lottery and gift enterprise in violation of Federal, State, and Masonic
laws, and requested to discontinue it. The officers and Past Potentates of the
Shrine in meeting assembled "determined that the Grand Lodge ' had no
jurisdiction in the premises and that the Shrine would proceed with the campaign to its conclusion.~· This the Grand Master reports was done, and twelve
of the participants were subsequently therefore tried Masonically, convicted,
and expelled.
Ten of the expelled petitioned for reinstatement and the Grand Master
recommended their restoration to good standing. The representative of the
blanket company neither appeared nor sought reinstatement.
The remaining defendant, according to the Grand Master, persisted in
his contumacy. He was a lawyer and the mover of the resolution of contumacy. His defense was simply denial of the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master recommended his expulsion.
The Committees on Jurisprudence and Appeals and . Grievances sustained
the action and recommendations of the Grand Master, concluding that "the
purposes of discipline had been accomplished."
The Grand Lodge adopted the reports of its committees and their finding
"that this Grand Lodge has full and complete jurisdiction of the matter of said
cause and of the accused."
Result-12 convicted and expelled; 10 of the 12 reinstated on petition; one
expelled with no appeal or · request for reinstatement; one expelled and appeal
denied, still contumacious.
Connecticut (1936):
(Grand Master): In one case which was called to my attention, an electrically lighted square and compass was displayed at night over a booth where
liquor, it was said, was openly sold. In another case, where money had been
raised by various forms of entertainment, a Masonic Charity Association was

or evade the Federal Amusement tax, I was asked to rule, "if the checks are
made payable to the Masonic Charity Foundation, will they be acceptable
as part of the Lodge assessments, laid by the Grand Lodge?"
My attention has been called or I have personally been asked to approve
of a game popularly known as "Bingo."
It has lately appeared in the daily press that the game "Bingo" had been
banned in one city on ,the ground that it was a form of gambling and in another
city the matter had been called to the attention of the prosecuting attorney.

tions wholly composed of Freemasons are generally regarded by the public as
Masonic orders. Thus the activities of the members in such organizations must
receive our consideration to the same extent that we consider their activities in
the subordinate Lodges,
"In general Freemasons are loyal to the principles and devoted to the high
standards adopted by our Institution. The few have been unable to absorb our
truths to an extent sufficient to guide them in their daily lives. These few
deserve our special attention as erring brothers who require further instruction.
"Let us therefore approach this problem by seeking the cooperation' of all
brethren in the maintenance of the high standard and integrity of our Institution,·
pointing out dangers to our Fraternity which they may not have realized. In the
first instance seeking their support as Freemasons_ working for a common purpose, but, failing to secure such cooperation and support, let us then deal with
them with all the courage, firmness and power at our command, to the end that.
Freemasonry may forever maintain its high standing in the eyes of. the world."

Florida (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Unfortunately, not to say shamefully, the Masonic horizon has been criss-crossed with a variety of question.
able money-raising schemes of late years, not always camouflaged by the seem·
ingly legitimate sale of dance and circus tickets and the like, but by boldly
employing recognized gambling devices.
All this was the result of financial losses and depleted treasuries due to
the back-wash of a wild economic era, and a general let down in ethics
following in the wake of a great World War.
It is generally agreed that all such schemes are un-Masonic and unworthy
the support or countenance of Masons of whatever station or grade. Grand
Masters, without exception, have been outspoken against the practice over
a period of years, condemning, scolding, temporizing, but the year 1936, as
gleaned, from various Proceedings, shows no let-up.
Nor is the practice confined to non-Masonic organizations headed by
Masons, but space in Masonic Temples is reported to have been let for the
operation of recognized gambling devices, with a "take" for the "House."
Grand Masters' Conference (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Under the head of Gambling
Devices and Lotteries the Grand Master quotes from paper from Most W orshipful Grand Master Claude' L. Allen of Massachusetts presented to the Grand
Masters Conference as follows:
"It is a deplorable thought that any Masonic Organization or any organization composed wholly of Freemasons should, for the purpose of raising money,
t,e willing to jeopardize the fair name of our beloved Institution by resorting to
lotteries or games of chance, in violation of the dignity and reputation of Freemasonry.
"What other organization may do is no concern to us as Freemasons. We
have our own landmarks and standards of morality and conduct. Let us not be
swayed by what others may do inconsistent with these high standards and principles. It is not a question of the legality of the various games devised.
"These brethren who believe that they are justified in going ahead with
these schemes if they can bring them within the letter of the law entirely miss
the whole point. They overlook the fact that they may still be guilty of a
Masonic offense when they bring Freemasonry into disrepute, or when their act
reflects upon our good name.
"The test of a Masonic offense is whether the acts of a member are of a
character that tend to reflect upon the good name of our Institution and thus
bring Freemasonry into disrepute.
"There would seem to be no doubt as to the power of the Grand Lodge to
determine the qualifications of its members even to 'the extent of arbitrarily
denying to them the privileges of joining certain other organizations. Organiza-

Kentucky (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Raffling is gambling,-a Masonic
offense. Any violation of the laws of God or of the state, involving moral turpitude, is a violation of Masonic law. Raffling is .gambling; gambling is a violation of the moral law and the laws of the state, and is therefore a Masonic
offense. The· use of gambling devices of any nature, such as raffles, lotteries,
punchboards, paddle wheels, spinning jenneys, and games of chance of whatsoever nature, for the raising of funds for charitable or other purposes, in
connection with circuses, carnivals, theatricals, musicals, birs, bazaars, games,
shows~ or entertainments of any description, whether held or operated under the
auspices of any Lodge of Free and Accepted ' Masons itself, or any of its auxiliary · organizations, such as clubs, band, drill team, drum or bugle· corps, .
orchestra, glee clubs, etc., also the giving away of chances on prizes whether
attached to admission tickets for such affairs, or otherwise, shall be strictly
prohibited.
Ohio (1936):
(Grand Master): As a future safeguar:d against the recurrence of gam•
bling in this jurisdiction, may I suggest to the Jurisprudence Committee the
adoption of the following change: The Grand Master of the Grand Lodge shall
have the power to suspend from all the rights and privileges of Masonry until
the next Annual Grand Communication the presiding officer, or others that may
be a party thereto, of organizations basing membership on Masonic affiliati?111
who persist in promoting lotteries, games of chance, and raffles of ·every kind·,
and character, after having been duly advised of our prohibitory regulations.
In medicine it is necessary for the physician to use two types of remedies
one for palliation, the other for cure. This palliative suspension of the presiding
officer of such organizations would certainly result in a curative effect.
The Grand Lodge adopted his recommendation.

schemes, and I trust that the time will never come when Masonic Lodge·St .or.
bodies composed of Masons find it necessary to violate either the Statute or.
Masonic law to obtain the necessary funds to carry on.

South Dakota (1935):
(Grand ,Master): Among the decisions passed upon by the ·Grand Master
was one with reference to lotteries. A Lodge proposed to give a dance, selling
tickets carrying a chance to win certain prizes, and the question put to the
Grand Master was, "Will this plan violate the Grand Lodge by-laws?" To
which the Grand Master replied: "It is perfectly legitimate for your Lodge to
sell tickets, but the matter of offering prizes cannot be endorsed by the Grand
Lodge."
Tennessee (1936):
(Grand Master): "Any club, association, organization, or society, composed
c,f Masons, which permits or encourages gambling, raffling, or any other immoral practice, is hereby declared an offense to good morals, and the character
of such organization may be established by reputation. Its members are subject
to trial for un-Masonic ci:mduct, and the Grand Master, by virtue of his office,
is empowered to dissolve and abate any such organization."
Texas (1935):
(Grand Master): "During the year I have been solicited, importuned, canvassed and cajoled by various and sundry individuals-some Masons and some
non-Masons-for the privilege of using the name and sanction of The Grand
Lodge of Texas in connection with promoting various sorts of advertising
schemes, lotteries, etc., during the Centennial which all Texans are preparing to
celebrate during the year 1936. The alluring 'bait' held out by this gentry was
usually such as an offer of 25% of the gross receipts of these schemes to be
donated to our Grand Charity fund, or to our Home and School-they to bear
all expenses, etc., and all they asked of us was the use of the good name of
Masonry, and permission to advertise the fact that their scheme was sanctioned
by The Grand Lodge of Texas. Needless to state that I refused any and all such
requests in no uncertain terms-in fact, I sometimes found it a little difficult to
comport myself with the dignity and restraint incumbent upon the Grand Master
in dismissing some of the more persistent solicitors."
Texas (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): But how is this for a record,
presented by Grand Master (Michigan) under "GAMBLING"?
"It is necessary that the settled law of this Grand Jurisdiction on the question of gambling should be stated, because some of our Lodges have advertised
lotteries, feather parties, punch boards, fairs, circuses, bazaars, raffling matches,
etc., for the purpose of raising money for Lodge purposes. Masonic Temple
associations have rented rooms for the purpose of permitting other organizations to conduct gambling games in the Temple."
Having quoted the law prohibiting gambling, he continues:
.
"The Committee on Appeals in a report in 1924 said: 'In our opinion, it is
Just as wrong for a Mason to gamble under the auspices of an organization
made up solely of Masons as it is to gamble under the auspices of a Masonic
Lodge.'
"Another flagrant incident of gambling came to light this year. A Masonic
Temple Association prepared a room for gambling, in which they maintained a
large munber of slot machines using different denominations of coins. They also
provided tables to be used for gambling with cards, for the use of which tables
they took a certain percentage of the money at stake. The officers of this Temple
Association boasted of the fact that they had an understanding with the prose-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

635

cuting attorney and the chief of police that so long as they allowed only Masons
to play, (italic ours) the place would not be raided."
Now the Grand Master comments:
"This is the most disgraceful conduct which has ever come to my attention
. Yet the Masters of the Lodges occupying this Temple not only permitted
the conditions to exist but profited by the ill-gotten gains of the gambling room."
Just too bad! But what about the responsibility of a Grand Master who
knows of and reports such conduct with never a word of Masonic discipline
having been applied. Oh, it is related that:
"I have been advised by the Secretary of the Temple Association that all
forms of gambling have now been removed from the Temple;"
and it is suggested that:
"In case of its revival, there should be some trials for un-Masonic conduct
on the part of Masons connected with the practice.''
We beg to be pardoned for the saying that this record would be much more
in keeping with Masonic teaching, practice and tradition, did it relate there were
"Charters lifted and trials for un-Masonic conduct had."
This record is that presented by the Grand Master himself. It reaches us
under cover of Grand Lodge Jurisdictions of this country, and without comment
therefrom, hence our restrained comment.
Wisconsin (1936):
(Grand Master): On March 2 my attention was called to the fact that
Zor Temple at Madison had adopted a money raising campaign involving certain lottery features which have been strongly disapproved in a number of
jurisdictions. I communicated with the national headquarters of the Shrine and
when the officers of Zor Temple were informed of the illegal nature of the
. undertaking, they promptly called the undertaking off and took steps to undo
what had been done. I wish to commend the officers of Zor for their evident
regard for their obligations as Master Masons and for their cheerful obedience
to constituted authority:
I should add that Tripoli Temple had been approached by the promoters
of the lottery, but before proceeding took the precaution to ascertain the attitude
of the Grand Master. When informed that he disapproved they promptly abandoned the idea.
Wisconsin Shriners have proved themselves good Masons, yet there is no
denying that the Shrine in some states is not reflecting credit upon the Craft.
The non-Mason regards the institution as an integral part of Freemasonry.
When thoughtless fez-bedecked brethren, many of whom have no interest whatjurisdictions. I communicated with the national headquarters of the Shrine and
. ever in Masonry, conduct themselves in public in a manner that creates a
mistaken notion of what Freemasonry really is, it becomes the concern of the
Craft. Imperial officers of the Shrine are constantly reminding their members
that they are first of all Master Masons and should not permit the conviviality,
which is so easily stimulated by so simple a thing as a red fez, to carry them
away; but anyone who has ever attended an imperial council session knows what
happens.
There is no trace of true Freemasonry in the Shrine. It is as foreign to
Masonry as any of the dozens of fraternities that men love to join and which
try to promote fellowship and mutual help, but so long as its membership is
made up exclusively of Masons, it must expect to conform to Masonic law and
principles.

Western Australia (1935):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Whatever else depression has
brought to ?- standstill, it has left alone the American Masonic urge for legislation. In consequence, Masonic law-making flourishes without need for an
impetus from President Roosevelt's "New Deal." What with Grand Masters'
recommendations, committees which admiringly. approve, other committees
which lick recommendations or amateurish (in a legal sense) resolutions into
scientifically legal shape-the said shape often taking the form of a verbal
Niagara, to say nothing of Lodges suggesting laws which they can scarcely
recognize as their offspring after the law committees have exercised their
artistry what time they have not "slaughtered the innocents,''-it would seem
that the words "and laws" should be inserted in a certain well-known passage
in Ecclesiastes, which would then read, "of making of books and laws there
is no end." Not long ago, the reviewer read of a Grand Lodge which passed a
law. Soon .afterwards, it did some more passing with the avowed object
of "clarifying" the law. And only recently, it has added to its achievements
by "clarifying" the clarification. It is conceivable that this last act may not
banish the Tyrrhenian darkness and that the Masonic isinglass will be used
to "re-clarify" the clarification, and so on, ad infinitum, until there will be a
re-re-re-reclarification, that will look like an attack of stammering or hiccoughs. And one may yet wonder whether Masonic legislation may not in fifty
years time reach such a size that Lord Halsbury's monumental work on the
statute law of England (22 volumes) will be comparable only as a needle is
to an anchor.
Western Australia (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Who has not heard of that inventive and tyrannical old-time ruler Procrustes ?-'he who designed an iron
bed and also a rule that all who slept in it must be adapted to its length.
If the unfortunate were too long, his legs were cut to standard; if he was too
short, his legs were stretched. And all this regardless of torture, pain, and
indignity. The Kansas budget committee invented a Procrustean series of
victims· out of by-laws, in presenting its budget. "Wherever there is a conflict
between these appropriations and the by-laws,'' said the committee, "we recommend that the by-laws be amended to conform to the amount appropriated."
And Grand Lodge answered and said, "Yea."

Wisconsin (1935):
(Grand Master): We had heard but one criticism of the Round Table
meetings in the past, that there were too many set speeches, and consequently
that there was not enough opportunity for discussion from the floor. We
accordingly eliminated any attempt for consideration, and are pleased to report
that as a consequence the discussion was much more free, entered into by many
of the Masters and Wardens present, and the conference really acted as a
ciearing house for the best ideas worked out by the different Lodges in the
state on the problems discussed.

We believe if the elective officers of a Grand Lodge could perhaps
borrow a leaf from the history of Russia and devise a continuous program
for five years, which would embody not only that outlined by the Gran~
Lodge but also their individual ideas for the advancement of the Craft, 1t
would in time produce beneficial results.
Every Grand Lodge Officer who in time ma! become the. Grand
Master has certain ideas or plans which he would hke to see carried to a
succes;ful conclusion. If through agreement, education along that line
could be continued during the time he was in line, when in a position to have
the same adopted there would be less lost motion and a better understanding of his program. If Masonry is to assume an active part in such spheres
as its Laws and Regulations allow, it can only be successful by continued
activity.

Utah (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This Grand Lodge (Minnesota)
has made provision for a new service, namely, that of a contact man, known
as the Grand Master's Representative, who is appointed by the Grand Master
for one year. His duties? They are manifold. He dealt with varied and difficult

that were to come up . for trial and was chairman of the Trial Commission.
These, and much besides, were included in his work.

(Grand Secretary): In the preparation of the Reports on Fraternal Correspondence for this Grand Lodge I have occasionally met with rather sneering
references to the attendance of Grand Lodge officers at those meetings (Grand
Master and Grand Secretaries' Conferences), characterizing such attendance as
"junkets." Now, that word "junket" has a significance which is about as savory
as the word "politics," or "politicians." Indeed, they not infrequently appear
together in print as a pair of misbegotten twins.
Observation and experience have convinced me that no Mason worthy of
the honor attaching to the position of Grand Master-and who has attended
any of those meetings-or to that of Grand Secretary, will think or speak of
the Brethren with whom he associates there for three days as being off on a
"Junket"! The Masons who annually gather in the nation's Capital for those
February meetings are drawn from all parts of the country; they are men who
have the confidence and esteem of the Craft in their respective Jurisdictions;
not a few of them are men of exceptional ability, and are recognized, nationally,
as leaders in Masonic thought and activities. They go there for a definite
purpose, and the character of the addresses, papers and discussions given place
on the programs indicate that they are not there on a "junket," and should leave
no ground for carping criticism.
Your Grand Secretary has no words with which, adequately to express his
appreciation of the privilege of attending those meetings and associating with
such men as are to be tnet with there.
Having said so much it occurred to me that I had opened wide the door
for the charge of ulterior motives. If that be so-so be it!

(Grand Master): As a subordinate officer of this Grand Lodge, I was
forced time and again to admit to myself my entire uselessness to the Craft.
I could not answer simple questions relative to the current policies of the
Fraternity, nor enlighten inquiring Brethren concerning Grand Lodge activities.
I was uninformed ahd had to keep still and look wise. My chief and almost only
duty was to take part in the opening and closing of the Grand Lodge. I know
the officers during my term must have felt quite the same as I did.
Would it not be a commendable practice to have regular meetings of
Grand Lodge officers from time to time, at which meetings matters of import-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

643

ance to the Craft could be discussed informally?-meetings at which the Grand
Master could inform those in lower offices of his hopes and ambitions, and
instruct them to carry his messages personally to the subordinate Lodges he
designated.
This policy would tend to make a closer and more democratic relationship
between the subordinate Lodges and the Grand Lodge. It would train the officers
as they progressed through the chairs, and allo·w the Masons of the State to
becoll!e personally acquainted with the men whom they were elevating to high
offices.
I recommend that quarterly meetings of the Line Officers of the Grand
Lodge be held to discuss the problems of the Craft and that provisions to meet
the expense of such meetings be made in the budget.

A LITTLE NONSENSE NOW AND THEN IS RELISHED BY THE
WISEST MEN
. To show that the Proceedings reviewed by the Correspondence Committee are not entirely devoid of humor, we give some gems of thought
culled from speeches, Correspondence Reports and remarks at social functions of the Craft contained therein. Whlie some may have evoluted from
Artemus Ward's time, they may perhaps break the monotony of a Report
of this character.
I will tell you a little story about a joint convention they had of the Grand
Army 9f the Republic and the Confederate Veterans, down at Richmond, I
believe. Both of the former enemies moved in some strength on that conven.tion.
Everything was going along nicely. There was a Confederate soldier who had
lost both arms, had one eye out, and had lost one leg, who was sitting there.
He was not exactly begging. He had his little tray handy and people did drop
in money as they passed. One particular Union man had done well in the world,
and he gave the old soldier a dollar. During the noontime they had served a
little wine, and as he passed he dropped five dollars into the tray. The man
thanked him again. That evening after a very fine dinner he gave him a
twenty dollar bill. The ex-rebel looked up and said, "I truly appreciate that.
It shows how fine and how forgiving those of you we formerly fought with
are." The Union man said, "Don't get me wrong. I am giving you all this
because you are the first rebel I ever saw that was trimmed up just to suit me."

*

*

*

*

*

*

One fellow present had had three or four drinks and got up and protested,
saying, "I don't want any temporary organization; I want a permanent one."
The politician who had called the meeting to order, insisted: "Sit down." "No
I am not going to sit down. I don't want a temporary organization. I want ~
permanent one." Thus he continued to protest, until finally the presiding officer
said to him, "You don't even know, in your present condition, the difference
between temporary and permanent." "Oh, yes, I do," came back the answer. "I'm
drunk. That's temporary. You are a damn fool. That's permanent."
They have been passing out another story on Noah in my section of the

and lexicographer-like not forgetting the fine distinctions between words, replied
very gently : "No, my dear. You are astonished. I am surprised."

District of Columbia (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : A number of rulings on the liquor
question appeared to be somewhat severe. The manager of a hotel which sold
liquor, an engineer in a brewery, the chief accountant in a grocery store which
sold beer, the foreman of a fruit and grocery company which sold beer, were
all barred. Also a man whose wife had a gasoline station and grocery store,
and who helped her with the business on Saturdays, which included the sale of
liquor, was barred from making application, because, said the Grand Master,
"even though the most of his time was spent elsewhere he was engaged in
the distribution of liquor'." In another case a young man whose father's drug
store was a depository for the state liquor board, and where the young man
worked, was refused admission. Nobody has got down to it yet, but if this
things keeps up we may soon find that to watch a brewery truck unload will be
considered a Masonic offense. ·
One Grand Master ruled that so long as the sale of liquor did not violate
any Federal or state law, persons engaged in the liquor business might petition
for the degrees, which is by far the most liberal dictum recorded in this
connection.
Grand Masters' Conference (1935):
Brother Yeo attended the Grand Master's Conference at Washington, D. C.,
in February, 1935, and was hoqored by selection to discuss problems arising
from the repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment. The paper which he there
presented he reproduces in his address; a capable review of a situation to which
many Grand Lodges are now compelled to give serious attention. Indiana prohibits the conferring of the degrees upon anyone who is in the habit of becoming
intoxicated or who makes it his business to manufacture or se11 intoxicating
liquors. The so-ca11ed respectable system of conducting the liquor business is
bringing many problems; for example, the drug and grocery clerk handling
the legal liquor in sealed packages. Indiana has held that the principal vocation
rather than the occasional duty should determine the petitioner's eligibility
under the law quoted above. Indiana has another regulation making the use of
intoxicating liquor as a beverage or the manufacture and sale of intoxicating
liquor to be used as a beverage a Masonic offense. Grand Master Yeo points
out that Masonry is tolerant,that it does not presume to dictate what its members may eat or drink, but that it does demand decency and tespectability in
the conduct of those who are under its jurisdiction. A broad clear-cut statement that will stand. He views these questions and problems from one
hypothesis only-Freemasonry is a strictly moral Institution. It is not within
the power of any legislative body to legalize that which is morally wrong.
Illinois (1936):
(Grand Master): The Grand Master (Nebraska) expressed the opm1on

directly and he therefore rendered several decisions holding that the law forbidding Masons from engaging in the manufacture or sale of intoxicating
liquors, including beer and wine, was binding not only upon the individual
engaged in such business but also to members of partnerships, the managers
or directors of corporations, to members of clubs, but not to minority stockholders in a corporation engaged in such business. He also held that prohibition

Minnesota (1936):
(Grand Master): The Grand Master was asked for his opm1on upon a
rather novel situation. There was a municipally owned liquor store, and the
question was whether the members of the city council violated the Masonic
code from the fact that the city council was responsible for, and controlled and
operated the liquor store. The decision of the Grand Master was that the
members of the council were not guilty of a violation of the Masonic code.

who sells liquor, a worker in a restaurant, a chemist in a distillery, a pharmacist

liquors as a beverage, ~s not the controlling factor."

THE MASTER'S HAT
Even in the early days of Masonry this question was present. In one
of the old Catechisms we find the question, " Where does the Master hang
his hat?" With the answer, "On Nature's peg." While the "plug hat"
still seems to be the insignia of the Master, some of them from their age
produce the same feeling as the well-known head gear· of Queen Mary and
Madam Perkins. The situation could be improved by either abolishing the
use of a hat, as in some of the European Lodges or else adopting a standard
one that never changes. To do this we would have to adopt the Massachusetts practice of using the three-cornered hat or some other form of "lid."
Florida (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : One Brother .objected, unless
the particular kind of a hat be prescribed. He didn't like the idea of the
Master wearing "any old hat,-soft, hard or what not, bowler or fedora, or
straw, and just because it is a hat, a tile or top piece." "There is no tradition
about it,-not a bit," he said, and furthermore, he said "it is purely an American
custom," and "not done anywhere else."
We are told that Masonry has certain "Landmarks."-Something unchangeable.-Some authors and some Grand Lodges list more and some less. There
is no universal agreement. Florida li~s none. The Master presiding while
covered is perhaps as much a "landmark" in American Masonry as any other
and about as often violated. But, unlike a member of the English House of
Commons, when addressing the Chair, he is not out of order, when presiding
uncovered.
New York (1936):
(Board of Custodians}: Masonic tradition has it that the Master of a
Lodge shall remain covered. The Master's hat is almost as much a symbol of
his office as the jewel appropriated to that station and we therefore recommend
that the wearing of a hat by the Worshipful Master be adopted by all Lodges
throughout this Grand J utisdiction.

*

*

*

*

(R.' .1W.'. Willicun C. Prime): Brethren, I don't know whether you know
or not, but the business of wearing hats is peculiar to America, so far as the
Master of the Lodge is concerned. It is. not done anywhere else. There is no
tradition at all about it,-not a bit.
If we are going to have the Master wear a hat as a symbol of his dignity,
it seems to me that it should be prescribed as to the kind of hat. It seems to

me that the encouragement of a man to wear any old hat,-soft, hard or what
not, bowler or fedora or straw, and just because it is a hat, a tile or a toppiece,-is not very wise. I have seen, and you have probably seen, in your own
neighborhood, Masters of Lodges in summer wear straw hats in the East.
lt is not dignified. Better no hat at all than that. But, if we are going to have
a law on the subject, I suggest that it be modified In the report and require
the Master to wear a silk hat,-I don't care of how old a vintage, but a silk
hat,-because it is becoming the office.
It may be that there is more than one Lodge in this J urisdiction that invests
· its Master Masons on being raised with a tile. I saw it some years ago I think
in North Tonawanda; and I think in a Masonic procession there I saw about
fifty years vintages of tiles. They were very interesting. T he reason too, as I
was told, was that a man should be equipped with an apron, and with gloves,
and with a hat to wear in his Masonic funeral procession,--or every procession,
but particularly funeral processions.
Now, I am presenting that suggestion to you, as one of common sense:
Either no law on the subject at all, or let the Master wear hi's hat or not,
as he likes; for I declare to you there is no tradition about it at all in Freemasonry throughout the world, and it is purely an American custom-if it is
a custom.

A LONG ROAD BACK
There are undoubtedly a large number of Members, wao by financial
reasons were forced to dimit or were suspended during the financial
debacle. Many of these might perhaps be restored through a proper approach, based on an investigation that would take into consideration the~
former interest in the Lodge as well as the financial reason causing their
severance.
The requirements that they must pay all arrearages would work a
hardship, even under the above plan. Some Jurisdictions have taken the
attitude that in view of the fact the Brother was not a member of the
Fraternity during his suspension, and therefore not entitled to any of its
rights or benefits, it is hardly just to expect him to pay for "a dead horse"
as a penalty of a privilege.
New York (1936):
(Judge Advocate): M.' .W.'. Christopher C. Mollenhauer, Grand Master
said (1934 Grand Lodge Proc., p. 49) :
"In view of the fact that during the last three years Brethren have been
unaffiliated for non-payment of dues, and having in mind the economic depression through which we have been passing and the fact that many such Brethren

652

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFQRNIA

may be desirous of again returning to the Craft, I recommend that there be
no fee charged to any Brother for reinstatement to membership in his Lodge,
provided said Brother has not been unaffiliated or non-affiliated for more than
five years."
The Committee on Constitutions expressed its hearty sympathy with the
Grand Master's recommendation recommended the adoption of the amendment
as it now appears.
From the expression of the Grand Master, it is apparent that his recommendation was predicated upon a desire that Brethren who through financial
difficulties had been unable to maintain their membership in their Lodges,
should not have their way made more difficult by the further financial barrier
of the $10.00 Grand Lodge charge for reinstatement.
The purpose of the amendment seems clearly to be in line with the policy
which has been advocated by Grand Masters during the period of depression,
that restoration to membership in his Lodge should not be made more difficult
for a Brother by requiring the payment of further charges.
Nowhere ·is the indication given that similar consideration should be
extended to those who desire their Masonic affiliation by obtaining membership
in another Lodge.
I am of the opinion, therefore, in view of these rpany evidences of legislative intent, that the amendment promulgated relieving unaffiliated or nonaffiliated Brothers from payment of reinstatement fees, is intended to apply
only to those cases wherein the Brother seeks to be restored to membership in
the Lodge of his former affiliation.

Nevada (U. S. A:)-were sufferers, the figures exceeding 140,000. Some of
these, probably a large majority, were victims of uncontrollaple circumstances
arising out of world conditions. Possibly included in the others was a more than

are victims of circumstanq:s which might and could have been avoided had
mqre attention been given to making Masons rather than members-had
Masonry been put into men rather than men into Masonry-had their Masonic
a.rdour received greater encouragement and guidance, and had it been realized
that to retain a fair membership in active standing is from the revenue point
c,f view as paying as making new members and not preventing the older ones
from dropping out. Having received them as members, is it not a 'Masonic
duty to get them back to us as quickly as possible. While it may be necessary
to wait till prosperity reappears to get back the sufferers from straightened
conditions, it may well be asked whether Masonic statesmanship is not equal
to the task of attempting to win back to our temples those who have ceased
to care. They are our brothers.

ODDITIES IN THE NEWS
Nova Scotia (1936):
(Grand Master): We all desire to see these losses made good, and I write
t0 make three suggestions as to the way in which you and your Lodge can
help.
1st-Go over the proceedings of Grand Lodge for the past ten years, and
list all the members of your Lodge who have been suspended. You will find
these names listed in the Proceedings under the head of "Suspended." Appoint a
small special committee carefully selected to go over this list and approach
those whose membership you consider should be regained.
2nd-Make a list of all your dimitted members for the past ten years.
Some have withdrawn because of financial reasons which may have now passed,
others possibly because of some real or fancied grievance. It is your duty in
every case to make an honest Masonic effort to secure their reaffiliation. Let
the same committee take this also in hand at once.
3rd-In addition to these two possibilities, there are in practically every
community a number of unaffiliated Masons. Approach them and persuade
them to affiliate with your Lodge.
Western Australia (1935):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The heavy decrease in Masonic
memberships in lit'erally all Jurisdictions speaking the English tongue is
beginning to be regarded in many quarters as almost a blessing in disguise.
it appears to be considered that after ·the Great War they were allowed to drift
into the Lodge after insufficient investigation, and that the Craft is well rid of
them as they were never true Masons at heart. To treat the brother who drops
out of active Masonic life as driftwood or dead timber may be correct in one
sense. Whether it is consistent with Masonic duty or responsibility, is quite
another thing. As already pointed out, most of the Grand Jurisdictions in the
English-speaking world are suffering from depleted numbers. Indeed, last

interesting.

A CHANGING WORLD
Observation by the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
from New Jersey (1935):
" Much of our present difficulty can be traced to the American trait
which makes mass and magnitude the criterion of success.
"Masonry in the old days was a simple organization; its dues were
intended to cover a ll financial wants; its benevolences were t he concern of
-the individual members. In these later years, all this has been changed.
L'Oi;lges and Grand Lodges have assumed property interests, foundations,
inves·tment problems. Benevolences are highly institutionalized. Activities
are carried out on a large scale. We may look back wistfully to the -0lder
and simpler Masonic code of living, but with Masoonry as it is today the
education and guidance of Lodge officers,· in matters of business and
finance is as essential to Masonic success as excellence in ritualistic or
esoteric work."
The Grand Master of Missouri also makes the following comment:
Respect for F reemasonry is too often sadly lacking from those to whom
we should look for the best, and when conferring degrees, indifference, poor
training, or lack of sincerity is plainly noticeable. The capable worker who is
really in earnest, whether Master or Steward, will make a happy and lasting
impression upon the candidate. Sometimes at funerals we behold an incompetent
Master attempting to render that sublime ritual, and bringing discredit upon
the whole body of Freemasonry. But the most serious offender is the brother
who, by misconduc~ brings the fraternity into disrepute.
A persistent clamor continues, to "Bring Freemasonry up to date," which
in reality means bringing it down to the level of questionable practices in
every day life, and to "excuse" some Freemasons who may do certain things
under the specious plea of necessity. The depression has broken down the moral
fiber of many men, who, as a result, do things they would never think of doing
under normal conditions. But Freemasonry demands that its followers live up
to its standards, and the problem is to bring the world up to Freemasonry.
Freemasonry is a venerable institution, whether it has existed for three
thousand years, or three hundred; it has withstood adversify, and has always
emerged stronger than ever. But it has never triumphed by compromising with
baser elements ; the charge given with the apron of the Entered Apprentice

658

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

forbids that. And finally, the Freemasonry that survives through the ages must
inspire men to lead honest, pure and upright lives, to be good citizens and true
to their government, to respect the sanctity of. the home, and finally to look
forward to a blessed immortality "in that House not made with hands."

THE MOVING FINGER WRITES .
The Proceedings of the average Grand Lodge from a Reviewer's standpoint may be divided into three parts. Under "Interesting" could be
grouped the Messages of the Grand Master, orations, historical papers and
matters of a like character. Under "Instructive" we would, of course, class
the Report of the Chairman on Correspondence and the work of an Educational Committee. Under "Superfluous" should be included the Roster of
Members and the long detailed reports of Certified Public Accountants
and Officers disbursing funds. The added high cost of printing, paper, etc.,
has caused the elimination of a large amount of "Superfluous" matter, which
would never have been dropped as a result of criticism.
Of course if a Grand Lodge believes that this has a value to the general
membership, or for their records, it is their individual affair and one that
should not be criticized.

the names of the parties in full.

Western Australia (1935):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): On more than one occasion I have
drawn attention to the custom in some Jurisdictions of printing full rosters or
registers of their Lodge membership. In some instances these lists reach
prodigious proportions. They become entitled to the application of the wellknown term "aldermanic proportibns," and suggest a return to those prediluvian
days when the mastodon, the mainmoth, the megalosaurus, and the labyrinthodon
stalked about the earth. That love which the pauline aphorism hath it "suffereth
all things," inspires belief that its more than generous dimensions were intended
for a good purpose, and not as a mere publicity stunt. But 1ts adaptability to
commercial purposes is indubitable. Secondhand book-sellers seem impressed
with this view, judging from what I saw on a large card in a secondhand book
store in a city in the United States. It bore the following legend: "Mail
Order Houses, Note I We have a number of Masonic membership rosters for
sale." And in an adjoining allotment there was a written notice on a private
bil.Jboard: "Gods for Sale." On inquiry, I found that "Gods" was the would-be
seller's way of spelling "goats." Think of it! Masonic and goat notices in
what one of Henry Cockton's character called "juxtaposition."
SAILS THAT CATCH THE WIND
The glamour of Masonry, perhaps to the average man, is due to the
thought that it is a Secret Society. Members connected with the Fraternity
by publicity have in the course of time perhaps removed that, even going
to the extreme of publishing what should properly remain unknown. Statements by others based, either on real or fancied knowledge, have also had
an influence. Grand Lodges, by advertising the activities of Masonic Homes
and in efforts to raise Endowment Funds have tended to make the general
public believe that one of our chief objectives is Benevolence.

The Grand Master of Kentucky ruled that it was permissible to organize a
ball club composed of Master Masons, but would not permit the use of the
emblem on the uniforms of players who were not Masons. It occurs to this

. . .. .

Individually it is our duty, whether Masons or not, to interest ourselves in
the business and politics of the Nation, not from the standpoint of class but
from the standpoint of good citizenship.
'
As for Masonry in business, that is something else again. We have a class
of business men who are Masons who would, if they were permitted, display
the Square and. Compasses on their show windows, for after all, Masons are
only human beings. And many applicants have been innocently led to believe
that Masonry ~as some all-po~erf~I genii, possessed of some magic property
calculated to bring about the m1lenmum for its votaries.

in Lodge offices and Grand Lodge offices where needed.

the custom has crept in of promoting Sunday picnics or motor outings for
members and their families and giving notice of the arrangements for same on
the Lodge circular. This is not permissible, and must be discontinued, as it is
not seemly that Masonry should identify itself with pleasure functions held on
the Lord's Day.
It is refreshing to find now and then a Grand Master who believes the
Sabbath Day should be observed in accordance with the standards laid down
by the founders of our nation and endeavors to hold the Lodges in his jurisdiction true to that standard.

Philippine Islands (1936):
(Grand Master): One feature of Masonic life and activities which, in
my judgment, requires regulation is the publication of Masonic activities
h. the daily newspapers. There has been undesirable pultlicity in the past.
Garbled accounts of Masonic functions and the publication of the names
of initiates and officers have done individual members and our cause considerable harm. We must always remember that s<ime of our Brethren are so
situated that they cannot afford to have their Masonic membership advertised to
the world at large. The quiet and unostentatious manner in which Masonry
works and carries on is one of its chief attractions. Enough information that
should never pass the tiled d<ior of the Lodge is leaking out as it is without
broadcasting Masonic activities through the medium of the nonmasonic press.
Accounts of Masonic activities carried on behind tiled doors, such as the conferring of degrees, elections, and private installations of Lodge officers, etc.,
should never be given to. the press. Publicity with reference to Masonic
necrological services, public installations, and social activities of the Lodges
should 1be limited and controlled. No information on Grand Lodge proceedings
should b~ given out except by, or with the approval of, the Grand Master or
the Grand Secretary. Let there be only such publicity as may be strictly necessary or 'plainly beneficial to our Institution.

Illinois (1935):
(Grand Master): The Craft is still suffering the consequences of defaulted
building obligations. Inquiries concerning these are constantly coming to the
office of the Grand Master from men and women past the self-supporting age
who invested their money' because of their faith in Masonry and undertakings
in the name of Masonry. Legally, the Grand Lodge has no responsibility. It does
have a moral obligation which requires that it prohibit the use of the name of
Masonry in oonnection with unsound· financial undertakings. I therefore recommend that no building project or business enterprise of any sort promoted
. by Masons as such and in the name of Masonry be permitted to .incur any
indebtedness without submission of the project to some C<lmmittee of this
Grand Lodge and under conditions fully apprising investors that the Grand
Lodge is in no degree lia:ble therefor.

PICTURES OF THE PAST
Temple Associations and Lodges by reason of extravagant or overbuilding projects are now suffering the inevitable results. Unfortunately
legislation by Grand Lodges to prevent such a condition was generally
taken after the damage was done. One of the most regrettable features was
that those not members of the Fraternity were often induced to invest.
The financial outcome has engendered bitterness toward the Organization
as a whole and of course given Masonry a bad name in certain quarters.

(Grand Lodge): The Pacific Mutual Insurance Company of California
brought suit in August, 1934, against Yuma Lodge No. 17, Yuma, Ariz., to
foreclose a first mortgage on a new building of Luma Lodge. The complaint
was in such form as t<> have permitted the insurance company to recover a

mortgage proper did not seem to satisfy the judgment and costs. The Grand

and the Grand Lodge lost its $6,000.00 loan it had made to Yuma Lodge in 1930.

WITHIN THE PALE
Attempts to circumvent the generally accepted rule that liquor must not
be served at Masonic gatherings under Masonic auspices or in Temples has
of course resulted in criticism. Where such occurrences took place they
were soon remedied so far as we recall. There is little deviation in any
Jurisdiction from the broad rule that Masonry and Liquor, like "Gasoline
and Booze," will not mix, except with disastrous results.

Utah (1936):
(Grand Master): On three different occasions Masters of Lodges asked
whether there was objection to the serving of beer with lunch after Lodge
meetings. My reply in each instance was that I considered it contrary to the
best interests of the Fraternity to permit beer, wine or spirituous liquor to be
served or drunk at any function held under the auspices of a Lodge, whether
iu a Masonic hall, a hotel :banquet room, or at a picnic or other outing. In none

having beer served but some of their members had suggested it. The officers
of the. subordinate Lodges in most instances do not know that the general
pr'actice of the Fraternity in this and other Jurisdictions, even before the passage of the Eighteenth Amendment, would preclude its use. This question has
come up for consideration in .many states during the past two years and the
serving of alcoholic beverages at Masonic gatherings has been prohibited by
many of the Jurisdictions, among which are: California, District of Columbia,
Ohio, Illinois, Oregon and Washington.

West Virginia (1936):
(Committee oii Jurisprudence): The Committee has given full c?nsid~ra­
tion to the question of dispensing :beer in the clubroom of the Masonic Building under a state license. This question is a serious one and while, as a
Committee, we do not criticize the conclusion reached by the Grand Master,
and appreciate fully the earnest consideration which he gave to it, yet we hold
it as grossly improper and unmasonic to set up a bar in such clubrooms for the
purpose of dispensing the so-called non-intoxicating beer. While there is no
statute prohibiting a gambling house or a house of ill fame in Masonic buildings,
yet every Mason would :be shocked if any such act was permitted therein, and
we believe that no Grand Master would hesitate for a moment to declare it a
species of unmasonic conduct and would not hesitate to arrest the charter of the
· Lodge that would permit it.
Therefpre, we recommend that the Grand Master of this Grand Lodge do
declare such action on the part of any Lodge as grossly unmasonic, and if the
action of any Lodge in so placing any bar in the clubroom of any Masonic
building be not immediately stopped, to arrest the charter of that Lodge at once.

THE WAY OF THE TRANSGRESSOR
Like the poor, the Report of Committee on Grievances and Appeals,
which covers the discipline of Members, is generally a part of the Proceedings. There are a few Jurisdictions, however, that do not contain such
material or where there is no cause. We believe that only the briefest outline of these unfortunate incidents should be set forth, but we cannot subscribe to the viewpoint that the name of the offender should not be given.
Finding a man guilty of an offense that warrants his severance from the
Fraternity, and then allowing the world at large, as well as the Brethren,
to labor under the illusion that he is still a member, we believe, shows too
much regard to one who has brought disrepute upon the Craft.
Consideration for offenders and minimizing their offenses is presenting
a serious problem in the administration of our criminal laws. Attorney
General Cummings and J. Edgar Hoover are authorities for this statement,
and a large part of their work is undone by maudlin sentiment or misplaced
sympathy.

by the Grand Lodge.

In a purely business transaction I am inclined to agree with the judgment
of certain of our sister Jurisdictions, who prohibit Masonic trials on charges
which merely involve the settlement of business transactions.
Masonic offenses may be of two kinds :-first, those which are purely
Masonic in origin and character, and secondly, those which are quite unrelated
to Masonry except as they may tend to lower the Order in the estimation of
the world at large.
If the act be one which shocks the enlightened conscience of r ight-minded
persons, then it violates t he moral law, whether or not it be also a crime, and it
is a Masonic offense.

Quebec (1936:
(Grand Master) : When the actions of a brother in his daily or private
life are such as to justify the adverse criticism and the proper contempt of
public opinion, it becomes at once not only the right but the duty of those
entrusted with the government of the Craft to take such steps against the
offending brother as may be appropriate and needful to purge our ranks of such
undesirables and thus convince the world at large that our Order will not
passively condone what society may properly condemn. We are the inheritors
of a proud past, and those who shall come after have a right to expect that we

673

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

shall hand down to them an institution with fair name untarnished and high
reputation unblemished.
As ·to those offenses which are not Masonic in origin and character but
which tend to degrade our institution in the estimation of the world at large, a
further element enters. Here the careful principle is the safeguarding of the
fair name of the Order. It has nothing to do with the internal management
thereof. If the act be one which shocks the enlightened conscience of rightminded persons, then it violates the moral law, whether or not it be also a
crime, and it is a Masonic offense. It would be impossible to state specifically
all the acts which might fall within this category. Many will readily suggest
themselves, while others may not be so obvious; but the test to :be applied in
all cases is the same, are the acts of a member such as may properly be considered reprehensible in the opinion of all fair and decent minded citizens in
the community? And if so, are such acts of such a character that they will
tend to reflect upon the good name of the Order if, .by silence and inaction; we
permit the offending brother to continue in good standing. If these two questions fairly admit of an affirmative answer, then such acts constitute a Masonic
offense and it becomes the duty of this Grand Lodge to take such action as may
protect and preserve its integrity.

Let's review the history of the project as stated by Most Worshipful John
M. Kinkel of Kansas. We quote:
"This Memorial was originally to cost $100,000.00. By 1916 the Association
was committed to a Temple to cqst not less than $500,000.00.
"In 1920 this was increased to $1,000,000.00, and later to $2,200,000.00.
"The report now is that there is invested in the Temple approximately
$3,500,000.00.
"Finally, it is estimated that the Temple will cost $4,000,000.00, to which
should be added an endowment fund of $1,500,000.00, making the total cost
$5,500,000.00."
When it is remembered that the Masons of America have subscribed and
. paid in something like forty times the original estimated cost of the project,
by no source of reasoning or imagination can it be truthfully said that the
project's present deplorable status is chargeable to lack· of stamina or dependableness of American Masonry.

Utah (1936):
(Chairman ·Correspondence Committee): Lodges do peculiar things sometimes. The Grand Master (Ohio) reported the case in which a member, who

resulted in expulsion. This case is not unique. About every year since we have
been preparing these reports, we have met with similar actions in one or another
Grand Jurisdiction. Ohio seems to have been unfortunate in this respect, as
two other cases were reported.

THE MONUMENT ON SHOOTER'S HILL

·
During the past year· that part known as Memorial Hall has been nearly
completed at an expenditure of approximately $65,000. A great statue of
Washington and mural paintings on the walls being all that is lacking to make
this part of the Memorial finished. Unfinished parts of the Memorial are an
Assembly Hall on the ground floor, the S ta te Memorial room on the fourth
floor, the Library on the sixth floor, and the Museum on the eighth. The third,
fif th and seventh floors are mezzanine. The ninth floor is the observatory.
At the date o<f the annual meeting of the association a total of contributions received was $4,030,647.45. Of said amount the sponsoring Grand Lodges
have contributed $3,673,502.58, and other organizations of Masons, together
with organizations having a membership based on Masonic affiliation have contributed $355,144.87.
The original plan of 'financing the Memorial was a voluntary contribution
of one dollar by every Mason on the membership rolls of the sponsoring Grand

North Dakota (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Anent the Washington Memorial,
the Grand Master of Missouri says :
"It is unfortunate that so much money has been expended on the erection
of this shrine to ·contain relics and mementoes of the great Washington and
then to know that the aforesaid relics and mementoes are still contained in an
cld, unkept and nonfireproqf building. The. Masons of the United States are
entitled to know whether the officers and members of Alexandria Washington
Lodge are complying with the spirit of their agreement to deposit these relics
in the Memorial Building, or are the relics being withheld so as to force the
Memorial Association into the donation of a free .Lodge room."
We confess to having heard similar complaints before but the fact of the
matter is that the memorial is in no shape to receive these priceless relics. The
replica room thus far consists of nothing but rough bare walls and an unfinished
concrete sub-floor and in no condition to receive anything even less valuable.
The fault is not that of Washington-Alexandria Lodge but of the Masons of
America in either planning too ambitiously or in not completing what they set
out to do. On our visit at Alexandria last February, we were assured that the
Lodge there was anxious to move the memorabilia at the earliest possible
moment. Surely the relics should be moved quickly from the fire-trap in which
they are now housed.

President Coolidge said that it was alright to let Nature take its course
but there was no law, human or Divine, that prevented any one ~rom assisting Nature. Solicitation in Masonry is prohibited but an active, sympathetic interest in Young Men and their Organizations rather than aloofness
or opposition would produce results. From experience this does not mean

Alberta (1937):
(Grand Master): There is a noticeable lack of applications from younger
men. One thing impressed me, that is in the larger centers Freemasonry is not
getting its "batting average" of younger men who have been fortunate enough
to establish security of position. This it seems to me calls for serious thought
and has raised in my mind several questions :
Has Freemasonry lost its appeal to the rising generation? Amid alf the
materialism of this age, the desire to possess without earning, the growing neglect
of the old conception of God and religion, idealism has not died out, and it is this
characteristic in the human mind upon which the seed of Freemasonry may be
sown and bear fruit. Many a mistake was made in the boom days and we are
still suffering from the consequences. An art that is founded on the operative
philosophy of men who spread cathedrals like brown lace across western Europe,
adorning them with stained glass, which stole brilliance from the sunlight, as
an expression of that philosophy and their own ideals, which meant more to
them than any material reward, should never lose its appeal.

South Carolina (1936):
(Committee on George Washington Memorial): There it is, unfinished.
During the year they tell us that over 150,000 people registered as visitors.
What was their impression? What story did this unfinished Memorial, with no
work having been done on it for over three years, tell? Simply this-Three
million men who call themselves Masons undertook a great task and they
cannot see it through; that Freemasonry in this country is not what some people
thought it was; that after all it must not amount to so much. That is the only
story that a lot of dust, dirt, loose slabs of marble and granite columns wrapped
around with paper covered with dust and doors warped and weather beaten
could tell. Like it or not, approve of its having been undertaken or not, it is
saying more and more in louder tones than all the voices of the three million
Masons of 'the United States.
·
.
I am informed that an organization, which I need not name, has been using
this unfinished Memorial as a basis for belittling and criticising Freemasonry
i~ Washington and Alexandria; that they are holding up to the people this
Memorial that we started and could not finish.

Montana (1936):
(Grand Master): There has existed and now exists, and probably always
will exist, among the brethren a diversity of opinion as to the value of the
Order of DeMolay and the Order of Rainbow for Girls. Many of the brethren
conscientiously feel that the support of these organizations is no function of
Masonry. Many others ardently believe that the active support of such organizations by Masonry is in accord with true Masonic teachings and principles
and should be encouraged.
I am of the belief that these organizations are rendering great service to
boys and girls approaching manhood and womanhood. They give a properly
directed outlet for the energies of these youthful citizens and inculcate in their
minds impressive lessons and high ideals. Through such organizations we are
assisting in the building of a greater citizenship which will result in great
benefit to our country and to our fraternity. It is my opinion that these organizations should be encouraged to the fullest extent by our fraternity.
Ohio (1936):
(Grand Master): In my Address as Deputy Grand Master, I asked this
question, "Is this national holiday, Washington's Birthday, not our opportunity
as a Fraternity to interest our sons in our Fraternity." This question has been
answered, my Brethren, as evidenced by more than one hundred letters that
have come to my office enthusiastically endorsing this program and expressing
a desire for its future continuance.
Shortly after returning to Dayton, a Masonic publication was handed to
me containing an article by a noted Masonic writer who stated, "It is a fact we
cannot deny that the thoughts of the younger generation are not toward
Freemasonry." At whose door may we lay this blame? Of course, there is only
one answer to this last question. Dad, father, the guardian of the moral and
character-building activities of his son. To me, this statement was a challenge
which I was willing to accept. May I quote at random some of the interesting
things that have been written to my office regarding this outstanding program.
One Master has said: "Judging from our experience the Lodge considers
'

Another has stated, "Many Brethren were pr;sent who had not attended a
Lodge meeting for. several years."

Rhode Island (1935):
(Grand Master): Primarily, Masonry needs leadership. The selection of the
proper timber from which to make a Master is of highest importance to every
LOdge and to which altogether too little attention is given. A large percentage
of our Lodges are in line. In one of those Lodges a young man was asked by
the brother who expected to be elected Master if he would accept a place
in line. He answered the question with an emphatic "No" and was requested to
see the "Old Man" as the Master of that Lodge was affectionately called. He
went to see the Past Master in question, and, in response to his inquiry, he was
told that the lOOth anniversary of the Lodge would occur in seven years and
he was being selected to be the Master of the Lodge on that occasion. That
is the type of Advisory Committee that is needed in our Lodges to look forward even for a period of years to insure the leadership that the Lodge needs
for best serving its membership and the Craft as a whole.
South Dakota (1937):
(Grand Master): Realizing that the average young man that is raised to
the sublime degree of a Master Mason is a high school graduate, or better,
and recognizing in him the thorough training he has had in memorizing, no time
should be lost in placing such material in office and endeavor to secure as much
"Ritualistic Proficiency" as possible from them in the first few years of their
services. Under a special urge the average graduate from our high schools will
memorize our ritual in a single year. However, this should not be expected of
him.
Follow the simple rule of filling the Junior Steward's place with these capable young men, and thereafter keep plenty of work for them to do; urge them
to progress, and if they will not, take them out of the line, for they are not only
a bad example for those to follow, but a hindrance to those whom they are
working with. The bees do not permit the drones to remain in the hives and
consume that which they did not produce, nor should a laggard, lounger, or a
· listless idler be left in the official lines of "Ritualistic Proficiency" in our
Constituent Lodges.
If this "Ritualistie Proficiency Program" is consistently carried on for
seven years, giving the Junior Steward of seven years ago an opportunity to

Utah (1936):
(Chairman Con·espondence Committee): Grand Master Purnell (Dela~
ware) indulged in some observations on "Religion," "Our Country'' and the
"Craft." For one we wish that the young men-college and university students,
who have recently taken oath not to bear arms for their country-not even in
it• defense should it be invaded-might take to heart certain of the sentiments
gathered under the second of these headings. We are sufficiently radical to say,
that in our opinion, when men, young or old, reach the point where they
voluntarily make oath that they will not defend their country, even when invaded by an enemy, they are not worthy of the protection and liberty and
opportunities for securing an education which this country affords them, and
that they are more dangerous to our institutions than are the organized red
radicals, who seek the overthrow of our government. While accepting the
gifts, they would smite the benefactor who provides them with all that makes
life worth the living. They place themselves in the position of those who would
slink out of harm's way while accepting the benefits of others' sacrifices. A
fine type of manhood is that !
BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS
Under this caption we embody the comments and criticisms of the
various Foreign Correspondents as far as published proceedings of our
8Sth, 86th and 87th annual communications.
These are only from the Reports received since the Grand Lodge
decided to again publish the work of the Committee on Correspondence
and necessarily omits those comments in the Proceedings received during
the years 1934, 1935 and 1936. Generally they were of the same tenor as
those hereinafter quoted.
Practically all of them noted with regret the absence of the Report
of the Correspondence Committee, as well as looking with favor upon the
actions of our Grand Lodge during the years above mentioned.
It should be a source of satisfaction to those who have served the
Grand Lodge of California to know that their efforts are looked upon with
favor by the various Reviewers, who are experts conversant with opinions
throughout the Masonic world. While there has been differences of
opinion and criticism, these have been handled from a broad Masonic viewpoint.

North Carolina:
California Masonry does much good to the cause of public education
by its annual observance of Public Schools Week, which is well nigh a
universal observance there. We could wish that there might be such in
equally effective manner in other states. Perhaps if we had it in North
Carolina, the ranking of our school system here would be nearer what
California ranks in public education among the states, and not so near
the absolute bottom among them all.
There is a very interesting report concerning clandestine Masonry in
California, by a special committee appointed to investigate such.

The address of the Grand Master shows a year of pleasing and constructive work.
The report of the Grand Secretary, John Whicher, is an excellent one
giving no indication of the fact that he is eighty-one years old. Surely hi~
mental vigor is unimpaired.
We are happy to note that it was voted to prepare and publish a report
on Foreign Correspondence and we will look forward with pleasurable
anticipation to next year's report.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation of the
world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000-5923.
Scottish Rite-Sarne as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology
is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 3760-5683. After
September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year th~ second temple was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the year of discovery."
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the temple of
Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.), "in the year of the
deposit."
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization of their
Order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118 from 1923---805.

Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing of
Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis (A. B.),
"in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing. Thus: 1923 and

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly speaking,
they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the
one called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United
States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the Cryptic
and the Templar Degrees.
The Symbolic Degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the Entered
Apprentice, the Feilow Craft and the Master Mason. They are called
Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.
The Capitular Degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the Mark
Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the Royal Arch.
The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred
in a Council of Hig.h Priests upon those who have been regularly elected
to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular
because ~hey are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic Degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the Royal
Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master. They are
called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret vault or underground passage.
The Templar Degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are the
Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes
from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the temple at Jerusalem
. from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd, inclusive. In the Sou·the.rn Jurisdiction of the United States (which includes
all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River)
the organization of the different Bodies, and the degrees conferred by
them, are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix,
15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to 30'; Consistory, 31 • to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33 °.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all states north of the
Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees conferred are:
Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council Princes of Jerusalem, 15°
and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33 •.
